Increasing the number of investors entails fostering the growth of savings. Fostering savings, in turn, require a sustainable macroeconomic environment, i.e. Low inflation environment. I am proud to say that the Bangko Sentral has been successful on this front. Average inflation last year has been cut to just 3.1% and the prospects for contained inflation this year despite recent developments are quite good. Widening the investor base also involves enhancing the transparency in the market. The availability of reliable and timely information on market players complements regulatory oversight by promoting market discipline. However, before one can enhance transparency, the accounting standards need to be improved. To address this, the BSP and the sec have both committed to implement IAS 39 and IAS 32 by 2005. Lack of reliable public information on the creditworthiness of corporate entities can also be remedied by the development of the credit ratings industry. The BSP has already recognized the sole credit rating agency in the country, and is now reviewing the application for recognition of one foreign rating agency. However, the presence of all these information would be all for naught if the investors are not educated about the methods for assessing the relative merits of the different instruments in the market. Towards this end, the BSP has formed a consumer education committee to design a comprehensive action program to strengthen financial literacy of consumers, as well as of key influence groups such as the mass media. Notable progress is being made. We have already made a major upgrade of our payment system by putting in place the Philippine RTGS or PhilPaSS. In addition, the BAP's fixed income exchange is scheduled to open this month. On the regulatory front, we are set to launch later this afternoon, also here in the Executive Business Center, the Financial Sector Forum which will seek to deepen coordination among its four participating agencies, namely: the BSP, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation (PDIC), and the Insurance Commission (IC). But in all these, we must not forget to continuously improve the corporate governance standards in the Philippines as this serves as the foundation in the further development of our capital market. Ladies and gentlemen, I thus wish you well in this workshop. May the session this afternoon be a productive exercise in identifying ways to advance capital market development in the Philippines. Thank you very much. (Note: Opening Remarks. Capital Market Development Council (CMDC) Workshop, July 5, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: 11th BSP Anniversary Message
Occasion: BSP's 11th Anniversary Celebration
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Members of the Monetary Board, fellow central bankers here at the BSP head office, the Security Plant Complex and our regional offices and branches. Good morning. And more appropriately happy anniversary! As late as Friday last week, the BSP Ad Hoc Anniversary Committee still did not know where exactly this flag raising ceremony will finally take place. While it preferred the podium, the committee nevertheless set up the Assembly Hall as an alternative venue if it rains. Very BSP,I should say. We would go to great extent to ensure that we attain our objective. And we did this past year. I must say that as a result of our collective efforts, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, once again, did very well. Truly, it has been a most challenging year for any monetary authority. In our case, not only did we have to navigate through an increasingly complex and difficult environment, we had to contend with a lot of noise from various fronts. Really, we do make a lot of noise in this country. I just wish it is true that noise drives away negativism and brings good luck. This way, the Philippines can be restored to its rightful place as one of the most vibrant and dynamic economies in this part of the world, where the quality of life is good. Well, this is still possible. If all of us, all sectors of our society, will work together and set aside personal differences for the common good. This is the reason why I am particularly proud of BSP. United by our vision, we continue to deliver on our mandate: we continue to have low and stable inflation that is well within target; benchmark interest rates that remain at single-digit levels and have therefore lowered the cost of doing business; and improving numbers of our key banking indicators that tell us we are on the right track in terms of making sure we have a sound banking system. But much remains to be done if we are to catch up with our more developed ASEAN neighbors. We have a capital market that is in its infancy. Much needed legislative reforms were slow in coming. After 10 years of lobbying for the elimination of the Documentary Stamp Tax (to develop the secondary market for long term paper), we finally got it in the last session; the Asset Securitization was just passed and is still awaiting the implementing rules and regulations. The much needed Corporate Recovery Act still needs to be passed. The protection of the investors is as important as the protection of the borrowers. In a developed capital market, there are just as many small investors as there are small borrowers. Other legislative work still has to be done - the banks have to work harder to do their share of developing the market. The regulatory environment has to be improved to ensure regulatory compliance and greater transparency from our own perspective. We still need vital amendments to our Charter if we are to be effective regulators, a pre-requisite for a really sound banking system, not to mention the fact that we still need the SSL removed from our Charter. Fortunately, recent legislation on this issue has been passed, we just have to work on ours. I think it is fair to say that BSP helped provide the silver lining for our economy. Independent observers here and abroad have noted it. Some even gave us awards in recognition. For these, I give credit to our formidable BSP team -- our employees, our officials, our Monetary Board. Today, BSP enters its 11th year practically alongside the newly-elected president's induction into office. It gives us reason to be hopeful that, this time, we will make a lot of headway in making life appreciably better for more Filipinos. I also expect this fresh wind of hope to inspire the corporate planning sessions that we will hold a few days from today. Our environment is constantly evolving and we have to make sure that we are able to correspondingly fine-tune our template for attaining the BSP vision. I will not bore you with the specifics on our gains in inflation targeting, the pursuit and promotion of good governance and the adoption of world standards and best practices in the banking sector. You must have read the circulars that were issued and routed to the staff as well as extensive media reports on the same. I do wonder if you have noticed, and this I would want to point out, that BSP is by design gradually breaking out from its exclusive and reclusive shell. It has gone into areas that have begun to give traditional esoteric central banking work a common or mass appeal. Our groundbreaker was microfinance which we continue to promote aggressively as our response to poverty alleviation. Anti-money laundering and small business-friendly rediscounting provisions have also been doing their share to strengthen BSP linkage with the public-at-large, in general, and with enterprising Pinoys in particular. Last year, we intensified our campaign for clean money both in form and content. There was a significant increase in the volume of mutilated and unfit notes that were turned in for exchange or retirement. We attribute this in part to the cooperation and support of the banks and the greater public awareness on the merits of keeping our money in circulation clean and in good condition. The clean note campaign, launched during our 10th anniversary, has been a good complement to our anti-counterfeiting efforts. This year, we go a step further. In partnership with the Department of Education, we will involve the schools in the campaign to protect the integrity of our currency. In addition, we will develop training and activity modules that will encourage students to develop the habit of regularly saving money. In this regard, we are re-launching, after more than a decade, a national savings campaign to instill among the children the habit of saving and to impress on them the vital role of savings to our economic development as well as to their future. Aside from working with schools, BSP will also be setting up an economic and financial literacy center that will cater principally to students. Our goal is to set up similar centers in our regional offices and branches. The center will provide students the opportunity to learn how seemingly esoteric economic policies and programs affect people's lives. This should serve them in good stead when it is their turn to lead the country. Information campaigns to protect the public from investment scams will also be pursued. We will also continue working with the financial sector in developing and implementing measures that will further enhance consumer welfare. These initiatives inject elements ordinary people can relate to. This could go a long way toward generating wider public support for BSP, especially when we would need it most. Internally, we have been moving on as well. ISO certifications raised the bar of procedures, systems and workplace planning and evaluation in our bank. Following the trail of the ISO certifications awarded to the entire Security Plant and the Systems Management Ofice, the BSP is working for at least three certifications more by the end of the year, and another in 2005. All departments, including the regional offices and branches, have joined hands to formulate the core program for the BSP's environmental and occupational health and safety management system to address the quality of our work environment and our commitment to the preservation of the quality of global environment. We aim to work for BSP's combined certification by end 2004 under ISO 14001 (for environment) and OSHAS 18001 (for occupational health and safety). It is important therefore that we all help in pursuing this program. Indeed, we now go about our central banking business in a mode more suitable to the current socioeconomic setting. Pretty soon, we will be moving more work at even a faster pace and utmost efficiency as our electronic reports, data and transactions are supplemented by teleconferencing, or what I would describe as electronic meetings. In the pipeline is the fine-tuning of the BSP organization. Last month, the Monetary Board approved the new BSP functional chart designed to address organizational needs that have emerged or evolved with the rapidly changing financial and corporate environments and the bureaucracy. This will involve the creation of eight departments and offices, namely, Office of the Security Plant Chief Superintendent, Procurement Office, Office of Regional Monetary Affairs, Center for Monetary and Banking Policy, Dept. of Economic Statistics, Human Resource Development Dept, International Dept and Management Services Sub-sector. On stream are the reorganization of some departments for sharper focus. For speedy response to manpower requirements, the Human Resource Dept. has been enhancing existing procedures on recruitment, selection and promotion, including the adoption of the chain promotion, forecasting manpower needs, and use of more advanced assessment tools. The results-oreinted performance evaluation system is also now being implemented. All these are expected to contribute to the greater efficiency and faster delivery of BSP services. Part of this morning's exercise is the renewal of our commitments as citizens, as BSPers and as civil servants. It is the people --you, us -- who will breathe life to these vows. And when we discuss human resource in this institution, the talk invariably leads to capability building and values enhancement that have become integral to the bank's year-round personnel development program. For the medium-term program for the period 2004-2008, BSP pursues an integrated approach to organizational performance management thru its service excellence program. This aims for every employee and officer of the BSP to deliver ever-improving value to everyone we serve, to improve BSP's overall effectiveness and capabilities and to enhance organizational and personal learning. In connection with personnel welfare, I have a piece of good news for you. We have time and again said that personnel welfare in this bank occupies a preferred slot in our priority lists. Last Wednesday, the Monetary Board approved a proposal that addresses the high cost of medical care these days. The Monetary Board approved the following: 1. Mandatory annual medical examination covering all BSP personnel for early detection of diseases, and 2. Increase in the maximum allowable ceiling for dread disease to P600,000 from P400,000 and the grant of an additional quota to be taken from the unutilized portion of the maximum allowable ceiling for the last five years. Much is expected from us, which is why the bank takes care of its people. After 13 top performing ratings from the Makati Business Club, we can rightfully claim and are duty-bound as BSP employees to protect and maintain a sterling reputation. A cut above the rest in the bureaucracy, we can be no less. I can go on and on with what we can do at BSP, but we have a full day ahead and I don't want to detain you any further. But please allow me a personal note. I want to thank you again for the most lavish expression of support that you have given me and our officials during the lowest point of our legal battle last year. That lowest point was the peak of my connection with you and it will remain etched in my memory. Last month, that issue was once and for all laid to rest with the courts deciding in our favor, a fitting footnote to a most eventful year. Together we delivered. And now for your most awaited moment-- again a manifestation of the bank's concern for your welfare --I would like to announce the 10 first prize winners in the anniversary raffle. Each one will receive P40,000. The names of the 50 winners for the P30,000 and P20,000 cash prizes are already posted in the elevators. To all the winners, my congratulations. (Note: BSP's 11th Anniversary Celebration, July 5, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: The Rural Banking System: Recent Developments and Key Challenges
Occasion: Induction Ceremony of New Officers Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Senen D. Glorioso, incoming President of the Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines (RBAP), Mr. Daniel R. Arcenas, outgoing RBAP President, RBAP Board of Directors, members of the association, ladies and gentlemen: good evening. It is always a pleasure for me to address RBAP whose commitment to innovation and excellence in rural banking is evident in its continuing work to improve the delivery of banking services to our local communities. RBAP has truly become a vital force in the industry, spurring the rural banks to work together towards building a solid and responsive industry. Status of the rural banking system Under conditions of modest economic growth and sound financial environment in 2003, the rural banking system turned in a commendable performance. Total resources of the rural banking system rose by 10.3 percent. The industry posted a 12.3 percent increase in deposit mobilization and a 9.1 percent expansion in capital accounts. The industry's overall asset quality continued to improve. NPL ratio fell to 12.1 percent at end-year 2003. For the last five years, the industry's past due ratio has been on a downtrend. On the other hand, ROPOA (gross) decreased by 1.7 percent at end-2003. These positive trends will have to be sustained if we are to effectively contain the stock of non-performing assets in the banking system. In relation to this, let me just remind those banks that are interested in availing the tax benefits under the SPV Law. You only have until April 8, 2005. Actually, the deadline is tighter since SPV s that can purchase NPAs will have to be organized by September 18, 2005. Given the tight financial situation, it is highly uncertain if congress will be willing to extend the deadlines. The industry also recorded significant improvement in bottomline figures. Profitability picked up as return on assets went up to 1.8 percent while return on equity further improved to 11.3 percent. All of these indicators suggest a vibrant rural banking system. As far as the industry's microfinance operations in 2003 are concerned, I am pleased with the very favorable outcome. Last year, 2 microfinance-oriented banks were opened, while an existing rural bank converted to a microfinance-oriented rural bank. As a result, total assets of microfinance-oriented rural banks reached P473 million from P31 million at end-year 2002. A couple of weeks ago, we have recognized successful Filipino microentrepreneurs who have made such a positive transformational impact on their respective communities with the help of microfinance institutions. Their success is proof of how microfinance can help in transforming the lives of the poor. Many of the winners were financed by rural banks. I hope you will continue to support the growing needs of the microenterprise sector through sustainable microfinance. Key challenges In due course, the performance of the rural banking system will depend on two main factors. Evidently, the overall economic climate will play a prominent part. And yet, this will not be the only major influence. An equally important factor is the progress on financial sector reforms and how this will affect the financial system over time. Against the backdrop of enhanced competition in the financial system, we have taken steps to institute key reforms that will lead to greater efficiency, effective risk management, stronger capital base and improved corporate governance standards in the banking system. To effectively carry out these reforms, we greatly rely on your cooperation and readiness to assume the heavy responsibility of ensuring the sustained viability and competitiveness of your respective institutions. The main challenge for the rural banking system is to establish itself as the lead catalyst in stimulating economic development in the countryside. Rural banks serve an important niche of our economy: the borrowers in the grassroots. This makes rural banks our major partners in countryside development. I am glad that the rural banking system has been very supportive of this endeavor. Your strong commitment to countryside development will enable us to meet the bigger challenge of building strong local economies for a more equitable economic growth. As a further initiative to develop larger and stronger countryside financial institutions (CFIs) that can cater to the diverse needs of the countryside clients, we have issued Circular No. 426 which sets the guidelines for the extension of the Countryside Financial Institutions Enhancement Program (CFIEP). The program is open to all CFIs, namely, rural banks, cooperative banks and thrift banks that meet the eligibility requirement set by bsp. Under the program, participating financial institutions are entitled to the following incentives: (1) relaxation of equity ownership ceilings for individuals, cooperatives and corporations for a period not exceeding 20 years and (2) waiver of penalties and other charges due on arrearages that may be redeemed under the program. Another challenge for rural banks and for the whole banking system, for that matter, is the development of a comprehensive strategy to raise the standards of corporate governance. Towards this end, we have issued pertinent regulations that are basically intended to enhance standards on transparency, accountability and fairness in the banking system. Strengthening bank governance also calls for improved standards on accountability. In line with this, we have further strengthened the standards for a bank's compliance function to better ensure adherence to relevant laws and regulations and sound practices. Concluding remarks At this point, I would like to call on the association, in particular, its new set of officers to remain true to its mission of providing quality service to the public through dynamic and responsible leadership. The outgoing officers have done a remarkable job. You have a tough act to follow! In the end, the key to continued viability of the rural banking system lies in its capability to fully serve the needs of its core clientele. For this task, you will have to be very efficient, competitive and innovative. Congratulations to the incoming officers of RBAP! Let me assure you that the BSP will remain your strongest ally in adopting a proactive approach to address the challenges ahead. Thank you and good evening! (Note: Induction Ceremony of RBAP Officers, Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines (RBAP), June 30, 2004, Century Park Sheraton, Manila)

Title: Opening Statement for FOCAP Meeting
Occasion: Breakfast Forum Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Over the past few years, the Philippine economy has been performing above most expectations, showing sustained growth and declining inflation despite a difficult global economic environment and domestic socio-political challenges. Our GNP, for example, grew by an average of 4.4 percent in 1999-2003 in real terms. In the first quarter of 2004, real GNP grew at a robust pace of 6.2 percent from its year-ago level, while real GDP rose by a higher 6.4 percent. However, the country's economic expansion remains modest when one considers our faster population growth and the quicker progress of other Asian countries. Many Asian economies have managed after the 1997 financial crisis to achieve output growth rates of nearly twice that of the Philippines. This is one of our biggest challenges. Thus, as we finally put behind us the may elections, we must now turn to the more difficult task of establishing and strengthening the foundations for rapid and sustained output growth for the long term. This higher level of output growth is crucial if we are to achieve a more meaningful poverty reduction program. Such an objective would require measures to address the key weaknesses and vulnerabilities that remain in the economy. These would include key concerns such as fiscal sustainability (which would include not only forceful deficit reduction but also debt sustainability), power sector reform, financial sector reform, export competitive-ness, and comprehensive infrastructure development. Even this short list is already a tall order for any government, particularly the task of restructuring the power sector. However, these are precisely the most critical tasks that the incoming administration will need to focus on in order to make a significant advance forward over the next six years. There being no better time than the present, then the nation should take this window of opportunity to direct its collective attention to addressing the key economic priorities for the medium term. I am now at your disposal for questions.

Title: The Financial System in Post-Election Philippines
Occasion: FINEX General Membership Meeting
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Franklin Isaac, President, Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines (FINEX), other officers and members of FINEX, distinguished guests, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. It is my great pleasure to address the general membership meeting of the largest organization of financial executives in the country, the FINEX. With the Philippines having just undertaken its most important electoral exercise this year, the timing is perfect--it is perfect for stocktaking and careful and cooperative planning for both private and public sectors. Such cooperation is crucial in ensuring that, within the next six years, the Philippines re-emerges as one of the vibrant economies in the region. The FINEX membership, comprising some 700 financial executives, CEOs, CFOs, entrepreneurs, public servants and academicians, possesses great potential as agents and champions of our national aspirations for economic progress. But first, it will be useful to remind ourselves of the recent challenges we face in the Philippines. On the domestic front, we continue to be affected by the political uncertainty arising from the protracted conclusion of the national election. The world is also observing how we shall keep our public finance aligned with our target; its sustainability remains an important public issue. Other equally important concerns involve the Philippine power sector as well as the challenges in the financial sector. I do not, of course, have to detail to you the shocks on the international front coming from the dramatic rebound in oil and other commodity prices. We have also to be prepared for the adjustments that may have to be made if the U.S. Federal reserve finally does the expected, and that is to raise its policy rates. How China and Japan and the rest of Europe will respond will definitely affect our menu of options in shaping our economic strategies. The economy in general The economy has performed above expectations in the face of all these challenges. GDP growth averaged 4.4 percent in 1999-2003, and, at 6.4 percent exceeded all expectations in the first quarter of 2004. The first quarter growth came on the back of about 7.7 percent agricultural growth, which may be attributed in part to good weather conditions, and to government efforts to improve the productivity of the agricultural sector. These productivity-enhancing measures provide an important example of how structural reforms can be expected to have permanent effects on stabilizing Philippine GDP, insulating it from the vagaries of weather conditions, and helping achieve price stability over the near term. Meanwhile, although inflation has risen slightly in recent months due to supply shocks, it averaged 3.8 percent for the first five months of 2004, still below the 4-5 percent target for 2004 and 2005. The BSP believes that supply-side pressures on inflation--such as the rise in the prices of food products, domestic pump prices of gasoline and other oil products and the adjustments in transport fares--that drove inflation upward recently, are temporary in nature and do not appear to lead to a permanent shift in the long-run inflation path. Nevertheless, continued soft demand conditions will help moderate any inflationary pressures that could emanate from supply shocks. Don't get me wrong: the BSP will remain anticipatory of any potential secondary effects of supply pressures on effective domestic demand which might require appropriate monetary response. Monetary policy is not written in stone. Yet we must acknowledge that our growth remains relatively modest considering the current pace of population growth and the performance of other Asian economies. We need to raise business confidence, improve productivity and enhance the country's competitiveness. In this regard, it is important that key issues must be addressed, including fiscal sustainability, power and financial sector reform, export competitiveness, comprehensive infrastructure support, a credible population management program, and socio-political stability. Clearly the upcoming administration has a heavy economic policy agenda. Status of the Philippine financial system Let me move to my sector of responsibility and your area of interest. In the last ten years, the financial sector has benefited from a number of liberalization and deregulation initiatives as globalization takes stronger roots in the Philippines. As a result, the Philippine financial system's underlying fundamentals has posted steady progress as of the second half of 2003. Institutional reforms continue to weave the system, driving indicators to improve including rising capital adequacy ratio, more stable non-performing loans (NPL) ratios and higher level of resources. Resolute operational and financial restructuring has also resulted in new business and revenues, with both banks and non-banks struggling towards profitability by keeping expenses in check, consolidating operations, shifting to more cost-efficient methods, business process outsourcing, system rationalization and a host of other operational improvements. Risk management has been elevated to a new level of strategic importance. Ladies and gentlemen, this is the better side of the balance sheet. Challenges for the Philippine financial system On the other hand, the BSP recognizes the need to continue fostering an efficient, stable and competitive banking system that supports the sustainable growth of the economy. Let me be more specific. Stronger regulatory frameworkTo strengthen the legal and regulatory framework for banking supervision, we are supporting key amendments to the BSP and PDIC charters aimed at reinforcing these institutions' regulatory capacities and empowering supervisors to deal with distressed institutions. Such proposed amendments to the BSP charter include: one, implementation of more frequent conduct of bank examination. Two, implementation of prompt corrective action on problematic/distressed banks to replace the strategy of forbearance and liquidity assistance. Three, restoration of the BSP's tax-exempt status. Four, imposition of stronger criminal and administrative penalties for violations of banking laws. Finally, exemption of supervisors and/or examiners from lawsuits incurred in the course of performing their duties. Without these amendments, it would be difficult to ensure that our bank regulator will be confidently bold when conducting his examination. On the other hand, amendments to the PDIC act should aim to strengthen the PDIC's mandate as statutory receiver and liquidator of closed banks and enhance public confidence in the banking system by providing greater protection to depositors. We would like to see a situation where our bank regulators will not hesitate to close a bank that is notoriously unworthy of public trust, or help a bank that has exhausted all its means but remains temporarily challenged by liquidity demand. The BSP is the lender of last resort, and not the lender of first resort. We will continue to avoid creating incentives for further financial instability. Improved supervision technology. Regulatory strengthening should be accompanied by measures to improve supervision technology. Planned measures over the medium term include: (1) revisions in the examination process to fully implement consolidated supervision and adopt the risk-based approach; (2) review of reportorial requirements for banks; (3) improvement of coordination with domestic regulators (sec, insurance commission and PDIC) and establishment of linkages with relevant overseas regulators. Financial sector restructuring. A system-wide restructuring strategy will have to begin with the large-scale disposition of banks' non-performing assets (NPAs). The legal and tax framework has been established to encourage banks to offload their idle assets and pare down significantly their NPAs. The BSP recently relaxed the rules governing special purpose asset vehicles (SPVs) to speed up the sale of the banking sector's NPAs. For example, the new guidelines set out alternative regulatory treatment of the sale of NPAs of banks and other financial institutions under BSP supervision to SPVs and to qualified individuals for housing. The BSP has also allowed banks to defer recognition of losses from NPA sales, and has recently even lengthened the deferral period from 7 to 10 years and backloaded the distribution. With these and other changes, banks will be able to greatly cushion the impact of NPA clean-up on their capital position. Capital market development. Developing domestic capital markets will help diversify risks away from the banking sector and provide an alternative pillar to cushion against external shocks, contagion and possible reduced access to international capital markets. This task essentially entails the establishment of the institutional framework for the proper functioning of markets for new securities, as well as the development of secondary markets for various securities. Efforts in this vein would include the establishment of a Philippine fixed income exchange to open hopefully by the middle of this year. This will centralize market transactions and provide the platform for the secondary trading of fixed-income securities. It would also entail the establishment over the period 2004-2008 of a domestic credit rating system. Corporate governance. Other banking sector reforms would consist of efforts to promote corporate governance reform and market discipline. This would include (1) passage of amendments to the corporation code; (2) creation of a corporate governance standards committee; (3) development and implementation of a system of corporate governance standards for financial institutions; (4) establishment of monitoring mechanisms on compliance with such prescribed corporate governance standards; and (5) promotion of compliance with International Accounting Standards (IAS) and International Valuation Standards (IVS). These are all meats, and perhaps too much and too tough to swallow one and all. It will hopefully simplify the many complex but interrelated developments happening in the financial system if I say that the first challenge is for the Central Bank to sustain its system-wide monitoring. This constant activity will ensure that the BSP will be in a stronger regulatory footing, understanding how potential macroeconomic shocks are transmitted through the larger economic system. The other important challenge is to ensure good bank governance through the banks' management team and board of directors and greater public disclosure of their true financial condition. Concluding remarks The efforts of the BSP form part of sustaining reforms that are seen to enhance the long-term growth and stability of the financial system as a whole. The objective is to make sure that the financial system deserves the public's confidence and that it effectively performs its role as an agent of economic growth. A stable financial system is certainly one in which all economic agents--households, business firms, financial services companies and the public sector--can with great confidence hold and transfer financial assets without so much worry on the risks of financial trouble. This is an environment we all want to achieve and keep for a long, long time. To this end, I challenge FINEX to do its share, and do it well. Thank you and good day. (Note: FINEX General Membership Meeting, June 16, 2004, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati City)

Title: Inspirational Message
Occasion: Awarding Ceremony and Appreciation Cocktails Land Bank of the Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It is a pleasure to join you this afternoon. I always look forward to this opportunity to address my colleagues in the financial sector. Today's awarding ceremony affords us with the chance to recognize outstanding financial institutions and sub-borrowers for their contribution to countryside development. More significantly, this occasion serves to further highlight the extent of the financial sector's involvement in accelerating rural development. I believe this is vital to all of us since one of our key roles as an industry is to serve as the lead catalyst in spurring economic development in the countryside. Admittedly, this is a very challenging role considering the widespread incidence of poverty in the rural communities. The overarching goal, therefore, is to find ways on how we can make a direct and immediate contribution to reduce poverty in these areas. The government has identified two key solutions in its medium-term program to alleviate poverty. One is to promote equitable, accelerated, and broad-based growth, based on free enterprise; and the other is to empower the poor to participate more fully in development through, among others, the efficient provision of basic services and the increase in access to productive assets such as land, rural infrastructure, and credit. We are getting much needed assistance in pursuing our twin objectives of promoting countryside growth and empowering the poor, judging by the heartening support of the various government and private institutions in the country. Land Bank is, of course, among those institutions that is actively involved in countryside development. Land Bank has successfully designed financial programs that have led to the expansion of credit outreach to priority sectors, namely the small farmers and fisherfolk; micro-, small and medium enterprises; agri-infrastructure; agribusiness; and agri- and environment-related projects. We are equally heartened by the commitment of our major partners in rural development, the Countryside Financial Institutions (CFIs) that serve and cater to the needs of our borrowers in the grassroots. The active role that you play in promoting countryside development will enable us to rise up to the challenge of building strong local economies for a more equitable economic growth. We are also strongly benefiting from the assistance being extended to us by the World Bank. Its Countryside Loan Fund, a credit facility under its International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) program, has helped in increasing the flow of investments and credit resources to the countryside. On our part, we at the BSP are ready to provide support to our financial institutions in building a truly progressive countryside. BSP initiatives A core aspect of the BSP agenda is the sustained implementation of banking reforms. I firmly believe that with sound reforms in place, we can further improve the efficiency and competitiveness of the banking system. This would effectively lead to a more resilient industry, one that is able to stand firm amid a tough financial environment. BSP reform initiatives constitute the upgrading of critical aspects of banking operations such as in the areas of capitalization, operational efficiency, product innovation, and governance. By operating in a prudent and sound manner, banks will be better able to provide efficient and reliable service to the public. And with millions of our countrymen living below the poverty level, most of them in the rural communities, the challenge for banks is to find better and faster ways of delivering banking services to these communities. The BSP supports the development of larger and stronger CFIs that can cater to the diverse needs of the countryside clients. Very recently, we have issued Circular No. 426 which sets the guidelines for the extension of the countryside financial institutions enhancement program (CFIEP). The program is open to all CFIs, namely, rural banks, cooperative banks and thrift banks that meet the eligibility requirement set by BSP. Under the program, participating financial institutions are entitled to the following incentives: (1) relaxation of equity ownership ceilings for individuals, cooperatives and corporations for a period not exceeding 20 years and (2) waiver of penalties and other charges due on arrearages that may be redeemed under the program. Microfinance agenda At this point, I would like to highlight BSP's commitment to promote sustainable microfinance as a response to the needs of the many enterprising poor in our society. I am glad that the industry, particularly, the rural banking industry, has been particularly supportive of this endeavor. Rural banks are proving to be an ideal delivery channel for microfinance. But we are still at an early stage, and the real challenge is for us to serve a greater number of the entrepreneurial poor who have yet to fully benefit from access to banking services. Let me remind you also that microfinance is a risk-taking business. This means that going into microfinance should never be used as an excuse to engage in unsound banking practices. We will not tolerate this. Presently, we are working on establishing a central credit information bureau, in partnership with the National Credit Council. One of the benefits of this project is that it will address the risks involved in microfinance operations. Among them are reducing the risk of credit pollution, promoting greater borrower discipline, and lowering credit risk especially on unsecured lending. The BSP is also committed to support the establishment of sustainable and viable microfinance institutions. We believe banking institutions are in a key position to meet the demands of the microenterprise sector. In relation to this, we are building on our initiatives to promote enabling policies, enhance training and capacity building, and actively engage in promotion and advocacy. In closing, let me assure everyone of BSP's commitment to champion economic development in the countryside. The strengthening of our local economies will lead to a more stable base for the national economy. Congratulations to all the winners! You have taken the lead in community financing and you have done a good job. You best exemplify the role of the financial sector as the principal catalyst in economic development. Let us continue to do our share in securing economic growth for the country. Thank you. (Note: Awarding Ceremony and Appreciation Cocktails (for the outstanding participating financial institutions and sub-borrowers of the Countryside Loan Fund and the Agricultural Loan Fund), Land Bank of the Philippines June 10, 2004, LBP Plaza, Malate, Manila)

Title: Inspirational Message
Occasion: Joint Luncheon Meeting Canadian and American Chambers of Commerce
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: 1. Introduction I appreciate this opportunity to speak to you about the BSP's assessment of prevailing conditions in the Philippine economy. As a central banker, I take advantage of every chance to communicate the BSP's views about inflation, the exchange rate, and other aspects of the economy with members of the business community. A central bank, after all, must consider itself ultimately accountable to the public, by virtue of the wide influence that it wields over the economic life of the nation. As such, central bankers have a duty to actively promote public discussion of economic issues that affect the welfare of businesses, consumers, wage earners, and other groups. Today I have the privilege of exchanging views with distinguished members of the Canadian and American business community in the Philippines. Most of you, I am sure, are no longer strangers to the intricacies of doing business in this country. What I would like to do, therefore, is to outline the BSP's views on what we may expect over the next year or so. My hope is that my talk will provide you a balanced assessment of the Philippines' economic prospects. I intend to focus mainly on the variables that directly influence the cost of doing business in the Philippines--inflation, interest rates and the exchange rate--things that are also of primary interest to the business community. 2. Review of recent developments Let me begin with a brief look at the recent developments in the economy. In the first quarter of 2004, the Philippine economy sustained its growth momentum on the strength of vibrant domestic demand. GDP grew at a robust pace of 6.4 percent, while real GNP grew by 6.2 percent from its year-ago level. This was driven mainly by consumer spending, which grew by 5.9 percent in the first quarter, stronger than the 5 percent rise recorded a year earlier, on account of election-related activities as well as increased OFW remittances and higher farm income. Export growth has also picked up due to the recovery in the world's major economies and our increasing trade with china. Most encouragingly, gross domestic capital formation rebounded to 16.2 percent after a contraction in the previous three quarters. This recovery was supported by investments in agricultural and industrial machineries, an improvement in construction spending and a build-up in inventories. On the production side, the three major production sectors, agriculture, industry and services all registered higher growth rates in the first quarter. The agriculture sector posted a year-on-year increase of 7.7 percent, the fastest pace in 15 years, on account of the impressive growth in the fishery sector and the strong rebound in rice production. The services sector likewise posted a strong growth of 6.4 percent in the first quarter from 5.5 percent a year earlier due to sustained expansion in transport, communication, and financial services. Meanwhile, industry also accelerated to 5.5 percent in the first quarter from 4.8 percent in the previous quarter, with manufacturing expanding by 4.3 percent on stronger consumer spending and export demand. Low inflation provided a supportive backdrop for stronger growth. Average inflation in the first five months of 2004 was 3.8 percent based on the 1994-base year CPI data and 4.1 percent using the new 2000-based CPI series. Both averages are near the lower end of the government's inflation target of 4‑5 percent for 2004. Despite the encouraging trends in growth and inflation, there remained some soft spots in domestic economic activity. The manufacturing sector, for example, continues to operate at below full capacity, with average capacity utilization at around 79 percent as of march 2004. Unemployment also remains relatively high at 11 percent as of January. Conditions for credit also appear to be relatively modest, as shown by the weak growth in total commercial bank loans, which has dwindled to less than 1 percent in march 2004. The weak loan growth has been traced to the climate of political uncertainty and the prevailing levels of non-performing loans which have compelled our banks to remain cautious in granting new loans. As a result, growth in the money supply or m3 also remains relatively weak, despite a mild recovery in April. The sluggishness in credit conditions has been accompanied by a moderate rise in market interest rates compared to the start of 2004. The average 91-day Treasury bill rate has gone up from 6.2 percent in January to 7.1 percent in May. The increase has been accompanied by a rise in average bank lending rates from 9.1‑10.9 percent as of end-January to 9.9‑11.9 percent as of end‑may. In part, this uptrend also reflects the concern among investors about the ability of the national government to meet its fiscal targets in an election year, and more generally about the sustainability of the fiscal position over the medium term. On the plus side, the peso has begun to recover after a period of election-related uncertainty and increased dollar demand. The nominal exchange rate averaged at P55.84 against the U.S. dollar in may from P55.98/US$1 in January-March as political concerns eased after the elections and higher inflows from overseas remittances added to the supply of dollars in the system. 3. Outlook and challenges Against such a background, what kind of performance can we expect from the economy in 2004?. I believe that our growth performance will continue to be robust in 2004 on the strength of private consumption spending on the demand side and strong performance from the agriculture and services sector on the production side. These sectors will propel GDP growth toward the 4.9 percent target for the entire year. As for inflation, our latest assessment at the BSP suggests that the outlook for inflation in 2004 remains consistent with the 4-5 percent inflation target for the year. However, supply-side factors such as transport fare adjustments, utility rate increases, and rising energy prices along with possible wage adjustments pose risks to consumer prices in 2005 and may cause an uptrend in average inflation above the 4-5 percent target. However, since the expected pressures on prices over the next year or so originate mainly from the supply-side, they are largely outside the influence of monetary policy and do not represent permanent shifts in the long-run path of inflation. Therefore, the prevailing risks to inflation do not require a monetary policy response from the BSP. Moreover, we believe that the continuing patterns of sluggish credit demand and moderate investment growth imply that the monetary policy stance should continue to support the economy and provide adequate stimulus to credit activity. The relatively modest improvement in investments constitutes a downside risk to the sustainability of growth in the medium term, and implies a need for caution in setting policy rates in the future. Monetary authorities recognize the need to preserve the stimulus to economic activity, and accordingly have kept the BSP's policy interest rates unchanged since July 2003. Nevertheless, the outlook for market interest rates will continue to be influenced by financial market perceptions of how well the government is doing in its efforts to manage the budget deficit. I am a bit optimistic in this regard, given the recent improvement in revenue performance. However, the incoming administration will need to follow this up with other revenue measures, and carefully explain to the public the critical importance of the fiscal measures that need to be put in place. The NG's performance in fiscal reform will also be important for the exchange rate. Movements in the exchange rate in the near term will continue to be tied to market sentiment on the government's commitment to critically needed structural reforms that will ensure continued growth in the medium term. Exchange rate volatility will be lessened by the strong inflows from remittances, but it can be minimized through forceful reforms not only in the fiscal sector, but also in power, infrastructure, and others. 4. Concluding remarks To sum up, there are good reasons to expect the Philippine economy to perform well in 2004, given robust consumer demand and a generally supportive macroeconomic environment. Over the longer term, however, the outlook for the economy depends mainly on how well the incoming administration is able to transform the electoral mandate and investor goodwill it has received into forceful measures to balance the fiscal budget, improve the investment environment, raise productivity, and enhance the country's competitiveness. The Bangko Sentral, for its part, intends to support these structural reform efforts by strengthening the banking sector and ensuring a sound monetary and financial environment for business and investment through prudent monetary policy. Let me now end by thanking the Canadian and American chambers of commerce for the opportunity to share my views on the Philippine economy. Your continued presence in the Philippines strengthens my belief that investors are able to see through all the political noise and continue to believe in our economic potential. It is my hope that you will stay the course with us as we march on toward sustainable growth for the long term. Thank you and good day. (Note: Joint Luncheon Meeting, Canadian & American Chambers of Commerce), June 09, 2004, Manila Peninsula Hotel, Makati City)

Title: The 2nd Citibank Microentrepreneur of the Year Award
Occasion: Awarding Ceremony 2nd Citibank Microentrepreneur of the Year Award
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Today we pay tribute to a select group of enterprising men and women who make up the roster of awardees in the 2nd Citibank Microentrepreneur of the Year awards. Each of them has a story to tell. What makes their stories exceptional is the fact that they are ordinary people whose ingenuity and perseverance have turned them into successful microentrepreneurs, with the support of microfinance institutions. Even more remarkable is the positive transformational impact they have had in their respective communities. Their courage and enterprising spirit have inspired others in their communities to similarly strive and venture into their own livelihood projects to attain better and more productive lives. Indeed, we can all draw inspiration from their accomplishments. Their success validates our belief that microfinance, indeed, has the power to transform the plight of our entrepreneur poor or the so-called e-poor. Let us therefore give the awardees a well-deserved round of applause. This microentrepreneur award is made possible by the enlightened support of Citibank. We fully appreciate the resources that Citibank has devoted to this worthy project. By encouraging the growth of micro businesses at the grass-roots level, we are promoting the development of local economies that are the foundation of sustainable and equitable economy in our country. We also acknowledge the continuing efforts of various organizations and microfinance institutions in the country in helping improve lives all over the country. We are truly grateful for your unwavering commitment to microfinance. In one of the studies made on microenterprise development, it was pointed out that the solution to the poverty problem would require, among other things, providing the poor people greater access to credit and capital. [1] this basically stems from the reality that without the means or the resources, the poor can never be productive, much less survive or see to their urgent personal concerns such as securing a job, getting an education, and having enough food to eat everyday. Through microfinance or by making loans available and providing job training, the poor are given the opportunity to engage in promising microenterprises. The poor can now have access to badly needed capital which they can use to start a small business of their own. Microfinance is the jumpstart they need to begin the process of meeting their most basic human needs. Microfinance gives the poor people hope. As an advocate of microfinance, the BSP aims to address this need by way of supporting the establishment of sustainable and viable microfinance institutions, particularly in the banking industry. Given their resources, banking institutions are in a position to meet the demands of the microenterprise sector. I am glad to report that banks, in general, have been quite responsive to our call for their greater involvement in microfinance. Together, 122 banks have so far provided about P2.5 billion in microfinance loans to nearly half a million microentrepreneurs. This is equivalent to an average loan of P5,000 each. Over time, we expect these numbers to increase exponentially. We have also gone full force in pursuing our three-part microfinance program that is essentially geared towards: (1) creating an enabling policy and regulatory environment for sustainable microfinance, (2) enhancing training and capacity building within BSP and the banking sector; and (3) actively taking part in microfinance promotion and advocacy. Very briefly, the highlights of this three-part program are as follows: We are currently working with the National Credit Council (NCC), in setting up a central credit information bureau. This project, although beneficial to the banking system as a whole, will particularly benefit microfinance operations by reducing the risk of credit pollution, promoting greater borrower discipline, and lowering credit risk especially on unsecured lending. We are also stepping up our training and capacity building program to enhance expertise of our general examiners, officers and employees, as well as the microfinance practitioners in the banking sector. This is being implemented through a series of training programs, workshops and exposure tours. For the benefit of the banking sector, the BSP has begun incorporating microfinance into the basic rural and thrift banking courses. We have likewise launched a Regional Advocacy Pprogram in 2003 in keeping with our promotion and advocacy agenda. Our goal is to conduct microfinance seminars in strategic regions in the country where we hope to entice potential practitioners. So far, we have conducted regional information seminars in 8 regions across the country. Another focus of advocacy is by way of establishing working ties with other institutions for a broader microfinance network. Towards this end, we have conducted briefings for major corporations, foundations and international organizations. We are also publishing a handbook on microfinance that should be useful for both microfinance institutions and potential borrowers. Indeed, if we are to achieve meaningful progress in our efforts to alleviate poverty in our country, we should all commit to work together in ensuring the long-term viability and sustainability of microfinance. Help can be delivered in various ways from various sources. Citibank, one of the world's biggest banks, has taken the time to create and manage a reward system for microentrepreneurs that has brought us together this afternoon. Let me share with you that no less than Jim Hunt, Citibank's country head, served as a member of this year's Board of Judges. So did foremost broadcast journalist and producer of the highly regarded Probe Team Cheche Lazaro; media executive Sandy Prieto, President of the Philippine Daily Inquirer, one of the country's biggest and most influential newspaper; Professor Ron Chua of the Asian Institute of Management's Center for Entrepreneurship; Nonoy Alindogan of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas; Steven Edminster, Governance Officer of USAID; and Secretary Villavicencio of the National Anti-Povery Council. As one of the judges myself, I can attest to the tough screening and evaluation process our winners went through. I can also tell you that based on what I saw and heard, our judges - individually and collectively - are true advocates of microfinance. Let us therefore give the members of our hardworking board of judges a warm round of applause. Indeed, no one should be too big, nor too small, nor too busy to be involved in promoting the cause of microfinance. As our awardees tonight have shown, in very convincing ways, microfinance offers the shortcut to alleviating poverty in our country. In closing, I extend my heartfelt congratulations to the winners. With courage and determination, you surmounted the odds and, in the process, became successful models in your respective communities. Your triumph over poverty serves as a shining example of Filipino ingenuity - just one of several virtues we Filipinos should be proud of. I am also happy to note that women no longer have a monopoly of the Citibank Microentrepreneur Awards. We have male winners this time around who can now serve as role models for Filipino men. Finally, I want to thank all of you for joining us this afternoon. With your presence, you have shown that you are one with us in promoting microfinance. Ladies and gentlemen, in a few days, we will celebrate our nation's independence. It is our hope that together, we can help many more of our countrymen move out of poverty into financial independence through microfinance. Maraming pong salamat. Mabuhay po ang ating mga winners, mabuhay po ang Pilipinas! -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [1] Source: UP Institute for Small Scale Industries (UP ISSI) (Note: Awarding Ceremony, 2nd Microentrepreneur of the Year Awards, June 04, 2004, Metropolitan Museum Manila)

Title: DENR and BSP: Forging an Enduring Partnership
Occasion: Inauguration of the DENR-BSP Mini-Forest Park
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Secretary Elisea Gozun, Udersecretary Rolando Metin, Undersecretary Renato Rueda, Director Julian Amador, Executive Director Cora Davis, other officers and staff of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources, special guests from the NGO community headed by Mrs. Narda Camacho, Ms. Juanita Abaquin and Dr. Metodeo Palaypay, our friends from media, fellow workers at Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, good morning. We are very happy that the partnership between the Department of Environment and Natural Resources and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas continues to bear fruit. As you can see, this mini-forest park houses a wide variety of trees and a profusion of flowers of different shapes and colors. It is truly a green haven that people from all walks of life can visit. That the park is within the National Ecology Center provides added incentive that a visit to this place will both be pleasurable and informative for those who want to do their share in taking care of the environment. Secretary Gozun, I assure you, the DENR has a partner in BSP for its efforts to protect and enhance our environment. This is the reason why our Monetary Board approved a donation of P3.9 million for the development of this mini forest park. The Secretary will also be happy to know that at the BSP's Security Plant Complex, right beside this mini-forest park, are environment-friendly projects we are particularly proud of. This includes a sewage treatment plant that allows us to recycle waste water; an environment-friendly tree-lined one-hectare parking area which used perforated materials that allow grass to grow underneath the parked vehicles; a new technology for recycling waste solution from our printing machines; and a briquetting system that allows us to recycle old banknotes for other applications, such as the paper weights we are providing our guests this morning. Indeed, we do not pay lip service to environmental protection. We walk the talk. The protection of the environment is our collective responsibility. Whether for health, economic and social reasons, it is an imperative that demands unyielding commitment from all of us. This commitment underpins the continuing investments of time and resources by Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas in projects that foster a better environment. With the signing of yet another MOA today, the DENR and the BSP continue their partnership in addressing mutual concerns through inter-agency cooperation. With a synergy such as this, I am confident the partnership between DENR and BSP will continue to grow and prosper in the years ahead. I understand the tree I am planting here today at the mini-forest park is the mangkono, the hardest of the Philippine hardwood species. I believe this is a fitting symbol for the enduring partnership between the DENR and the Bangko Sentral. Marami pong salamat sa inyong lahat. (Note: Inauguration of the DENR-BSP Mini-Forest Park, June 04, 2004, National Ecology Center, Quezon City)

Title: Welcome Remarks
Occasion: Dialogue with Exporters
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Ladies and gentlemen, good morning: I am extremely grateful for this opportunity to once again bring together our exporters and policymakers to discuss issues of common concern. We've been doing this for some time now, and I think on the whole our meetings have been quite productive and useful for everyone involved. I also think that this is a particularly good time to assess the prospects for the export sector and figure out what we can do to improve its performance. I'm sure you'll agree that the Philippine export sector's growth of 1.4 percent in 2003 somewhat pales in comparison with the growth rates reported by its Asian counterparts. Like everyone else in the region, our exporters faced the slower-than-expected pickup in global demand, particularly for electronics products, but in addition they also had to contend with numerous domestic problems, such as high input costs, inadequate infrastructures, and security problems, which created a difficult environment for investments in manufacturing and dampened order placements from overseas buyers. We need to continue examining some of these problems together and determine how we can best address them. This is why we have extended our invitation to officials from the Department of Energy and the Department of Labor and Employment, as well as to the Department of Finance, Department of Trade and Industry and the Philippine National Police. Last December the BSP projected a 10 percent increase in export revenues in 2004, after consultation and discussions with the industry. This will be supported by the pickup in demand for Philippine goods as a result of the global economic recovery that is now well underway. Although we are inclined to maintain our 10 percent forecast, the available export figures for the first quarter of the year were somewhat weaker than expected, and I hope that this forum will give us a better feel of how the industry's performance will shape up this year so that we can adjust our projections accordingly. Let me now end by saying that these meetings are part of the BSP's efforts to strengthen the economic policymaking process and also to support the Philippine export industry. Let me therefore thank my colleagues from the different government agencies and the representatives of the export sector for taking the time to join us here at this forum. I look forward to hearing all your views this morning. Thank you very much. (Note: Dialogue with Exporters, June 01, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Malate, Manila)

Title: Inspirational Message
Occasion: 2004 BSP Family Day Celebration
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Magandang hapon sa inyong lahat! Have you enjoyed your day? Thank you for sharing this day with us and bonding with the bigger BSP family. Indeed, we the mainstays in BSP are happier and inspired to do more when our children, spouses and kin understand and appreciate our work a little better. I congratulate the BSP Cultural and Sports Committee and the Ad Hoc Family Day Committee for successfully putting together this whole-day affair. Our congratulations, too, to those who will be declared winners today. On my way here, I could not help feeling like a winner myself. The sight of an endless stream of broad smiles, and the mingling of laughter, pleasant chatter and exuberance all around were certainly exhilarating. This, I thought, is my BSP family. I would like to think you share the same feeling of belonging that I have now amid your presence. The BSP family is embedded in our corporate culture, ensconced in a cocoon of confidence and trust that BSP will continue to preserve it. BSP upholds the "Family Day" tradition precisely for this reason. But, it is not the only reason. Our "Family Day" is at the same time a symbol of the Bangko Sentral's commitment to the family as a basic social institution. By the way, our constitution expressly recognizes the sanctity of family life. I can say we in the Bangko Sentral have always been conscious of this fact. I liken the BSP family to a laboratory for rearing good citizens and active participants for nation-building. The "Family Day" is a process of renewal of sorts. This day of bonding serves as a reminder that a family bigger than our own, also requires our attention and care. Moreover, we continue to build on our strength so that our family members -- alone or together -- will have better capability to share of themselves and what they have with others outside the family circle. The challenge to each and every Filipino today is to transcend limiting family concerns and get involved in the larger community. How far has our BSP family gone along this line? This is something that I hope you would think about later in the comforts of your homes. Again, thank you for coming and enjoy the rest of the day. (Note: 2004 BSP Family Day Celebration, May 28, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Closing Reception US$500 Million BSP Term Loan Facility
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Members of the Monetary Board, distinguished representatives from the participating banks, co-workers at the Bangko Sentral, friends from the media, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. We have successfully closed another term loan facility last April, just a few days before the national elections. Amidst the political developments and the tight timetable, we were pleased to see participation from a diverse creditor base. As with our past deals, more than twenty institutions joined this term loan facility. Recent statistics show that the economy has been performing well. The April inflation figure of 4.1% is well within the target of 4% to 5%. The budget deficit as of end-March 2004 at P56.8 billion was below the program level of P58.9 billion for the first quarter. Non-performing loans are trending down. As of February 2004, NPLs of commercial banks stood at 14.2% of total loans compared to the 15.1% recorded in the same period last year. On the international front, exports are picking up with the economic growth of our trading partners. Exports increased by 7.1% in March 2004, bringing year-to-date growth to 6.3%. Higher export growth translates to higher imports of raw materials. For the first three months of 2004, imports grew by 6.4%. Foreign direct investments in the country have significantly increased, too. Direct investments from non-residents for the first two months of this year reached US$140 million, compared to just US$15 million during the same period last year. We believe that despite the current political noise, the Philippines can sustain this good performance. As previously announced by the Bangko Sentral through a press release, this term loan facility will refinance Bangko Sentral's obligations due in the second half of this year. I am delighted to see again the participation of banks who are already creditors of the Bangko Sentral under existing facilities. On behalf of the Bangko Sentral, I thank you all for your continuing confidence, commitment and participation. Finally, let me extend our appreciation to the group of arrangers which includes the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited, HSH Nordbank, Standard Chartered Bank, Mizuho Corporate Asia (HK) Limited, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, DBS Bank Limited and Mitsubishi Securities (HK) Limited, for their commitment; and congratulate them for successfully arranging this facility for the Bangko Sentral under challenging circumstances. Thank you and good day. (Note: Closing Reception, US$500 Million BSP Term Loan Facility, May 20, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila)

Title: Corporate Governance Reforms in the Banking Sector
Occasion: High-Level Working Meeting on the Corporate Governance of Banks
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It is an honor for us to participate in this high-level discussion on corporate governance of banks. In the aftermath of the 1997 Asian financial crisis that saw several banking systems around the region come under stress, we have embarked on a wide-ranging set of banking reforms in the Philippines to better insulate the economy from future crises. In our view, improved corporate governance in the banks and other financial institutions that we supervise is the most fundamental of these reforms. BSP's Governance Reform Agenda Our reform agenda is centered on promoting greater adherence to the enhanced standards on transparency, accountability, and fairness. At the bank organization level, we have made it very clear that this is to be led by the board of directors in which final authority and full responsibility is vested. It is a sad and disturbing reality that at the root of most bank failure cases we have encountered, the failure of board oversight in the face of insider abuse has been a recurring theme. The comprehensive amendment of the General Banking Law in year 2000 has given us the critical foundation to pursue governance reforms more vigorously. In particular, the amendments provided us the clear legal basis to enforce fit and proper standards for the qualification and disqualification of bank directors and key officers. The law also required a minimum of two independent directors in an effort to counter-balance potential insider abuse. We have parlayed these basic legal requirements to reinforce the corporate governance framework of banks, including defining the duties and responsibilities of bank directors, individually and as a collective board. In 2002, we launched a mandatory orientation program for bank directors, outsourced to reputable training organizations, with the objective of familiarizing them on their primary duties and responsibilities particularly on risk management oversight. These responsibilities involve setting policies and strategies, identifying key risk areas, and monitoring corporate performance as a means to achieve growth, profitability and financial stability. Failure to attend this training is a ground for the disqualification of a director. It is imperative that bank directors know and understand the nature and scope of these oversight responsibilities. Directors should also not be able to offer the excuse that they do not know what's going on. With the growing complexity involved in running a bank, regulators need to work even more closely with the board directors who are in a far better position to monitor bank activities. As regulators, legal and physical limitations make it extremely difficult to closely monitor bank behavior especially in preventing insider abuse. Building on these early initiatives, we are taking steps to encourage professional certification of bank directors to raise the standards further and maintain the professional and ethical practice of bank directors. Many of our new regulations on enhanced risk management in line with Basel Committee recommendations necessitate directors to improve their competencies. We are especially advocating more training on specific aspects of corporate governance, particularly with regard to the proper functioning of banks' audit committees, risk management committees, and governance systems, in compliance with global standards. Accreditation of external auditors Another key aspect of our corporate governance reform agenda is to focus on the critical role of independent external auditors in promoting financial transparency. In particular, external auditors should be able to provide an objective assessment of the effectiveness of controls over financial reporting and disclosure. In order to better achieve this objective, we issued new guidelines in October 2003 prescribing the rules and regulations that shall govern the selection, appointment, reporting requirements and delisting for external auditors of banks, their subsidiaries and affiliates engaged in allied activities and other financial institutions subject to BSP supervision. These build upon ground rules adopted earlier in may 2000. The key principles of these rules and regulations include avoidance of conflict of interest situations, periodic rotation of audit partners, affirmative reporting responsibilities to bank supervisors of significant issues and adherence to international accounting standards and practices. In order to strengthen credit risk management in banks, we are also working with the Securities and Exchange Commission to strengthen financial reporting standards of banks' corporate clients. Very clearly, substandard and unreliable financial reports prejudice sound credit decisions that end up ultimately hurting everyone through reduced credit access and higher cost of credit. The idea is to create strong incentive for corporate borrowers to use only external auditors that are committed to upholding proper auditing and accounting standards. Those entities that opt not to abide by this discipline will have to pay a price by way of adverse credit treatment. Once these new guidelines are fully implemented, we hope to raise the level of professional standards in accounting and auditing to promote greater financial transparency not only to the regulatory authorities but also to the broader public. Shift to International Accounting Standards In support of promoting greater financial transparency, the Philippines is also preparing to shift to International Accounting Standards or IAS by 2005. With respect to banks, the BSP has set in motion a process to migrate our banks to this accounting standard subject to the resolution of certain issues that are now being discussed at high level between the IASB and the international banking industry. Credit Bureau and Credit Rating Agencies The BSP is also seeking to improve overall transparency in the financial system by sponsoring the formation of a central credit information system as a means not only of improving credit access and lowering borrowing cost, but also to promote a strong culture of responsible borrowing. Complementing this initiative, we are likewise encouraging the formation of domestic credit rating agencies to strengthen market discipline. Enhancing Financial Literacy The BSP is complementing its efforts to improve overall transparency with a program to empower financial consumers through a well-targeted financial literacy program. The objective of this program is to enable the public to properly use the financial information being provided to achieve more informed decisions and enhance market discipline. Further Regulatory Reforms I would also like to update you on our continuing efforts to upgrade our prudential standards in a manner that promotes bank transparency. In this regard, our most recent initiatives involve better measurement and disclosure by banks of their credit concentrations particularly to connected parties. These new rules expand considerably on long-standing limits by requiring measurement and reporting on a consolidated basis. Role of Compliance System and Compliance Officers Strengthening bank governance also calls for improved standards on accountability. In line with this, we have required banks to establish a compliance system that is intended to ensure a bank's identification of relevant laws and regulations, analysis of risks of non-compliance and prioritization of compliance risks. We are presently looking into a proposal to further rationalize the compliance system on the basis of recent recommendations made by the Basle committee. Basically, the proposal concerns the compliance function and how it can be duly upgraded to conform to corporate governance best practice. Conclusion All of the above corporate governance initiatives form an integral part of the BSP's broader banking reform agenda that aims to strengthen the financial sector and reduce overall vulnerability. As the supervisor of the banking system, the main challenge for us at BSP lies in ensuring the basic safety and soundness of banks. In response to this challenge, we fully intend to be an active proponent of better corporate governance. Building a culture of corporate governance at the institution level can help create a stronger and more effective financial intermediation. In time, this can lead to an environment that is conducive to sustained growth and economic stability. (Note: High-Level Working Meeting on the Corporate Governance of Banks, May 13, 2004, The Guildhall, London)

Title: Opening Remarks
Occasion: Course of Financial Programming and Policies
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Henri Ghesquiere, Director of the IMF-Singapore Regional Training Institute (IMF-STI), the professional staff of the IMF-STI- Mr. Rajan Govil, Mr. Anthony Makin and Mr. Neil Saker, the IMF Resident Representative to the Philippines, Mr. Vikram Haksar, deputy governors, colleagues in government, co-workers at the Bangko Sentral, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.
