The Bureau of Customs has also been a proactive innovator in this area as it moves to fully convert to electronic collection of duties at all ports of entry. The SEC has likewise embarked on an electronic corporate registration process linked to a local bank electronic platform. Other government agencies are likewise moving in this direction to collect fees. Sixth, we note an innovative local project to allow small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to potentially benefit from e-banking by creating electronic documents to speed-up the factoring of SME receivables thus increasing access to credit and lowering financing costs. I'm sure there are many more but I've just noted those that are especially interesting. For our part, in addition to our regulatory role, we are directly supporting the healthy growth of e-banking in the Philippines through the provision of a major payment infrastructure through the creation of PhilPaSS. This is our local version of a Real Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS) for large value interbank payments. It is vital for reducing settlement risk that can have potential systemic risk for the financial system. Already, PhilPaSS has linked with the ROSS system to achieve greater safety in settlement of government securities. ATM switches are also linking up with PhilPaSS to allow settlement of net claims of banks against each other. Likewise, it has become the basis for payment versus payment (PVP) settlement of foreign exchange transactions. Conclusion At this point, let me conclude by saying that e-banking is providing a major driving force for change in the local banking industry. It challenges our banking institutions to rethink the old ways of doing business. Equally, it challenges us, as regulator, to adopt new approaches in order to keep pace with market developments without being an obstacle to progress. Before I get carried away any further, let me again thank HSBC for the invitation. Accept my heartfelt congratulation for the successful launching of your guide to treasury and cash management in Asia-Pacific 2004 and the introduction of HSBCNet. Thank you and good afternoon. (Note: Launching of HSBC's Guide to Cash and Treasury Management in Asia Pacific (2004 edition), February 17, 2004, Makati Shangri-la Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Press Conference on the 4th Qtr 2003 BSP Inflation Report
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Good morning, everyone. Transparency is a hallmark of good monetary policy, and for this reason the BSP continually strives to bring across its policy message to the public and present its view of the future inflation environment. This is the main reason why we publish a quarterly inflation report, and we would like to thank everyone here for joining us at this morning's presentation. Among other things, the presentation by MD Guinigundo will show that the BSP's expected path for inflation continues to be favorable. Inflation should see a moderate increase in 2004-2005 as GDP growth strengthens, aggregate demand conditions improve, and cost-side adjustments exert their influence on consumer prices. Average headline inflation is expected to remain broadly in line with the Government's target of 4-5 percent for both 2004 and 2005. In the meantime, the stance of monetary policy will continue to emphasize prudence in responding to the changes in the outlook for inflation and output growth, keeping always in mind the potential risks to the future path of inflation. Let me end by saying that the BSP remains strongly committed to good monetary policymaking. This includes ensuring our accountability, which we try to do by formally submitting ourselves to public judgment on the basis of the Government's inflation targets. It also implies making sure that the stance of monetary policy is properly communicated by means of a comprehensive, well-organized and lucidly written document such as the inflation report. We therefore welcome your feedback on the contents of the report and hope that you will continue to support the BSP's efforts in communicating its monetary policy strategy to the public. Thank you and good morning. (Note: Press Conference on the 4th Qtr 2003 BSP Inflation Report, January 30, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Launching of the Second Citibank Microentrepreneur of the Year Award
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen! Welcome to the Executive Business Center of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. I am pleased and honored to join you this morning in launching the second Citibank microentrepreneur of the year award. Today we officially begin the search for remarkable individuals who, with the support of microfinance institutions, were able to liberate themselves from the clutches of poverty and became successful in their own right. At the outset, I would like to commend Citibank and the Microfinance Council of the Philippines for their strong advocacy for microfinance. This award that you are collaborating on is certain to stimulate the progress of microfinance in the country. By recognizing successful micro-entrepreneurs, you are encouraging the growth of microenterprises which, if properly motivated and managed, can serve as the driving force to invigorate local economies. This will definitely help boost our efforts to fight poverty in the country. With the success of the first Microentrepreneur of the Year Award, we now face the challenge of making this year's search even better in terms of putting together the selection criteria and refining the guidelines to benefit a larger segment of the microfinance industry. I call on all microfinance practitioners here - representatives from the banking sector, cooperatives, non-government organizations - to help us in drawing up a list of possible awardees for this year's search. I urge you to submit the names of your microfinance clients whom you believe embody the core values espoused by microfinance, namely, ingenuity, patience, hard work, honesty, responsibility, among others. With a broader selection base, we can give due credit to deserving microentrepreneurs. I am positive that there are many more unsung heroes out there who reinforce our belief that microfinance can indeed be a powerful tool in improving one's quality of life. Their success as microentrepreneurs is also your success. As microfinance service providers, you are in a key position to help bring about change in the lives of your clients. With your continued support, the entrepreneurial poor can have access to capital which they can use to help put up a small business and increase their income. This way, the poor can truly rise above their difficulties and lead better, more productive lives. At Bangko Sentral, microfinance is, and will continue to be, our humble share in the nationwide campaign against poverty. Where are we now in our microfinance agenda? As far as the banking sector is concerned, we have made substantial progress in pushing for microfinance initiatives. For the record, close to half a million borrowers have been granted loans by the banking sector. As of 30 October 2003, we have a total of 122 banks engaged in microfinance activity. So far, these banks which consist of 2 microfinance-oriented thrift banks, 3 microfinance-oriented rural banks and 117 rural and cooperative rural banks with some level of microfinance operations were able to give out microfinance loans amounting to P2.5 billion to 432,475 borrowers. While these numbers are encouraging, we, at Bangko Sentral, are bent on surpassing them as we go along in our initiatives to encourage the establishment of more microfinance-oriented banks and the setting up of microfinance operations of existing banks. We have gone full force in pursuing our three-part microfinance program that is essentially geared towards: (1) creating an enabling policy and regulatory environment for sustainable microfinance, (2) enhancing training and capacity building within BSP and the banking sector; and (3) actively taking part in promotion and advocacy. We are currently working on establishing a credible and comprehensive credit bureau model in the country. A credit bureau will ensure the presence of a more transparent information system and lead to an improved credit process. It will also serve to prevent high incidences of credit pollution where one client borrows from multiple institutions. The BSP has also launched a regional advocacy program in 2003 in keeping with our promotion and advocacy agenda. Our goal is to conduct microfinance seminars in strategic regions in the country where we hope to entice potential practitioners. So far, our regional information seminars have brought us to 8 regions across the country. This year we hope to reach more potential microfinance practitioners, as well as institutional partners for existing microfinance institutions. It is heartening to know that we are not alone in this endeavor. We need all the support we can get if we really want to move forward and see more productive results in our fight against poverty. This Citibank project will go a long way in creating role models for microfinance institutions and client entrepreneurs among the very poor. Let us work hand in hand in fighting poverty so that we may achieve progress as a nation. Thank you. (Note: Launching of the Second Citibank Microentrepreneur of the Year Award, Citigroup & Microfinance Council of the Philippines, January 28, 2004, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Annual Reception for the Banking Community Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Good evening ladies & gentlemen. Happy new year to all of you. It has been the tradition at the Bangko Sentral to gather its friends at the beginning of the year to greet each and everyone and to extend our thanks for their cooperation and understanding in the year that passed. It is no different tonight - except that we have a lot to thank for. Your unwavering support for the institution of Bangko Sentral and for me personally has been deeply felt and greatly appreciated. On behalf of the Monetary Board and all of our co-workers at the Bangko Sentral, thank you very much indeed! I need not disrupt the camaraderie we are enjoying this evening, so I shall be brief and to the point. 2003 was a challenging year for all of us. Just consider the following events that took place: The war in Iraq, where hostilities are still raging Remember SARS and how serious its effects were We still see clips of the massive destruction and suffering caused by the earthquake in Iran Closer to home, we recently had the landslides in Leyte and surrounding areas Remember the "pyramiding scams" pursued by the AMLC and other agencies of government Then the Oakwood incident! Who among you did not cringe when two international rating agencies downgraded the credit of the country? Remember how surprised we were when the Governor of the Bangko Sentral was suspended by the Court of Appeals! How about the country's chief justice of the supreme court being impeached! And the recent resignation of the Secretary of Finance whose parting words were "We are in a fiscal crisis"! Despite the backdrop of the foregoing grim events, the economy managed to perform creditably with positive results. GDP for the year will likely meet our target; propped up by domestic consumption, pick-up in agriculture and I.T. sector, increase in call centers, and recovery in the banking sector. Inflation of just over 3% versus target of 4.5% to 5.5%, a remarkable feat in our economic history Interest rate averaging 6.264% for the 91-day T-bill versus target of 9.5% to 10.5% target, a major accomplishment FX volatility at 4.2%, lowest in 6 years Ability to settle foreign exchange debts, the record amount of maturity during the year, and still able to pre-fund some for future servicing and Fiscal performance better than target. This year we anticipate the monetary and banking policies to be neutral to cautious in stance, have focus on strengthening the banking system, enhance corporate governance, promote the development of capital market, enhance risk management, and be supportive of micro-finance activities. 2004 is an election year, and the political noise is already upon us. Recognizing this as a factor to be considered, the Bangko Sentral shall continue to maintain and implement the mandates given to it by the constitution and the statutes. Bangko Sentral shall keep that same spirit in doing its job despite what transpires around us. Lastly, let me mention that the results of our working together in the past year were given international recognition through the awards given to me as Governor. I am proud of them, our trophies. I am more deeply touched however by the continuing trust and confidence in my own person that you have expressed during the period I was the object of a vile accusation that led to my suspension. Your faith in me continues to inspire me to move on. By the way, the suspension is under appeal. And so, we can now say, we are ready to face 2004. Handa na po tayong lahat! Thank you and good evening to all. (Note: Annual Reception for the Banking Community, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, January 7, 2004, Fort San Antonio Abad, BSP Complex)

Title: Christmas Message
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Good afternoon, fellow workers at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. Maligayang pasko po sa inyong lahat...Pwede po bang itanong...Maligaya po ba ang pasko natin? I must say that 2003 has been an exciting roller coaster kind of year for our country and for BSP, this is one year characterized by ups and down we could not have anticipated. Through all these, there was one clear thing that emerged: The unity of purpose that binds BSPers is the one thing that kept us going! In the end, the upside prevailed....Today, accolades and recognition from respected local and international institutions remain a trademark of BSP and its people. These recognition for excellence did not come easy; Together, we planned and worked hard for it. And because we remained focused and united, we successfully delivered on our mandate: We kept prices stable and the banking system generally healthy. Let us therefore give all BSPers a round of applause! But a word of caution....Next year is bound to be tougher....With all the political noise that gets louder by the day and an increasingly competitive global economic environment. More than ever, therefore, we should not be distracted...We should remain focused on serving our country by remaining true to our mandate...and by committing to do better every day. I can tell you that given the challenges ahead, the members of the Monetary Board are confident BSPers will again rise up to the occasion and deliver on its mandate...for we are united....we are committed...and we are prepared. We have crafted our mission and vision statements. We have identified the critical areas that we need to work on to further streamline our operations. We have laid down the BSP blueprint which will guide us in the years ahead. And we continue to build and upgrade our infrastructure to provide a positive working environment for our people. As you all know, we now have an ISO-Certified Security Plant Complex, a world-class Employees' Dining Hall and Executive Business Center, and pretty soon, all of us can enjoy good coffee and light snacks at our Bridgeway Café. You will be happy to know that the Bridgeway Café and our new Executive Dining Room at the third floor will be inaugurated next week and should be ready for regular operation by mid-January. Yes, many good things came our way in 2003 and many more should come our way in 2004. The Christmas season is the perfect time for counting our blessings and sharing our happiness with our co-workers. But while we celebrate and enjoy our good fortune, let us not forget the less fortunate who need our help. There are many ways within and outside BSP through which we can extend a helping hand to others. Let us do so with a happy heart and open hands. In the meantime, as Assistant Governor Nesting Espenilla said, the Christmas Party Committee prepared an exciting program for all of us....so let's go on and enjoy our party. Again, on behalf of the members of the Monetary Board, a merry Christmas to all of you!! (Note: BSP Christmas Program, December 18, 2003, PICC)

Title: Payment Systems Reforms and Anti-Money Laundering Initiatives
Occasion: Induction of Officers, Clearing Officers Club, Inc.
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Jorge B. Dungo, Mr. Rolando S. Rojas, the COCI Board of Trustees and members of the Clearing Officers Club, Inc.. Good afternoon. I am honored and pleased to be with you on this special day, on the occasion of the induction of the officers and trustees of the COCI. Our institutions, the Bangko Sentral ng pilipinas (BSP) and the COCI are bound by a common objective, that is to promote a healthy and vibrant financial system. The importance of the role of the club in ensuring and maintaining an efficient financial system cannot be over-emphasized. You play a very critical role in promoting the safety and efficiency of our strategically vital check payment system, our workhorse payment system today. One only has to look at the high volume of checks that passes thru the clearing house daily. But down the road, there are still many challenges in payments system reform as our economy's needs expand and as payments innovations come in. In 2002, we have taken a major stride down that road when we rolled out the PhilPaSS, our real time gross settlement system for large value payments among banks. More recently, a payment versus payment system was launched to support the efficient settlement of peso-dollar exchange transactions. Coming up is the establishment of a modern debt securities, clearing and settlement system in connection with the expected launching mid-next year of the fixed income exchange. No less exciting are the innovations in retail payments systems especially in the area of electronic payments. These include things like more innovative uses of credited debit cards in conjunction with the internet, payment postal services, expanded usage of ATMs, and the use of mobile phones in payments transactions. Admittedly, we are still at infancy in use of these payments alternatives but the trends are unmistakable. Worldwide, use of paper checks is on the decline against other forms of non-cash payments and even checks are being converted to electronic documents at a much earlier stage through arrangements like check truncation. In line with the innovations in payments systems, our legal framework will need to be upgraded particularly in terms of how we handle issues of enforceability of transactions, finality, bankruptcy, and security arrangements. This should form part of the priority legislative agenda of the next congress. The COCI can play a role in guiding us through an evolutionary process as we smoothly transform from current dominant payments arrangements. Your collective experience will help promote an orderly change. Apart from payments systems reform, i would like also to update you on the anti-money laundering issue which is our common concern. As you are all aware, our country is still in the list of non-cooperative countries and territories or NCCT by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), an agency created a decade ago by the G7 economic powers to coordinate international efforts to combat money laundering. Inclusion on the NCCT list means we run the risk of being the subject of adverse advisories which will signal to international banks and other financial institutions to take caution when handling any Philippine-based transactions. This will not only render more inefficient and costly our international payments including remittances, it will also likely discourage foreign parties from investing or doing business in the Philippines. The stakes are clearly very high for our country. In spite of the enactment of Republic Act No. 9160 (The Anti-Money Laundering act), as amended by Republic Act No. 9194, the Philippines still remains in the non-cooperative category. Just to give you an idea, the most notable amendments of R.A. No. 9160 are (1) the lowering of the threshold amount for covered transactions from P4.0 million to P500 thousand and the grant of authority to BSP to inquire into or examine any deposit or investment with any banking institution or non-bank financial institution in the course of the regular or special examination of the concerned institution to ensure compliance with said law. We have yet to convince the international community that our law meets all the established standards in the fight against money laundering. On the part of our depositors, the Anti-Money Laundering Law should not cause them any apprehension. They are still protected under Republic Act No. 1405 (The Bank Deposit Secrecy Law), as amended. Likewise, R.A. 9160, as amended, provides adequate safeguards to protect depositors and investors. While banks and all covered institutions are required to report suspicious transactions, this however, does not give them the liberty to make malicious reports because the law also prescribes penalties for malicious reporting. In summary, we can say that Republic Act No. 9160, as amended, has laid down the legal framework for a strong anti-money laundering program. We believe that this is already sufficient justification for removing our country from the list of non-cooperative countries. We expect that the Philippines will soon be removed from said list. But we should not be complacent. Just like money launderers who continue to explore new means to commit and cover their crimes, we should continue to vigorously fight money launderers. The Bangko Sentral and the SEC, in close coordination with AMLC, are presently evaluating the possibility of placing large-scale money changers and other non-bank remittance entities under appropriate regulatory cover. This may include a tighter licensing and monitoring of these enterprises to reduce the risk of these being made conduits for the flow of laundered funds. As in all endeavors, the campaign against money laundering should be a joint effort of the government and the private sector. In this regard, I strongly encourage your association to help us improve our arrangements for effectively stopping money laundering activity. Before I get carried away any further, let me again congratulate the newly elected officers and trustees of the Clearing Officers Club. Let us join forces both in promoting payments system reform and in fighting money laundering. Thank you and merry Christmas to all. (Note: Induction of Officers, Clearing Officers Club, Inc., December 15, 2003, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Coming Home to Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Occasion: Luncheon Program for July 2002 - June 2003 BSP Retirees
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Magandang hapon po sa inyong lahat. Clearly this is a happy occasion for all of us. Alam po ninyo, as Monetary Board Member Nonoy Alindogan, Deputy Governor Andy Suratos, AssistantGovernor Marc Siongco and I were distributing the plaques of appreciation, the one thing that was so obvious were the big smiles of our honorees today: our retirees. Onstage, their happiness is quite contagious! On this basis, I consider this program in honor of our retirees a success. I therefore congratulate Governor Andy Suratos, Director Dong Asperilla and the HR Department for this well-organized program. Palakpakan po natin sila. Our intention in hosting this lunch is to honor and thank our retirees for their dedication and loyalty to Bangko Sentral. So, I am glad to see that they are pleased with our program. On the other hand, it is possible that our honorees are simply happy to see us again.... and happier still to be back here at Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. Tanungin natin ang ating mga retirees: Are you happy to be back at BSP? Well, if you are happy coming home to BSP, you are welcome to come and visit.... anytime you miss us. As you know, BSP retirees even have their own office here at the 11th floor of the multi-storey building. This is just one way of making sure you stay connected to Bangko Sentral. As in a relay, while the retirees may have passed on the torch to us....we need you to watch and cheer us on....as we continue to face the many challenges ahead. The mandate of Bangko Sentral is clear: To ensure stable prices and a stable banking sector. And with the new BSP mission and vision statement, we have identified the values of integrity, excellence and patriotism as our guiding principles in crafting our roadmap toward providing a better life for Filipinos. How do we measure up against our mandate? You will be happy to know that BSP is doing quite well. We have been successful in keeping prices stable at low levels and the banking sector stable. Of course, in this imperfect world, others will still find fault in BSP. This is where you, the retirees, can help us. As you know by now, it is not enough that we do the right thing; other people must know and understand why we do the things we do. So please, within your family and circle of friends, help people understand BSP and its policies; for only when people understand can Bangko Sentral count on their support. I also wish to tell you that Bangko Sentral is launching a national economic and financial literacy campaign starting next year that should also keep the public aware of economic opportunities available to them while keeping clear of scam artists who victimize people of their hard-earned money. And so, beyond merely keeping in touch, I hope retirees will be part of our economic and financial literacy campaign. Looking at the profile of the retirees here with us today, I saw that two ladies hold the record of having the longest service years: Leonida Alvis of DLC and Fe Calaycay of SRSO. Each of them served BSP for 42 years! Palakpakan po natin sila. On the other hand, the distinction of being the youngest, in terms of service years, surprisingly belongs to.....Dr. Romeo Gavino who served BSP for 17 years. Palakpakan din po natin siya. From what I hear, there is one person among you who is well-loved, not because of his position, but because he really and truly exemplified the best of what a BSPer can aspire to be: I am referring of course to Assistant Governor Andy Rustia. Palakpakan po natin siya! Once again, let us give all our retirees a warm round of applause. I know that all of you deserve your retirement. However, retirement is not a finish line. Like BSP, you must constantly reinvent yourself to adapt to a changing environment. You have harnessed your talent in the service of BSP and the country; in the process you have provided for your family. Now, it is time to set new goals you should aspire for. Always, it is fulfilling to support a cause larger than yourself. Continue to share the knowledge and wisdom you have accumulated over the years. So I enjoin all of you to continue serving not only your family but also your community....our country. On behalf of the Monetary Board and our co-workers at Bangko Sentral, I wish you all a meaningful and joyful Christmas as well as a healthy and prosperous 2004! Marami pong salamat. (Note: Luncheon Program for July 2002 - June 2003 BSP Retirees, December 03, 2003, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Regional Initiatives in Developing the Regional Bond Market
Occasion: "Asia Pacific Political Risk, Project Finance and Export Credit Summary 2003", Asian Development Ban
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Secretary Jose Isidro Camacho, guests, colleagues in the financial industry, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. I am pleased to take this opportunity to assess with you some of the important initiatives in mobilizing long-term capital in the Asian region, notably the creation of a regional market for debt instruments. The necessity of developing the Asian bond market The Asian region has recovered relatively swiftly since the financial meltdown experienced starting 1997. The resulting improvement in macroeconomic performance and the mechanisms for regional cooperation that were either established or strengthened during the recovery phase bolstered the pursuit of joint economic initiatives among the countries in the region. One of the recent joint initiatives by Asian economies is the development of a regional bond market. Pursuing this would require drawing several lessons from the experience during the financial crisis of 1997-1998. The first lesson is the need to avoid the "double mismatch" problem namely, currency and maturity mismatches. The second lesson is the need to reduce the corporate sector's over-reliance on the banking sector for funding its projects. To address these concerns, the monetary authorities in the region are working towards the upgrading of their individual bond markets and the development of an Asian bond market. A well-developed Asian bond market will enable the efficient utilization of savings within the region by serving as a channel through which available long-term savings are matched with long-term investment needs. It will help mitigate maturity and currency mismatches as fund users are allowed to borrow in their own currencies and channel long-term funds into carefully chosen projects. The development of a regional capital market will also promote the preservation of foreign capital and savings in the region. This will help stabilize capital flows and thus avoid a repeat of the 1997 Asian crisis. A two-pronged approach in developing the regional bond market Beyond words, the authorities in the region are now pursuing a wide range of initiatives to develop the regional bond market. These efforts are being undertaken on two fronts. At the local level, national authorities are undertaking measures to accelerate the development of their own domestic bond markets. At the regional level, a region-wide bond market is being developed. It is envisioned that well-developed local bond markets will eventually form the nucleus of this pan-Asian bond market. Development of local bond markets An increasing number of east Asian countries have been giving the development of their own capital bond markets a high priority in their reform programs. Some countries began by addressing the major impediments in the development of their bond markets. Their efforts are focused on areas such as creating a benchmark reference rate and improving market infrastructure. In the Philippines, we are undertaking a host of measures to strengthen the local bond market in preparation for the establishment of a regional bond market. For example, the market infrastructure has been upgraded with the launching of a real time gross payment settlement (RTGS) system known as the Philippine Payment System or PhilPaSS in December 2002. The PhilPaSS is intended to cover transactions in the equities, fixed income, money and foreign exchange markets. The upgrading of our payment and settlement system is expected to minimize settlement risk and thereby allow primary and secondary markets to function more effectively. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) has also been supporting the establishment of the Fixed Income Exchange (FIE) that is tentatively scheduled to begin operations in the second quarter of 2004. This exchange will provide the platform for the secondary trading of private and public fixed-income securities such as government securities, commercial papers and asset-backed securities issued by companies. The Philippines is also working towards an investment-friendly tax environment. The BSP has been supporting the removal of the Documentary Stamp Tax (DST) on the secondary trading of financial instruments. The DST increases the cost of financial intermediation and thus discourages the secondary trading of securities. A bill for its removal is now pending in congress. The government has also issued 2-, 3-, 4-, 5-, 7-,10-, 20- and 25-year fixed rate treasury bond/notes over the past decade.This has resulted in a longer-yield curve for the public sector debt, providing the needed variety and various degrees of liquidity in the market. The BSP recently approved the application of a preferential reserve requirement of 2 percent on Repo transactions of banks. This move will help reduce transaction costs and is expected to spur more activity in the secondary market for government securities. At the same time, the Philippine government has been pursuing measures to deepen the asset securitization market. The BSP is supporting the enactment of the Securitization Bill, which will set the legal and regulatory framework for securitization in the Philippines. Another important element in developing the bond market is the presence of a strong credit rating system. The mandatory rating requirement for all bond issues instituted by the Philippine government is expected to help in the assessment and pricing of risks and increase transparency for all bond issues. It should also induce demand for ratings services, making it a more profitable venture. To ensure that the quality of ratings and that the reliance of regulators as well as industry players on credit ratings are well placed, the monetary board of the BSP recently approved the rules and regulations that will govern the recognition and derecognition of domestic credit rating agencies for bank supervisory purposes. The regulation prescribes minimum eligibility criteria, which include, among others, objectivity, independence, transparency, credibility, and compliance with internal procedures and certain disclosure requirements. At the same time it requires that credit rating agencies should have the financial capability to invest in the necessary technological infrastructure and employ sufficient professional analytical staff and thus ensure the proper discharge of their duties and responsibilities. Development of an Asian bond market On a regional basis, simultaneous efforts are being undertaken on two fronts--the demand and supply sides. On the demand side, the Executives Meeting of east Asia-Pacific Central Banks (EMEAP) created the Asian Bond Fund (ABF) initiative. In June 2003, the EMEAP-member countries launched the US$1 billion Asian Bond Fund for investment on dollar-denominated Asian Bonds (ABF1). Currently, EMEAP is studying the extension of the ABFto a fund for local- currency denominated Asian bonds or the ABF2. This initiative is expected to serve as catalyst for private investors to consider investment in Asian issues. On the supply side, the ASEAN+3 and Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Finance Ministers' Meeting (APEC FMM) are addressing issues relating to, among other things, the issuance of new debt instruments, bond rating and enhancements and infrastructure improvements. Meanwhile, the Asian Cooperation Dialogue (ACD) has been providing technical support and helping in the dissemination process to gather critical political support. To deepen the regional bond market, there are initiatives to encourage the issuance of more sovereign bonds to improve liquidity in government bond markets and help establish benchmarks. Moreover, the floating of asset─backed securities linked to loan packages of banks or receivables by corporations is also being studied to widen the variety of instruments available in the market. Fair credit ratings are a key element for an active regional bond market. To improve the quality of credit ratings in Asia, an Asian Credit Ratings Board (ACRB) is being proposed, under the ASEAN+3 framework, to provide training to local rating agencies and collect regional data to ensure/improve the consistency and accuracy of ratings. The ACRB is not intended to replace international rating agencies but is expected to complement their presence in Asia. The other aspects of an efficient market infrastructure are work in progress. One, bond settlement systems in individual countries should be improved to strengthen cross-border settlement mechanisms within the region. Second, the use of securitization and enhancements such as guarantees is being explored to reduce the difference in risk appetite of borrowers and credit ratings of issuers. Finally, efforts are also directed in narrowing the cross-country differences in the rules and regulations relating to bond transactions in the region. Differences in market regulations, documentary requirements and taxation, among others, translate into additional cost in doing cross-country investments. Conclusion Let me conclude by saying that the authorities in the Asian region are pursuing a comprehensive approach to the development--at both the local and regional levels--of Asian bond markets. Such initiatives are expected to benefit investors and market participants. In particular, the development of the regional bond market is a long-term endeavor and requires the active participation of the private sector. In fact, we have been receiving valuable inputs from private financial institutions and multilateral organizations on almost all fronts of institution and capacity building critical to developing an efficient regional bond market. We continue to count on their support in the future to transform this vision into a reality. Short of this, the Asian region will always be at the receiving end of the adverse shifts in the short-term funds from the banking system. Thank you. (Note: "Asia Pacific Political Risk, Project Finance and Export Credit Summit 2003, Asian Development Bank, November 03, 2003, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Signing of the Agreement on the Payment versus Payment System for the USD-Peso Foreign Exchange
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Ladies and gentlemen, it is a pleasure to welcome all of you to the signing of the agreement on the Payment Versus Payment System for USD-Peso Foreign Exchange Transactions. In the past decade, the Philippine payments and settlement infrastructure has undergone tremendous change and improvement as we endeavored to keep pace with the ever-growing technological developments in the international financial markets. Moreover, the growing sophistication of the markets make the need to address the various risks involved in the settlement aspect of trading very evident. Thus, the evolution of our payments and settlement system from a purely paper-based setting to an electronic environment was inevitable. Currently, with the Bureau of Treasury's Registry of Scripless Securities (ROSS) and the BSP's PhilPaSS, government securities transactions and interbank deals are now settled by electronic means. The automation of these two settlement systems has served to make banks' trading activities more efficient and mitigate risks that our institutions are exposed to in the conduct of our operations. Today, we take another step in aligning our payments and settlement system with those of other countries as we enter into the agreement that will formally set in place the payment versus payment system. In putting together this undertaking, we have been guided by the international best practices as classified by the Bank for International Settlements. It is our goal that the realization of this project will diminish settlement risks inherent to USD-Peso transactions, which in turn will encourage greater trading activity, enhance market liquidity and encourage growth in the financial sector. Our nation, along with the rest of the global community, is facing challenging times and it is important that we, in the financial sector, do what we can to encourage the economy to grow. At this point, I would like to encourage everyone to be actively involved in this undertaking. Out of the 42 member banks of the Bankers association of the Philippines, 39 have already tendered their applications for access to the system. However, only 24 banks are actually using the system. Let's not be shy about being part of this enterprise. We must keep in mind that it is not enough to create and maintain an efficient electronic payments and settlements system. The real challenge lies in continuously improving the said system in order to keep abreast with the developments in the global community and to address the growing and changing needs of the consumers. Here's looking forward to more successful ventures as we continuously work to strengthen our financial system. Thank you and I wish everyone a good morning. (Note: Signing of the Agreement on the Payment versus Payment System for USD-Peso Foreign Exchange Transactions, November 25, 2003, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Strengthening Risk Management in Philippine Banking
Occasion: Inaugural Meeting Professional Risk Managers International Association (PRMIA)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It is a great pleasure and honor for me to speak at this inaugural meeting in the Philippines of the professional risk managers' international association (or PRMIA). PRMIA comes to the Philippines at a most opportune time when we are deeply engaged in reforming the Philippine banking system. Its advocacy for the promotion of sound risk management standards and practices globally is something that we strongly believe in. We therefore welcome PRMIA Philippines as a natural partner and ally in upgrading Philippine banking standards to match the best in the world at least in terms of optimizing the delicate balance between prudence, efficiency and effectiveness. The impetus for reform The business of banking and finance has changed dramatically especially in the last decade in the face of deregulation, rapid advances in information and communications technology, and constant innovation in financial technology. These have greatly expanded the opportunities not only for financial institutions but for economies as a whole. But progress has come at the price of increased complexity that has had implications for the proper monitoring and management of risks. The genie is now out of the bottle. As a bank regulator, our job is not to seal it back in again, but rather make it work for the greatest common good while minimizing potentially destabilizing excesses. Indeed, this changed agenda has preoccupied the international banking regulator community and directly led to the original Basel Accord in 1988 prescribing risk-based capital norms. But because the process of innovation has been very dynamic, the original accord has had to be periodically updated. Even now, Basle ii is being finalized to make the framework even more risk-sensitive. We have closely monitored all of these developments. However, it took the enactment of the revised general banking act in 2000 to finally give us the clear legal basis to adopt the evolving risk based capital standards. On July 1, 2001, BSP circular no. 280 came into force, formally bringing the Philippine banking system into Basle I world. On July 1, 2003, the market risk component of the revised Basle I, took effect under BSP circular no. 360. These two circulars have significantly elevated the risk management consciousness of the local banking community. But by no means these were the only ones issued in the last three years designed to strengthen the quality of risk management. The lessons of the 1997 Asian financial crisis were also an important driver for reform. Its painful consequences, still being felt today, have concretely illustrated to all market players and regulators the impact of benign neglect of risk management especially during the heady days of economic boom. Mr. Andrew Crockett, the former General Manager of the BIS and Chairman of the Financial Stability Forum, was clearly on the mark when he observed that "...indicators of risk tend to decline during upswings and to be lowest at, or close to, the peak of the financial cycle, i.e. just at the point where, with hindsight, we can see that risk was greatest. And yet, there is a sense in which risk increases during upswings, as financial imbalances build up, and materializes in recessions...". The region has of course now seen the materialization of that risk. It should be a powerful motivation for all of us to step up the upgrading of our risk management standards and practices. If we fail to learn from history, then we are doomed to relive it. Corporate governance reform The BSP is deeply committed to strengthen the quality of risk management in Philippine banking as a fundamental element of a wide-ranging banking reform agenda. We are starting from the most basic building block, promoting sound internal corporate governance in banking institutions, under the leadership of an active and competent board of directors. We have seen far too many cases of banks getting into trouble where the root cause can be traced to lack of board oversight. It is essential that the board of directors provide the moderating counter-weight against excessive risk-taking in order to maximize the long-term value of their institution. In this regard, we have focused on two main iniatives: (1) ensuring fit and proper directors and officers and (2) clearly defining the duties and responsibilities of the board and its directors as individuals. Following this approach, among others, we have in place a mandatory director exposure program designed to sensitize directors to good corporate governance principles and practices in general and the concepts of sound risk management oversight in particular. We strongly believe that it is essential to build an effective internal constituency for risk management. Without meaningful board level appreciation of risk management, the whole exercise will just become a compliance issue, an annoying cost of doing business to be minimized, rather than a core element of strategy for the banking organization to achieve its goals. Capacity building Commitment needs capacity to achieve results. We acknowledge that the concept of risk management is intuitive but its effective practice requires high level technical skills that need to be nurtured and reinforced so that risk professionals will have the necessary credibility to restore the proper balance in the risk versus return equation. The training of risk management professionals, both market practitioners and their regulators, is a top priority. For the BSP, as bank regulator, training is necessitated by our shift to risk-based approach to bank supervision and our commitment to align our domestic standards with international banking standards notably the Basle principles. The demands for effective implementation of anti-money laundering programs, a critical operational risk area, have further underscored the need for training. We have adopted a collaborative approach with the private sector in seeking to mutually build up and reinforce our skill sets. For example, we have been closely working with the industry to develop risk management manuals and operating conventions firmly grounded on international best practices while being attuned to domestic operating considerations. These subsequently form the basis for joint training so that we can more rapidly elevate risk management practice. The training approach will benefit from a credible skill certification process that can validate the acquisition of knowledge and the acceptance of the proper ethical standards. In this regard, we would expect all risk professionals in the Philippine banking industry to eventually obtain certification as professional risk managers under the PRMIA program or other equivalent programs. In addition to training, the BSP is prioritizing the establishment of institutions that enhance the capacity for risk management. This is actually an all-encompassing agenda that includes capital market reform initiatives such as support for the establishment by the private sector of an electronic fixed income exchange and related securities clearing and settlement systems. It also includes enhancements of the payments systems such as implementation of RTGS for large value payments. We also advocate for legislations that rationalize the tax structure, that allow the introduction of a greater variety of financial instruments as well as that set up transparent rules for the conduct of business and the resolution of problem cases. We are also paying attention to the role of reputation agents like external auditors and domestic credit rating agencies. We are pursuing a definite game plan to either encourage the formation of new players or the reform of existing players in this important area to assist us in cleaning up the banking system by activating the compelling force of market discipline. A vital institution that we are nurturing at this stage is the formation of a comprehensive central credit information bureau out of the existing fragmented industry that has not really been that effective in monitoring debtor track record. This is an important project that will help control credit risk not just by providing creditors with timely and relevant information. More importantly, it will help promote a culture of credit responsibility. It will also lead to greater credit access at much more reasonable cost to ordinary borrowers who know how to live up to their commitments. We have a good idea of how we will bring about a central credit information bureau as we have been extensively consulting on this issue for some time now. Our next step is to commission a study to thoroughly work out all of the key legal issues on both the operational aspects as well as consumer protection issues. We hope to have the system in place by next year. The road to Basel II Looking ahead, the forthcoming agreement on Basel II looms large in the consciousness of risk professionals and bank regulators. I am convinced that the Philippines is well on the way to meet its requirements by the time it comes into force around 2006. In a sense, many of the concrete initiatives we are taking today constitute vital preparatory steps towards substantive compliance. But we are not underestimating the complexity of this undertaking that requires the putting together of so many pieces to form the complete picture. No doubt Basel II, once we adopt it here, will have a profound impact on Philippine banking, for the greater good. We should start feeling the positive effects well before 2006 as banks strengthen their risk management processes and improve efficiency. As opportunities for excess returns from excessive risk-taking disappear, banks will have no choice but to maximize their efficiency and innovativeness in order to thrive. This will further drive the streamlining and consolidation of the banking industry. Concluding remarks Let me now conclude. I am greatly excited and encouraged by how the domestic banking industry is constructively responding to the myriad challenges facing the system and our economy. Its evident commitment to upgrade the quality of risk management is a shining example. I strongly urge you to sustain the effort. The value of risk management, to paraphrase former U.S. Fed Reserve Bank Governor Laurence Meyer, is not so much in the profits that are earned but rather lies in the catastrophic costs that are avoided. Thank you and good day (Note: Inaugural Meeting, Professional Risk Managers' International Association (PRMAI), November 21, 2003, Mandarin Oriental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Closing Remarks
Occasion: 9th Conference Series on Good Governance and Responsible Citizenship
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. It is an honor to take part in this 9th conference series on Good Governance and Responsible Citizenship. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has always been a staunch advocate of corporate governance. We strongly believe in the importance of promoting sound corporate governance practices especially in banks. Judging by the theme of this conference, "Bridging Corporate Governance Initiatives in East Asia", and listening to the different speakers, we can see how extensive is the work being done to promote corporate governance. The rallying call seems to be to spread the good news of corporate governance or suffer the consequences. I think we know firsthand the effects of poor governance. The 1997 financial crisis was a vivid reminder. And indeed, many vexing issues that we continue to confront today find their roots in the basic failure of governance practices. As far as the Philippine banking sector is concerned, I am happy to report to you that we have been making steady progress towards building a strong corporate governance regime. Our corporate governance agenda is primarily designed to strengthen our financial institutions. Along this line, we have taken steps to improve standards on transparency, accountability and fairness. A critical aspect of this agenda is the promotion of effective corporate directorship. We have recently concluded our mandatory orientation program for bank directors. Overall, the industry has been quite supportive of this undertaking. I especially commend the directors of universal banks for their one hundred percent attendance. We have also initiated measures to strengthen the accreditation process of independent external auditors. This is being done to uphold high ethical and professional standards in accounting and promote greater transparency through enhanced coordination and sharing of information between external auditors and regulatory authorities. The new guidelines governing the accreditation of external auditors is embodied in BSP Circular No. 410 dated 29 October 2003. Strengthening bank governance also calls for better standards on accountability. In line with this, we have required banks to establish a compliance system that is intended to ensure a bank's identification of relevant laws and regulations, analysis of risks of non-compliance, and prioritization of compliance risks. We are set to improve upon this further in line with recent recommendations of the Basle Committee. We are also set to fully adopt prescribed international accounting standards by 2005. These core initiatives form an integral part of the broader banking reform agenda aimed at strengthening the financial sector and reducing overall vulnerability. Good governance in the banking system cannot be effected by BSP alone. We rely heavily on the support of every bank. It is the quality of good governance at the individual bank level that is deemed crucial to the creation of a strong and effective banking system. At this point, I would like to assure everyone of the BSP's unwavering support and leadership in advancing governance reforms in the country. I commend both the organizers and the participants in this conference for their commitment to pursue governance initiatives. Your work should go a long way in building a strong foundation for corporate governance in East Asia. Thank you very much. (Note: 9th Conference Series on Good Governance and Responsible Citizenship, Institute of Corporate Directors, November 19, 2003, Edsa Shangri-La, Mandaluyong City)

Title: Inspirational Message
Location: Multi-Story Building, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Occasion: Basic Security Training Graduation Ceremony, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Magandang umaga sa inyong lahat. Dumating din ang araw ng inyong pagtatapos sa ikatlong Basic Security Training ng Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. Woody Allen, the famous Hollywood director, said, "50 percent of success is showing up." But I think you will agree with me, especially after you have gone through 60 days of grueling training, that the other 50 percent is in sticking to what you have set out to do and completing it. Congratulations to all our graduates. I especially commend your batch for completing the course without any casualties. Your group remained 40-strong from start to finish. Palakpakan po ninyo ang inyong mga sarili. But this does not make your batch unique; the first batch did the same. What makes your batch unique is that, for the first time, two female guards--Melody and Rubi Rosa--went through the same back-breaking exercises as the males did. Palakpakan po natin silang dalawa. I went through your eight-page course syllabus and I counted around 60 training items, ranging from the familiar orientation on BSP to a class on Dactyloscopy and Poroscopy. I noted that you also had several days devoted to actual range firing. I am confident that you have learned the fundamentals, techniques, and methods involved in the various aspects of security operation such as intelligence, investigation, physical security, and bank security. It has been said, "Chance favors the prepared mind." A significant part of your training focused on preparing you to respond to emergency situations. With your training over, you can now go back to your posts armed with all the theories and techniques you have learned. Half of you will go back to secure and protect our offices in Manila and Quezon City; the other half will do the same in our regional offices and branches. In doing your job of securing BSP's property, employees, and visitors, bear in mind that that is your unique contribution to price and financial stability. Day and night, we can concentrate on doing the work of central banking secure in the knowledge that we have trained security people like you to keep our premises safe.Maaasahan -- kung kaya't inaasahan -- namin kayo. I would also like to congratulate the Security, Investigation, and Transport Department or SITD for successfully conducting this training for the first time. Of course, SITD could not have done it without the cooperation of the BSP Institute, branch operations, and other offices of BSP that sent their experts to assist in the conduct of the training or give lectures on specific topics. Maraming salamat sa inyong lahat. Continuously improving the skills of our security people is an integral part of our effort to become a world-class monetary authority. That is why training programs like this enjoy the support of the Monetary Board. I look forward to an even better Basic Security Training next year. Again, congratulations to all the graduates. Thank you, and good morning. (Note: "Basic Security Training Graduation Ceremony, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, November 14, 2003, Multi-Storey Building, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Testimonial Lunch in honor of Governor Buenaventura hosted by the Bankers Association of the Phils.
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I would like to thank the business community through the four prestigious associations - Bankers Association of the Philippines, FINEX, Makati Business Club, and Management Association of the Philippines for this testimonial lunch. The accomplishments that have been shown and recognized are the results of the great efforts - not only of myself - but also of the Monetary Board and all of my fellow-workers at the Bangko Sentral. Some of them are here - so I would like them to stand up to be recognized for excellent performance. The past three years at the Bangko Sentral have been difficult as well as challenging. That would be an understatement. But they have also been very rewarding. You have been most supportive and I appreciate on behalf of all of us at the Bangko Sentral the continuing confidence and trust you have given us. On a professional level, the experience has given me a broader perspective in understanding the role of the institution as it affects the economy and how it impacts the businesses and lives of our countrymen. On a personal level, it has given me a deeper insight into people. I have become more introspective about the importance of relationships and the meaning of loyal friendship. Especially throughout the tough, rough times. These are moments when we have to make decisions for the greater good, beyond friendship. Rest assured that these decisions are made objectively and in the interest of the country. The international recognition we have received is an honor, unexpected but deeply appreciated by myself and our institution. It is timely that the Philippines is ranked among the top four in the world. And we are proud to share this honor with all of you as you are an important component of the efforts that led to it. It also validates the efforts we have made to provide stability for the economy and strengthen the financial system. Please allow me to give you some of what we in the Bangko Sentral have done during my watch in the past 3 years, 4 months and 8 days. You will note that the countdown began on day one. 1) On the principal mandate of the Bangko Sentral, which is "Price stability conducive to a balanced and sustainable growth of the economy", monetary policies have resulted in the inflation rate going down to record lows. In October it was 2.7% or a year-to-date rate of 3.2%. 2) With lower inflation, the Bangko Sentral has brought down interest rates to 7%, the lowest in over 10 years. The bench-mark 91-day T-bill rate also went down from an average of 8.8% p.a. in the year 2000 to 5.5% p.a. in October this year. 3) The peso value has remained aligned with other currencies and is presently around P53 per US$, down from a high of P55 per US$ in early 2001. 4) The gross international reserves have remained at healthy levels over the last few years and at the end of October stood at US$15.9 billion, equivalent to approximately 5 months' imports of goods and services. Allow me also to mention certain policies adopted and pursued during the last 3 years which to a large extent contributed to the attainment of the foregoing results. 1) At the beginning of 2002, the Monetary Board started to implement the inflation targeting framework which focused and refined the means of controlling inflation. This shift in methodology is proving effective. 2) We have liberalized the rediscounting policy which now permits greater access by the different sectors of the economy, including housing construction and acquisition. 3) Over the past several years, the housing sector has been given regulatory flexibilities. They include the relaxation of "risk weight" as a charge to capital, an increase in loan valuation from 70% to 80% of the real estate collateral, even higher in certain instances, and compliance eligibility to the Agri-agra Law. 4) Policies and regulations have also been adjusted for the small and medium enterprises, and microfinance borrowers. They include access to credit and technical training. 5) Good corporate governance policies and regulations have been in place since 1997 and have now been re-emphasized with the cooperation of and coordination with other government agencies, more specifically the S.E.C., as well as the private sector. 6) Sound monetary policies on interest rates and foreign exchange have contributed to the increasing volume of foreign exchange remittances from OFWs. The estimate now is that these remittances would reach a record high of US$8 billion. Our OFWs are really making valuable contributions to the country's economic development 7) The global thrust in containing money-laundering activities has placed the Bangko Sentral as an important participant in the enforcement of the Anti-Money Laundering Act passed in 2001. The Governor of the Bangko Sentral chairs the Council, which includes the SEC cChairman and the Insurance Commissioner as members, that implements this law. I would like also to mention a few challenges that the Bangko Sentral faces today. 1) In the efforts to strengthen the banking system, the Bangko Sentral has been working with Congress in the enactment of an Asset Management Company law that would ease the burden of non-performing assets of banks. The Bill has now passed both houses of Congress and will be deliberated upon by the Bi-cameral Committee very soon. 2)> As Chairman of the Anti-Money Laundering Council, I have also been engaged in reconciling the very stringent requirements of the FATF with the sentiment of Congress. Several important issues remain, and hopefully the proposed amendments to the AMLA would resolve them. The stakes here are high, as an impasse may keep the Philippines in the FATF list of non-cooperative countries that would be sanctioned. Any sanctions would certainly impact our OFWs in their remittances of foreign exchange into the country. Efforts are being exerted to avert such consequences. Proposed amendments to the Charters of the PDIC and the Bangko Sentral are also in our agenda. These would give more teeth to the enforcement powers and capabilities of both institutions, necessary to keep a healthy and stable banking system. The Bangko Sentral shall likewise be actively participating in the deliberations of important legislative pieces, like those involving tax matters and the capital market development area. These are important tasks ahead of us. We earnestly ask for your continuing cooperation and active support in pursuing the mandates given to us by our statutes. We at the Bangko Sentral are committed to continue to do our best in the most objective, equitable and professional manner. Thank you again and good day. (Note: Testimonial Lunch in honor of Governor Rafael B. Buenaventura, hosted by the Bankers Association of the Philippines, FINEX, Makati Business Club and Management Association of the Philippines, November 13, 2002, Peninsula Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Keeping the Public Trust
Occasion: 103rd Civil Service Anniversary Message delivered during the BSP Flag Raising Ceremony
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Magandang umaga sa inyong lahat. As we mark the 103rd anniversary of Philippine Civil Service, let us take time to pause and reflect on the essence of being a civil servant. We have been told again and again that a public office is a public trust. It is such a truism that it is enshrined in our law. At BSP, we know what trust is all about. It is about integrity, excellence, and patriotism -- the values we at BSP live up to. At a time when political distractions abound, BSP remains focused on its mandate to maintain price and banking stability. And we have good results to show for it: benign inflation and record low interest rates. We have also made a quantum leap in terms of promoting good governance. Specifically, BSP is at the vanguard of ensuring transparency such that even highlights of the Monetary Board meeting on policy rates are regularly released to the public. Thus, BSP almost always receives the honor of being rated as the top-performing government agency. This is a continuing validation that we are not just doing our job...but that we are doing it quite well. For indeed, it is not enough that we accomplish our objectives; it is equally important that we do so with professionalism, excellence, and integrity. And we have...and we continue to do so. Kaya palakpakan po natin ang ating sarili. And reflective of the way we adhere to the values we hold dear...honesty and integrity have names and faces here at BSP. Let me identify some of them. We have Mr. Argie Bacalso, Security Officer II at our Cebu Regional Office, who recovered a snatched cell phone and cash and caused the arrest of the snatcher. We have Mr.Samuel Montilla, Mr. Randy Pinuela, and Mr. Vicente Reya, all Security Officers posted in Cebu, who promptly contained a vehicular fire incident and avoided further damage. We have Ms. Aurora Acazar, Administrative Services Officer III from the Internal Audit Office, who unselfishly contributed to help improve the facilities of one elementary school in Antique. We have Mr. Simon Aganan, Audio-Visual Aids Technician IV from the Corporate Affairs Office, Mr. Beltran Abucayan, Security Officer from the Security, Investigation, and Transport Department, and Mr. Restituto Espiritu from the Office of the Monetary Board, who all returned "lost and found" cash to their owners. Palakpakan po natin silang lahat. By helping others, employees of BSP exemplify the overarching objective of BSP to provide a better life for Filipinos. Indeed, for as long as one out of three Filipinos remains poor, we cannot be complacent. And so, let us continue to work together to alleviate poverty in our country. Isapuso at isagawa po natin ang Civil Service anniversary theme na mag- "Sama-sama...tulong-tulong republika patatagin". I end my message by urging all of you to stand tall as BSP employees; stand tall as civil servants. Mabuhay po tayong lahat!

Title: Closing Remarks
Occasion: 2003 BSP Strategic Planning Conference (Part I)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Almost a year ago, we made an initial attempt to synchronize the planning and budgeting activities of the Bangko Sentral. It was the first conference with a theme highlighting the need to respond to change. And, it was the first planning exercise which involved active participation by top management. It was indeed a milestone in the history of strategic planning in the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. During the past two days, we reached another landmark in our strategic planning process as we tried to blueprint the future of BSP in the next five years. I believe this is the first time in the entire history of the bank that a medium-term plan is formulated. The plans concretized during the pre-planning activities that started in July and the outputs during this two-day planning conference, have certainly moved us closer to our vision. We now have a clearer, more defined picture of BSP five years from now. Yesterday, we discussed our strategic intent as the guardian of price stability. With our goal of achieving long-run price stability, we shall continue to refine our approaches with respect to the framework used for the conduct of monetary policy including the use of monetary policy tools such as credit policy, reserve requirement and open market operations as well as the mechanism that fosters efficiency in the foreign exchange market. Likewise, we shall provide efficient banking services through more effective currency management and branching operations. We discussed earlier today our design for a world-class banking supervision, focusing on our medium-term strategies towards strengthening the banking system of the Philippines. We have outlined four strategic initiatives: (1) further enhancements to the regulatory framework; 2) improvements in supervision technology; (3) promoting corporate governance reform and market discipline; and (4) introducing capital market reform initiatives. While we have drawn the blueprint of a world-class monetary authority by focusing on its core functions, we still need to design the organizational requirements of our planned initiatives. The two-part structure of this year's planning conference is a deliberate move to enhance our strategic planning process. The output in the last two days shall serve as inputs to part two of the conference to be held this October, when we shall deliberate on the organizational requirements of the strategies we have formulated for monetary policy and banking supervision. This new approach will provide ample time to formulate plans and programs in the following areas of organizational capability building: organizational development, human resource, information technology, and physical facilities and infrastructure. The medium-term budget of BSP that will ensure the implementation of all our plans shall likewise be formulated this October. Our planning activity does not stop as we go back to our respective offices. Starting tomorrow, each department and office will need to fine-tune and finalize their respective strategies and action plans according to the strategic intents in monetary policy formulation and banking supervision. During the first part of this conference, the Chairman of our Corporate Monitoring Committee took stock of the accomplishments relative to the commitments made in last year's planning conference. I would like to take this opportunity to commend all the BSP departments and offices responsible for these accomplishments. Thank you for your continued support, for your cooperation in the implementation of our initiatives, and most of all, for your firm dedication to work towards the achievement of the objectives we have set for the year. Your untiring efforts have once again made BSP the most respected government institution in the country. I would also like to commend the technical and administrative arrangements made by the Corporate Planning Office. From a three-man team last year, its personnel complement has since doubled to six. Similarly, its responsibilities have expanded as its mandate continues to evolve. As I thank and congratulate each one of you today for the very enlightening and productive part one of the strategic planning conference, I would like to enjoin your continued cooperation and dedication. When we have concluded part two of the strategic planning conference and completed the blueprint for BSP in the next five years, I would like to think that we have left a legacy that will leave an indelible mark on the institution as a world-class monetary authority. Once again, thank you and congratulations. See you all in Tagaytay this October. (Note: 2003 BSP Strategic Planning Conference (Part I), September 12, 2003, Executive Business Center, BSP)

Title: Opening Remarks
Occasion: 2003 BSP Strategic Planning Conference (Part I)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I. Introduction Our gathering today reminds me of the words of Sun Tzu, a famous Chinese military general. He said "...With careful and detailed planning, one can win; with careless and less detailed planning, one cannot win. How much more certain is defeat if one does not plan at all! From the way planning is done beforehand, we can predict victory or defeat..." Last year, we hammered into place the BSP's vision and mission statements. Guided by our vision to become a world-class monetary authority, we prepared a set of agreements to help us realize this goal. This year, our corporate planning office or CPO set out on an awareness program to make our employees claim ownership of the BSP vision and commit themselves to its pursuit. CPO went to our offices all over the country to cascade the BSP vision and mission statements to all employees and caused the mounting of posters containing the BSP vision and mission statements in all departments and offices. As you very well know by now, the recitation of the vision statement during the weekly flag-raising ceremony has been institutionalized, all the more to remind every BSPer of his commitment. More recently, our vision and mission statements were translated in Filipino "Para mas madaling isapuso". II. Strategic planning Today, we take off from there and plan some more to raise the probability of success in the achievement of our goals. Indeed, I cannot overemphasize the importance of planning and planning well. In the late fifties and sixties, long-range planning was the trend. Long-range planning is generally considered to mean the development of a plan of action to accomplish a goal or set of goals over a period of several years--the major assumption being that current knowledge about future conditions is sufficiently reliable to enable the development of these plans. More recently, however, as a result of a dynamic and changing environment, organizations have shifted to a new mode of planning, popularly known as strategic planning. Strategic planning aims to ensure the organization's ability to successfully respond to environmental changes. More specifically, it helps an organization focus its energy, ensure that members are working toward the same goals, and assess and adjust the organization's directions in response to changed conditions. Strategic planning is, however, just a management tool. It cannot substitute for the exercise of judgment by leadership. The leaders of the organization will ultimately need to sit back, ask and seek answers to the questions: "What are the more important issues to respond to?". And "how should we respond?" It is likewise important to note that strategic planning becomes useful only if it leads to strategic management. This means that plans are translated into actions through the formulation of: a) an organization's vision and mission in light of changing external factors; b) development of a competitive strategy to achieve the mission; and c) creation of an organizational structure which will provide the necessary resources to carry out the strategy. III. The task at hand In the next two days, we shall again be immersed in the strategic planning process to identify the programs and projects that would lead us closer to our vision. For the first time, we shall attempt to draft a medium-term plan for the bank, focusing on its core functions of maintaining price and financial sector stability. We shall also define measures that need to be adopted if we are to ensure effective banking services through an efficient currency management system and responsive branching operations. The successful implementation of all these action plans will hinge on the timely provision of adequate resources--man, machines and facilities. That is why we will hold another planning session specifically on organizational capability building one month after the completion of this conference. This will allow us to discuss fully the strategies that we need to implement to provide the resource requirements that will support the plans and programs agreed upon in the next two days. IV. Conclusion This is our second annual strategic planning exercise. Hopefully, this exercise will make strategic planning become part of our daily routine to guide us though the complex decisions that we have to make as we work towards becoming a world-class monetary authority. Finally, with your active participation, I trust that this strategic planning session will provide us with a clearer picture of where and what we want to be five years from now. Thank you and good day. (Note: 2003 BSP Strategic Planning Conference (Part I), September 11, 2003, Executive Business Center, BSP)

Title: Opening Remarks
Occasion: Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Good morning friends, ladies and gentlemen of the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP). Thank you for inviting me once again to your forum. When I met FOCAP members in July of last year, I just marked my third year anniversary as BSP Governor. I mentioned then that I was half way through my term as BSP Governor. Today, I still have about 1 year and 10 months remaining in my term and I expect to finish my term. Looking forward, in terms of economic performance we anticipate sustaining the momentum of the economic recovery despite some fluctuations in the financial markets. A review of the recent performance shows that the economy is indeed on a sustainable growth track. During the first half of the year, the economy posted a real GDP growth of 3.85 percent vis-à-vis the 3.97 percent growth in the comparable period last year. This expansion was remarkable in that it was achieved amidst external and domestic shocks, including the Iraq war, the outbreak of SARS and adverse weather conditions. In fact, the Philippines proved to be one of the most resilient in the region as some countries posted negative growth during the second quarter of the year. At the same time, year-on-year inflation eased anew to 3.0 percent in August from 3.3 percent in the previous month, bringing the average inflation to 3.0 percent for the first eight months of 2003.
