These figures are well below the full-year target helped mainly by steady food inflation, fairly stable non-food prices and prudent monetary policy. The benign inflation combined with lower foreign interest rates have enabled the BSP to relax monetary policy stance. BSP's policy rates, which were last changed on 15 March 2002, are now at 6.75 percent for the overnight borrowing rate and 9.0 percent for the overnight lending rate, the lowest levels since May 1992. This accommodative stance, together with the improved fiscal performance and ample liquidity in the system, was reflected mainly on the decline of market interest rates. The rate of the bellwether 91-day Treasury bill during the last auction was 5.225 percent. Moreover, concerns over the ability of the National Government to meet the budget deficit have diminished with the marked upturn in revenue collections combined with the mindful forbearance in fiscal spending. For the period January-July 2003, the fiscal deficit amounted to P95.4 billion, compared to P131.8 billion deficit in the same period last year. In the banking sector, NPLs have continued to come down to 15.13 percent as of June 2003 from 15.33 percent a month-ago. However, we expect a substantial improvement in the level of non-performing assets of the banking system as banks seriously consider taking advantage of the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) Law to clean their balance sheets. A survey conducted by the BSP recently showed that nearly half of the 43 members of the BAP are in various stages of availing the incentives in the SPV Law through various avenues, which include among others, exemption from taxes and staggered compliance to the reserves provisioning of the BSP. In the foreign exchange market, we have recently experienced some volatility, with the peso-dollar rate averaging around the P55.06/US$1 in recent days from a year high of P52.54/US$1 in May 2003. This was due mainly to a combination of temporary, seasonal economic factors (e.g., higher dollar demand by importers, low foreign exchange inflows from OFWs) and non-economic factors (e.g., political issues and security concerns). In response to the recent sharp depreciation of the peso, the BSP, on 28 August 2003, suspended for the second time during the year the tiering scheme for banks' short-term deposits with the BSP. The move is a preemptive monetary measure to prevent adverse impact in inflationary expectations. The suspension of the tiering scheme is expected to selectively siphon extra liquidity in the system which can be used for excessive hedging activities in the foreign exchange market. I will end my opening statement at this point. I now welcome any questions you have wanted to ask me. I also look forward to receiving comments or suggestions from you which I have always found to be insightful. Again good morning and thank you for this opportunity. (Note: Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines, September 10, 2003, Mandarin Oriental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Building Capabilities Through MABS Service Providers
Occasion: Regional Roundtable Conference, RBAP-MABS Luzon and Visayas
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Atty. John V. Owens, Mr. Daniel Arcenas, our colleagues from USAID and RBAP, ladies and gentlemen: good afternoon. I am both pleased and honored to join you today as we mark another milestone in the development of sustainable microfinance in the country. I congratulate RBAP and USAID for their tireless efforts to promote microfinance through continuous trainings focused on sound microfinance practices and capacity building. Microfinance is a serious business. Institutions that want to engage in microfinance should be well-prepared and fully committed to uphold best practices and high performance standards. This is the rationale behind our efforts to promote training and capacity building as a key strategy for developing a vibrant microenterprise industry. I believe the microenterprise access to banking services (MABS) program has done much to contribute to this agenda. The MABS program has certainly come a long way in providing training and technical assistance to rural banks. The MABS program enables rural banks to build on the technical expertise needed for a successful microfinance venture using the MABS approach. The MABS approach to microfinance is systematic and is thus deemed comprehensive as it involves various aspects of microfinance operations. It is worth mentioning that since 1998, more than 110 rural banks have benefited from the MABS approach and are now operating profitably by offering loan and deposit services to approximately 260,000 microenterprises. [1] Today we are all keen about taking part in the launching of the MABS service providers (MSPS), another major initiative of RBAP under the MABS approach training and technical services program. With the presence of MSPS which have been extensively trained in microfinance operations, we can better promote sustainable microfinance by helping banks develop the capability to provide financial services to the entrepreneurial poor. The Bangko Sentral has been actively promoting training and capacity building in microfinance. We now have included microfinance in the basic rural and thrift banking courses that we regularly conduct. In addition, we have introduced the BSP Microfinance Regional Advocacy Program last January 2003 as a way of encouraging more banks to go into microfinance. Under the program, the BSP will be conducting a series of information seminars in strategic regions in the country. The very first seminar was held in our Cebu Regional Office. Presently, we have 3 microfinance-oriented rural banks and 115 more banks with some level of microfinance operations and servicing around 350,000 borrowers. With the launching of MSPS, we hope to significantly increase the number of banks engaging in microfinance, while at the same time developing their capability to provide microfinance services. In the process, we hope to be able to reach out to the many enterprising poor who need access to basic financial services. With that, I would like to issue a call to rural banks to continue to support us in advocating sustainable and viable microfinance operations in the banking sector. Congratulations to the newly accredited MSPS! We strongly rely on you to make sustainable microfinance a success. Thank you very much. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [1] Data from MABS (rural banks have so far extended loans to over 90,000 micro-borrowers and are providing deposit services to almost 170,000 micro-depositors). (Note: Regional Roundtable Conference, RBAP-MABS Luzon and Visayas, September 5, 2003, Pan Pacific Hotel, Manila)

Title: Keeping Faith in the Face of Adversity
Occasion: BSP General Assembly
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Dear fellow workers at Bangko Sentral: I am overwhelmed...I really am so touched and overwhelmed by your support. Salamat. Salamat po sa inyong lahat. As you all know, I was in the United States, representing our country on official business, when I learned of the court decision suspending me for one year. You can imagine how shocking it was...for me and my family. I was further saddened to learn that there were other BSP officers given the same penalty - Deputy Governor Bert Reyes, Managing Director Dolly Yuvienco, Director Candon Guerrero and retired BSP Director Tom Aure. Let me tell you, it meant a lot to us to know that there are so many people who support and believe in us. In my case, it was a source of comfort knowing that many institutions and prominent personalities were speaking out to defend BSP, when I was thousands of miles away and unable to respond to misleading charges. Ang sabi nga ng aking mahal na asawa, hindi ka pala nag-iisa. But ladies and gentlemen of Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas....I assure you, we did the right thing. Bert, Dolly, Candon and Tom were right. Let me explain, the facts of the case. First, the owners of Urban Bank themselves voluntarily closed the bank by declaring a bank holiday in April 2000. Inaccuracies and blatant falsehoods have been used to blame other people for this. Actually, the reason is really quite simple: Urban Bank ran out of cash. Now, you may ask, what happened to the money of the depositors of Urban Bank? Records show that the management of Urban Bank used P4.6 billion of depositors' money to buy doubtful receivables of its investment affiliate UrbanCorp Investment, Inc. or UII. The proceeds were used to service massive withdrawals and pretermination of placements of UII clients, among whom are relatives of bank officials. In other words, the purchase was made to favor UII investors, at the expense of Urban Bank's depositors. Mr. Borlongan, former president of Urban Bank, has publicly declared that he considered both the Urban Bank and the investment house affiliate to be the same integral unit; that there is no distinction between the two companies. This is a most irresponsible view. The bank and the investment house were two separate corporations with different stockholders: the interest of one is not the same as the interest of the other. Accordingly, charges of estafa have been filed in court by the Department of Justice against 11 respondents, including Mr. Borlongan. The cases are pending in Regional Trials Courts in Makati city. Clearly, the Monetary Board did the right thing...by acting promptly and decisively in placing the bank under receivership. By doing so, we prevented the dissipation of its assets, protected the integrity of bank records, and safeguarded the interest of the depositors, creditors and the general public. Placing Urban Bank under PDIC receivership, paved the way for its purchase by Export and Industry bank and its subsequent rehabilitation. Unfortunately, the Court of Appeals ruled that the memorandum recommending the placing of Urban Bank under receivership a day after it declared a bank holiday, "was done in an arbitrary manner violative of fair play and committed with grave abuse of discretion." This, we believe, is an unfair decision, which we will now appeal. Our examiners had been monitoring the financial condition of Urban Bank months before it declared a bank holiday. Therefore, we knew the following: 1. That its non-performing loan ratios had been consistently exceeding the industry average; 2. That for three months up to April 25, Urban Bank had been depending heavily on inter-bank borrowings, exceeding P5 billion a month, to meet its mounting liquidity requirements; and 3. Urban bank was capital deficient as it could not meet the P2.4 billion capitalization of a commercial bank. In other words, the bank was capital deficient, illiquid, and unable to pay its liabilities as they became due. These findings were confirmed in Urban Bank's letter dated April 25 advising the BSP of its declaration of a bank holiday. Please note additionally that before the closure: 1. Urban downgraded from universal bank to a commercial bank, and with a further request to downgrade once more to a "holding company." 2. Urban had made appeals for assistance from the Bangko Sentral. 3. BSP was trying to arrange a take-over by a stronger bank. 4. BSP offered to give an emergency loan which was declined as it would not sound nice in public. 5. PDIC offered to provide a loan which Urban declined for lack of collateral. Very clearly, the closure of Urban Bank cannot be described as abrupt and done in haste. As such, we are confident of our stand: professionally, legally and morally. We believe therefore that, in time, our courts will rule in our favor. I explained all of these today, because it is important that you know...and believe...that we did the right thing in the case of Urban Bank. I want you to be able to declare -with conviction- to your friends and family, that BSPers are professionals; that they can rely on the integrity of our actions and intentions. Outside the courts, as you have seen and heard, there is a groundswell of public support for BSP in this case. It is the same public that consistently votes for BSP as the top-performing government agency. They believe. They have kept the faith. I appeal to all of you therefore not to let our people down. In doing our work, let us continue to be guided by the values of integrity, excellence and patriotism. These are the very same values we have enshrined in our vision statement. The legal setback we encountered is temporary. You can be sure, we will exhaust all legal remedies available to us. We shall not be intimidated. We shall persevere. We shall prevail. Once again, on behalf of Bert, Dolly, Candon and Tom - our Urban heroes, we thank you for your heartwarming and spontaneous support. Finally, I just want to say this:...it really feels good to be back among friends. Muli, marami pong salamat sa inyong lahat. (Note: BSP General Assembly, August 28, 2003, BSP Assembly Hall)

Title: Presentation of Megalink's Electronic Settlement Facility
Location: PNB Financial Center, Roxas Blvd., Pasay City
Occasion: Launching of Megalink's Electronic Settlement Facility between Megalink and BSP
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Distinguished officers and members of the banking community, my co-workers at BSP, ladies and gentlemen: good afternoon. Today we mark another milestone in the Philippine banking system with the launching of Megalink's electronic settlement facility, a joint undertaking between Megalink, Inc. and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. This new electronic settlement facility is expected to further minimize the banking system's exposure to settlement risk. By connecting with PhilPaSS, the Philippines' version of a real time gross settlement system for large value payments that we introduced in November 2002, Megalink's electronic facility will be able to approximate real time, final and irrevocable gross settlement of the network's financial transactions via direct debit or credit to member banks' demand deposit accounts with BSP. Since settlement will occur frequently during agreed intra-day settlement time windows based on an electronic settlement file that is electronically sent by Megalink to BSP for posting, the process will significantly reduce the gap between the actual completion of the network's ATM transactions and actual settlement of network funds. Prior to the new system, settlement is completed with a two-day lag. To ensure an exclusive point-to-point connection and secure passage of data from Megalink to BSP, the system will be electronically linked with PhilPaSS through a leased line. Other risk management measures include the use of a high-quality data encryption mechanism and contingency backup. Likewise, all transactions will be processed using built-in security features for validating settlement and payment instructions, auditing information, and verifying status of transactions. The BSP is satisfied that these features will guarantee accurate and reliable transmission of information. With the linkage of Megalink's electronic settlement facility to PhilPaSS, we hope to maximize utilization of our real-time gross settlement system. By extending rapid settlement to primarily retail payments, the new system will boost our efforts to modernize our payments infrastructure for a more stable and globally competitive financial system. These initiatives should generate greater confidence in the integrity and dependability of our banking system. At this point, I would just like to stress the importance of your commitment to comply with the policies and guidelines specified in our memorandum of agreement. We require all participating banks to observe proper control and security procedures to ensure operating efficiency and sound implementation of risk management practices. We have a shared responsibility to ensure, at all times, the sustained viability of our financial institutions. BSP cannot accomplish the job alone. We need your full cooperation and support. A major component of BSP's comprehensive banking reform agenda is to develop critical financial market infrastructure and systems that reduce our risks and boost our efficiency. We are sustaining implementation of other key banking reforms that are mainly geared towards: (1) strengthening the supervisory framework; (2) restructuring the local banking system; and (3) improving corporate governance standards and risk management. In closing, I would like to commend the officers and members of Megalink, Inc. for their initiative, resourcefulness, perseverance and dynamism to see this project through. Let us sustain our partnership so that, together, we can achieve our common goal of developing our economy. Thank you. (Note: Launching on Megalink's Electronic Settlement Facility between Megalink and BSP, August 27, 2003, PNB Financial Center, Roxas Blvd., Pasay City)

Title: PRIME-ing the Local Banking Industry
Occasion: Launching of Prime Magazine, Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines (BMAP)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: These are exciting and interesting times for the banking sector. With the recent passage of the Special Purpose Vehicle Act governing the cleanup of bank's non-performing assets, the recent amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering Act, good governance reforms, benchmarking with international banking standards, and further improvements in credit access of SMEs and micro entrepreneurs, there is a whole new landscape that is unfolding for the banking sector. For the banks, all these reforms, as well as the new issues that go with it....have to be properly understood, analyzed and implemented. And by the same token, bank customers also need to understand these reforms and emerging issues. Clearly, we needed to have a new forum to ventilate all these issues and concerns. And, appropriately, it is the Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines, or BMAP, which recognized this need. Thus, we are here tonight to witness the birth of Prime Magazine, a monthly magazine that will focus on issues and concerns affecting the local banking industry. Based on its initial issue, Prime Magazine provides good value for money, as it is full of useful information on the business of banking and investment. That it also serves as lifestyle and leisure guide is a bonus. I am sure BMAP and the staff of Prime Magazine--led by executive editor Roni Tapia-Merk, editor-in-chief Raul Dancel, and managing editor Samuel Caezar Peralta--started this venture with their eyes open....well aware of the difficulties of keeping a magazine running. But with the support of all the bankers present here tonight, Prime should last and continue to evolve with the banking sector. To us at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Prime Magazine represents yet another vital communications link between the regulators and the regulated. Through its pages, we can have a continuing dialogue on emerging issues. It is in this light that I have agreed to write a regular column for Prime magazine, starting in its next issue. To me, this is a good opportunity to be able to communicate directly to both the banking industry and to bank customers - both depositors and borrowers. Indeed, the need to communicate and be understood is an advocacy that we at the BSP are committed to pursue. This is the reason why, among others, BSP produced an authoritative book on money and banking written by BSP specialists, who are either policy-makers or administrators involved in daily central banking operations. For those who want to know more about money and banking in the Philippines, get a copy of our brand new book, entitled "Money and Banking in the Philippines-Perspectives from Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas." We have a table here where you can place your orders. If you noticed, like good marketers, we have also distributed flyers of our book. And just to remind you, please do not forget to submit your subscription to Prime magazine as well. Before I end, I just want to share a bit of good news. Today, the Makati Business Club survey revealed that Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas was rated by its respondents, once again, as the best-performing among 35 government agencies. This could not have happened, if the banking sector did not do its part in sustaining national economic growth. I therefore share this award with the banking sector. Ladies and gentlemen. We all want the banking sector to succeed. Let us therefore keep our communications channel alive and healthy. Thank you all and good night. (Note: Launching of Prime Magazine, Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines (BMAP), July 24, 2003, Metropolitan Museum of the Philippines)

Title: Message
Occasion: Recognition and Culminating Activity for the MSEP-1 Graduates (Batches 1 - 6)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Brother Andrew Gonzales, Vice President for Academics and Research of the DLSU System; Mr. Francisco del Rosario, Executive Vice President of the Professional Schools Inc. of the DLSU System; Mr. Philip Juico, Dean of the Graduate School of Business; MB member Valdepeñas, MB member Alindogan, MB member Salazar, MB member Quintos, Deputy Governor Reyes, Deputy Governor Tetangco, our training partners from De La Salle University; my co-workers in the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, good morning: Congratulations to the graduates -- or should I say the survivors --- of the Management Skills Enhancement Program Level-1. Indeed, after hurdling three arduous weeks of lectures, group discussions, presentations, and case studies, you certainly deserve a resounding round of applause! I would like to acknowledge the cooperation of all the five sectors of the BSP for helping make the initial six offerings of the MSEP-1 a success. In particular, I would like to cite the Supervision and Examination Sector and Banking Services Sector for having sent the most number of participants to the program. The Graduate School of Business of De La Salle University also deserves a round of applause. I am pleased that the BSP Institute's training partner in MSEP is one of the leading institutions that has established a niche in the area of management and business. In the conduct of the MSEP-1, I am happy to say that they have met our expectations. And today, like a parent attending his child's graduation, I take pride in recognizing all of you for graduating from MSEP-1.More specifically, I would like to recognize the accomplishments of: Celedina P. Garbosa of SED IV, who incidentally got a perfect 4.0 in her GPA; Alec M. Badiola of SED III; and Henry M. Sungsai, also of SED IV; who were awarded the gold and silver medals for academic excellence; The 17 bank officers who were given bronze medals on academic achievement; and The three groups who were awarded with plaques of recognition for presenting the most innovative projects on savings and cost reduction on operational efficiencies. We just had our first Program on Awards and Incentives for Service Excellence, or PRAISE, last Monday. I believe the projects of MSEP would qualify as contenders for this award. I am therefore asking the PRAISE Committee to consider the MSEP group projects so that these outputs can be given appropriate recognition. In the back-to work assessment that the BSP institute conducted among selected heads of departments and offices who sent participants to MSEP-1, I am happy to note that there was overwhelming affirmation and recognition of the positive contribution of MSEP-1 both from the participants' perspective as well as from the supervisors who evaluated their performance. Moreover, not a few inquired about a follow-through course. With such encouraging feedback, I am happy to announce that the BSP Institute has already scheduled the pilot run of MSEP-2 this year, tentatively set for August. MSEP-2 will focus on the advanced management modules that cover strategic I.T. and resource management. Furthermore, lectures will touch on the concepts of creativity and innovation, process and quality management, and the use of technology; and integrate them with change management and ethical leadership. I cannot overemphasize the need to continuously build capability in the bank. One major area of concern is building leadership successors. "The thing that wakes me up in the middle of the night is not what might happen to the economy or what our competitors may do next; it is worrying whether we have the leadership capacity and talent to implement the new and more complex global challenges." This is a quote from David Whitman, the Chairman and CEO of Whirlpool Corporation. I perfectly understand his concern. Bottom line, he's talking about keeping Whirlpool Corporation a viable business concern in a globally competitive world. So you must appreciate how much more worried I should be, considering that the BSP is the guardian of the Philippine economy. We must therefore ensure a consistent supply of quality leaders in the bank. Potts and Sykes' study on executive talent led them to say that good executives do not grow on trees. Responsible corporations, they added, "grow" them over a period of years through nurturing and developmental experiences that allows them to master the ultimate executive responsibilities. It is therefore essential that the BSP should have a system to "grow" its own executives. MSEP is just one of these developmental experiences that are part of a management succession plan. As a component of the management succession plan, MSEP shall henceforth be a pre-requisite for promotion to any supervisory or managerial position in the bank and I instruct the HRMD to develop the mechanics for this. I appreciate the concern of managers and department heads who have to keep on postponing their attendance in developmental training in order to meet their daily accomplishment requirements. But meeting these short-term obligations have to be well balanced with the need for sustainable success in the long term. Training and development are among our long-term strategies. The need for successors is already upon us. Almost yearly, one or two from among our top management leave us to retire. Recognizing the urgent need for leaders and the time it takes to develop them, I enjoin all department heads to seize the opportunity to participate in or send participants to this training program as a first step towards "growing" our own leaders. Let us do our part in ensuring sustainability of this institution by contributing our high potential staff to the leadership pool. Send them to MSEP because from the graduates of MSEP will come the candidates to our acceleration pool for management succession. As I leave you with these thoughts, let me once again congratulate our MSEP graduates and wish everyone a good day. (Note: Recognition and Culminating Activity for the MSEP-1 Graduates (Batches 1 - 6), July 23, 2003, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: BSP PRAISE Awardees - Raising the Bar for Excellence
Occasion: BSP PRAISE Awards Ceremony
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Members of the Monetary Board, fellow workers at Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. Good morning. It is my personal belief, that in any organization, the most important resource is its people...the human resource. Here at Bangko Sentral, we definitely have a huge goldmine of employees who serve with integrity, utmost professionalism, and passion for excellence. This is the reason why I strongly believe that BSP is the best among government institutions in the country today. And so, this morning, we should rightfully congratulate everyone who works at Bangko Sentral. Let us give ourselves a round of applause. Ladies and gentlemen of BSP. I ask you to mark this day as a BSP milestone. Today, we honor our first set of awardees under our Program on Awards and Incentives for Service Excellence...or PRAISE. You might say that if BSP is the champion team, then our honorees today are the MVPs - our most valuable players. Let us therefore honor them with another around of applause. Congratulations to the awardees for outstanding department: Internal Audit Office for the Top Management Sector; Treasury Department for the Banking Services Sector; Supervisory Reports and Studies Office for the Supervision & Examination Sector; BSP Institute for the Resource Management Sector; Department of General Services for Security Plant Complex; The Davao Regional Office for being named Outstanding Regional Office; And last but not the least, the Investor Relations Office for earning the Special Office Award and the Legazpi branch for winning the Special Branch Award. Through teamwork, they accomplished their plans with flying colors. Let us also congratulate the three winners of the Suggestions Award: Jimmy Balidiong, Paolo Galimba and Primitiva Jose. Your innovative ideas will surely bring about marked improvements at the Bank. Our 31 academic awardees also deserve special commendation for successfully balancing work, studies and family priorities. They exemplify the tenacity with which BSPers pursue their goal. Lastly, we honor the extraordinary dedication to duty of our 33 perfect attendance and punctuality awardees. They were not only present every working day, they were also punctual, strictly observed scheduled break times and remained on the job until dismissal time, for the whole year! I must say, our awardees this year have raised the standards of excellence at BSP. And this is just the beginning; more awards will be given out before the end of this year, including the Model Employee Award. Tough act to follow? Well....there is a Chinese proverb that says: "...behind every able man, there are always other able men." Next year could be your turn. I am confident therefore that in 2004, we will have an even bigger and better harvest of PRAISE awardees. Again, I thank all of you for making BSP a winning team through all these years. Marami pong salamat. (Note: BSP PRAISE Awards Ceremony, July 21, 2003, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Remarks
Occasion: Signing Ceremony, RCBC Tier II Capital Issuance
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I congratulate RCBC for the successful issuance of its subordinated notes in the amount of P5 billion. This will significantly boost RCBC's regulatory capital base since this will qualify as Tier 2 capital which we now recognize in line with the Basle Capital Accord Principles. In taking this step, RCBC manifests its will to stay competitive and strengthen its position as one of the country's premier banking institutions. As supervisor of the banking system, the Bangko Sentral is strongly committed to lead the banking system to build a solid capital base which is the foundation of a stable financial system. Since the 1997 Asian crisis, we have accelerated our initiatives to introduce meaningful reforms in our financial system. A key initiative is the adoption of a risk based capital adequacy framework as prescribed under Circular 280 and Circular 360. This is a process that will continue as we steadily align our regulatory standards with best international practices. However, RCBC's issuance is notable as well for pioneering a peso denominated issue specifically targeted to our nascent domestic capital market. I hope this will open the door for other similar issues and thus invigorate the capital market. The development of the domestic capital market is a major initiative. I realize that many elements need to fall into place to achieve this goal. But I believe that many important steps are now being taken including the creation of a fixed income exchange and it's supporting, clearing, settlement and custodial systems. Another important step are legislative initiatives to reduce the friction cost of secondary trading and to create the legal framework for asset securitization. Regulatory arrangements that inhibit capital market development are also being reviewed. From another perspective, this issuance is also significant for enlarging the mix of financial assets that the public can invest in with adequate safeguards. As we develop new instruments, hopefully we can also discourage the vulnerability of the public to investment scams in their earnest desire to achieve better returns for their hard earned savings. For all of these reasons, once again I congratulate RCBC for its bold initiative. I encourage our banks to sustain our cooperative efforts to strengthen the banking system and develop the domestic capital market. Thank you and good day. (Note: Signing Ceremony for RCBC's Tier II Capital Issuance, July 16, 2003, RCBC Plaza, Makati City)

Title: Towards a Resilient Rural Banking Industry
Occasion: Induction of Officers and Directors, Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Daniel Vidal R. Arcenas, incoming president of the Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines (RBAP), Mr. Jerry B. Coloma, Jr., outgoing RBAP President, RBAP Board of Directors, members of the Association, ladies and gentlemen, good evening. I am pleased to join my fellow colleagues in the banking sector. We are bound by a common objective, that is, to promote a healthier financial system. As such, we are all concerned about the state of our financial institutions. Let us look at how the rural banking industry is doing at present. Assessment of the rural banking industry I would like to commend the rural banking industry for staying resilient in spite of difficult domestic and global conditions. As of March 2003, the rural banking system demonstrated overall soundness: expansion in assets, steady growth of deposits, increasing capitalization, and reasonable profitability. The industry's total resources stood at P82.2 billion or 11.6 percent higher than last year's P73.7 billion. Deposits grew by 14.2 percent to P56.3 billion from P49.3 billion a year ago. Capital accounts increased by 8.9 percent to P13.3 billion from last year's level of P12.2 billion. In terms of profitability, average return on assets was at 1.4 percent while return on equity was at 8.7 percent. It is also worth mentioning the improvement in overall asset quality. The industry's NPL ratio declined to 14.0 percent from 15.1 percent a year ago. Still, I would like to encourage the industry to work doubly hard in containing the stock of non-performing assets (NPAs) which remain a severe problem, so that you can undertake new lending and resume your primary role in fund intermediation. The enactment of the Special Purpose Vehicle Act (SPV Act) last January is a major BSP initiative relating to the resolution of the NPA problem. This would pave the way for the creation of privately owned asset management companies (AMCs). The Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of the Act took effect on 9 April 2003. This sets in motion the sale of NPAs with fiscal incentives to special purpose vehicles and, in the case of residential loans and foreclosed residential assets, to individuals. In connection with the implementation of the SPV Act, we have issued a Memorandum to all banks/NBQBs containing procedural guidelines for the sale of such NPAs to fast track the regulatory approval process while maintaining full transparency. The BSP is working closely with other regulatory agencies, such as SEC and BIR, in implementing the Act. I strongly urge you to consider using the new law to reduce your NPAs. We have sweetened the package by allowing deferred recognition of losses on eligible transactions. Moving on, let us now consider the challenges that rural banks face today. Challenges and key reforms The difficult domestic and global economic environment pose serious challenges to rural banks. Now, more than ever, there is need to institute reforms that would ensure the sustained viability and competitiveness of the industry. To hurdle these challenges, rural banks need to embrace reforms that would improve overall efficiency, strengthen risk management, build up capital base, and enhance corporate governance standards. We are here to support you all the way. Our efforts to strengthen the banking reform agenda is basically geared towards helping promote greater safety, efficiency and competitiveness in the banking industry. One of the key reforms in our agenda is the promotion of better governance in our financial institutions. The broad corporate governance reform agenda is a fundamental challenge that we, as a nation, face. Let us do our part by ensuring that there is fairness, accountability and transparency in the way we conduct our business. Furthermore, we also need to promote leadership integrity in the entire industry, beginning with the board of directors in whose shoulders rest the responsibility of ensuring the presence of sound work ethics and effective risk management systems within the institution. Thisis the fundamental reason why we have taken the initiative to empower bank directors through training. We want directors to understand the nature and scope of their responsibilities which involve setting policies and strategies, identifying key risk areas, and monitoring corporate performance as a means to achieve growth, profitability and financial stability. Our records indicate that as of May 2003 around 60 percent of rural bank directors (from 635 rural banks) have participated in our mandatory orientation program. [1] What happened to the other 40 percent? What happened to the 139 rural banks who have not sent a single director for training? Remember, we even extended the deadline up to 30 June 2003 so that we can come up with a perfect attendance and more importantly, avoid the situation where we would be forced to disqualify directors. Now we must act. Our ongoing agenda on corporate governance constitutes the following initiatives: Supporting more training on specific aspects of corporate governance, particularly in improving banks' audit functions, risk management systems, and governance systems. We hope RBAP can continue to play a role in providing such training. Encouraging professional certification of bank directors to raise the standards and maintain the professional and ethical practice of bank directors; and Supporting objective monitoring of progress in corporate governance practice. Finally, I would like to highlight BSP's commitment to promote sustainable microfinance as a response to the needs of the many enterprising poor in our society. I am glad that our rural banks have been particularly supportive of this endeavor. The number of banks involved in microfinance lending has steadily risen since we first implemented the project in 2000. We now have 119 banks engaged in microlending with total microfinance loans amounting to P2.2 billion spread out to 394,613 borrowers. [2] However, I have to remind you that going into microfinance is a risk-taking business. Without the necessary adherence to sound practices, it can create bigger problems. Microfinance should not be an excuse for unsound banking practices. Conclusion At this point, I would like to call on the association to remain steadfast in promoting a healthier rural banking industry. Your efforts will certainly help spur growth and development in the countryside, leading to more efficient and responsive services. Ultimately, this will aid in promoting a stronger and more vibrant economy. Thank you and good evening! ----------------------------------- [1] Source: BSPI - Status Report on Corporate Governance Seminar [2] Source: Data as of May 2003. Updates on BSP Supervised/Regulated Financial Institutions, March 2003

Title: Message
Occasion: First Annual Meeting of Respondents to the BSP's Quarterly Business Expectations Survey
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Distinguished guests, friends, colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon: I will begin by thanking everyone for joining us here at the first annual meeting of respondents to the BSP's quarterly Business Expectations Survey (BES). Economic policymaking is a difficult occupation. We look at a big body of information, and because macroeconomic policy, particularly monetary policy, takes time to fully affect the domestic economy, it is important for economic managers to have a good idea of where the economy is going several quarters into the future. One of the important elements considered by economic managers is how the public views the outlook for the economy. This is particularly true for the monetary policy of the Bangko Sentral. Public expectations are an important channel through which monetary policy affects the economy, and having information on expectations about the economy is extremely valuable to the formulation of monetary policy. Initiatives like the BES, therefore, help monetary authorities get timely information on how the business sector is responding to the current macroeconomic environment. The BES indicates to us the economic outlook of business and industry. It is extremely useful because it contains their short-term economic prospects and their own adaptive business strategies. In turn, we at the BSP are able to craft more solidly-based, more market-informed monetary and banking policies which are more forward-looking than one based on nostalgia. The need for timely information about economic expectations and business activity cannot be overemphasized. Policymakers in the Philippines and the rest of the global economy continue to struggle to engineer a sustained recovery in the face of generalized economic weaknesses. The future path of economic policy can only be established on the basis of strong and reliable data on the progress of economic activity. In our own case, based on the results of the last BES survey, we are now seeing some indications of a steady, even if modest, rebound in business confidence in the Philippines. This has been due largely to the positive turn of recent events, particularly the early resolution of the war in Iraq, the significant downtrend in world petroleum prices, the strong recovery of the peso, the modest but improving pattern of domestic demand, and evidence of rising export orders from the U.S., Europe and Asia. Such evidence bolsters our belief at the BSP that our monetary policy is on the right track, and we hope that these expectations will eventually be translated into stronger economic activity that will lead to higher and sustained growth. This is the good news that we must be awaiting. We, your public servants at the Bangko Sentral, are very grateful to the business community for the continuing support extended to the BES. This Survey Respondents' Meeting, which we hope to conduct on a regular, annual basis, aims to strengthen further the partnership between the BSP and the private sector in building up our information system for economic analysis and applying international best practices in policy-making. Today is your opportunity to suggest to us how we can further improve and expand the survey and how best to disseminate the survey results to the public. I should also emphasize that the quality of the BES survey results derives in large part from the timely responses and reliable information provided to us by the survey respondents, who made time to fill out our questionnaire. The primary benefit of the survey will accrue not just to policymakers but also to the business community. The data will also be useful to the business because it will help sharpen your planning and pricing decisions. We have bigger plans for the survey, as indicated by the staff. Let me just reiterate these plans: first of all, we plan to expand the coverage of the Survey to include the regions outside Metro Manila, and make greater use of composite indicators. Starting next year, we will also be giving out awards to the best BES respondents as a token of our appreciation for the business community's support for the BSP. We will be announcing the criteria and mechanics shortly. We also intend later on to complement the BES with a similar survey on consumer sentiment. Our overall goal is to design something along the lines of the Bank of Japan's Tankan Survey, which provides Japanese policymakers with timely snapshots of various key aspects of the Japanese economy. Over the medium term--with the support of the business sector--we hope to implement a comprehensive system of leading indicators that would tell us the likely path of business and consumer activity in the Philippines. In conclusion, I wish to paraphrase a very telling quote: A nation whose government and its people walk together will always get to its destination. Our common goal is to achieve economic prosperity for our nation and people. When you help us and support us to sharpen our ability to improve on monetary and banking policy, you are also helping us deliver a better economic deal to our people. Mabuhay po tayong lahat. (Note: 1st Annual Meeting of Respondents to the BSP's Quarterly Business Expectations Survey (BES), July 4, 2003, Philippine International Convention Center (PICC))

Title: Official Launch and Inauguration of The PICC Forum
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Secretary Gordon, special guests, friends, ladies and gentlemen. Good evening. On behalf of the Board of Directors of PICC, I thank all of you for joining us tonight at the official launch and inauguration of the PICC Forum. It is said that "A picture is worth a thousand words." To me, however, there is nothing better than being here...to see and experience the PICC Forum. As you can see, this is a place which lends itself to a wide variety of uses, depending on the need of our customers. It can be an exhibition area, host a convention, or serve as venue for formal occasions, sports events or product launching. In keeping with the latest international trend, we have provided the PICC Forum with built-in flexibility to adapt to the requirements of our customers. The Forum therefore transforms the PICC Complex into an integrated convention and exhibition center in the region. As owner of PICC, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is bullish about the strategic upgrade and renovation program of the Complex. With the region on a recovery mode from the fallout caused by SARS and the Iraq situation, the Philippines is well-placed to catch the uptrend in business activities. Ladies and gentlemen. The service sector is one of the country's major employers and dollar earners, but we have yet to tap its full potential. I hope therefore that you will also help market the Philippines as a destination and promote PICC, in particular, as a convention center. Help bring money into the country. In our case, PICC's trademark for "providing professional service with a smile" gives it a distinct advantage over other convention centers in the region. Of course, having an extremely dynamic and creative Tourism Secretary gives us an added edge for attracting international business for PICC in particular. We are therefore looking forward to busy months ahead for PICC in serving both local and international customers. In the meantime, be among our first customers and help us spread the good news about the PICC Forum. Thank you all for coming. (Note: Official Launch and Inauguration of the PICC Forum, July 03, 2003, PICC, Manila)

Title: Recent Economic Developments, Prospects and BSP Initiatives
Location: MS Philippines Floating Restaurant, South Harbor, Manila
Occasion: Luncheon Meeting, Rotary Club of Manila
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Renato A. Ampil, president of the Rotary Club of Manila, other officers and members of the Rotary, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. I welcome this opportunity to dialogue with you about our economy from our vantage point at the Bangko Sentral. As community business leaders in your own right and as concerned citizens, we are all stakeholders in what is happening around us. Let me begin with our assessment of the current economic environment, and then the key challenges ahead, and BSP's policy initiatives. The economy in brief What's the big picture? Despite the generally weak global environment, the country continued to post favorable economic performance. For the first quarter of 2003, GNP growth stayed robust, benign inflation reigned, low interest rates and a relatively stable peso exchange rate prevailed. Real GNP and GDP grew by 5.6 percent and 4.5 percent, respectively, propped up across the board by the strong performance of the services, industrial, and agriculture sectors. Economic growth has been fostered in a low-inflation environment. The slower increases in the prices of both food and energy-related items caused average inflation rate for the first four months of 2003 to settle at just 2.9 percent. Consequently, average inflation for 2003 is expected to be well below the original government target of 4.5-5.5 percent. During the first four months of 2003, the 91-day Treasury bill rate averaged 6.1 percent, slightly higher than a year ago but still quite low by historical standards. The slight uptrend in T-bill rates mainly reflected market uncertainty over the impending war in Iraq. However, with that issue now resolved, the T-bill rate has settled at 5.5 percent as of the latest auction. The balance of payments (BOP) as of the first two months this year remained in surplus of US$55 million As a result, the country's gross international reserves reached $16.1 billion as of end-May 2003. This is sufficient to cover 4.5 months imports of goods and services. The country preserved its favorable foreign exchange liquidity position due to sustained export growth and steady flow of workers remittances. The banking system at a glance As far as the Philippine banking system is concerned, it continued to manifest overall stability in the face of many uncertainties in domestic and global conditions. Key financial indicators of the Philippine banking system in 2002 reflected overall soundness: steady growth of deposits, resumption of lending, increasing capitalization, and improving profitability. Total resources aggregated P3.5 trillion as of end-December 2002, up by 6.6 percent from a year ago. The banking system also recorded 7.0 percent increase in deposits, 2.5 percent loan growth, 4.6 percent increase in capitalization, and near doubling in net income after taxes (NIAT). However, the large holdings of non-performing assets (NPAs) remains a major issue. At end-year 2002 total NPAs stood at P504.2 billion, equivalent to a little over 14 percent of total banking system assets. Two-thirds comprised non-performing loans and the balance represented acquired assets or ROPOA. This overhang of NPAs continues to put pressure on affected banks and poses a major obstacle to full resumption of lending activity. It is imperative to reduce the stock of NPAs to more manageable levels. After more than a year of painstaking work with Congress, the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) Act was finally enacted last January. This would pave the way for the creation of privately owned Asset Management Companies (AMCs). It is our major initiative to resolve the NPA problem. The implementing rules and regulations (IRR) of the Act became effective on 9 April 2003. This sets in motion the sale of NPAs with fiscal incentives to special purpose vehicles and, in the case of residential loans and foreclosed assets, to individuals. Through this approach, we expect to mobilize fresh private investments, especially foreign investments, to resolve the NPA problem. We have also issued a Memorandum to all banks/NBQBs containing procedural guidelines for the sale of such NPAs to fast track the regulatory approval process while maintaining full transparency. The BSP is working closely with other regulatory agencies, such as SEC and BIR, in implementing the Act. Last week, the Monetary Board decided to allow banks to also defer recognition of losses arising from such NPA transfers subject to full disclosure and dividend restriction. This is intended to provide further incentive to banks to get rid of their NPAs soonest. Towards sustaining reforms Despite a generally improving outlook for the economy, there is a pressing need to address a number of challenges. At the forefront is the critical task of containing the budget deficit primarily through better revenue collection. The success in achieving fiscal stability will greatly assure sustained economic growth with low inflation and peso stability. We all need to fully support the government in its drive to improve revenue collection and rationalize fiscal expenditures without compromising the need to address social and development objectives. As a monetary authority, we will also stay firmly committed to our basic mandate of sustaining low inflation. Since last year, we have adopted an explicit inflation targetting framework to ensure that BSP stays focused and accountable on inflation performance. Moving on to the banking system, our basic agenda is to ensure basic safety and soundness of the system as a whole and to promote greater efficiency of the financial system. Key reforms involve: (1) the strengthening of the regulatory and supervisory framework in line with international standards, (2) promotion of better corporate governance in banks, and (3) development of critical financial market infrastructure and systems. We are actively promoting corporate governance reforms in the financial system through empowerment of the board of directors collectively and as individuals. We started by more clearly defining their duties and responsibilities. We followed through by requiring all bank directors to go through a mandatory orientation course or else face disqualification as directors. We would like to build on the momentum already achieved by: Supporting more training on specific aspects of corporate governance, particularly with regard to the proper functioning of banks' audit committees, risk management committees, and governance systems, in compliance with global standards. Encouraging professional certification of bank directors to raise the standards and maintain the professional and ethical practice of bank directors. Supporting objective monitoring of progress in corporate governance practice. In the area of financial market development, the BSP has sustained the initiative to improve our basic infrastructure. In November last year, we launched the Philippine Payment System or PhilPaSS. This is a real time gross settlement system compatible with international standards designed to minimize settlement risk for high value payments between banks and reduce possible contagion should a crisis occur. We are also strongly supportive of a BAP project to develop a fixed income exchange which will allow the efficient secondary market trading of government securities and other securities that may be issued by banks and other private issuers. The development of a local bond market is a critical goal that will promote a healthier and more efficient financial system. We are presently too dependent on the banking system for financing developmental needs leading the unnecessary fragility as banks try to meet long-term financial requirements with essentially short-term funding sources. We are likewise signing a Memorandum of Agreement with the Philippine Clearing House Corporation to establish a world-class cash management center, a facility that will provide an efficient and cost-effective system of handling and processing currency notes for circulation. These reforms all form an integral part of the BSP's broader banking reform agenda that is geared towards further strengthening the financial sector, reducing our overall vulnerability and promoting a high level of efficiency. But we also recognize that the basic building block of a strong financial system is the quality of human resources behind it. As a modest contribution, we will be launching today on the occasion of our 10th anniversary " Money and Banking in the Philippines - Perspectives from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas." This is intended to be a textbook for college-level students. Finally, let me end by highlighting our efforts to develop a banking system that is also responsive to the needs of the many enterprising poor in our society by actively promoting the concept of sustainable microfinance. This is not a doleout program but a means of providing access to savings and credit to the poor so that they can help themselves and live a life of dignity that they deserve. The number of banks involved in microfinance lending has steadily risen since 2000. Presently, a total of 119 banks are engaged in microlending As of May 2003, microfinance loans amounted to P2.2 billion spread out to 394,613 borrowers. [1] Conclusion I would like to end my talk by expressing my gratitude to the officers and members of the Rotary for this opportunity to share with you our plans for securing sustainable growth for the country. We are strongly committed to pursue these initiatives in keeping with the spirit of the BSP vision: "To be a world-class monetary authority and a catalyst for a globally competitive economy and financial system that delivers a high quality of life for all Filipinos More power to the Rotary Club of Manila! Good day to all! ------------------------------------- [1] Source: Updates on BSP Supervised/Regulated Financial Institutions, March 2003

Title: Message
Occasion: MOA Signing on Clean Note Policy and Book Launching
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Special guests from the Commission on Higher Education and the academe, fellow bankers, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. On behalf of the Bangko Sentral, I thank all of you for joining us today. To us, your presence is a firm indication of your commitment to ensure the success of the projects that we have launched this morning - the Clean Note campaign and the BSP textbook on money and banking in the Philippines. The Clean Note Policy is not new and our bankers know this. The New Central Bank Act, our Charter, refers to it under Section 56 which states: "The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas shall withdraw from circulation and shall demonetize all notes which for any reason whatsoever are unfit for circulation and shall replace them by adequate notes. (flash slide on basis for clean note policy) BSP cannot do this on its own, and called on banks' participation in pursuit of this objective. It issued Circular No. 61 in 1995, Section 19 of which states that "Currency notes considered unfit for circulation shall not be re-circulated, but may be presented for exchange to or deposited with any bank." Chapter IV entitled "Clean Note Policy" of this Circular also provided the guidelines and procedures that banks and their branches shall observe for the fast withdrawal from circulation of unfit Philippine currency. Sorting and classifying cash deposits into clean or fit notes and dirty or unfit notes by series and by denomination before turning these over to BSP as required under the Circular have apparently become a real load to banks in terms of both manhours and cost. The processing of both fit and unfit notes invariably ended up with BSP. I must say this has kept us from fully attaining our clean note policy objective. (flash slides on unfit notes) These slides will give you an idea why sorting and classifying can be really tedious. We have mounted samples of unfit and mutilated notes for a closer look at the details. Our banks and BSP have been getting together for some time to put together a less costly scheme that will facilitate and improve the retirement and replacement of unfit currency. The need for clean notes in circulation has become more pronounced with the recent call for clean money because of tourism concerns as well as the public apprehension over the spread of SARS. BSP is ever conscious of its responsibility to maintain the integrity of the Philippine currency, and dirty money certainly do not help this cause. Neither does it inspire respect for our currency. Thus, the launch of the Clean Note Policy Campaign. With the Bankers Association of the Philippines, Chamber of Thrift Banks and Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines as partners in this campaign, we expect the retirement and replacement of unfit currency to be faster and more efficient. Another cause for our optimism is the Cash Management Center which shall be established jointly by BSP, the Philippine Clearing House Corp. and the BAP in our Security Plant Complex in Quezon City. It is a clear response of the banking system to the initiative of BSP for greater bank participation in the efficient circulation of fit notes in the system. (insert slide on cmc diagram) The CMC, to be run by PCHC, will provide cash management services currently provided by BSP. Simply, CMC will process and recycle notes on behalf of the commercial banks and pass unfit notes to BSP, among other services within the parameters set by BSP. Thus, we will be dealing only with the CMC in servicing the cash requirements of banks. Certainly, there are other benefits for both BSP and the banks that will accrue from this arrangement as shown on the screen. (flash slides on benefits of the cmc) (flash slide on the campaign tagline) (flash slide on the book cover while rbb is talking about the text book) We are particularly honored by the presence of leaders in our education sector, led by Dr. Manuel Punzal, Commissioner of the Commission on Higher Education, at the launching of BSP's book, "Money and Banking in the Philippines - Perspectives from Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas". With the publication of this textbook, BSP signals the start of a more proactive stance in helping elevate the quality of education in our country, particularly in the area of money, credit and banking. Our objective is to make more and more people understand the philosophy that underpins our monetary policy. BSP's twin mandate is to keep prices and the banking system stable, the basic ingredients for sustaining investments and economic growth. As such, our Monetary Board believes it is important that we provide our youth a solid background on this subject. We hope therefore that schools and students will find this BSP textbook most useful. We have made this 438-page book affordable, at five hundred pesos (P500) a copy, to make it accessible to students...and others who want to know more about the business of money and banking in the Philippines. This represents good value for money, if I may say so. We understand of course that public schools, state colleges and universities may not have sufficient funds for acquiring reference books. We are therefore donating two books each to all state colleges and universities through the commission on higher education. We will also be giving one book each to all the schools represented here this morning, as a way of saying thank you for making our 10th anniversary celebration truly meaningful. As for the banks represented here today....we have sales counters outside especially prepared for you. I hope you understand that the money we will generate from its sales will allow us to produce more materials for our schools. Again, on behalf of BSP and the members of the Monetary Board, I thank all of you for joining us this morning. (Note: MOA Signing on Clean Note Policy and Book Launching of "Money and Banking in the Philippines - Perspectives from Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas", July 3, 2003, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas

Title: Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas @ 10
Occasion: BSP's 10th Anniversary Celebration
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Magandang umaga at maligayang anibersaryo sa inyong lahat Fellow workers at BSP. The tradition here at BSP is to have the governor deliver the equivalent of the bank's annual report during anniversary celebrations. However, as I was entering BSP's gate 6 this morning, our streamer proclaimed that now, we are also celebrating Savings Consciousness Week....savings consciousness. As we all know, time is gold. And so today, BSP's 10th anniversary, I will practice what we preach. I will save time...and deliver a brief speech. This is not to say that BSP's first 10 years does not deserve a traditional 30-minute speech. However, I think that with all the news reports, bulletin board posters and our ever reliable BSP grapevine, I am sure you all know that BSP has been doing its job quite well....and that we have been getting both national and international recognition for our performance. In fact, international ratings group, while critical of certain aspects of government policies and programs, almost always end up citing sound and responsive monetary policies of the BSP as a source of strength and stability for the country. So far, BSP policies have yielded low & stable inflation and interest rates, a relatively stable currency, comfortable international reserves level, as well as an increasingly stronger banking system. With inflation running at 2.7%, the country is enjoying one of the rare periods in the country's history when prices have remained relatively low and stable. This has, in turn, pushed interest rates down to their lowest levels in ten years, a factor which has kept investments and production going...and employment opportunities growing. Equally important, BSP's pro-active role in providing an operating environment conducive for banks' increased participation in microfinance, housing and SME lending have been cited as a trailblazing activity for a central monetary authority. In short, the BSP concerns itself not only with major financial transactions but even those at a micro level, because our objective is a better quality of life for all Filipinos. What I want to discuss with you today is why and how we are able to achieve all of these. To me, the reason is clear: the BSP is a world-class monetary authority. It is world-class because of its people...and its people value integrity, excellence and patriotism. In short, even before we crafted and articulated BSP's new vision and mission statements, the people of BSP have long been guided by these values. This is the essence of the people of BSP. At the very least therefore, let's give ourselves a well-deserved round of applause. On behalf of the other members of the Monetary Board, I thank all of you for making our policies work....I am sure you have noticed that in the last ten years, there have been many improvements and additions to the benefits package you receive, of course, within the limits allowed by law. This is your Monetary Board's way of showing its support and appreciation for the excellent work you have been doing. I guess, your question is: "Can we give more?"...Well, we will...if and when the Supreme Court decides in favor of the petition of the non-exempt employees, or if and when Congress approves our recommended amendments to the BSP Charter, whichever comes first. I assure you, we share your sentiments here so we continue to work on this. In the meantime....you can all look forward to winning in our special anniversary raffle to be held this afternoon!. Good luck sa inyong lahat. In addition, all BSP employees will receive a simple, but meaningful memento of our 10th anniversary. Like this. (Gov. RBB to hold up a copy). This is a fitting keepsake for the people of BSP who make this institution a good role model for government agencies. This is the reason why, I am proud to be a part of Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. But ladies and gentlemen of BSP...while we are good, we definitely can be better. For as long as one out of three Filipinos live in poverty, we cannot claim complete success. In fact, we recognize that the work ahead is going to be tough, more difficult, and more complex, even as the stakes get higher. Therefore, we at the Monetary Board are giving closer attention to developing our people to cope and carry on, in the tradition of excellence BSP has been known for. We will continue to seek and develop your potential, give you the opportunity to grow, to be exposed, to be challenged and to take on bigger responsibilities...for you will continue to lead BSP long after we at the Monetary Board have left. Well, I promised you a shorter speech this year. However, just to make sure you do not forget our milestones and memorable moments, we have prepared a photo exhibit on BSP's first 10 years at our main lobby. And for posterity, we are launching this morning, a textbook entitled "Money and Banking in the Philippines - Perspectives from Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas." With this textbook for college students, we present an authoritative book on money and banking based on the authors' deep and broad experience in BSP, either as policy-makers or administrators involved in daily central banking operations. Let me mention the authors who generously shared their time and expertise to produce this book: Monetary Board member Vince Valdepenas who also served as Chairman of the Editorial Board; Deputy Governor Andy Suratos; Deputy Governor Bert Reyes; Deputy Governor Say Tetangco; and officers Dr. Cyd Amador; Dr. Francisco Dakila; Dr. Tobby Marcelo; Dr. Geraldine Reyes; Dr. Magno Torreja; and Dr. Olive Vital, who all hold the Ph.D. degree in economics. On my part, I wrote the preface and the books' overview. Don't we deserve a round of applause?...Salamat sa inyo. Of course, we are also launching a new public service program to mark our 10th year. This morning, we will sign a Memorandum of Agreement with the heads of the Bankers Association, Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines and the Chamber of Thrift Banks to implement, on a nationwide basis, our Clean Note program. Under this, all banks are committed to accept unfit currency from the public and replace it with new banknotes and coins. In other words, ayaw natin ng dirty money. Papalitan ito ng bago. As you are aware, our currency is a symbol of our country. So, all of us here at BSP should rightfully lead the campaign to handle our currency with respect. By the way, we have produced, in cooperation with channel 4, a TV plug or commercial which will inform the people about our Clean Note program. Watch it at a special preview before the start of the raffle at the cafetorium. Ang payo natin sa mga tao: "Ingatan ang ating salapi, larawan ito ng ating yamang-lahi."....exactly the way we care for BSP. Thank you all and happy 10th anniversary! (Note: BSP's 10th Anniversary Celebration, July 3, 2003, BSP Complex Manila)

Title: The Challenge of Being the Governor of Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Occasion: June Networking Event, British Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Chairman Geoffrey Short, Mr. Simon Morris, officers and members of the British Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good evening. Alan Greenspan of the U.S. Federal Reserve once said that few modern institutions in a democratic society receive greater public scrutiny than the central bank. This should come as no surprise. The unique powers of the central bank provide it with the ability to affect the economic life of a country. Its ability to influence interest rates, the exchange rate, and the general functioning of the banking system affects not only financial intermediaries, depositors and borrowers, but also businesses and ordinary consumers. Congressman Jose Roy, the author of the law which created the Central Bank of the Philippines in 1948, correctly described it as an institution which affects the very life of every man, woman and child. In the Philippines, one out of three Filipinos live below the poverty line. Taken in this context, you can imagine the weight of responsibility and challenges that a central bank governor has to contend with. Having spent my career as a banker in the private sector for 34 years, a third of which was in the Philippines, you could say that I was an old hand in terms of dealing with central banks. I believed, it was a matter of shifting perspective: from regulated to regulator. Easier said than done, of course. I came on board as BSP Governor in 1999, just when banks and economies were dealing with the fallout from the Asian financial crisis. Since then, we had to deal with the consequences of natural and man-made disasters, including New York's 9-11, the Middle East conflicts, SARS, and the skirmishes in Mindanao. Given this scenario, how did we, at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, fare? The mandate of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is to ensure the stability of prices and the banking sector. Our overriding objective: to provide the proper environment for sustained long-term economic growth of our country. To me, all things considered, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has been effective, insofar as delivering on its mandate is concerned. Let me be more specific. First, prices have stabilized. Statistical data bear us out on this: in the 10-year period covering 1983 to 1992, inflation averaged 14.2% in the Philippines. In 1993 to 2002, the first ten years of Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, average inflation dropped to 6.8%. In the first five months this year, average inflation had slowed down further to 2.8%. Now, about the banking sector. Even in the face of prolonged tough and uncertain domestic and global conditions, good news prevailed in the banking sector. Thus, while there were some banks that were having difficulties, key financial indicators of the Philippine banking system in 2002 reflected overall soundness. In 2002, we saw steady growth of deposits, resumption of lending, increasing capitalization, and higher bottom line figures. In more concrete terms, the Philippine banking system recorded a 7 percent growth in deposits; a 2.5 percent loan growth; a 4.6 percent rise in capital; and a 98% percent improvement in net income after taxes. In fact, consolidated net income of the banking industry in 2002 was its highest in five years at p28 billion. Capital adequacy ratio of the sector also remains well above international standards. It is fair to say that a sound supervisory and regulatory environment, the implementation of a broad set of financial reforms, and the generally proactive stance of Philippine banks have helped foster growth and sustain viability in the banking industry. Basically therefore, BSP has responded well to the challenges coming its way, in the four years that I have been there. Throughout this period, it has stood strong and remained resilient in discharging its twin responsibilities of keeping prices stable and of keeping the banking system sound and healthy. In turn, this helped provide an operating environment conducive to sustained economic growth. The advent of lower inflation has allowed BSP to pursue a growth-supportive monetary policy that has encouraged a downtrend in market interest rates. For instance, the benchmark 91-day treasury bill rate averaged 5.4% in 2002, down from 12.3% in 1993. Key economic indicators validate that we are well and truly on the right track. In the first quarter this year, our economy grew better than expected. In fact, the Philippines ended up among the highest in Asia. Our GNP was up 5.6% while GDP expanded by 4.5%. I am not saying, it will be easy sailing for us from now on. But what we have accomplished so far gives us the confidence to proceed with the reforms we have started. Going forward, the key to sustained viability of the banking system over the medium and long term depends on sustaining reforms that enhance corporate governance structure, improve operating efficiency, strengthen risk management and build up capital base. The passage of the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) act of 2002 should go a long way in addressing non-performing assets (NPAs) which have been a millstone around the neck of the banking sector. Through asset management companies, we expect a lowering in impaired assets of banks. This should enable them to undertake new lending and resume their primary role in fund intermediation. Asset clean-up is a very important first step; but right behind it are the challenges of replenishing bank capital and of achieving fundamental operational restructuring to achieve better efficiency, competitiveness, and risk management in the much tougher banking environment ahead. All three issues are closely inter-linked with the quality of corporate governance. Even as banking reforms and adherence to good governance strengthen the banking system in the years to come, I expect we will have less, but bigger and stronger banks; weak banks would have been merged or absorbed by healthier and vibrant banks. With the liberalization of the entry of foreign banks, Philippine banks, under the reciprocity rights specified in R. A. No. 7721, can do business in other countries, subject to certain requirements. In this regard, I look forward to seeing a greater number of our banks expanding their operations abroad and competing in the global financial arena. I foresee that a number of our banks will be at par with their foreign counterparts in terms of resources, efficiency, and solvency, offering a full range of services as a financial supermarket. I also foresee that microfinance will be a regular item in the lending portfolio of most banks. So far, response to BSP's call for bank's greater involvement in microfinance has been good, especially from the thrift and the rural banks. Indeed, microfinance is an advocacy BSP is committed to promote as the sector's contribution to alleviating poverty in the country. Others see microfinance as a purely social responsibility; to me, sound banking and microfinance go together. Microfinance, with its extremely high repayment rates, is a viable undertaking. On our part, we at the BSP will continue to apply the appropriate mix of monetary policy instruments and sector reforms to enhance the long-term growth and stability of our banking system. Our objective is to make sure banks deserve the public's confidence and that the banking system effectively performs its role as an engine of economic growth. Thus, while it is inevitable that certain individual banks will continue to face difficulties, I am confident that the Philippine banking system as a whole will continue to grow and serve the country well. The remainder of my term as Governor will be devoted to preserving the BSP's standard of excellence, and continuing our efforts in applying international best practices to the conduct of monetary policy and banking supervision by the Bangko Sentral. I am pleased to tell you that our efforts to align BSP with international standards have been recognized here and overseas. BSP has frequently figured among the top performing government agencies in the surveys of the Makati Business Club. In October last year, New York-based magazine Global Finance chose me as one of the top four central heads in the world. They gave me a grade "A" rating along with the central bank chief of Sweden, Australia and the Bank of England. And last week, BusinessWeek magazine ranked me among the 25 Asian leaders at the forefront of change. I was the only central bank governor who made it to the list. Now you ask me: How is it being Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas? My answer is this: it is such an honor to serve as Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas for the distinct privilege it gives me to serve my country and our people. And it is also such an honor for me to work with the people of BSP who are so committed to high standards of excellence. Just to give you an idea of what I am talking about. In January 2002, BSP shifted its monetary policy framework from monetary aggregates to inflation targeting. Since then, we have been receiving very positive feedback from various institutions, such as the Bank of England and the IMF, on our successful shift to inflation targeting.
