Recently, I came across a study by noted European economists which rated the inflation reports produced by 20 inflation targeting central banks. The rating was based on quality and comprehensiveness of the information provided and how convincing the inflation report is judged to be. This is important as it serves as the main document for articulating the central bank's monetary policy strategy. I am very pleased to tell you that the BSP inflation report scored fairly well in the ranking, placing ahead of more experienced inflation targeters such as Canada, Australia, Israel and Peru. Of course, the number one on the list is the Bank of England. Still, for a relative newcomer such as the BSP, a rank of number 11 in a field of 20 is not bad. Give us more time and BSP will be higher up there. After all, the Bank of England is older than Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas by at least 300 years. I have been asked how heavy my burden is as Central Bank Governor. I am telling you, it is heavy; but because of the excellent support I get from my co-workers at BSP, I still have time in fact to improve my golf swing. In other words, it is a job that I love to do, challenges and all. Thank you and good night. (Note: British Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines, June Networking Evening, June 17, 2003, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Strengthening Links with Our Partners at PNP
Occasion: Flag Raising Ceremony, Philippine National Police
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction Good morning ladies and gentlemen. Allow me to welcome you all to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas and to thank you for inviting me to keynote this timely event. The discussions that will take place here today on the sustainability of the economic gains we have achieved so far is of particular relevance when taken in the context of Filipino culture. We are a nation that likes celebrating our successes. I guess this is why we have fiestas, although not as much now in Metro Manila as in the provinces. It is a good custom because it is our way of thanking the Lord and our patron saints for giving us good weather and the right elements for either a good harvest or for whatever positive results we seek from our efforts and hard work. It is not only good, it is also a lot of fun. But somewhere along the way, we yield to our huge hangovers and forget where all the merriment came from. We begin to relax and go back to a very laid back attitude until we reach a stage of inertia. We forget that we have to regain the energy and momentum to get back to work and continue to nurture the seedlings that have nicely grown from our earlier efforts until they eventually die on us and we are left with having to start again from scratch. I am talking about a very common trait among us Filipinos. We refer to it as "ningas cogon". As economists, you are all aware that the Philippines lagged its Asian neighbors in growth and development. While I laud the fact that our historical growth had been steady and sustained on account of strong consumer spending, we just never seem to grow at rates that befit our potential as a nation. Our nation has a wealth of resources, the most important being our human capital resource, which is now being recognized as one of, if not, the best in many skill-based sectors globally. We have a wealth of amazing natural wonders that are far more beautiful than many of the tourist attractions I have seen in the foreign countries I have visited. Yet, somehow, and I am troubled by this, we can't seem to overcome our inertia. We need to overcome this cultural peculiarity because other than that, we have all that it takes to become a tiger economy. And I have no better desire than for our nation to become a regional growth driver. Recent performance Last year, the Philippine economy displayed newfound strengths, enabling it to overcome the political shocks caused by the domestic transition in political leadership, the global correction in the high tech sector, and the 911 incident in the United States. Our DGP grew at a modest pace of 3.4 percent in 2001, outperforming all the projections of independent analysts. We all know the reasons behind such growth by now. We all had a plan for growth and we pursued it. We persisted and with much perseverance and professionalism, we prevailed. The plan carved out by the Government is one that aims for higher growth over the medium term, one that aims for sustainable development, one that seeks excellence. With ningas cogon in mind, we ourselves doubt if we can attain such growth objectives. So far this year, our targets appear to be highly attainable. In fact, based on trends we are seeing, the numbers continue to surprise us on the upside. The economic team is therefore looking to review the targets. Prudent fiscal and monetary management will still be our main guiding principles. Fiscal discipline from last year produced amazing results in bringing down our cost of borrowing and perceived risks. Hence, the team effort put forth by the economic managers in order to achieve such results deserve praise and encouragement. At the BSP I also laud the efforts of the Monetary Board and the rest of the institution for an effective monetary program that, in working with Government, has aided in bringing inflation down to levels we have not seen in a very long time, and has restored stability in our local currency. I am also happy to note that our international reserves are at levels beyond international benchmarks. Indeed our fundamentals are nearly back in shape. But so much work remains to be done if we are to achieve faster growth. Targets for 2002 and beyond Allow me to focus, however, on one task we need to do as a people. This is the inertia that has long gripped this nation. We need to get out of a box that has held our minds and psyche hostage. It is that box that prevents us from seeking our true potential as a nation. This box, I believe, is borne out of emulating a known Filipino legend we all know as Juan Tamad. Elementary teachers talk about him in schools. He comes across as a comic relief. Local movies even glorify him because he is quite entertaining. Unknowingly however, Juan Tamad has become deeply engrained in our minds as a local legend. But a very dangerous one, because the values he stands for keep us boxed up into mediocrity. Until now, many Filipinos like focusing on what it is that they cannot do, instead of exploring the many options available to achieve their goals. A favorite past time is self flagellation. Mistakes are glorified. Problems dominate conversations with little or no attention spent in coming up with real solutions. There is perception that problems will find their own solutions. This reminds me of the picture of Juan Tamad lying under a tree waiting for the fruit to fall into his mouth instead of getting up, picking the fruit and putting it into his mouth. Little does he know that a passerby could come by to grab the fruit, and he would live to wonder where he might have gone wrong. Similarly, many times as a nation, we miss opportunities because of inertia. Subconsciously, we allow more aggressive competitors to grab them. Hence, we have lagged behind the tiger economies of Asia in the last two decades. Fellow economists, we have been given another opportunity to pursue our goals with more vigor and valor. Let us rid our minds of the legendary Juan Tamad. In the context of nation building, he is not in the least funny. He has nothing good to teach us. He is lazy, idle, unproductive, and he has no future ahead of him. Pursuing the plan For nearly a year now, the Government has been communicating its plan for sustainable growth and development. Materials are available for anyone who cares to know about this plan. NEDA has a book on it. We launched it in briefings and have gone around the world and the country talking about it. We also have websites that contain this plan. I strongly believe, however, that plans need to be pursued. You see, Juan will die a very sad death from starvation, because he doesn't dare lift a finger to reach for his goal. Along the way, he might even be cursing the Government for not doing anything about his problem. But shame on Juan for being such a loser. As far as I am concerned, he is an alien and one that should be removed from Filipino consciousness. He does not deserve the kind of attention he has been getting. And so, I challenge you all to get up and pursue your goals. You cannot forever wait for government to give you everything. You are this country's most valuable resource. Put yourselves to good use and become millionaires over time. Millions don't just come from game shows. They also come from hard work. Persistence pays Be persistent. Don't let anything get in your way of achieving your goals. I recall not so long ago when we had to deal with heavy speculative attack on the peso. But our goal of keeping prices stable amid a mandate of maintaining a market driven foreign exchange system proved quite a challenge. Persistence paid. We looked for ways to solve the problem. When hiking reserve requirements proved insufficient, we resorted to harsher measures such as identifying and imposing penalties on speculators. Such moves, gained for us the respect of the financial community and up until now, without having to put good money after bad, our currency remains stable. Perseverance Perseverance will likewise help you endure challenges. The change in political leadership last year brought with it pressures for me to step down from my current position. But I kept myself focused on my mandate and worked even harder with my constituents. What you see now are the fruits of our hard labor, but fruits that we still need to guard until they are ripe for the picking. Professionalism Finally, the most enduring characteristic that we need to exercise in achieving our plans and our objectives is professionalism. This encompasses many other values we need to keep in mind. First is self appreciation for the innate skills we are gifted with. Enough of self flagellation and negativism. Let us get into the habit of counting our blessings. Second is honing such skills so we can achieve efficiency and expertise in the fields we choose to enter. Excellence is the key to becoming a tiger but excellence can only be achieved through dedication, constant practice, and exposure. Third is the ability to draw respect from your constituents. But drawing respect means giving it first and complementing that with hard work. Conclusion If you came here this morning to listen to me give you an earload of monetary policy, you must be disappointed. As a senior member of the economic team, I feel it is my duty to set the tone of the discussions that are yet to unfold today. Plans and goals are very important. But we sorely lack in implementation because first, we have to work toward adopting the right attitude. I hope I have given you enough this morning to guide you toward this direction. We need advocates of good values and work ethics because as far as I'm concerned, they are the key elements for sustainability. Join me in waking up a new and exciting character for the Filipino, one that is currently sleeping soundly in our subconscious. So that perhaps, one day, our children and theirs will begin learning about the life and times of Pedro Talipag, whose last name aptly stands for talino at sipag. Thank you very much and have a pleasant day ahead of you. (Note: "Regaining Economic Momentum: Macro and Micro Approaches", Annual Meeting, Philippine Economic Society, March 14, 2002, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila)

Title: New Year's Message 2003
Location: Fort San Antonio Abad, BSP Complex, Manila
Occasion: Annual Reception for the Banking Community
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Good evening ladies and gentlemen... Tonight, I will refrain from talking about monetary policies and banking fundamentals. You read and hear about that every single day in the papers or on radio and television. Instead, I would like to share with you a few thoughts about my term to date as the BSP Governor, simply because it has lent much color to my life as a person and to the Bangko Sentral as an institution. When I was offered the job as Governor of the BSP, I had reservations because I had no experience working in Government. It was a scary thought crossing the line from the private sector to the public sector. I kept thinking then that the risk was high because I was happy enough being in my comfort zone heading up one of the biggest local banks. But my desire to serve the country prevailed. And the rest is history. Now, you're stuck with me until 2004. When the impeachment trial for former President Estrada happened, my job became much harder and heavier. The stability of the whole monetary system was put to extreme test. We, at the Monetary Board, became very concerned about the economic well being of the country. But all those things came to pass swiftly. Thanks to People Power 2, a new administration was installed and the BSP survived the pressures of that historic event. Yet, new pressures arose. Some quarters wanted me to step down, while a few analysts and speculators started hitting on the peso. With the monetary system still on shaky ground, I listened to rational and reasonable advise from people who understood the demands of my job and my primary goal of keeping things in the monetary system in order. My resignation would have meant giving in to mob rule. It would have put the economy at risk. Moreover, it would have compromised the integrity of the Bangko Sentral, which is an institution that is, and should remain independent, and free of any political bias. Those pressures have likewise disappeared and the peso is now as steady as one can hope for given an equally challenging global environment. In retrospect, I could not have thought of a more colorful term for a BSP Governor. The events that took place in 2001 was a blessing in disguise because it became a defining moment for the role of the BSP Governor and the institution as a whole. It gave all of us a unique opportunity to assert our independence, our ability to transcend politics and to rise above challenges that, at that time, seemed to many to be as disastrous as the argentine crisis. We also feel fortunate that the new administration has recognized that independence and has since worked closely with us in achieving a common goal of promoting macroeconomic stability, long-term growth and development, and winning the war against poverty. And so, my dear friends in the banking community, we approach 2002 with increased confidence that, with your continued support, cooperation and increased understanding, we can achieve greater goals for the Philippine economy. I strongly believe that the Philippine banking system has come of age. It is ready to take bigger steps toward increasing its global competitiveness. It can deepen its market reach toward small-scale borrowers with a view to mobilizing resources in areas where growth opportunities are abundant, but are currently restricted by the lack of financial liquidity. The BSP, together with the executive and legislative branches of Government, will be steering you toward that direction with the aid of increased efficiency and supervisory powers, incentives, and legislative support. We realize that we need to make these new directions appetizing enough for you to chase and to pour resources into them. We are also committed to increased transparency. We realize that a successful economic program requires communicating our agenda to all our stakeholders. In fact, for the first time in Philippine history, the BSP and the National Government has included in its agenda holding regular economic briefings for both the local and international business community and the media. Just like stockholders meetings, these briefings make us account for our performance against program targets and rate ourselves accordingly. We provide analyses and allow ourselves to be grilled by the audience. As such, we develop a two-way communication process, because we know that feedback is just as important in the proper execution or implementation of our policies. To prove how strong an advocate I am of open communication within its legal confines, I am, perhaps, the only Central Bank Governor who can be reached wherever I am in the world, that is through texting. It is a proven theory, as far as I am concerned that, suspicions and speculations are bred by secrecy or by providing cryptic information. We will also focus on good corporate governance as one of the measures in improving asset quality in the banking system. We continue to seek amendments to the BSP Charter, which will enhance our supervisory powers, and raise our standards for credit risk assessment. This will be complemented by our commitment to shepherd congress into passing the bill creating special purpose asset vehicles so that we can authorize the entry of financing firms that help in liquefying our non-performing assets. While 2001 was a blessing in disguise, let us all hope that we have seen the end of it because, for health reasons, I can only take it and all of its pressures once in my lifetime. Meanwhile, let us welcome 2002 with open arms, and with an air of renewed optimism knowing that we, as a nation have been able to withstand crisis with flying colors. We now look forward to the chance to prove ourselves worthy of higher recognition by the international community, because I know by heart that the Filipino mind, talent, and spirit are among the finest in the world. Thank you very much and I wish you all the best for 2002. Have a pleasant evening. (Note: Annual Reception for the Banking Community, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, January 11, 2002, Fort San Antonio, BSP Complex, Manila)

Title: BSP and USAID: Joining Forces in the Fight Against Poverty
Location: Executive Business Center, BSP Complex, Manila
Occasion: Signing of the BSP-USAID Memorandum of Understanding on Technical Assistance Program
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Director Michael Yates, our other friends from the USAID, my co-workers at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, special guests. Good afternoon. Once again, we thank the USAID for its timely support for BSP's efforts in promoting microfinance, our flagship program for poverty alleviation. Under our Memorandum of Understanding on a Technical Assistance Program for Microfinance, BSP will get a much-needed boost in strengthening its capability to properly regulate and supervise microfinance operations of rural, thrift and commercial banks in the Philippines. Microfinance operations have peculiarities that set it apart from traditional banking practices. This program therefore should help us craft prudential regulation standards and discipline...through appropriate examination procedures, while allowing flexibility and keeping an open mind to the uniqueness of microfinance. The end goal is to promote microfinance as a viable tool for improving the lives of our entrepreneurial poor, while protecting the financial system from unsound practices. USAID's support comes at the right time because the number of institutions engaged in microfinance has been increasing, following of BSP's strategy of providing the appropriate policy and regulatory environment for microfinance. Right now we have 2 mirofinance-oriented thrift banks and 2 microfinance-oriented rural banks established under a BSP circular issued just last year. These four banks have been in operation for a period ranging from just one month to one year; and yet, they have been able to reach out to 35,000 microfinance clients already. In addition nearly 30 banks have significant microfinance operations: on the average, about 30% of their portfolio is dedicated to microfinance. Further, there are over 80 rural banks who are engaged in microfinance. These are the banks linked to the microenterprise access to banking services program, which, by the way, USAID also supports. About eight more microfinance-oriented banks are in the pipeline. It is also interesting to note that many other microfinance groups including cooperatives and NGOs are signifying interest in similarly transforming into microfinance-oriented banks. To sustain this momentum and ensure the long-term viability of microfinance institutions, we do need to institutionalize microfinance supervision at BSP. We need to do this so that even if we are no longer around, a strong and vibrant microfinance sector will continue our fight against poverty in the Philippines. Once again, I thank USAID for its continuing support to BSP, to our country and the Filipino people. Mabuhay kayo! (Note: Signing of the BSP-USAID Memorandum of Understanding on Technical Assistance Program on Microfinance, December 16, 2002, Executive Business Center, BSP Complex, Manila)

Title: Joining Hands for a World-Class Philippine Payment System (PhilPass)
Location: Executive Business Center, BSP Complex, Manila
Occasion: Launching of the Philippine Payment System (PhilPaSS)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Good afternoon to our partners in the banking community, our visitors from the IMF, our friends from the media, my co-workers in government, ladies and gentlemen. Once again, BSP and the banking community are proving that the best way to move forward, and to reach a common goal, is through cooperation...working things out and taking joint responsibility for its outcome. And so, once again, together, we mark another milestone toward strengthening the Philippine banking system, this time, with the launching of a real-time gross settlement system or what is generically known as RTGS. BSP itself has invested over P100 million to set up PhilPaSS, our version of an RTGS deemed by the Bank for International Settlements as essential for the growth and stability of a national payments infrastructure system. With PhilPaSS, systemic risk is minimized as real-time high value payments between banks are made using their deposit accounts with BSP. This allows BSP to monitor liquidity positions of participating banks throughout the day, on a transaction-by-transaction basis, so settlements are made only when banks have sufficient funds. In other words, PhilPaSS is a vital component for ensuring sound risk management. Based on a soft launch which started last November 22, PhilPaSS has been averaging P100 billion a day from settlements of participating universal and commercial banks as well as a number of thrift banks and investment houses. By September next year, this volume will increase some more as PhilPaSS transactions will include bank settlements for government securities issued by the Bureau of Treasury. Indeed, the challenge before us is to maximize utilization of a real-time payments infrastructure system such as PhilPaSS. For instance, banks can now offer to do guaranteed payments with final and irrevocable settlement to large corporate customers, including multinationals. Irrevocable settlements provided by PhilPaSS can also be of value to retail customers of banks when, for instance, a transfer of house ownership goes together with a guaranteed real-time payment. In the future, PhilPaSS may also be linked with the Philippine Stock Exchange for real-time settlement of stock transactions using the delivery versus payment mode. By the way, BSP has set up mirror sites to serve as backups for PhilPaSS to ensure the system's smooth and uninterrupted operations. All of these should generate stronger confidence in the integrity and dependability of our banking system. May I just point out that even as we work to provide a modern banking infrastructure, parallel efforts are being made by BSP for reforms that would create a more stable and globally competitive banking sector. This includes working closely with Congress for the passage of an asset management company law that would ease the burden of non-performing assets of the banking sector. The bill has now passed both Houses of Congress and is being deliberated upon by a bi-cameral committee. As of June 30 this year, non-performing assets of the banking sector reached P520 billion, equivalent to 14.9% of total assets of Philippine banks. Another legislative reform that banks should watch out for is the amendment of the Anti-Money Laundering Act to match the requirements of the Financial Action Task Force. We need this to spare our country from possible sanctions imposed on so-called non-cooperative nations. The stakes involved here are high, as FATF sanctions are bound to delay remittances of millions of our overseas workers to their respective families. On the average, OFWs send $ 500 million a month to the Philippines. May I also take this opportunity to inform all of you that the FATF has warned the public against unscrupulous parties claiming to charge, on its behalf, alleged clearance fees for fund transfers. So, to the banks present here, help protect our OFWs from these fraudulent charges. Before I get carried away any further....I just want to reiterate that we at BSP are indeed proud to have our own real time gross settlement system with PhilPaSS and we thank all of you for joining us this afternoon. Let me also take this opportunity to be the first to greet all of you a Merry Christmas. Thank you all. (Note: Launching of the Philippine Payment System (PhilPaSS), December 12, 2002, Executive Business Center, BSP Complex, Manila)

Title: The First Citibank Microentreprenuer of the Year Award
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Magandang hapon po sa inyong lahat. I must say, this is one memorable afternoon for all of us. Finally, the members of the Board of Judges in this First Citibank Microentrepreneur of the Year Award get to meet the winners: these inspiring women who, individually and collectively, fortify our belief that microfinance can indeed be a powerful tool for improving one's quality of life; that given the right support, Filipino ingenuity, patience and honesty can produce amazingly good results. The story of your success and accomplishments should encourage many of our kababayan to be equally resourceful in identifying business opportunities within their respective communities. You are true investors; you generate employment; and you foster economic growth. And all of you have plans to expand your business. Truly, in your own way, you are doing a lot to help your country. Tulad ng ating mga overseas workers, kayo po ay mga bagong bayani ng ating bansa. Again, let us give all the winners a round of applause! Of course we must also give due credit to all microfinance institutions who support microentrepreneurs. You also deserve a round of applause. Let us also congratulate Citibank for immediately heeding and responding to Government's call for support for microfinance, the national flagship program for poverty alleviation. I understand this is the first time, anywhere in the world, that Citibank is embarking on an advocacy program for microfinance. It is remarkable, therefore, that it took Citibank, one of world's biggest banks, to fashion a program to reward microentrepreneurs in the Philippines. Indeed, no one is too big, nor too small, in the fight against poverty. For instance, Father Barcelon tells us that in Mindanao, they met some of their program beneficiaries to evaluate whether microfinance was really making a difference. A father of six, who received a microfinance loan of just a thousand pesos, told Father Barcelon that this spelled the difference for his family to graduate from eating just once a day, to having three meals daily. And in Negros, a federation of microfinance organizations is now able to provide insurance at very affordable rates not only to their 40,000 member-borrowers but to their spouses as well. Certainly, as microfinance beneficiaries become successful, they gain purchasing power that spur economic activities and generate surplus funds that find its way to the banks as deposits; deposits that can help fund other business ventures. And so, through microfinance, we are not only alleviating poverty; we are also laying the foundation for solid and sustainable growth in urban centers and the countryside. This is the reason why Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has been a principal advocate and supporter of microfinance. So far, BSP has issued four Circulars that recognize and promote microfinance as a legitimate banking operation. BSP Circular 272, issued in early 2001, laid down the guidelines to implement the provisions of the General Banking Law of 2000 on microfinance operations. Through Circular 273, BSP lifted the moratorium on the issuance of licenses for the opening of new thrift and rural banks, as well as branches for existing banks, to encourage banking institutions to venture into microfinance. On the other hand, Circular 282 opened a rediscounting window to refinance the loan portfolio of microfinance-oriented rural banks and provide additional liquidity for micro lending Finally, Circular 324 issued early this year, included thrift banks among the eligible borrowers under the BSP microfinance rediscounting facility. I am happy to announce, that BSP's strategy of providing the appropriate policy and regulatory environment for microfinance is already bearing fruit. Right now we have 2 mirofinance-oriented thrift banks (Opportunity Microfinance Bank and Microenterprise Bank) and 2 microfinance-oriented rural banks (Vision Bank and Banco ng Masa) established under Circular 273. (This does not include card which was established before the circular). These four banks have been in operation for a period ranging from just one month to one year; and yet, they have been able to reach out to 35,000 microfinance clients already. About eight more microfinance-oriented banks are in the pipeline. It is also interesting to note that many other microfinance groups including cooperatives and NGOs are signifying interest in similarly transforming into microfinance-oriented banks. In addition, there are over 80 rural banks who are engaged in microfinance, even if they are not a fully microfinance-oriented bank. These are the banks linked to the Microenterprise Access to Banking Services Program. Please note that our National Awardee this year, Ms. Josephine Alima, is a client of FICO bank, a rural bank in Isabela. I also wish to report that so far, eight banks with over 7,000 clients have availed of BSP's rediscounting window, and more are being processed. Indeed, we can say we are on the right track. As part of our continuing efforts to mainstream microfinance within BSP and the banking community, we have initiated the following: A comprehensive training program to develop a core group of examiners, supervisors and regulators knowledgeable in microfinance operations; A review of our Manual of Regulations to make it more attuned to microfinance operations. BSP is doing this under a USAID-funded technical assistance program; The incorporation of microfinance as part of the rural and thrift banking courses; Workshops and exposure trips for our bank personnel to successful microfinance institutions to keep them abreast of the latest methodologies and technologies in the field; The creation within BSP of a microfinance committee that provides the overall direction of BSP's microfinance initiatives and a microfinance unit that serves as coordinating body to ensure continuity of the programs and projects; A regional advocacy program to promote microfinance in a roadshow that will cover BSP regulations on microfinance, best practices, and inspiring success stories. Actually, BSP's involvement in promoting microfinance extends beyond the banking community. Among others, BSP is participating in the national effort to establish a regulatory framework for microfinance. I am narrating all of these things to underscore the importance BSP attaches to microfinance. For indeed, we need to gather as many advocates as possible to work together in alleviating poverty, which afflicts one out of three Filipinos. In fact, no less than President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo has declared that microfinance represents the cornerstone of her administration's poverty alleviation program. And so, to all of you who are here this afternoon, continue in spreading the good news about microfinance. Be an advocate. Help our country. And to all the men who are here today and who are out there, I challenge you to prove yourselves equal to these successful women. Come and join the microfinance sector, so that we would have at least a token representative in the ranks of Citibank's microentrepreneur awardees. Catherine Weir here assures me that men entrepreneurs were, and will be, given equal opportunity in Citibank's microentrepreneur awards race. Again, on behalf of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, congratulations to Citibank, the microfinance institutions and to all our successful microentrepreneurs. Muli, magandang hapon sa inyong lahat. (Note: The First Citibank Microentreprenuer of the Year Award, November 19, 2002, Metropolitan Museum, BSP Complex, Manila)

Title: Welcome Remarks
Location: Executive Business Center, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila
Occasion: Joint Governance Advisory Council - Capital Market Development Council
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Good morning. I am pleased to welcome all of you today at the Executive Business Center of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas for the Joint Governance Advisory Council - Capital Market Development Council Working Sessions on Moving Forward with Governance Reforms in the Philippines. Title: Closing Remarks
Location: Century Park Sheraton Hotel, Manila Fellow bank supervisors and regulators, distinguished resource p
Occasion: Closing Ceremony, SEACEN-FSI Workshop for Bank Supervisors and Regulators
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Fellow bank supervisors and regulators, distinguished resource persons: Mr. Thomas Morck of the Deutsche Bundesbank, Mr. Roland Raskopf of the BIS Financial Stability Institute, SEACEN Centre Officials: Mr. Cheong Kwok Yew and Mrs. Wong Yoke Mei, co-workers in the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, honored guests and friends, good afternoon! It is indeed an honor for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas to co-host this workshop jointly with the SEACEN Centre and the Financial Stability Institute of the Bank for International Settlements. We are grateful to the course organizers for bringing together such a notable team of experts in the fields of securitization, risk management and the new capital accord. Four and a half days surely is such a short time to fully cover these broad subjects. However, judging by the course syllabus (not to mention your looks this afternoon), I believe that you have had some grueling discussions on the current trends in global financial markets and the subsequent impact of these trends on the way financial institutions do business these days. Having done so, I am certain you now have a deeper understanding of the underlying principles of asset securitization, risk management and new capital accord. A solid and firm understanding of these subjects are but some of the must-have tools for bank supervisors and regulators to remain effective in our ever increasingly becoming sophisticated banking environment. I agree with what Mr. Brad Shinn of the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institution said on the first day of this workshop. It is really quite easy to get lost into the technical details of asset securitization. This is particularly true if the uninitiated is faced with the maze-like complexity of the specially structured securitization transactions. I am sure that everyone here will also agree when I say that Asian banks are not that far behind their counterparts in Europe and in the Americas when it comes to the offering of new, innovative and complex financial products. Neither are we in the early stages in the evolution spectrum of credit business models. Using Mr. Bill glass' presentation, I believe Asian banks are now in the middle stage as most Asian banks are into active portfolio management. Moreover, Asian banks are already inching their way into the third stage - advanced credit portfolio management. These banks are now transforming their risks into marketable products. They are, as a consequence, also investing in highly sophisticated risk management technologies. Also, I am particularly happy to note that you have been introduced to a scenario of future directions in banks' risk management practice. The experiences of banks in more mature financial markets certainly provide a comprehensive frame of reference for us supervisors and regulators in this part of the world. Notwithstanding our country differences, our main task, as supervisors and regulators, remains that of ensuring that financial institutions under our respective jurisdiction operate in a safe and sound manner. Accordingly, it is but proper to update and upgrade our regulatory and supervisory tools to international best practice/standards in the light of the new developments. Doing so will surely enhance our chances of success in effectively performing our main function. Compliance with the new capital accord, with its focus on flexibility and risk sensitivity, is a major step towards this end. Understanding the new accord is of paramount importance. I am sure that this workshop has gained headway towards this direction given the presence, particularly of Mr. Stefan Hohl and Mr. Roland Raskopf. We are indeed grateful to all the resource persons and the course organizers for selflessly sharing their valuable time and expertise. And to all the 33 participants, congratulations. Let me commend all of you for your diligence and active participation not only during the regular sessions as well as in the non-technical aspects of this workshop. You are enriched not just by the new learnings and technical knowledge but no less so by the new friendships you have formed. I cannot overemphasize the value of these networks especially when you find yourselves needing to act quickly in a crisis. Who knows? As a final note, I call on you to exercise greater vigilance in guarding and promoting the financial stability in our respective jurisdiction. That certainly is not a simple task. Hence, we need to work out a more intensive collaboration. I wish all of you a pleasant and an enjoyable city tour this afternoon. Also, have a nice trip home. I am looking forward to seeing you all again in the near future. Thank you once again. (Note: Closing Ceremony, SEACEN-FSI Workshop for Bank Supervisors and Regulators: Asset Securitization, Risk Management and the New Capital Accord, November 08, 2002, Century Park Sheraton Hotel, Manila)

Title: CFAs: Developing a Culture that Rewards Ethical Behavior
Occasion: 2002 CFA Charter Award Ceremonies, Association of Investment Professionals - Manila
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: (Thank you Gina for that generous introduction. I understand Gina carries the distinction of being the only female president in Asia of a Chapter of the Association of Investment Professionals.) Magandang gabi po sa inyong lahat. You must forgive me if I open my speech with a cliché, for this is truly how I feel. I am honored to be with you tonight, when 14 more individuals are awarded the globally-recognized Chartered Financial Analyst designation. I understand from your President that the Association of Investment Professionals - Manila (AIPM) now has 42 CFA members. This means that tonight, the number of CFAs in our country increased by 33%! If AIPM can sustain this growth rate, things are likely to get better faster in our financial system. I am sure all of you here tonight realize that more than ever, the financial community, here and overseas, need investment professionals who can be relied on to provide excellent service, while adhering strictly to the industry code of ethics. Our 14 new CFAs went through a minimum of three years of rigorous studies, three levels of examination and demonstrated commitment to ethical behavior to earn this globally recognized stamp of excellence and integrity. We salute you for your perfect anticipation and timing. And so, ladies and gentlemen, let us give our new CFAs a round of applause. Indeed, given the range and magnitude of corporate misdeeds we hear and read about from overseas, good corporate governance is what the world needs today; CFAs definitely will play a key role in ensuring that the guiding principles of fairness, accountability and transparency are religiously followed. Now, it is no longer enough that one is a skilled professional who can contribute much to the bottom line; ethical behavior is a must. Individuals and institutions have since learned that, in the end, adherence to ethical behavior makes a lot of business sense; that short-term gains made at the expense of ethics, generate penalties so severe that can send executives to prison and companies to bankruptcy. Overseas, in the United States especially, companies are hiring what are now called "ethics cops." Their job is to develop a corporate culture that rewards fair play and respect for law. Precisely the standards of CFAs. I hope all CFAs present here tonight are doing their own share of helping develop a culture of fair play and ethical behavior in their respective institutions. We do need to spread the word; and practice what we preach. Walk the talk, in other words. I am sure you have heard of this company who was providing ethics consultancy services; this year, it was found guilty of illegal business practices. Obviously, this consultancy firm knew the ethical rules; however, its people succumbed to pressure. Pressure. That is the one thing CFAs like you must guard against. At all times, you must protect your independence. Of course, this is easier said than done. As the mentor of Harry Potter said, it is much more difficult to adhere to your principles when you are going against friends. We all know that unlike many industries, the margin that separates ethical from unethical conduct in the investment business is not always so clear. It is only with a clear understanding of how to apply rules, regulations and ethical guidelines that investment professionals can safely avoid ethical quandaries and properly serve their clients and employers. Investment professionals are obliged to exercise diligence and thoroughness in all areas of investment decision-making process. As CFA charterholders, you are now fully equipped to do this function. Let me talk a little about parallel concerns we have at Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. BSP's mandate is to serve as guardian of price and banking stability. Economies need a stable environment to ensure sustained growth. At BSP our bank examiners have to guard against people and institutions which can threaten the stability of the banking sector, through the irresponsible and illegal use of other people's money. Fortunately, we have a lot of good men and women at the BSP who are not afraid to do the right thing, even in the face of pressure and possible lawsuits. Of course, even I am not spared from these lawsuits. What is important is for us to remain focused and adhere to ethical practices, come what may. Sometimes, you may feel alone, confused, even afraid. But I have seen enough of the world to be able to tell you that by and large, the truth will prevail and vindication will come your way. Even now, I see this at BSP. For instance, in the last two surveys of the Makati Business Club, BSP emerged as the top performing government agency. Imagine what more we can do if BSP itself will have CFAs in our midst. I was therefore happy to learn from Gina that AIPM has a scholar from BSP - our Bank Examiner Mary Anne Chong. I am also happy to announce to you that we are now processing the papers of CFA Michael Oliver Manuel who will join the Monetary Policy Unit of BSP's Department of Economic Research. I assure you, BSP is behind you in encouraging the development of more CFAS in our country. Good governance should be fundamental not only to banks but also to the whole financial system as it engenders public trust and confidence that are inherent to the fiduciary business. That your organization has established a career-development path with the highest standards for investment professionals through your CFA program is a big contribution to our initiatives for good corporate governance. I therefore commend AIPM and its officers for their missionary zeal in promoting the cause of CFAS. May your tribe increase. Marami pong salamat. (Note: 2002 CFA Charter Award Ceremonies, Association of Investment Professionals - Manila, November 07, 2002, Manila Peninsula Hotel, Manila)

Title: Closing Remarks
Location: Executive Business Center, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila
Occasion: BSP's Strategic Management Process Conference
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Before I bring this conference to a close, I wish to highlight the significance of this conference that makes it stand-out among our past conferences: It is our first attempt to synchronize the planning and budgeting activities of the bank. From here on, I look forward to the implementation on a more permanent basis of a planning- programming-budgeting continuum, where agreed strategic plans during the conference are translated to specific programs and projects, whose budgetary implications are incorporated in the bank's medium-term financial program; It is also the first effort to monitor organization-wide our activities based on key result areas instead of on a per project basis arising from individual action plans of departments; It is our first conference with a theme, highlighting the need to respond to change with a "best practice" orientation as can be seen from the choice of workshop topics; It is our first undertaking where top management - the Monetary Board and Deputy Governors - participated actively in a pre-conference strategic management workshop. I likewise look forward to similar exercises in future conferences to ensure a meeting of minds between the policy formulators and the program implementers on the direction that the Bank would take in the near- and medium-term to bring us closer to our vision of being a world-class monetary authority; It is our first conference conducted entirely on weekdays. I know all of you look forward to future conferences not falling on a week-end--that can be arranged; and Finally, it is the first conference organized by the CPO which at present is a three-man team, within a two and a half month period with a very modest budget. I wish to commend the organizers of this conference in this respect. Certainly, the active participation of all of you was crucial in making this activity a productive and useful exercise. The cross-sectoral constitution of each workshop group was intentional. It would have been more manageable if the workshop groupings were on a sectoral basis. The Supervision and Examination Sector could have been assigned the Basel Core Principles of Banking Supervision or the Resource Management Sector the Resource Infrastructure Group. But this was not done. The organizers of this conference believe that a cross-sectoral grouping would ensure that each group would benefit from the varying degree of richness in experience and exposure of the individual members. Based on the depth of the presentations and discussions today, they were right. This conference has indeed been a forum for the sharing of valuable information, insights and ideas from all participants. I wish to congratulate all of you for a job well done. The CMC chairman reported significant accomplishments within a six-month period on previous years' Corplan agreements and within a two-month period on the April Corplan agreements. I wish to commend all BSP departments/offices responsible for such an accomplishment. I also wish to commend the technical and administrative arrangements made by the Corporate Planning Office for the conference, notwithstanding time and budgetary constraints. As I officially close this conference, I urge all of you not to stop at visioning. We should walk the talk. I expect to see positive results from the plans and strategies laid out for the Bank during this conference. Thank you and again congratulations to all. (Note: BSP Strategic Management Process Conference, October 24-25, 2002, Executive Business Center, BSP, Manila)

Title: Opening Remarks
Location: Executive Business Center, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila
Occasion: BSP's Strategic Management Process Conference
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I. The BSP Vision In March this year, the Monetary Board approved the BSP's vision and mission statements, which were products of long and impassioned debates among middle management during a series of pre-conference workshops in February and March. The BSP's vision statement, which should serve as a guide post to all our efforts states that: "the BSP, imbued with the values of integrity, excellence and patriotism, aims to be a world-class monetary authority and a catalyst for a globally competitive economy and financial system that delivers a high quality of life for all Filipinos." In early September, the corporate planning office facilitated a visioning and direction-setting workshop among the BSP's top management consisting of the Monetary Board members and the deputy governors. The workshop gave top management the opportunity to revisit the BSP vision statement and ponder on what it means operationally, and the commitment it entails from each of us in the BSP. Compared with the vision statements of other central banks, ours stands out because it gives high priority to the promotion of three important values that should define the conduct of our work as the independent monetary authority of the country. By espousing the value of integrity, we articulate our desire to perform our mandate with sincerity, honesty and uprightness worthy of respect and emulation by those we supervise; by promoting the value of excellence, we express our dedication to achieve a level of competence in service delivery comparable with the more respected central banks in the world; and by upholding the value of patriotism, we affirm our selfless commitment to the service of the Filipino people and the country. Moreover, our vision of a world-class monetary authority--a leading practitioner in the region--attests to our highest aspiration to play the role of a catalyst in driving the Philippine economy to new heights. II. Visions ahead Keeping the BSP vision in mind, I foresee: A BSP implementing best practices in monetary policy setting, resulting in stable inflation conducive to growth and comparing favorably with our Asian neighbors; A financial system with fewer but bigger and stronger banks resulting from an effective consolidated banking supervision; A satisfied BSP work force transformed into a learning community that is productive, competent, highly responsive to client needs and the challenges of change; A BSP infrastructure equipped with the state-of-the-art facilities and technologies able to safeguard information and property; enhance work productivity; promote employees' welfare; and respond to contingencies. III. What needs to be done Noted futurist Joel Barker once said, "Vision without action is merely a dream. Action without vision just passes the time. Vision with action can change the world". Now that we have defined our vision of what the future BSP should be, the next step is to chart the courses of action that would lead to the realization of this vision. This is the main objective of this conference. To achieve this objective, it is important to keep in mind that our success in realizing our vision would hinge on our capacity to hone further our strengths, mitigate our weaknesses; manage threats; and maximize opportunities. It also demands from each employee of the bank, regardless of rank, ownership of and total commitment to the vision. This is where your role as senior officers of the bank could be pivotal. Your actions should reflect ownership and commitment to the vision at all times. IV. Commitment of top management On my part, I am committing top management to a role model leadership--practicing what we are preaching; to establish the foundations for a holistic development of each employee in the bank and to assure each employee of self-fulfillment through satisfaction in the workplace. V. Conclusion As in the past, I am confident that our 1 ½ days conference will be characterized by candid and constructive discussions on how the bank can lay the foundations that would enable it to anticipate and respond to the challenges of change today and in the future. Considering the "many firsts" in this conference, I expect to see the first strategic plan of the BSP formulated as a result of this conference. May this conference dictate the necessary actions that we need to do today in order to achieve our objectives tomorrow. Thank you and good day. (Note: BSP Strategic Management Process Conference, October 24-25, 2002, Executive Business Center, BSP, Manila)

Title: Welcome Remarks
Location: Executive Business Center, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, Manila
Occasion: Annual General Meeting, Microfinance Council of the Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction Distinguished officers and members of the Microfinance Council of the Philippines, Inc. (MCPI), ladies and gentlemen: good morning. I am happy to welcome all of you to the Executive Business Center of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. It is always a pleasure for me to address the Council whose tireless works in the field of microfinance have led to the fast-tracking of microfinance projects in the country. Hosting this annual general meeting is BSP's way of showing invaluable support to the Council's objectives. Today's assembly affords us with an overview of the developments in microfinance. I hope this meeting will provide the perfect venue for assessing performance -- thereby making way for further improvements -- and setting appropriate goals for the promotion of microfinance. BSP and microfinance As you very well know, the promotion of microfinance has been identified as the signature project of the BSP in full support of the national agenda on poverty alleviation. Toward this end, the BSP has taken bold initiatives in the areas of establishing an enabling policy and regulatory environment, capacity building, promotion and advocacy. I am happy to report to you that we have made significant progress in pushing for microfinance initiatives. As a matter of fact, we have taken further steps by streamlining microfinance operations within the BSP. We have started to enhance the process of internalizing and institutionalizing microfinance by creating a Microfinance Committee (MFN Committee) and a Microfinance Unit (MFN unit) within the BSP. Generally, the MFN Committee is tasked to provide the policy framework and overall direction on BSP's microfinance initiatives, as well as oversight on the activities of the proposed microfinance unit in the BSP. On the other hand, the MFN Unit is envisioned to quarterback and liaise with the different operating units such steps and activities that may be needed to implement the committee's decisions, directions and initiatives. Evidently, we are continually looking for ways to increase our knowledge and capability to promote sustainable microfinance. We believe there is still a lot of work to be done. With the continuous need of the poor for financial services, as well as with the increased number of new entrants in the field of microfinance, the challenge before us has never been greater. It is, therefore, heartening to see that the Council has bravely risen to this challenge. MCPI programs At this point, I would like to cite the Council's major contributions in spearheading microfinance. The Council's responsive programs and pro-active networking have led to the improved performance of its members, as well as an increase in its membership, which now includes four rural banks. Likewise, the establishment of performance standards for your members, augmented with the conferences and training courses that you have conducted, has instilled the importance of sustainability and viability in microfinance operations. Indeed, only sustainable microfinance institutions (MFIs) can provide continuous access to quality financial services for the entrepreneurial poor. I am happy to note that your members are adopting these standards and are seeing the positive effects both on their financial operations, as well as in the depth and breadth of their outreach. Also worth mentioning is your work in providing useful information and valuable insights to practitioners, policymakers, and the general public. Future challenges I will not take a minute longer as I know that there is a lot that we have to accomplish today. The coming year presents the Council with even greater tasks. Among others, the regulatory framework for microfinance, which was recently approved by the National Credit Council, gives the MCPI an important responsibility of being the repository of information of microfinance NGOs. Transparent and accessible information is crucial in ensuring sound operations by MFIs, specifically NGOs as they are not regulated. Ultimately, the collection of complete, correct and comparable data can set the groundwork for establishing a rating agency and credit bureau for MFIs across the formal and informal sector. With the able and dynamic membership of the Council, I am confident that you will see the rewards of your efforts in the near future. Rest assured that the BSP would remain dedicated in working towards the development of sustainable microfinance programs in the country. More power to the Microfinance Council! Thank you and good day! (Note: Annual General Meeting, Microfinance Council of the Philippines, September 11, 2002, Executive Business Center, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas City)

Title: A Monetary Policy Framework to Support Economic Recovery and Maintain Price Stability
Occasion: Joint General Meeting, ACI Philippines, MART and TOAP
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction Mr. Horacio Cebrero III, President, Association Cambiste Internationale (ACI) Philippines--the Financial Markets Association; Mr. Roberto Juanchito Dispo, President, Money Market Association of the Philippines (MART); Ms. Ma. Elena Sarmiento, President, Trust Officers Association of the Philippines (TOAP); distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, good evening. I take great pleasure in speaking before the joint general membership meeting of the ACI Philippines, the Money Markets Association of the Philippines, and the Trust Officers Association of the Philippines. The membership of your respective associations, indeed, constitutes the front-liners and market movers whose views and decisions wield considerable influence over the economy. I am, therefore, quite aware of the importance that this general membership meeting presents as a venue for a frank exchange of ideas and assessment of direction of the economy. I have been requested to update you on the latest policy issues involving growth and inflation targets. I hope that this occasion will provide an opportunity for a fruitful exchange of views on the subject. Despite some difficult challenges, the economy fares much better today than it did at the beginning of 2001, when several domestic concerns and a weak global economy dampened both domestic and external investor confidence. In 2001, exports contracted by 16.7 percent, as our major trading partner, the United States, suffered an economic slowdown. Today, despite a still-weak international environment, there are indications that the business cycle has bottomed out. The foreign exchange market has broadly stabilized and external trade has started to move up, although some uncertainty regarding the pace of global economic recovery remains. On the domestic front, inflation has gone down considerably, allowing wide latitude for monetary authorities to reduce interest rates to historic lows and help support economic recovery while ensuring that the price stability objective is met. Banks have remained resilient and stable and the banking system's asset quality remains manageable. Maintaining price stability... The BSP's focus on achieving price stability has been enhanced by the switch since January 2002 to inflation targeting as a monetary policy framework. Under this framework, the authorities pre-announce the inflation target over a given time horizon. If the target is not met, the BSP will be required to explain the reasons and map out the measures that it will take to get back on track. Thus, there is greater accountability for its actions on the part of the BSP. The framework, therefore, will help the BSP build its credibility by demonstrating consistent adherence to the price stability objective. In the process, inflation targeting is expected to promote greater transparency in the conduct of monetary policy, thus facilitating the functioning of efficient financial markets. For 2002 and 2003, the Government's target for annual inflation has been set at 4.5-5.5 percent. Since the BSP is the institution primarily in charge of promoting price stability, it is appropriate that I begin today's discussion with an assessment of the inflation outlook. We note that the Ateneo Center for Economic Research has assessed inflation management as "the greatest success of the current government", and attributed the low inflation rate to the combined effects of favorable agricultural production, trade liberalization and prudent monetary policy. [1] As you know, inflation remained muted at 2.9 percent in August. This brought the average inflation rate so far to 3.3 percent for January-August 2002, which is about one percentage-point below the lower end of the Government's target range for 2002. The favorable inflation environment and lower foreign interest rates created room for a careful easing of monetary policy. Policy rates have declined by 800 basis points since the BSP started to ease policy rates in December 2000. The inflation record so far, coupled with favorable supply conditions, broad stability in the exchange rate and continued soft--though improving-- demand conditions, support the BSP's expectation of a generally calm inflation outlook for 2002. Some inflationary headwinds could still surface over the policy horizon, however, and may contribute to inflationary pressures beginning in the first half of 2003. There are uncertainties concerning the full impact of the anticipated El Niño weather phenomenon on agricultural output, a possible uptrend in world oil prices, possible adjustments in power and water rates and their expected second round effects on the prices of other commodities and on wages, as well as market concerns over the fiscal deficit and external pressures on the peso. There is, therefore, some possibility of inflationary pressures surfacing in the first half of 2003. Going forward, therefore, there is a need for continued caution in setting the monetary policy stance. Given the preceding factors and the uncertainty over the robustness of the world economic upturn, the Monetary Board has decided to keep the interest rates on the BSP's overnight borrowing or RRP rate and overnight lending or RP rate at 7.0 percent and 9.25 percent, respectively, which are the rates that have been maintained since 15 March 2002. The Monetary Board is of the view that the current monetary policy stance is appropriately supportive of the economy's growth and price stability objectives. For the rest of the year, therefore, the BSP sees the need to allow past monetary easing measures to flow through the economy to have a firmer indication of the extent to which recent policy moves have been transmitted to the real sector. At the same time, the BSP is of the view that monetary policy should continue to focus on ensuring conditions that will strengthen domestic demand. This involves keeping policy rates steady in order to foster a low market interest rate environment that is supportive of the country's growth objectives while ensuring that price pressures are contained. In summary, notwithstanding the aforementioned risks, we can be confident of attainment of inflation targets for 2002 and 2003, helped by the currently benign inflation environment....conducive to a balanced and sustainable economic growth With the easing in monetary policy, the benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate fell from an average of 12.2 percent in January 2001 to 5.7 percent in January-June 2002 and further down to 4.9 percent in July-August 2002. As of the 2 September auction, the 91-day t-bill rate stood at 5.2 percent. Reflecting this trend, bank lending rates declined from a range of 16.5-18.2 percent in January 2001 to 8.0-9.8 percent in August 2002. The generally low interest rate environment is expected to exert a favorable impact on overall prices by helping reduce the cost of capital for firms and the debt service burden of corporates. The decline in interest rates is also expected to provide impetus for investment and consumption, and help support our economic recovery. To this end, we are heartened by the higher-than-expected 4.5 percent and 5.2 percent second quarter 2002 growth rates in GDP and GNP, respectively. The economy's growth was broad-based and was sustained by healthier demand from both domestic and foreign markets. In terms of sectoral composition, although agriculture slowed down in the second quarter, industry recovered strongly. Moreover, the decline in investment slowed down, suggesting a bottoming out. The strong industrial recovery was led by manufacturing, which grew by 5.0 percent. Growth in services continued to be led by double-digit growth in communications. These developments further bolster our confidence that the Government's full-year growth targets of 4.0-4.5 percent for real GDP and 4.5-5.0 for real GNP for 2002 will be met. For 2003, the Government is targeting growth of 5.4-5.9 percent for GDP and 5.5-6.0 percent for GNP, based on a projected recovery in investments and exports. To this end, key legislative measures are needed to push the economic reform agenda forward and attract both foreign and domestic investors. These measures include passage of the Special Purpose Asset Vehicle (SPAV) Law, which will allow the inflow of millions of dollars into the country. Recent developments in the fiscal position have raised some concern regarding the Government's ability to control the budget deficit for 2002, and the possible negative implications of such a deficit on the attainability of the Government's growth and inflation objectives. We should, however, place matters in their proper perspective. Given the prevailing low interest rate environment, the benign inflation outlook, and the generally strong state of the economy, the BSP can flexibly and comfortably accommodate a moderate overrun in the fiscal sector. As a result of our better-than-expected monetary performance, the deficit does not currently warrant a monetary response. The BSP can continue to pursue its monetary policy stance with the expectation that market interest rates will remain in their current range. The Government's approach to deficit reduction is aggressive fiscal discipline--expenditure control throughout the Government coupled with concerted efforts to increase revenues. The reforms include instituting an e-filing and payment system as well as VAT audit and internal audit systems. These reforms, together with aggressive regulation enforcement and accelerated prosecution of tax evaders, are already producing results in terms of increased revenue collection. External position We have so far achieved a much improved balance of payments (BOP) position, with a higher surplus in the current account and a substantial improvement in the capital and financial account. The BOP for January-May 2002 yielded a surplus of US$1.889 billion, as opposed to the US$797 million deficit for the comparable period last year. The current account posted a US$3.182 billion surplus, buoyed by a strong growth in merchandise exports, as increased demand from Asian markets compensated for the lower demand from the U.S. and Japan. In July, exports grew by 23.0 percent year-on-year, in line with the improving electronics sector. Meanwhile, imports of goods expanded in June by 9.3 percent. The import recovery reflected in part replenishment and inventory build-up as the manufacturing sector geared up in expectation of a more robust domestic demand. Portfolio investments have recovered strongly. From a net outflow of $938 million in January-May 2001, portfolio investments during the first five months of 2002 posted a net inflow of $1.429 billion. The positive external position has helped raise our gross international reserves (GIR) to $16.1 billion as of end-August 2002, higher than the end-December 2001 level of $15.658 billion and the projected level of $14.8 billion as of end-2002. The preliminary end-August level of international reserves remains comfortable, providing ample cover for 5.2 months' worth of imports of goods and payment of services and income, or alternatively equivalent to 1.4 times the amount of the country's short-term external obligations based on residual maturity. The adequate international reserve position has also helped support orderly adjustment in the foreign exchange market. Recently, there was some impact on the peso from some concerns on political and fiscal issues and the possible vulnerability of emerging markets, including the Philippines, to the Brazilian debt contagion. Of late, the peso has stabilized, standing at P51.709/US$ as of 4 September 2002. As we adhere to a flexible, open exchange system, this development reflects our strong macroeconomic fundamentals, healthy international reserve position and improving trade balance. Continuing challenges and response The ever-changing domestic and international environment poses continuing challenges. Thus, the policy reform process is a work in progress. In addition to stabilizing inflation, the BSP is working at narrowing gaps with regional counterparts through structural reforms. Financial liberalization and globalization called for changes in the structure of the banking system and at the same time created new risks faced by bank management. Our financial reform efforts have been, therefore, directed toward preparing domestic banks to effectively compete in a globally integrated banking environment. As a result, Philippine banks are now better prepared to handle potential volatility in capital flows, following the adoption of the risk-based capital adequacy framework in July last year. Banks' aggregate resources stood at P3.47 trillion as of end-June 2002, slightly higher than the end-December 2001 level of P3.40 trillion. This growth in resources was underpinned mainly by increased deposit mobilization and capital build-up. Also, the banking system's capitalization remained more than adequate relative to international norms and the statutory floor. Using the new risk-based capital adequacy framework adopted in July 2001, commercial banks' CAR reached 13.2 percent in September 2001, which remains well above the BSP's 10.0 percent statutory floor and the Bank for International Settlements' (BIS) 8.0 percent standard. The reforms we adopted to enhance good governance also have served to strengthen the banking sector. Nevertheless, lending activity remains weak. As of end-June 2002, commercial banks' loans outstanding was 3.7 percent lower than the year-ago level. This is traceable, in part, to the banks' cautious stance in extending new loans in an effort to curb any further weakening in the quality of their assets as banks' non-performing loans remain relatively high. However, with the recovery in domestic demand--as indicated in the strong second quarter growth in GDP--and measures to address the non-performing loan problem in the banking sector, bank lending activity is expected to gain momentum. The Government's macroeconomic polices will continue to be directed towards strengthening the economy's resiliency against vulnerabilities that can undermine growth over the medium term. To this end, let me summarize the BSP's policy thrusts: Maintenance of price stability. Reduction of uncertainty in the rate of inflation will encourage both households and investors to undertake longer-term decisions. Commitment of resources to long-term savings vehicles and investment projects will help ensure that the Philippines experiences stable and sustainable economic growth. Adherence to a flexible exchange rate policy. With a market-determined exchange rate policy, the BSP hopes to improve its foreign exchange monitoring system for better recording of events and developments as well as assessment of market conditions. Promotion of bank lending while addressing the high NPL levels. The BSP fully supports private sector asset management initiatives that will unburden banks of non-performing assets and help restore bank soundness and profitability. As a medium-term strategy to reduce NPLs, the BSP is supporting the passage of the SPAV Law, which seeks to provide the legal framework to encourage private investment in non-performing assets of banks through the creation of SPAVs. In line with the Government's renewed efforts to spur the development of capital markets, the BSP endorses the proposed Securitization Act which aims to establish the legal and regulatory framework for capital markets in the country, including the creation of a favorable market environment for a wide range of asset-backed securities. We are also supporting strategies to rationalize the taxation of the capital market, promote new debt and equity instruments as well as to expand institutional players in the market in order to make it a more effective source of financing the requirements of development. Further strengthening of the banking sector, including through the continued formulation of the implementing rules and regulations of the General Banking Law of 2000, continued improvement in the BSP's supervisory framework over the banks and pursuit of amendments of the BSP Charter. Enhancement of efforts to combat money laundering. We will work for the country's removal from the Financial Sction Task Force (FATF) list of non-cooperative countries and territories in the fight against money laundering. Modernization of the payment infrastructure. To enhance operational efficiency, reliability, speed and timeliness as well as limit the settlement and systems risk of payment and settlement transaction, the BSP shall implement fully the Real Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS). In the end, we hope to be rewarded with greater efficiency in the financial system and in the allocation of resources, an enhanced role of intermediation in ensuring broad-based, sustainable development and a regulatory environment that is up to the challenges of the times. As key market movers, your decisions matter critically in the allocation of investible resources for the future. Although your invitation called for my speech to indicate the likely directions of the Philippine economy, let us not forget the fact that the best way to predict the future is to make it happen. Together, we can shape our future. Thank you and good night. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [1] Ateneo Center for Economic Research and Development First Quarterly Economic Briefing, 15 August 2002

Title: Taking the High Road
Location: Tower Club, Philamlife Tower, Makati City
Occasion: International CEO Forum on Ethical Business Practice, IABC
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Dr. Estanislao, Ms. Freeman, officers and members of the International Association of Business Communicators, special guests, friends. Good morning. I must say, IABC is one organization that is attuned and responsive to the needs of the time. Indeed, given the range and magnitude of corporate misdeeds we read and hear about from overseas, good corporate governance is what the world needs today. As Dr. Estanislao points out, the important elements of good governance are fairness, accountability and transparency... transparency. This is a job that calls for good and honest communicators. The point of transparency is to inform- accurately and simultaneously - so that your stakeholders are able to make their own independent judgment. I was therefore quite pleased to note that you chose to name today's event as "taking the high road, an international forum on ethical business practice." Indeed, 'taking the high road' might as well be the mantra for corporate governance. Let me make it clear, however that even before these practices were embodied in a code now called corporate governance, the rudimentary elements thereof are already reflected in various sections of the Manual of Regulations (MOR). This is the code of rules covering BSP-supervised financial institutions. Now, let me give you my perspective on this timely subject. Good corporate governance in banks In developing countries such as the Philippines where the domestic capital market remains largely undeveloped, certain conglomerates and family groups end up dominating the business sector. This is not necessarily bad, per se, since they do take on the responsibility of serving as domestic engines of growth. Given that governments in developing countries lack resources, this is a vital role that such groups play. On the other hand, regulators need to make sure that interlocking ownership of such groups does not give rise to undue advantage over other stakeholders. The challenge for regulators therefore is to ensure a level playing field for stakeholders... that the same standards are made to apply to everyone these groups do business with. Fairness, in other words. At the same time, executive officers of corporations must be held accountable for their actions. They must answer for their acts...or non-action. In particular, weak standard of governance has been blamed for the crises that have hit the international community, including the Philippines. Since then, a consensus has emerged that countries must adopt and implement a body of best practice standards, one of which is a standard for corporate governance. Fortunately for us in the Philippines, we have a Dr. Estanislao who has been tireless in his advocacy of governance reforms and has been conferred the International Corporate Governance Network Laureate Award for 2002. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, as a principal advocate of good corporate governance, continues to work closely with Dr. Estanislao. For instance, the Institute of Corporate Directors which he heads is one of four groups accredited by BSP to conduct governance workshops for banks, along with De La Salle University, Development Finance Institute, and Bankers Institute of the Philippines. For your information, BSP has made it mandatory for all the members of banks' Board of Directors to undergo a special seminar on governance by December this year; otherwise they shall be deemed temporarily disqualified, until they complete such seminar. As most of you are aware, the primary mandate of BSP is to serve as guardian of price and banking stability. Accordingly, BSP has been instituting structural reforms geared at raising the standards of corporate governance in the financial sector.
