Given this overall picture, clearly the industry will be well advised to prioritize and to promote the basic improvement of asset quality among its membership. Otherwise, this will be a severely limiting factor that could consign many banks into permanent low gear. Need for Action For many rural banks, there is need to move quickly and aggressively to reduce the volume of non-performing assets and to accelerate the build up in loss provisions against non-performing assets. As of end-December 2000, the total provisions represent only about a quarter of total non-performing assets, thus adding to the concern on underlying solvency. The Bangko Sentral will soon be coming up with new proposals to induce banks to accelerate the build up in loss provisions especially on acquired assets which have rapidly accumulated. At industry level, we hope that the RBAP will take a leading role in exploring viable options for orderly balance sheet clean-up that respond to the special needs of the rural banking industry without necessarily calling for the expediency of a government bail-out which will just be a non-starter given current fiscal realities. For example, in commercial banks, we are aware that there are now initiatives to set up private asset management companies as a market-driven solution to this type of problem. Admittedly, the short-term measures to mitigate bad assets will add to the pressure on rural banks but they may be our most pragmatic responses. The alternative of simply waiting for better times to roll in to outgrow the problem may prove too little, too late and condemn a bank to mediocre performance for a long time. That will probably be costlier in the long run for the banks' stakeholders and for the economy. On the other hand, banks that act decisively can expect faster recovery and thus be in a strategically advantageous position for a quick rebound as the economy recovers. At present, the new administration is firmly committed to attaining a moderate but sustainable economic growth rate. The Bangko Sentral will actively support that objective by keeping inflation low, interest rates reasonable, and the exchange rate relatively stable. Already, interest rates today are at their lowest since the Asian financial crisis in 1997 and we have made significant progress in reducing exchange rate volatility. Further reform initiatives Looking back at the experience, there is clearly a need to further strengthen the institutional capability of our banks to deal with risks, especially credit risks, in a disciplined manner that promotes financial safety and soundness without unreasonably hampering profitable operations. After all, a healthy banking system must first of all be a profitable system. In addressing these issues from a regulatory perspective, we are being guided by evolving international best practices particularly in the critical areas of institutional governance and transparency, risk-based capital, and risk management. The common denominator of these initiatives is to promote institutional self-control rather than to impose external constraints and limits on business decisions. In order to promote better bank governance, the monetary board recently approved Circular 283 which clearly defines the duties and responsibilities of the Banks' Board of Director both collectively and as individuals. It is based on the principle that the Banks' good governance is the primary responsibility of the Board of Directors. The new Circular amends Circular 130, issued in 1997 by expanding on the key duties and responsibilities in line with best international practice. Among the new features, it calls for the Board to: (1) conduct the affairs of the bank with high degree of integrity; (2) monitor, assess and control management performance; (3) adopt and maintain adequate risk management policy; (4) meet regularly; (5) keep individual directors and shareholders informed; and (6) conduct regular performance assessments of all key personnel including the Board of Directors. The Circular also aims to have a Board of Directors composed of competent and active members who can each contribute to the effective governance of the institution and the attainment of its objectives. Moreover, there will be a follow-on Circular in the near future which would implement fit and proper tests for directors and officers as provided for in the new General Banking Law. One of the requirements will be for all bank directors to undergo at least a one-day seminar where they will be given orientation on their duties and responsibilities and other related topics. The same Circular will also operationalize the concept of independent director of which two must be present in the Board of Directors as provided for in the new General Banking Law. We are now also reviewing the current rules on disclosures with the end in view of expanding the amount of relevant information now required to be regularly provided to the public. The objective is to let the market have sufficient basis for making informed decisions on the financial performance and condition of a bank so that good bank behavior will be promoted. It is increasingly clear that the lack of information to the public in the past has made it easier for bank management to misbehave. It also placed too much burden on the already overstretched resources of bank supervisors. Another initiative that Bangko Sentral will be pursuing is the strict implementation of risk management standards in our banks in the context of a risk-based examination approach. For example, it is our experience that far too few of our banks have sufficient systems in place to systematically review their loan portfolio and assign proper risk classifications and provisions as may be warranted. Many banks have come to rely on Bangko Sentral examiners to do this for them and this has hampered the efficient conduct of bank examinations. Under risk-based examination, our examiners will now increasingly focus on the quality of a bank's internal decision making processes rather than auditing its transactions. And as you are now also probably aware, we also recently issued Circular No. 280 prescribing risk-based capital requirements. Essentially, it is a standard that matches the bank's capital against its risk-weighted assets and prescribes a minimum capitalization ratio of 10 percent. This further reinforces our emphasis on proper deployment of the bank's resources with due regard to the trade-off between risk and return. Microfinance Opportunities We are complementing our new regulatory initiatives by recognizing the potential role of microfinance as a banking product that fits the reinforced risk management standards while allowing our banks especially rural banks to meet the credit needs of the enterprising poor. In this regard, I would like to commend the RBAP for its proactive role in working with foreign donors and experts to mount a viable microfinance program in select rural banks in Mindanao. I understand that because of its success, the new technology is now being propagated to other rural banks and other areas outside Mindanao. On our part, the Bangko Sentral has rapidly responded to this new development by issuing implementing rules to allow collateral free microlending based on well-defined and proven standards. We have also partially lifted the moratorium on the establishment of new banks to accommodate the formation of microfinance-oriented banks. Finally, we have opened a rediscount window for microfinance loans of qualified banks to encourage the participation of existing banks. We are strongly supporting legitimate microfinance programs because it delivers much needed credit to a segment that has long been denied adequate credit access. It is a potentially powerful weapon to combat poverty. At the same time, it is an opportunity for upgrading the credit management skills of our smaller banks and for introducing them to state-of-the-art but user-friendly information technology specifically adapted for credit risk management. Concluding remarks Let me now conclude my presentation. I strongly believe that our rural banking system will continue to play a very important role particularly in the delivery of banking services to our countryside and to economic groups that have the greatest need for economic opportunities. Because of this, it is vital that you succeed. However, success is not a birthright. It is something that you need to constantly work for. The business of banking has undergone profound change in the last couple years as competition has intensified, globalization became more pervasive and as financial market volatility has become more entrenched. All of these require new approaches both in the way banking is conducted and the way it is regulated and supervised. Rapidly, the margin for complacency is being eliminated for all of us. I am confident, however, that the rural banking community will stay attuned to the new realities and that it will evolve new strategies and remake itself with the same determination and tenacity that has enabled it to hurdle so many challenges in the past. Thank you and good day.

Title: Policy Thrusts and Prospects in an Uncertain Global Economic Environment
Occasion: General Assembly Meeting, Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction Ladies and gentlemen, good evening. It is a great pleasure to join this gathering of the officials and members of the Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry in the Philippines. The Japanese business community has been an important partner of the Philippines in our drive to boost investments and create more employment opportunities. The close economic ties of the Philippines with Japan are seen in the significant trading and investment relations between the two countries. Japan is the third biggest market for Philippine exports, accounting for about 15 percent of Philippine goods sold abroad in 2000. Also, imports from Japan accounted for almost 20 percent of total imports. Furthermore, Japanese companies contributed more than US$1.8 billion in direct investments in the last 3 years, about 21 percent of the total foreign direct investment inflow during that period.[1] In fact, for the first quarter of this year, this trend continued as several big Japanese corporations reportedly expanded their operations in the Philippines.[2] One may observe that the trend for large Japanese corporations now is to look for alternative manufacturing bases which offer cheaper labor. We believe, and I think most of you would agree, that the Philippines enjoys certain key advantages as an alternative destination for investments. The labor cost in the country remains relatively competitive. More importantly, the Philippines offers a large pool of highly skilled professionals including engineers. The Government has also been consistent in its policy of encouraging investments, providing various incentives to priority investment areas. One advantage of the Philippines as an investment site, which we are trying to reinforce, is the relatively stable macroeconomic environment. Another advantage is the sound and efficient domestic banking system. These are areas which the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) has an active participation in, and will be the focus of my talk in the next few minutes. However, before focusing on the developments and issues in the monetary and banking sectors, I will first elaborate on the key elements of the domestic and international environment that policymakers and the private sector have to contend with. A Challenging Environment We are all aware that the Philippines was subjected to episodes of domestic political tensions since late last year. Increased political tension was experienced during the impeachment proceedings last year, the EDSA II People Power in January, the arrest of the former President in April, and the violent May 1st rally. Depreciation pressures on the peso and decline in stock prices accompanied these events. Nevertheless, the Philippines emerged with its democratic institutions intact and with the basic strength of its economy preserved. We have undergone a peaceful transition of Government that has been upheld by the Supreme Court. Even as some recent controversy has surfaced, the foundations for a stable political infrastructure--which is essential for the viability of long-term investment in the country--have been laid. Moreover, the impact of the political disturbances on financial markets are temporary and this is reflected in the subsequent recovery of the peso-dollar rate and in the rebound in the performance of the Philippine Stock Exchange Composite Index. The generally peaceful conduct of the recently concluded National Elections also galvanizes the strength of democratic institutions in the country. While the domestic political environment continues to improve, we meet today at a time of great uncertainty for world economic growth. This challenging external environment, highlighted by the slowing down of the U.S. and Japanese economies, looms as a dark cloud over the horizon for both developed and developing economies. This development could have significant effect on the economic performance of Asian economies in view of the importance of the U.S. and Japanese markets as destinations for exports and as a source of investments. Specifically, growth in the export sector could be expected to soften and the inflow of foreign investments could be subdued. On the other hand, lower interest rates and growth prospects in developed economies could lead to a reallocation of capital portfolios. Whether or not this will lead to strengthened capital inflows to particular economies will depend on the ability of those economies to demonstrate good track records in terms of attaining macroeconomic and financial stability, and to lay down, through appropriate structural reforms, the foundations for sustainable economic growth. The Philippine Government is aware of this, and in response has strengthened its commitment to implementing sound and consistent macroeconomic policies as well as pursuing the necessary reform agenda. Let me now focus on what the BSP is doing to contribute to macroeconomic stability and to the structural reform process. Monetary Developments and Policy Stance The focus of monetary policy for this year will continue to be the maintenance of low inflation while providing sufficient liquidity to meet the country's growth requirements. Inflation averaged 6.8 percent during the first four months of 2001. This is within the Government's target of 6-7 percent for the whole year. Moreover, expected improvements in supply conditions and stability in the foreign exchange market suggest that inflationary pressures will abate starting the second half of this year, and these increase our confidence that the inflation targets will be met. These favorable expectations have actually supported some flexibility in the conduct of monetary policy. Benign inflation for the first quarter of the year, improving but still relatively weak domestic demand, the presence of spare capacity, and broad exchange rate stability justified monetary easing. Since December 2000, the BSP has reduced policy rates by a total of 550 basis points. The overnight borrowing (RRP) and lending (RP) rates now stand at 9.5 percent and 11.75 percent, respectively, back to the levels a year ago. The benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate fell from an average of 12.23 percent in January 2001 to 9.90 percent in April, while average bank lending rates fell from a range of 16.46-18.23 percent to 13.49-15.11 percent during the same period. From zero growth in January 2000, outstanding loans of commercial banks rose by 5.7 percent year-on-year in February 2001. The decline in interest rates is expected to have a pro-growth bias as it would provide impetus for investment and consumption. The BSP's commitment to price stability will be enhanced further by the adoption of inflation targeting as the framework for monetary policy in the second half of 2001. By stabilizing prices, inflation targeting will encourage longer term saving and investment, and will deepen the role for longer-term financial intermediation. With some volatility in most currencies of the region, we likewise reiterate our commitment to maintain a market-oriented foreign exchange rate policy under a freely floating exchange rate system. Exchange rate determination will be left to market forces, with some scope for occasional actions to maintain orderly adjustment in the foreign exchange market. Banking sector developments and the reform process The Philippines' banking system remained fundamentally sound amidst the Asian financial crisis and the challenges that faced us last year and in more recent periods. This resilience by the banking sector is demonstrated by several key indicators. The banking system's total resources increased on an annual basis by 18.6 percent, to P3.5 trillion in January 2001. This represented a significant improvement over the 10.5 percent growth as of end-December 2000. Asset quality remained manageable. As of February 2001 the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio of commercial banks stood at 16.48 percent. The NPL ratio of commercial banks has been within the 14-16 percent range for about a year now. However, the broad stability in the exchange rate and the decline in interest rates as well as the pick-up in bank lending activity are expected to have a favorable impact on banks' NPL situation in the future. It may also be noted that no public funds have been used in the Philippines to purchase non-performing assets or recapitalize financial institutions. The banking system remained adequately capitalized. As of end-December 2000, the average capital adequacy ratio reached 16.4 percent, well above the BSP statutory floor of 10.0 percent and the Bank for International Settlement's (BIS) standard of 8.0 percent. Preliminary data on the real estate exposure of commercial banks showed that the ratio of real estate loans to total loans declined slightly to 11.3 percent as of end-December 2000, from 11.6 percent at end-December 1999. The current ratio remained far below the 20 percent ceiling imposed by the BSP. The credible performance of the banking sector in the past few years may be attributed to the wide-ranging reform measures started even two decades ago. In fact, the BSP has continued to undertake steps to further strengthen the financial system in recent years. Let me discuss briefly some of these recent policy actions. The BSP has instituted major reforms in financial supervision and regulation. The recently passed General Banking Law of 2000 (Republic Act No. 8791) provides the overarching framework for financial regulation. Under this framework, financial reform efforts continued to be geared towards strengthening the banking system, improving transparency, putting in place internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy, and enhancing competition in the banking system. An avenue for fostering competition is through the further liberalization of the ownership participation of foreign banks in the local banking system to 100 percent within seven years after the effectivity of the GBL 2000. The BSP has tasked a committee to formulate the implementing rules of the new law. So far, Circulars have been issued pertaining to foreign stockholdings, outsourcing of banking functions, guidelines on microfinance loans and the adoption of risk-based capital adequacy standards aligned with international norms. Other areas being reviewed by the committee pertain to revised guidelines governing the composition of the board of directors of banks, the observance of the fit and proper rule on the management of banks to better protect depositors and the general public, and revised guidelines governing the single borrower's limit. To further improve risk management in the financial system, the BSP continued to institute regulatory changes: The BSP has changed the focus of its supervision from a purely compliance-based and checklist-driven assessment of banks' conditions to a forward-looking and risk-based framework. The BSP has also begun to supervise financial conglomerates on a consolidated basis, including consolidation of limits on foreign currency exposures between banks and their affiliated foreign exchange corporations, and a consolidated approach to addressing bank solvency. The BSP, in collaboration with the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP), is upgrading the existing payment system into a Real Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS) that will cover transactions in the equities, fixed income, money and foreign exchange markets. Once fully operational, the RTGS would offer a powerful mechanism for limiting settlement risks. In response to current trends towards increased use of the internet in banking, the BSP has laid down the requirements for banks seeking to provide e-banking services. This is to ensure that banks planning to provide these services have in place a risk management process that is adequate to assess, control and monitor associated risks. To promote bigger-capitalized banks that can be better equipped to meet the demands of the new globalized environment, the BSP continues to encourage mergers and consolidations through the provision of incentives. The policy also reduces moral hazard since owners have more of their wealth at stake. In response to the global drive against money laundering, the BSP, since July 2000, has undertaken important actions on the matter. We have issued a number of Circulars in 2000 which bring the country's regulatory regime on anti-money laundering closer to international standards. These Circulars require banks to take reasonable means to determine the true identities of their clients and report suspicious transactions. In addition the BSP continues to actively support initiatives--including legislation--aimed at enhancing the effectiveness of activities to curb money laundering activities. On the legislative front, the reforms in the General Banking Law of 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the New Central Bank Act. These amendments aim to enhance the BSP's supervisory powers and operational independence, improve prudential standards and promote greater competition in the banking system. Key reforms would include the grant of authority to the BSP to conduct more frequent banking examinations and greater scope and strength of administrative sanctions. Concluding remarks With the improvement in the domestic political environment, we see the uncertainty of the global economic environment as one of the major challenges for policymakers. In response, we continue to enhance our commitment to fighting inflation and to pursue the needed financial sector reforms. We believe this strategy would form the sound basis for a sustained non-inflationary growth and for continued viability of long-term investments in the country. For this year, we expect the country's GNP to expand by 4-4.5 percent and by another 4.9-5.4 percent next year. Meanwhile, inflation is seen to average 6-7 percent for the whole year and by 5-6 percent next year. We have no doubt that the economy can again weather any challenge that external factors may pose for this year. The prospects are favorable for long-term investments and I hope that all of you will continue to be our partners in our drive for strong economic growth. Thank you and good evening. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [1] Includes data reported by BOI, PEZA, SBMA, and CDC [2] Toshiba transferred production of its notebook-type personal computer from the US and the manufacture of its DVD-ROM from Japan, Nihon Ceramics constructed a new plant for its production of sensors, Sumitomo Jyukikaikogyo set up a new plant for machinery components, NEC increased its production of its modems

Title: An Assessment of Philippine Compliance with International Standards in Banking
Occasion: "The Implementation of Financial Architecture in Asia - An ADB-FSF Seminar"
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I am deeply honored to participate in this seminar on the implementation of a strengthened financial architecture in Asia. In the Philippines, particularly in the banking system, we have intensified our structural reform efforts in response to vulnerabilities highlighted by the Asian financial crisis. These initiatives have significantly improved our compliance with the core principles for effective banking supervision as articulated by the BASLE Committee. Key Strengths of the Philippine Banking System Even prior to the core principles, the Philippines already had in place a set of basic banking laws that establish a clear and reasonably effective legal framework for the supervision and regulation of the banking system. We believe that this has been instrumental in somewhat mitigating the impact of the Asian financial crisis on the banking sector. The General Banking Act, comprehensively updated and amended into the General Banking Law of 2000, is a key element of the legal framework that defines the chartering of Philippine banks, prescribes binding standards of prudent behavior, and defines their manner of supervision. The General Banking Law is closely complemented by the Central Bank Act of 1993 which established an independent central bank, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), that has primary responsibility for both monetary policy and the supervision of the banking and financial system. The independence of the BSP in discharging its responsibilities is guaranteed by no less than the Philippine constitution. We also have a long-established deposit insurance system administered by the Philippine deposit insurance corporation (PDIC), patterned after the U.S. FDIC, that forms part of the safety net. The PDIC supports the oversight of the safety and soundness of the banking system and plays a role in the orderly resolution of problem banks. The supervisory framework defined by these basic laws and institutions provides US with the ability to readily uphold a critical mass of the BASLE core principles for effective banking supervision. Recent enhancements As duly noted by the World Bank, we have been taking additional steps since 1997 to further upgrade our compliance with international banking standards. These include: Structural improvements: Consolidation of the banking sector through incentives for mergers and acquisitions, restrictions on branch expansion, higher capital requirements, and greater foreign competition. Better prudential regulation: Implementation of risk-based capital requirements, tighter loan classification and provisioning rules, implementation of mark-to-market on securities portfolio, better consolidated reporting, tighter implementation of connected lending limits, limits on real estate exposure, and more conservative collateral valuation. Improved supervision: Shift from checklist approach to measurement of risks, monitoring of top 200 borrowers, better on- and off-site supervision, higher monetary penalties, expanded powers for inspectors, improved and formal plans for prompt corrective actions, development of systemic contingency plans, and better coordination between BSP and PDIC. Improved intelligence and transparency: Implementation of a basic early warning system as well as a bank performance rating system, and more comprehensive and timely industry analysis. Improved management of market risks: Better matching of foreign currency assets and liabilities, expanded liquidity cover against foreign currency liabilities, closure of regulatory loopholes on transactions of bank-affiliated FOREX corporations. Improvements in corporate governance and disclosure: Accreditation of external auditors, specifications of duties and responsibilities of bank directors, fit and proper tests for directors and officers, reporting of suspicious transactions, "know your customer" rules, fuller disclosure of shareholders, quarterly publication of statement of condition and key financial indicators as well as non-performing loans, and related party lendings. Challenges ahead Notwithstanding the significant progress to date on banking reforms, we remain acutely aware of remaining gaps that hamper our full compliance with the core principles. These will be addressed, many in the context of new legislation. A key legislative priority is the further strengthening of the legal framework for resolving distressed banks by providing, among others, the BSP and PDIC with sufficient powers to override consent of existing shareholders in cases of severe capital deficiency. We are also seeking better protection for regulators from suits and other legal challenges in the exercise of their duties. These would involve further amendments to basic banking laws particularly the general banking law and the charters of the BSP and the PDIC. We are also working for a comprehensive law that will criminalize money laundering activities and facilitate the cooperation of banks and other financial institutions in related investigations. To support anti-money laundering efforts and to strengthen the general ability of supervisors to monitor abuses in the banking system, we are likewise seeking a judicious dilution of current highly restrictive deposit secrecy laws to achieve a more reasonable balance between protecting the confidentiality of deposits and preventing the use of the banking system to hide criminal activities. In particular, we favor allowing bank supervisors to look into suspicious deposit transactions strictly following a well-defined administrative process. In addition to the preceding legislative priorities, the BSP will continue to push for other amendments to the BSP charter which we believe will further strengthen its institutional capacity to discharge its duties independently and effectively. These include full exemption of BSP personnel from salary standardization and the exemption of BSP from taxation especially on its open market operations. We are also seeking greater flexibility to impose higher monetary penalties when appropriate, to conduct consolidated supervision of banks and their non-bank subsidiaries and affiliates as well as their parents, to determine the frequency of on-site examinations, and to impose additional capital requirements on individual banks when warranted by specific risks. In addition to legislative initiatives, we are emphasizing the training of bank examiners in risk-based examination. We are also reviewing examination procedures accordingly. To strengthen off-site surveillance, we are accelerating our shift to electronic reporting and are increasing our investment in electronic databases and computer-based analytical tools. Finally, we are working closely with other regulators particularly the PDIC and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to further strengthen coordination in the supervision of banks and their non-bank affiliates. Conclusion The Philippines is firmly committed to strengthening its banking and financial system in response to the challenges of globalization by putting in place critical structural reforms and fully adopting a supervisory framework in accordance with best international practices. We have already made significant progress. We are determined to complete the task. Thank you.

Title: Philippines: Monetary Sector, External Sector and the Financial System
Occasion: Country Presentation of the Philippine Panel, 34th ADB Annual Meeting
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Ladies and gentlemen, I am pleased to have the opportunity to be able to talk on two of the primary policy areas of the central bank of the Philippines: Monetary Policy and the Banking System. Developments in the Monetary Sector Inflation. Inflation was relatively subdued. In 2000, due to favorable weather conditions and the Central Bank's resolve to keep monetary aggregates within programmed levels, the average inflation for 2000 was at 4.4 percent, well below the government's full-year target of 5.0-6.0 percent. During the first quarter of 2001, inflation averaged 6.8 percent, which was within the Government's target of 6-7 percent for the whole year of 2001. This year, inflation is expected to be relatively higher during the first semester due to the lagged effects of a weaker peso, higher petroleum prices and wage adjustments that happened in late 2000. However, improvements in supply conditions and prospects for continued stability in the FOREX market are expected to contribute to a trend decline in inflation in the second half, to around 5 percent by December. Market and policy interest rates. The 91-day T-bill rate averaged 9.9 percent in 2000, down from the 10.2 percent average in 1999. However, the benchmark 91-day T-bill rate reached a peak of 16.7 percent in late 2000 (6 November auction) as the monetary stance was tightened. Subsequently, the benchmark interest rate gradually declined as the Central Bank steadily eased its monetary stance due to the decline in political risk premium. From December 2000 to 20 April 2001, the Central Bank reduced its policy rates by 550 basis points. The overnight borrowing (RRP) and lending (RP) rates now stand at 9.5 percent and 11.75 percent. They are back to the levels of a year ago. Domestic liquidity and credit. Domestic liquidity growth began to pick up in 2000, with m3 rising by an average of 12.1 percent during the year as economic growth strengthened. Latest data shows that domestic liquidity grew by 12.8 percent in February 2001. The expansion in domestic liquidity has been supported by increased bank lending. From a zero growth in January 2000, outstanding loans of commercial banks rose by 5.9 percent in February 2001. Developments in the Foreign Exchange Market The peso averaged P44.20/US$1 in 2000, depreciating by about 13 percent relative to the 1999 average peso-dollar rate. The peso reached a high of about P55.00/US$1 at the height of the political crisis in mid-January. However, since then the peso has strengthened steadily. Of late, the movement of regional currencies, the emergence of corporate demand and some political tension have contributed to downward pressures on the peso, with the peso trading around P50- P51/US$ in April. Developments in the External Sector The gross international reserves of the country continues to provide a comfortable cushion to our external obligations. As of end-March 2001 international reserves stood at US$14.7 billion which is about 4.4 months worth of imports of goods and services. The external debt of the country also remains manageable at US$52.06 billion as of end-2000, with short-term obligations comprising only 11.0 percent of the total. Developments in the Banking Sector The positive developments in the monetary and external sectors are complemented by the favorable performance of the banking system. Capital adequacy. The banking system is comfortably capitalized. The banking system's capital-to-risk assets ratio was 16.4 percent p/ as of December 2000, well above both the BIS standard of 8 percent and the statutory floor of 10 percent. The successive increases in the minimum capitalization requirement of banks and the ongoing consolidation process helped Philippine banks maintain their relatively strong capital positions. Quality of loan portfolio. For commercial banks, their non-performing loan (NPL) ratio was at 16.0 percent in January 2001. The NPL ratio of commercial banks has been within the 14-16 percent range for a year now. However, the broad stability in the exchange rate and the decline in interest rates as well as the pick-up in bank lending activity are expected to have a favorable impact on banks' NPL situation going forward. Real estate exposure. The exposure of commercial banks to the real estate sector continues to be moderate at 12.3 percent of total loans (as of end-September 2000). This is well below the central bank's ceiling of 20 percent. Central bank policy directions As to the policy direction of the Central Bank... Monetary policy The thrust of monetary policy will continue to be guided by the pursuit of the Central Bank's primary mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to a balanced and sustained economic growth. Expectations of a trend decline in inflation by the second half of this year and the stabilization of the financial markets gave the Central Bank scope to ease monetary conditions early this year. As stated, the Central Bank reduced its key policy rates by a total of 550 basis points since last December. The gradual relaxation of monetary policy should help establish a more supportive environment for business activity. The Central Bank will continue to monitor and assess carefully the risk stemming from possible inflationary pressures. Further Central Bank policy rate cuts will be calibrated vis-à-vis economic and financial developments, and would be considered carefully with a view to observing an appropriate differential with international interest rates. To further improve the central bank's capability to pursue its mandate of maintaining price stability, an inflation targeting framework will be adopted in the second half of this year. Under this framework, government authorities will pre-announce the inflation target over a given time horizon. If the target is not met, the central bank has to explain the reasons and spell out the measures that it will take to get back on track relative to the target. This forward-looking framework is expected to help the central bank build its credibility by demonstrating consistent adherence to the price stability objective. In the process, the framework will promote greater transparency in the conduct of monetary policy, thus facilitating more efficient markets, as well as greater accountability on the part of the monetary authorities. Exchange rate policy The Central Bank will continue to support a floating exchange rate system, with some scope for occasional Central Bank action to smooth out sharp fluctuations and maintain orderly market conditions. In this regard, the Central Bank continues to monitor developments in the foreign exchange market, with a view to determining the appropriate policy response. Banking sector policy In the banking system, the Central Bank's focus remains to be the promotion of a globally competitive banking system that is strong, sound and resilient as well as able to intermediate funds effectively and manage risks efficiently. Legislative framework. A key reform measure is the General Banking Law (GBL) of 2000 or R.A. No. 8791, which was passed last may 2000, now forms the basic legal fabric governing the banking system. The law enhances the competitiveness of the banking sector, improves the prudential standards and strengthens the effectiveness of the central bank's supervision over banks. A number of circulars to implement some of the provisions of this new law have already been issued by the central bank including those pertaining to foreign stockholdings, outsourcing of banking functions, guidelines on microfinance loans and the adoption of risk-based capital adequacy standards aligned with international norms. The reforms supported by the GBL 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the Charter of the Central Bank. The amendments will reinforce the autonomy, authority and capacity of the Central Bank not only to regulate and supervise the banking system but also to more effectively implement monetary policy. Key initiatives include the restoration of the tax-exempt status of the central bank; the relaxation of the deposit secrecy provision which would allow the monetary board to inquire into deposit accounts of a suspicious nature; the grant of authority to the Central Bank to conduct more frequent banking examinations; and the imposition of broader and more stringent administrative sanctions. The Central Bank has also strengthened the efforts to combat money laundering activities. We have issued a number of circulars in 2000 which bring the country's regulatory regime on anti-money laundering closer to international standards. These circulars require banks to take reasonable means to determine the true identities of their clients and report suspicious transactions. In addition the Central Bank continues to actively support initiatives -- including legislation -- aimed at enhancing the effectiveness of activities to curb money laundering activities. Supervisory and Regulatory Framework. Aside from the changes in the country's banking laws, an ongoing initiative by the Central Bank is the improvement of its supervisory framework in line with the evolving structure of the financial system. This upgrading of capabilities would ensure that supervision will remain effective in fostering the safety and soundness of the country's banking system. An important step in this effort is the adoption of a more forward-looking and risk-based bank supervision framework. This involves the re-orientation of the bank examination process towards improving the quality of decision processes rather than just compliance with rules and regulations. Another dimension of the upgrading is the implementation of consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates. This approach facilitates a more comprehensive assessment of the risks involved in the banks' activities. The Central Bank has also started to improve the regulatory framework in anticipation of the expected growth of e-banking. General guidelines for banks planning to offer e-banking services have been issued to ensure that they have rigorous internal controls and comprehensive risk management systems that can adequately take into account the risks involved in these new banking activities. Existing rules and regulations are being reviewed continuously in order to align prudential standards with international best practices. The Central Bank is also encouraging the restructuring of the local banking industry. In a more globalized financial landscape, domestic banks need to mobilize sufficient capitalization and to strengthen risk management systems to compete in this challenging environment. This strengthening can be assisted through mergers and acquisitions and through greater participation of foreign financial institutions. In 1998, the World Bank granted a $300 million Banking Sector Reform Loan (BSRL) to the Philippines. The BSRL was in support of structural reforms needed to help the banking system withstand difficulties faced by the Philippines during the regional financial crisis and build resistance against future shocks. The Philippine Government is on track with most of its reform commitments under the BSRL and has already drawn on part of the loan. One of the requirements for the release of the remaining tranches is the privatization of the Philippine National Bank (PNB). Currently, the Government and the majority stockholders are developing measures to ensure the continuing viability of the bank. They include various reforms in the bank's structure and operations. The steps being undertaken are preparatory to the eventual sale of the government's equity either in a joint-sale or on its own. Privatization is still the ultimate goal for PNB. Market Infrastructure. The Central Bank is also supporting the modernization of the market infrastructure for the financial system. In line with this, a key initiative supported by the Central Bank is the upgrading of the existing payment system into a Real Time Gross Settlement System to enhance operational efficiency, reliability, speed and timeliness of payment transactions. This will not only foster a more efficient banking system but also help develop the capital market. Microfinance Loans. The Central Bank is also extending support to the social development agenda of the government within the limits set by its charter. In this regard, the Central Bank has released guidelines to govern the microfinance operations of banks.[1] through this initiative, the Central Bank hopes to contribute to the efforts to bring more resources and opportunities to the marginalized sectors of our society. Thank you and good day. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- p/ Preliminary [1] Last January, the Central Bank issued a circular on microfinancing loans to implement some of the provisions of the GBL. These provisions relate to the application of market-based interest rates by lending institutions to enable them to recover the financial and operational costs of their micro finance operations. The Central Bank is also finalizing guidelines for the opening of a rediscount window for rural banks and cooperative banks engaged in microfinance. This facility will support small banks that have achieved efficiency in their microfinance operations, without sacrificing prudential standards.

Title: Sustaining Economic Recovery Through Sound Monetary Policy
Occasion: * 4th Monthly Business Meeting, Chamber of Real Estate & Builders' Association, Inc. (CREBA)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Charlie Gorayeb, officers and members of the Chamber of Real Estate and Builders' Associations, inc. (CREBA), distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, good morning: I would like to begin by thanking CREBA for inviting me to its 4th Monthly Business Meeting this year. Occasions such as this one remind policymakers like myself about the importance of the dynamic and synergistic relationship between the government and the private sector in the efforts to sustain economic growth. Introduction Our shared task is to build a path to strong recovery and sustained non-inflationary growth. As we gear up towards a more broad-based economic recovery in 2001, the role of the private sector becomes more important in providing the sustaining momentum for economic growth. I speak in particular of the real estate sector as represented by groups such as CREBA with its large and influential membership. The real estate sector is vital to the national economy as a prime mover of the housing sector. Housing, as you know, has long been a priority program of the government both as a major component of social policy and an instrument for economic growth. The role of housing as an essential channel for economic pump-priming is particularly important because of its impact on ancillary industries, which include the basic building materials sector and the construction sector. On the other hand, the role of government, and the BSP in particular, in sustainable growth consists of providing a supportive economic environment for vigorous productive activity through sound and coherent macroeconomic policies. I would like to discuss briefly with you this morning the BSP's efforts in this regard and how they have affected the real estate and housing sector. Ensuring a sustainable recovery The BSP's efforts to ensure a supportive macroeconomic environment have centered on preserving price stability, which is the BSP's primary mandate, while also broadly supporting the economy's output growth objective. Ensuring a reasonably low level of inflation helps reduce the uncertainty in economic decision-making, so that individuals and businesses have a reliable basis for long-range decisions and plans. Our efforts to keep inflation in check have so far been successful. Actual inflation continues to be well on track relative to its projected path for this year, holding steady at 6.7 percent in March and averaging at 6.8 percent in the first quarter. Latest readings on inflation also indicate a declining trend towards the end of the year. This makes us confident that the inflation target of 6.0-7.0 percent for 2001 is well within reach. The favorable inflation environment has also enabled us to provide broad support to the economy's growth objectives. Over the last few months, the BSP has brought down interest rates through an accommodative monetary policy stance. Beginning December 2000, key BSP policy rates were reduced by a cumulative 550 basis points. This has led to the downtrend in market interest rates. The 91-day Treasury bill rate, for example, has fallen from a high of 16.72 percent in November 2000, when political tensions were running high, to 9.855 percent at the latest auction on 23 April. Similarly, banks' lending rates have fallen to a range of 13.4-15.0 percent for the period 2-6 April 2001 compared to 18.3-20.1 percent in the first week of December. Benefits to the economy Our policy actions have continued to pay off in terms of a healthier economic picture. Recently, we have seen indications of stronger private demand in terms of rising power sales and faster growth in bank lending. Meralco power sales rose by 9.4 percent year-on-year in February, up from the 6.3 percent increase registered in the previous month. The total loan portfolio of our commercial banks has continued to grow steadily with a year-on-year increase of 7.8 percent in January. With these positive indicators, we expect to see sustained economic activity this year, as quarterly GDP growth is expected to accelerate beginning in the second quarter to produce an average annual GDP growth of 3.8-4.3 percent for 2001. The combination of subdued inflation, easing credit conditions and broad stability in the foreign exchange market should pave the way for a continued decline in interest rates in the remainder of 2001. Lower domestic interest rates, together with improved financing conditions, should provide a boost not only to real estate and construction activity but also to the overall economy. These conditions will allow domestic demand to take over the reins of growth while external demand remains weak due to the global economic slowdown. Business confidence is part of the key to raising domestic demand and the best way for the government to boost private sector confidence is to reaffirm its abiding commitment to policy reforms. In this regard, we realize as well that financing is vitally important to the key economic sectors such as real estate and housing. To this end, the BSP has continued to pursue reforms to create a stable, sound and globally competitive banking and financial system. We believe that better financial intermediation will give freer rein to vigorous business activity. Broad key measures in banking and financial reform include the implementation of the General Banking Law (GBL) of 2000 (R.A. No. 8791). The GBL is aimed at strengthening and modernizing the basic legal framework for the banking system. It is also expected to foster greater public confidence in the banking system through better supervisory and enforcement capability of the BSP, improved prudential and regulatory standards, and greater competition in the banking industry. This will be complemented by proposed amendments to the Bangko Sentral Charter aimed at reinforcing the BSP's autonomy, authority and capacity to both regulate the banking system and implement monetary policy more effectively. Other initiatives include the improvement of the BSP's supervisory framework (for example, through the adoption of forward-looking and risk-based bank supervision) and the strengthening of the local banking industry through consolidation and increased participation of foreign financial institutions. The BSP is also supporting the development of our capital markets through the modernization of the market infrastructure of the financial system (via the upgrading of the existing payment system into a real time gross settlement system) and the promotion of the securitization of long-term deposits to help spur domestic savings and deepen the local capital market. The package of BSP initiatives also comprises specific issuances aimed at supporting the housing sector. These include BSP Circular No. 211 (dated 29 September 1999), which established a BSP rediscounting window for the socialized and low-cost housing loan papers of qualified commercial, thrift and rural banks. We also issued a Circular-letter (dated 23 November 1999) exempting loans to low- and middle-cost housing developers under the government's National Shelter Program from the 20 percent aggregate limit on real estate loans of banks and from the reduction in the loan values of real estate collateral (from 70 percent to 60 percent of appraised value). Meanwhile, BSP Circular No. 218 (dated 23 November 1999) exempted banks, in certain cases, from the requirement of hiring an independent appraisal company to appraise collateral to support loan restructuring. These BSP issuances are part of the wider government initiatives to ensure the viability of the country's housing program by lowering the cost of housing loans and facilitating better access to financing. Concluding remarks The role of the BSP in ensuring broad-based and sustainable growth consists of providing a supportive economic environment in which businesses can thrive. We do this through our unwavering commitment to sound macroeconomic policy and financial sector stability. At the same time, our collective efforts toward sustainable growth require the crucial participation of the private sector. This includes the real estate sector's role in providing the impetus for key sectors such as housing. I am pleased to note that CREBA continues to be at the forefront in this area. As your president Mr. Charlie Gorayeb said, "creba has always been a partner of government in promoting its pro-poor programs, specifically, providing a roof for every Filipino." I hope your organization will continue to work with the government in pushing forward our common agenda for a sustainable economic future. Thank you. (Note: 4th Monthly Business Meeting, Chamber of Real Estate and Builders' Associations, Inc. (CREBA), April 26, 2001, Hotel Inter-Continental, Makati City)

Title: Ensuring Sustainability of Economic Development
Occasion: 1st General Assembly
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I welcome this opportunity to discuss with you the ongoing reforms in the financial sector. These days political news tends to obscure the crucial work being done quietly away from the limelight. I hope to rectify this by sharing with you our recent initiatives and what we have charted to do further in the future. Prospects for 2000 By and large, Asia is now back on its feet. The region's snap back from recession has been remarkable for both its speed and timing. For the Philippines, the favorable assessment by the recent IMF mission adds to expectations of an even stronger economy this year. For example, real GNP growth is expected to easily hit the target range of 4.5-5.5 percent this year as industry and services continue to recover. Inflation is projected to average between 5 and 6 percent after reaching well below the target for 1999. In the external sector, a sizable projected current account surplus will help build up gross international reserves to $17.1 billion by yearend. We are also moving closer to fiscal consolidation. Fiscal authorities are expecting a reduction in the consolidated public sector deficit from 3.4 percent of GNP in 1999 to 2.9 percent this year. First-quarter revenue collections suggest that the national government's target deficit of P62.5 billion for 2000 can be achieved. Ensuring Sustainability The immediate challenge now for Asian leaders is to sustain the cyclical upturn and translate it into robust long-term growth. This means stepping up reform efforts. In the Philippines, financial reform initiatives have drawn heavily from the lessons of past crises. In addition, as former World Bank Chief Economist Joseph Stiglitz argued, we also need to reshape our methodology in favor of looking at the microfoundations, for instance, of bankruptcy and fear of default so that our analysis is more complete. Reform Initiatives To do this, the Bangko Sentral has focused on strengthening governance, upgrading regulatory standards, and building up the BSP's independence and capabilities as regulatory authority. Let me cite some of the measures we have put in place. Promoting better bank governance means improving transparency and raising the quality of bank management. Hence, we have required more detailed quarterly reporting from banks on NPLs, risk assets, return on equity and DOSRI loans. We also drew up guidelines on the duties of banks' directors to improve the quality of management. Improvements in regulatory standards involve introducing changes in the definition of non-performing loans and tighter requirements for loan classification and loan-loss provisioning to conform with international standards. Upgrading the BSP's supervisory capacity means using a more dynamic, forward-looking and risk-based approach to bank supervision. In this regard, we have conducted seminars and dialogue with foreign and local institutions to train and upgrade the skills of BSP personnel. Future Policy Thrusts Needless to say, the work does not stop there. Further banking reforms will have to deal with increasing sophistication in the financial environment. The reforms that I have just outlined centered mainly on the banking system because the BSP's authority is precisely built on that bedrock. This is not to say, however, that we are neglecting the other crucial areas of financial reform. We remain ever aware of the need to develop sources of long-term financing and of putting up the necessary infrastructure for developing the capital markets. In fact, reforms have already been proposed aimed at resolving issues on the taxation of financial transactions. The BSP is also working closely with the BAP and the other financial associations on the establishment of best practices for (1) risk management, including credit risk rating, market risk process, propriety and compliance test; (2) accounting and valuation standards, such as marking-to-market and stress testing; (3) the origination and underwriting of securities; (4) trading and market making; and (5) trust and asset management. Appropriate working groups have been put in place in order to ensure that specific work programs are carried out within specific time tables. We are likewise working with the BAP in developing a market for fixed-income instruments (such as REPOs) and making the payment and settlement system more efficient through the real-time gross settlements (RTGS) project. This is expected to be operational within the year. Supervisory authorities are also improving the monitoring of banks' off-balance sheet transactions to obtain a more complete and accurate assessment of portfolio risk. One crucial point in this long laundry list of planned measures is that they cannot be implemented without the proper macroeconomic environment. Therefore, the Bangko Sentral's abiding commitment to price stability remains as crucial as ever to continued reform and the sustainability of economic growth. Stable price levels are a key ingredient to strong and sustainable growth, since they reduce uncertainty so that, to quote Alan Greenspan, "expectations of change do not become major factors in key economic decisions." Thus, the Bangko Sentral is planning to shift to inflation targeting as the framework for conducting monetary policy in 2001. Among other things, this involves determining and announcing an explicit inflation target, and making regular reports on the performance of monetary policy. This framework raises both the level of transparency in the conduct of monetary policy and the BSP's accountability to the inflation goal. In closing, I would like to reassure you of the Bangko Sentral's unstinting commitment to financial reform and macroeconomic stability. I think I can say, without being immodest, that our record largely speaks for itself. This country's long history of financial reform largely helped shield it from the worst of the past crisis. We intend to continue and build on that tradition. However, we cannot do it all on our own. The task of upgrading the capabilities and practices of the financial system also requires the initiative of industry groups like mart, the BAP and other associations. I am therefore grateful for the invaluable cooperation and support extended to the BSP by the financial community. I hope our partnership will continue to prosper in the years to come. Thank you and good evening. (Note: 1st General Assembly, MART, April 25, 2000, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati)

Title: Credit Management in the New Economy
Occasion: 25th National Credit Congress, Credit Management Association of the Philippines (CMAP)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction I am very pleased to join this gathering of distinguished credit and finance executives of the member-companies of the credit management association of the Philippines. The theme of this year's national credit congress ----- credit management in the new economy ----- is a fairly broad canvass to work on and I am grateful for the flexibility you are giving me in choosing the specific issues to develop. As credit professionals, i think we can all readily find common ground in taking a look anew at developments in our banking system which stands at the very heart of the national credit mechanism. The current situation Nearly four years after the outbreak of the Asian financial crisis, many countries in the region including ourselves are still sorting out the mess. Although we have fortunately managed to avoid the worst disruptions, we have not been immune from the crisis and its effects. The banking system today continues to labor under the heavy burden of the bad credit decisions of yesterday. The non-performing loan ratio, 16 percent for the commercial banking system as of end-January 2001, remains uncomfortably high. In addition, the volume of acquired assets and rescheduled debt have also significantly increased. There is little comfort that our overall asset quality situation is still significantly better than those in other crisis countries. These developments have inevitably eroded bank profitability, eaten away at scarce bank capital and reduced appetite for new lending. What should be done? Reversing the dangerous tide calls for resolute action by government and by the financial institutions. One cannot simply wish away the problems by assuming that we will be able to grow our way out of trouble. That may be especially unrealistic at this point in light of the dimming economic outlook for our key trading partners, notably the united states and Japan, which would limit our own ability to rebound more quickly. Indeed, in the ASEAN region, economic growth is forecasted to slow down to 3 percent this year. In the Philippines, GDP growth is projected at around 4 percent. Two things need to be done quickly. First, we have to address the weakened balance sheet condition of some of our financial institutions by expediting both the clean up of bad assets and the replenishment of capital when necessary. Second, we need to introduce genuine internal reforms in our institutions to improve credit decision-making processes and avoid future problems. In light of fiscal realities and on moral hazard grounds, the government cannot be expected to shoulder the main burden of the balance sheet clean-up. This must primarily be the responsibility of the concerned financial institutions and their owners. But government can play a constructive and supportive role by, first of all, taking a more realistic view on the tax treatment of loan loss provisions along the lines of international best practice. I am particularly referring to allowing the tax deductibility of specific loan loss provisions. I believe there is also scope for meaningful government support by way of strategic enhancements to essentially market-driven mechanisms either to take out bank assets or to re-capitalize banks. There are already existing models we can look at. The Bangko Sentral has been playing a catalytic role in the clean-up process by forcing the issue on realistic valuation of loans and other assets through its regulations and enforcement actions. Key initiatives include tightened policies on loan classification and provisioning, on marking-to-market of securities portfolio, and on asset appraisals. We have also recently issued BSP circular 280 implementing the risk-based capital framework which would officially take effect on July 1 this year. Under this framework, which is based on the basle capital accord, banks' assets will be categorized into 4 risk buckets with risk weights of 0%, 20%, 50% and 100%, respectively. Both on-balance and off-balance sheet assets are included. Banks will need to maintain, on a daily basis, a minimum eligible capital level equivalent to at least 10 percent of total risk-weighted assets. However, the definition of eligible capital is broader than the conventional concept since it includes so-called tier 2 or supplementary capital such as long-dated subordinated debt. In addition, the minimum capital ratio has to be maintained on stand-alone basis by the bank and also on banking group-wide basis if it has financial subsidiaries. By hardening the capital constraint, this is expected to affect in a fundamental way how banks allocate their scarce capital resources bearing in mind the relative risks of their asset choices. The framework will also be evolving in the future in the direction of increasing sophistication of risk measurement which will put an even greater premium on the quality and discipline of credit management. Towards an improved credit process A clean-up of the balance sheet is not enough. More critically, we need to thoroughly reform our credit processes precisely to avoid the kind of headaches we face today that are ultimately extremely costly to the economy. There is a basic need for better corporate governance in our credit institutions. Banks are not the private reserve of their primary shareholders to be used as a ready source of cheap credit. But all too often, this principle may have been honored in the breach. At ground level, our bank examiners play a constant cat-and-mouse game with some of our banks in identifying so-called DOSRI lendings that are very imaginatively concealed. When you analyze it, most of our recent bank failures and near-failures can ultimately be traced to insider abuse. The Bangko Sentral is determined to raise the governance standards of our banks. We will soon be issuing new regulations defining clearly the duties and responsibilities of the board of directors --- the body that should be primarily responsible for ensuring sound corporate governance. This would be backed-up by fit and proper rules on bank directors and officers, that include the rules for disqualification, as provided for in the New General Banking Law. The GBL has also provided us the legal basis to issue strengthened regulations on DOSRI loans and the single borrowers limit. Both regulations are also in the pipeline. On a more general note, we need to recommit ourselves to sound credit management principles that we may have started to take for granted. The monetary board has recently approved a proposal for the establishment of minimum standards for a comprehensive credit risk management system that should be consistent with international standards. This shall be done in consultation with the Bankers Association of the Philippines and other banking associations. This would lay down the basis for more rigorous credit assessment standards including the wide and consistent use of internal credit grading systems. The development of a strong credit culture will also be assisted by the development of private providers of credit information like credit bureaus as well as local rating agencies. The Bangko Sentral recognizes the need to nurture these institutions as a means of fostering credit discipline as well as to expand access to credit especially of smaller enterprises based on performance rather than collateral. In this regard, the Bangko Sentral is open to information sharing arrangements with legitimate institutions subject to certain safeguards as set out in a formal memorandum of agreement. A final note To achieve excellence in the rapidly changing environment, sound credit decisions at your level is essential. Management must adopt mechanisms to safeguard your institution from unsound transactions. On our part, the BSP will adjust to the changing needs of the system by continuously improving the supervisory and regulatory framework. I urge you to continue to work in partnership with us in achieving excellence within individual institutions and in attaining our quest for a stable, sound and globally competitive financial system. Thank you and good day. (Note: 25th National Credit Congress, Credit Management Association of the Philippines (CMAP), April 20, 2001, Hotel Inter-Continental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Welcome Remarks
Occasion: IMF-World Bank Seminar on Standard and Codes in the New Int'l Financial Architecture
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Charles Enoch, Ms. Lynn Aylward, Mr. Axel Peuker, distinguished guests and participants to the IMF-World Bank Seminar on Standards and Codes in the New International Financial Architecture, friends and colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good morning: Let me begin by thanking all of you for joining us here in this seminar. We are very fortunate to have with us today three distinguished officials from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank (WB) who will talk about current international initiatives in standards and codes for economic and financial areas such as statistics, the monetary and financial sector, the fiscal sector and corporate governance. The need to establish international standards and codes for all countries should be clear to most of us here. Our experience with macroeconomic crises in the past decade has heightened the need for a policy framework to minimize the effects--if not prevent altogether--these crises. Good economic citizenship is an important part of macroeconomic crisis prevention, and good citizenship implies adherence to internationally accepted standards, principles, and guidelines of good practice for economic, financial, and business activities. Adherence to these good practices helps ensure the proper functioning of not only individual domestic economies and financial systems but also the international financial system as a whole. Initiatives in these areas contribute to the collective good, and require the collaboration of both the public and private sectors. One important initiative is the collaborative effort between the IMF and the World bank to monitor and assist various countries in the observance of international standards and codes. This effort includes, among other things, the Reports on the Observance of Standards and Codes (ROSCS), which are experimental case studies on individual countries' observance of international standards. The ROSCS and other recent developments in data standards, fiscal transparency, corporate governance, guideline concerning accounting and insolvency, are the subject of this morning's presentations. With its decades-long history of continuing economic reforms, the Philippines has already made good progress in observing the standards and codes of good economic citizenship. Nevertheless, I believe today's presentation and discussion will greatly help the country build further upon its track record. I hope that this seminar will open up further discussion and cooperation in these areas to help the Philippines take further steps along the road to better economic citizenship. Thank you and good morning. (Note: IMF-World Bank Seminar on Standards and Codes in the New International Financial Architecture, April 19, 2001, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Promoting the Growth and Stability of the Banking System
Location: Resident Lounge, Ayala Center, Makati City
Occasion: Monthly Membership Meeting, Australia-New Zealand Chamber of Commerce (Philippines)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I. Introduction Mr. William f. Mason and Mr. Chris Ward, President and Executive Director, respectively, of the Australia-New Zealand Chamber of Commerce (Philippines), Inc.; friends, ladies and gentlemen, good evening. It is my distinct pleasure to address this monthly membership meeting of the Australia-New Zealand Chamber of Commerce. Together, our three countries share many common interests in the region, and the Australia-New Zealand chamber of commerce has contributed significantly to the promotion of these interests, be they in cultural, social or economic affairs. My talk tonight will focus on the importance of promoting the growth and stability of the banking system in a globalized environment. After experiencing a setback due to the Asian financial crisis, most of the affected economies in the region recovered rather quickly, and seemed poised for a take-off into sustainable growth. However, recent uncertainty about the extent and duration of the slowdown in the U.S. economy, coupled with the fragile recovery in Japan, have underscored the importance of international developments on the region's growth prospects. The increased mobility of cross-border capital flows that has accompanied globalization and the greater economic linkages among countries call attention to the crucial issue of the stability and efficiency of our financial systems. This evening, I will, therefore, First present briefly the important aspects of the current international environment that could bear on the performance of the economy for the coming year; and point out the role that a healthy financial sector plays in supporting sustainable growth; Then update you on the present state of the Philippine banking system; Next, go over the policy reforms that the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has done in order to prepare the financial system to meet these challenges; and Finally, present the policy reform agenda in the medium term. II. The Challenge from a Possible Global Economic Slowdown The importance of implementing a structural reform program for the economy in general and the financial sector in particular is underscored by concerns about the near-term prospects of the global economy. The anticipated slowdown in the U.S. and Japan could impact disproportionately on the ASEAN economies, and on the information technology (it) sector in particular, in view of the importance of the U.S. and Japanese markets as destinations for ASEAN exports. Central forecasts of economic growth in the U.S. have fallen to 1.5-2.5 percent in 2001, from 3.5 percent in 2000, while structural weaknesses in the banking and corporate sectors are expected to hold down the growth of the Japanese economy to a little over 1.0 percent. However, an IMF paper cites significant room for policy maneuver in both the fiscal and monetary areas in most advanced economies, with the exception of Japan, and, as a result, the paper argues that there is a chance that recovery could start in the second half of 2001. What do these developments mean for emerging market economies? Growth in the export sector could be expected to soften and the inflow of foreign investments could be subdued. On the other hand, lower interest rates and growth prospects in developed economies could lead to a reallocation of capital portfolios. Whether this will lead to strengthened capital inflows to particular economies or not will depend on the ability of those economies to demonstrate good track records in terms of attaining macroeconomic and financial stability, and to lay down, through appropriate structural reforms, the foundations for sustainable economic growth. With regard to the financial system, the challenge is to sustain its growth and stability in the midst of these fast-moving global developments. Any disruption in the intermediation process of the financial system will inevitably have negative repercussions on the rest of the economy. As a result, the soundness of the banking system and the adequacy of the supervisory framework have generated considerable interest. Allow me to discuss these with you in some detail. III. State of the Philippine Banking System The Philippines has emerged from a crisis-prone year with its democratic institutions intact and with the basic strength of its economy preserved. Through this and through the Asian financial crisis, the Philippines' fundamentally sound financial system has served us in good stead. A two-decade history of close supervision, sustained banking reforms, and implementation of timely pre-emptive measures have helped develop a financial system that is able to withstand transitory shocks arising from both domestic and external sources. Key banking sector indicators reflect this: The banking system's total resources increased by 10.4 percent in 2000, to P3.3 trillion. Asset quality remained manageable, despite a recent uptrend in non-performing loans as a result of the pass-through effects of higher interest rates and the depreciation of the peso. As of end-2000, the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio of the banking system was 15.0 percent, higher than the 12.7 percent recorded at end-1999. In particular, the NPL ratio of commercial banks improved to 16.0 percent in January 2001, after peaking at 16.3 percent in November 2000. In comparison, the end-December 2000 NPL ratios were 17.7 percent for Thailand and 18.8 percent for Indonesia, and the end-January 2001 ratio was 9.4 percent for Malaysia.[1] While the ratios have fallen faster in some of the other affected Asian economies, these declines have reflected largely the off-loading of NPLs to public restructuring agencies. By contrast, no public funds have been used in the Philippines to purchase non-performing assets or recapitalize financial institutions. The banking system remained adequately capitalized during the year. As of end-December 2000, the average capital adequacy ratio reached 16.4 percent, lower than the previous year's 17.5 percent but well above the BSP statutory floor of 10.0 percent and the Bank for International Settlement's (BIS) standard of 8.0 percent. The decline in the capital adequacy ratio was attributable to the increase in the required valuation reserves. While the real estate exposure of commercial banks rose slightly to 12.3 percent as of end-September 2000, from 11.6 percent in December 1999, the ratio remains far below the 20 percent ceiling imposed by the BSP. In the face of the anticipated correction in international equity markets and the subdued mood for foreign investment, the financial sector's efficiency in fund intermediation and risk management would play a key role in determining how well the Philippine economy performs this year. Let me, therefore, discuss some of the recent steps that the BSP has undertaken in order to further strengthen the financial system. IV. Reforms and Policy Directions The BSP has instituted major reforms in financial supervision and regulation. The overarching framework is provided by the recently passed General Banking Law of 2000 (Republic Act No. 8791).
