Some of the more important features of the GBL 2000 include: (1) granting authority to the Monetary Board to require banks to adopt internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy; (2) providing for stricter rules governing bank exposure to directors, officers, stockholders and related interests (DOSRI); (3) strengthening current regulations with respect to transparency practices; (4) adopting a fit-and-proper rule test for appointment of senior bank officials; (5) further liberalizing the ownership participation of foreign banks in the local banking system to 100 percent within seven years after the effectivity of the GBL 2000; and (6) granting authority to the BSP to regulate electronic banking. The BSP has tasked a committee to formulate the implementing rules of the new law. So far, circulars have been issued pertaining to foreign stockholdings, outsourcing of banking functions, guidelines on microfinance loans and the adoption of risk-based capital adequacy standards aligned with international norms. The BSP also instituted regulatory changes so as to improve risk management in the financial system: The BSP has changed the focus of its supervision from a purely compliance-based and checklist-driven assessment of banks' conditions to a forward-looking and risk-based framework. The BSP has also begun to supervise financial conglomerates on a consolidated basis, including consolidation of limits on foreign currency exposures between banks and their affiliated foreign exchange corporations. The definition of past due loans was tightened.[2] To promote sound risk management in large-value transactions, the BSP, in collaboration with the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP), is developing a Real Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS) that will cover transactions in the equities, fixed income, money and foreign exchange markets. Once fully operational, the RTGS would offer a powerful mechanism for limiting settlement and systemic risks in the interbank settlement process. In response to current trends towards increased use of the internet in banking, the BSP has laid down the requirements for banks seeking to provide electronic banking services. This is to ensure that banks planning to provide these services have in place a risk management process that is adequate to assess, control and monitor associated risks. A policy of encouraging mergers and consolidations has been in place for some time. This recognizes the fact that bigger-capitalized banks can withstand better the increased volatility of capital flows, and are, therefore, better equipped to meet the demands of the new globalized environment. The policy also reduces moral hazard since owners have more of their wealth at stake. The BSP offered incentives in support of this policy, including allowing banks to amortize their goodwill up to a maximum period of forty (40) years. In addition to the foregoing measures, the BSP has adopted key reforms that strengthen the foundations for good governance in the financial system. Among other areas, these reforms address the need for: Management integrity and adequacy of training and experience. The BSP has provided guidelines governing the responsibilities of banks' boards of directors and the election/appointment of bank directors and officers. Transparency and disclosure. The BSP has instructed all banks to disclose publicly detailed quarterly information on their non-performing loans, classified loans and other risk assets, amount of general and specific loan-loss reserves, return on equity, and insider (DOSRI) loans. V. Looking Ahead Moving forward, a major plus factor for the Philippines is the greatly improved and stabilized political situation which has improved confidence. In addition, fiscal authorities have committed to firmly address the fiscal deficit through a combination of expenditure restraint and--more importantly--improvements in tax collection efforts and administration. The outlook for inflation in 2001 is also favorable, with indications that inflationary pressures will abate starting the second half of this year, to average 6-7 percent in 2001. It may be recalled that inflation remained steady at 6.7 percent in march relative to its month-ago rate. These factors provide greater flexibility to the BSP to pursue its primary mandate of maintaining price stability for sustained economic recovery and growth. The inflation-targeting framework--which the BSP plans to implement in the middle of 2001--embodies this commitment through its emphasis on transparency, accountability and a forward-looking perspective. By stabilizing prices, inflation targeting will encourage longer term saving and investment, and will deepen the role for longer-term financial intermediation. Flexibility in monetary management will also help support attainment of the 4-4.5 percent growth target for GNP. On the legislative front, the reforms in the general banking law of 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the New Central Bank Act. These amendments aim to enhance the BSP's supervisory powers and operational independence, improve prudential standards and promote greater competition in the banking system. Key reforms could include the relaxation of the deposit secrecy provision which would allow the monetary board to inquire into deposit accounts of suspicious nature; grant of authority to the BSP to conduct more frequent banking examinations; and greater scope and strength of administrative sanctions. With respect to another area of recent concern, the BSP issued in 2000 a number of circulars which bring the country's regulatory regime on anti-money laundering closer to international standards. These circulars require banks to take reasonable means to determine the true identities of their clients and report suspicious transactions. Recognizing the importance of legislation, the BSP is advocating the passage of House Bill No. 5216, also known as the Anti-racketeering Bill, which would make money laundering a crime in the country. Moreover, the BSP is currently working with the Bankers association of the Philippines to come up with guidelines regarding a proposal that will give banks and regulators the right to examine foreign currency deposit unit accounts under certain conditions. I hope that the foregoing discussion has gone some distance in convincing you of the vibrancy of the economic reform program in the Philippines and the continued strength of the banking system. My invitation is for you to take part in the efforts of nation-building in the Philippines. With the improved political environment and the fundamental strengths of the economy backed up by the government's firm commitment to needed reforms, there is sound basis for a take-off into sustained non-inflationary growth and for continued viability of the long-term investments in the country. Thank you and good night. ---------------------------------------------- [1] Data for other Asian economies come from the Asian Development Bank ASEAN Economic Outlook 2001 (April 2001). [2] The entire outstanding balance of a loan/receivable would now be considered as past due when the total amount of arrearages reaches ten percent (10%) of the total loan receivable balance.

Title: Keynote Address
Occasion: E-Commerce Product Launch, Union Bank of the Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It is my pleasure to keynote this evening's event. The importance of this event goes beyond the walls of Union Bank and its customers and partners as well as stakeholders. Its implications are quite far-reaching, extending to the way Philippine firms conduct business and the way consumers transact their dealings. Dramatic changes are occurring in the structure of banking. The environment has become so dynamic largely because we continue to grapple with technological innovations and globalization brought about by increased interdependence of markets and financial flows. Tonight, Union bank and partners Visa and Thyron are unveiling two e-banking products that will take e-commerce in the Philippines to the next stage of development and onward from there. Chairman Ortiz had earlier outlined what merchant establishments can do with the payment gateway, and what consumers can do with Eon Visa Electron. The main attraction is Union Bank's payment gateway, the Port. This is the first time a payment gateway is being made available to Philippine merchants and retailers. The implications --as we noted--are tremendous. The Port expands the payment options and accessible markets of Philippine merchants. Hence, Philippine merchants who otherwise could not sell locally and abroad through the internet--because they are not connected to an internet payment facility--can now link up with the Port and consummate the payment part of the transaction. This is indeed a much welcome development, because it could enable more Philippine export sales through the internet by giving Philippine businesses an opportunity to break out in the world market as well as enabling existing exporters to expand their global reach. Thus, the availability of this gateway facility will contribute significantly to today's efforts to boost exports and speed up the recovery process. Exports remain as one of the country's strong growth drivers. Not only the exports industry, but the retail trade industry as well stands to benefit from this development. Last year, the Retail Trade Liberalization Act was passed, opening the industry to increased foreign competition. With this internet payment facility, local entrepreneurs can compete more effectively with their foreign counterparts. So, part of my advice to Unionbank is to tell their merchant customers that, because of this technology, borders are increasingly being rendered seamless, with the end-result that their markets can potentially expand to include the whole world. On a more general level, this initiative is thus supportive of the government's efforts to further promote both domestic absorption and exports in order to fire the engines of economic growth. The Bangko Sentral is, therefore, quite pleased to see these banking innovations because they are good for the global competitiveness of Philippine business. I normally order my books from amazon.com because they're reasonably priced and delivered fast. If a Philippine supplier later on emerges that is price-competitive, operationally efficient and image-and-media-savvy enough to at least match the amazon.coms of the world, then I don't see any reason why you and I won't buy from that supplier. As I scan the possibilities in the horizon, the payment gateway might help unlock the entrepreneurial talents and competitiveness of many Philippine businesses. It is not impossible if the next logistics company to challenge UPS, DHL and Federal Express would be an enterprising Philippine outfit. This is not far-fetched given that Philippine entrepreneurs are quite adept at innovating, particularly those who understand the challenges presented by a wired world. I must commend Union Bank and partners Thyron and Visa for taking the initiative. In particular, I would like to commend Tito Ortiz for crusading e-commerce in the Philippines. A crucial segment in e-commerce is, of course, the payment leg; otherwise e-commerce is not consummated. What Union Bank is doing is providing the payment leg by bringing proven world-class technology into the Philippine market. That is a clear, positive contribution to the evolution of the Philippine e-marketplace. For our part as your central bank, I wish to give you my assurance that the Bangko Sentral under my watch remains accommodating and supportive of the ongoing evolution of e-commerce in the Philippines, which is led by the private sector, as should be the case. Like the private sector, the Bangko Sentral is responding to the demands of e-commerce. We have ongoing initiatives such as the Real Time Gross Settlement project, which is expected to enhance operational efficiency, reliability, speed and timeliness of payment transactions in the face of rapidly increasing volume and value of transactions. The RTGS system, once in place, will offer a powerful mechanism for limiting settlement and systemic risks in the interbank settlement process, thus ensuring stability of the whole financial system. Another initiative is in the form of interbank call loans, which are now electronically linked to the BSP's financial accounting system, among others. However, as transactions involving this type of technology grow in volume and complexity, there is a need to identify, assess and manage the risks attendant to these transactions. The BSP has already undertaken initial steps towards this direction. It has issued some requirements to be imposed on banks seeking or already providing e-banking services to ensure that these banks have in place a risk management process that is adequate to assess, control, and monitor associated risks. My challenge to union bank and other Philippine banks who are at the forefront of e-banking is this: make sure transaction security and integrity as well as client confidentiality are never compromised. These are the non-negotiable items as far as Bangko Sentral is concerned. E-commerce is a new and unfamiliar terrain to many of us, and we have to be very careful. For sure we at the BSP are as vigilant as ever in monitoring and providing safeguards for the general public with respect to these banking innovations. This is indeed an auspicious evening. Thank you and good evening. (Note: E-Commerce Product Launch, Union Bank of the Philippines, March 29, 2001, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Recent Developments in the Philippine Economy
Occasion: Philippine-American Chamber of Commerce Trade Mission, Makati Business Club
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I take great pleasure in joining the participants in this trade mission led by the Philippine American Chamber of Commerce, Inc. Today, you have come at an auspicious time when the country is reviewing its directions and priorities in an effort to achieve faster economic recovery and a more conducive business environment. I therefore welcome this opportunity to update you on the Philippine economic situation, particularly on developments in the monetary and banking system. Real sector Let me start with the real sector developments. · In the face of challenges from the domestic and international fronts last year, the Philippine economy managed to pull off a respectable performance. Real GNP grew by 4.2 percent, well above the 3.7 percent posted in 1999. The economic expansion was underpinned by a more balanced and broad-based growth among the major sectors of the economy. · This growth picture in 2000 continues to be validated by key advance indicators. On the supply side, the production index has been on the rise both in value and in volume. On the demand side, exports continue to grow although at a slower pace. Power sales remain strong, while appliance sales have rebounded from a declining trend in 1999. Commercial bank lending also continues to be favorable, showing a 7.8 percent growth in January this year, up from a negative 0.2 percent growth a year ago. However, imports growth has remained low, and passenger car sales have declined in the first two months of the year. Monetary sector Notwithstanding the pick-up in economic activity last year, prices have remained generally stable. · Inflation averaged 4.4 percent last year, compared to the 6.7 percent recorded in 1999. This was also well below the program range of 5-6 percent in 2000. For the first two months of this year, inflation averaged 6.8 percent, well within the program range of 6-7 percent for whole year. · Moreover, benign inflation was achieved despite inflationary pressures from oil price and transport fare increases and the depreciation of the peso, which fed into wage adjustments. · Overall, in 2000, monetary policy was supportive of economic growth, despite some tightening episodes in May, September and October to smoothen out some instability in the financial market. The calibrated adjustments in policy rates during these episodes were eventually offset by policy rate cuts since December as broad stability in the market eventually prevailed. Since December last year, we have reduced our policy rates by 500 basis points. · As a result, interest rates have begun to ease toward the end of the year. This was true both for the benchmark 91-day T-bill rate and the bank lending rates. · The easing of the monetary stance resulted in the expansion in domestic liquidity by 4.6 percent in 2000, and further to 12.2 percent in January this year. This expansionary trend was reflected as increases in the public and private sector credits, with the bulk of bank loans going into manufacturing and other key sectors of the economy. Fiscal sector · In the fiscal sector, the fiscal position was a source of concern in 2000 as the National Government deficit exceeded the target for the year. Nonetheless, it is helpful to note that the increasing use of domestic sources to finance the shortfall did not lead to a precipitate increase in market lending rates. · For this year, fiscal consolidation is a tall order that will require fiscal discipline on the part of the government. Fiscal prudence is expected to be achieved through: improvement in tax collections, improvement in tax administration, and rationalization of government expenditures. External sector · In the external sector, the current account posted a hefty surplus in 2000, owing to brisk exports and low import growth. The overall balance of payments, however, showed a deficit due to a weaker financial account. · As of end-February 2001, our international reserves remained high at $14.2 billion, which is equivalent to 4.2 months of imports of goods and payments of services, and more than enough to cover our short-term obligations. · The country's external debt remained manageable, with the bulk of total debt stock accounted for by medium and long-term liabilities. Owing to this and good export numbers, the country's debt service burden has also remained manageable at 12.5 percent compared to 17 percent, which was observed in the early 1990s. · Meanwhile, the peso started appreciating slightly toward the end of December 2000 on account of foreign exchange inflows and the progress in the political situation during the period. But in early January this year, the peso was again subjected to some pressure owing to political uncertainties at that time. However, following the change in administration in mid-January, the peso has since improved and stabilized. The banking system · In the banking sector, our banking system has remained sound as evident in its steady level of resources and manageable banking ratios. · As of end-December 2000, total resources of the banking system reached P3.3 trillion, compared to P3.0 trillion a year ago. · The capital adequacy ratio of banks at 15.6 percent as of end-December 2000 was well above the 10 percent minimum requirement and the 8 percent international standard. · Meanwhile, the quality of commercial bank assets continued to be manageable. As of end-December 2000, the NPL ratio of commercial banks fell to 15.1 percent from 16.3 percent a month ago. · In addition, our banks' real estate exposure at 12.3 percent of total loan portfolio as of December 2000 was way below the 20 percent ceiling imposed by the BSP. · n general, our banking system remains healthy and resilient and continues to be an efficient transmission channel of monetary policy. Outlook · Overall, if the economy's performance last year is any indicator, we are moving toward a more broad-based growth, even as we strive to rise to the challenge of fiscal consolidation. For this year, the government expects the economy to grow by 4.0-4.5 percent in terms of GNP and by 3.8-4.3 percent in terms of GDP. Growth is expected to be underpinned by the continued strength of the services sector. Meanwhile, inflation is expected to be in the range of 6.0-7.0 percent. · With the stabilization of the domestic political situation, business confidence has continued to improve. One indication is the result of the business world-audit & surveys worldwide joint survey for the last couple of months, which showed a significant rise in the business confidence index. External environment · In the external front, macroeconomic developments in the major industrial countries are expected to continue to exert a major influence on domestic economic developments. Upside factors that are being monitored include: the moderating trend in world oil prices and lower U.S. interest rates; while risk factors include a slower growth in the U.S. economy as well as potential weaknesses in the economies of Japan and the European Union. The Philippines as an ideal investment site · In addition to the country's sound macroeconomic performance, the positive economic outlook, and the supportive external environment that we have discussed earlier, one other factor that makes the Philippines an ideal investment site is its high-quality workforce. · As most of you would know, the country has a large pool of highly trained, English-speaking manpower. · In 1999, the PERC survey ranked the Filipino worker first in Asean and second in Asia in terms of quality, cost competitiveness and availability. · Around the same period, the Meta Group's Cyber Atlas ranked the Philippines first among 47 countries in terms of availability of knowledge workers. This was based on the country having more qualified IT engineers, more senior managers and higher enrollment in higher education. Policy thrusts · I have given you some broad-brush strokes on the state of the Philippine economy. With the recent change in administration and the return of business confidence, faster economic recovery is clearly underway. · For its part, the Bangko Sentral will continue to pursue its primary mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to a balanced and sustained growth of the economy. · One major policy thrust will be the implementation of the shift from monetary targeting to inflation targeting. This is expected to improve further the transparency and consistency of monetary policy, and consequently its effectiveness. · In the banking sector, efforts to further strengthen and modernize the banking sector will continue to be pursued. This will include: finalizing the rules and regulations implementing the General Banking Law of 2000; improving risk management and the payment and settlement infrastructure; encouraging mergers and consolidations; pursuing amendments to the BSP charter; and strengthening efforts to combat money laundering. In closing, I wish to thank the organizers of this mission for the opportunity to present the current monetary and banking environment in the country. I hope that the members of the mission will be able to spread the word about the more positive prospects now prevailing in the economy. Thank you and good day. (Note: Philippine American Chamber of Commerce Trade Mission, Makati Business Club, March 23, 2001, Hotel Inter-Continental, Makati City )

Title: Outlook for Monetary and Banking Policies in the Philippines
Occasion: Business Conference, The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It is with great pleasure that I join this gathering of the top executives of multinational companies in the local business community. Of late, I have attended a number of similar sessions with leaders of the business community and have had interesting discussions with them. I am sure that we will also have productive exchange of views today. The BSP has two major responsibilities under its charter. One, to provide policy direction in the areas of money, banking and credit. Two, to supervise the operations of banks and regulate finance companies and non-bank financial institutions performing quasi-banking functions. Allow me then to provide you with a broad outline of the BSP's policy thrust in these two areas. Monetary policy The thrust of BSP monetary policy will continue to be guided by our primary mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to a balanced and sustained economic growth. Monetary policy stance was generally accommodative for most of last year as inflation remained largely subdued. However, there were tightening episodes, particularly in may and in September-October, in response to emerging inflationary pressures and the narrowing of interest differentials which contributed to volatility in the foreign exchange market. These episodes were characterized by increases in our key policy rates as well as in liquidity reserve requirements. However, as the foreign exchange market began to achieve stability in December, monetary policy was gradually eased. Further boost in the stability of financial markets was achieved with the peaceful resolution of the recent political impasse. Expectations of declining inflation and the stabilization of the financial markets have provided more room for easing of monetary conditions and helped establish a more supportive environment for business activity. Thus, this year saw the continued gradual relaxation of monetary policy. Since December last year, the BSP has already reduced its key policy rates by a total of 450 basis points. In the near term, the BSP sees some potential for further easing of the monetary policy stance. Inflation for this year is expected to be relatively higher during the first semester due to the lagged effects of a weaker peso, oil price hikes and wage adjustments late last year. However, improvements in supply conditions and prospects for continued stability in the foreign exchange market are expected to lead to a downtrend in inflation in the second half. This anticipated downtrend in inflation and the easing bias of the U.S. Fed will provide the BSP with greater latitude for further cuts in the BSP's policy rates. However, this has to be weighed alongside the need to maintain an appropriate interest rate differential to encourage investors to keep their peso- denominated assets. There may also be downside risks that dictate a circumspect approach in further reducing policy rates. As such, the BSP will continue to watch closely developments in the financial and fiscal sector and more importantly, the emerging inflationary scenario to guide its subsequent actions. To further improve its capability to pursue its mandate of price stability, the BSP plans to formally shift to inflation targeting as the framework for conducting monetary policy by the middle of this year. Under this framework, government authorities will pre-announce the inflation target over a given time horizon. If the target is not met, the BSP will be required to explain the reasons and to spell out the measures that it will take to get back on track. The framework, therefore will allow the Bangko Sentral to build its credibility by demonstrating consistent adherence to the inflation goal. In the process, the framework will promote greater transparency in the conduct of monetary policy, thus facilitating more efficient markets, as well as greater accountability on the part of monetary authorities for its actions. Banking sector policy In the banking system, the BSP's focus remains the promotion of a stable, sound and globally competitive financial system. The BSP envisions a banking system that is strong, sound and resilient as well as able to intermediate funds effectively and manage risks efficiently. A key reform measure is the change in the legislative framework for the banking system. The General Banking Law (GBL) of 2000 or R.A. No. 8791, which was passed last May 2000, now forms the basic legal fabric governing the banking system. The law gives the BSP flexibility in supervising the banking industry and upgrades the country's banking laws to meet global standards. A number of Circulars to implement the provisions of this new law have already been issued by the BSP including those on the definition, classification, powers and scope of authorities of banks, outsourcing of banking functions, foreign stockholdings, and microfinancing loans. The reforms supported by the GBL 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the Charter of the Bangko Sentral. These amendments are important if we are to reap the full benefits offered by the GBL. The amendments will reinforce the autonomy, authority and capacity of the BSP not only to regulate and supervise the banking system but also to more effectively implement monetary policy. A specific amendment to the New Central Bank Act will among others relax existing barriers to the fight against money laundering. We are proposing to Congress that the Monetary Board be allowed to look into deposits of more than P50 million in an individual account, provided that there is reasonable ground to believe that such an account is being used in relation to any fraud or irregularity. This will effectively restore the authority of the Monetary Board under the old Central Bank Act, which was deleted under the New CB Act, to inquire into deposit accounts of a suspicious nature. The BSP is also currently working with the BAP on guidelines that will give banks and regulators the right to examine FCDU accounts under certain conditions. Under the plan, non- Philippine resident depositors will be asked to sign a voluntary waiver on secrecy upon opening an FCDU account in any Philippine-based bank. To raise the level of awareness of the general public and the authorities concerned, the BSP and the BAP institute have sponsored and will continue to sponsor seminars on money laundering. Related to this effort, the BSP is supporting the passage of a legislation which would, among others, make money laundering a crime in the country. Aside from the changes in the country's banking laws, an on-going initiative by the BSP is the improvement of its supervisory framework in line with the evolving structure of the financial system. This upgrading of capabilities would ensure that supervision will remain effective in fostering the safety and soundness of the country's banking system. An important step in this effort is the adoption of a more forward-looking and risk based bank supervision framework. This involves the re-orientation of the bank examination process towards quality of decision processes rather than just compliance with rules and regulation. Another dimension of the upgrading is the implementation of consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates. This approach facilitates a more comprehensive assessment of the risks involved in the banks' activities. The BSP is also in the middle of pursuing important changes in the regulatory framework for banks. Regulatory standards are being aligned with international norms and internationally- accepted best practices. Transparency, on the part of both market participants and regulators, is being emphasized to promote better bank governance and more effective market discipline. The entire regulatory framework is in fact being reviewed to plug any remaining loopholes. The regulatory gaps between banks and non-banks are being closed to avoid regulatory arbitrage activities. The remaining regulatory loopholes on foreign exchange trading are likewise being addressed. The BSP has also started to address the need to improve the regulatory framework with the introduction and anticipated growth of e-banking. We have already issued general guidelines for those banks planning to offer e-banking services to ensure that banks have rigorous internal controls and comprehensive risk management systems that can adequately take into account the risks involved in these new banking activities. The BSP will remain vigilant for developments in the banking community and innovations in technology so that we can finetune our policies accordingly. The BSP is also encouraging the restructuring of the local banking industry. In a more globalized financial landscape, we realize that domestic banks need to mobilize sufficient capitalization and to strengthen risk management systems to compete in a more challenging and globally integrated banking environment. This strengthening can be assisted through mergers and acquisitions and through greater participation of foreign financial institutions. The BSP is also supporting the modernization of the market infrastructure for the financial system. In line with this, a key initiative supported by the BSP is the upgrading of the existing payment system into a Real Time Gross Settlement system to enhance operational efficiency, reliability, speed and timeliness of payment transactions. This will not only foster a more efficient banking system but also help develop the capital market. Another initiative being supported by the BSP that can enhance the development of the domestic capital market is the plan to securitize long-term deposits. The proposed scheme involves the pooling of funds deposited for at least five years into certificates of deposits that can be traded in the secondary market. This scheme can help spur domestic savings and deepen the local capital market. The BSP is also extending support to the social development agenda of the government within the limits set by its charter. Last January, the BSP issued a Circular on microfinancing loans to implement some of the provisions of the GBL. These provisions relate to the application of market-based interest rates by lending institutions to enable them to recover the financial and operational costs of their micro finance operations. This was complemented by the lifting of the moratorium on the licensing of new thrift and rural banks to allow the entry of microfinance-oriented banks. The BSP is also finalizing guidelines for the opening of a rediscount window for rural banks and cooperative banks engaged in microfinance. This facility will support small banks that have achieved efficiency in their microfinance operations, without sacrificing prudential standards. Through this initiatives, the BSP hopes to contribute in the effort to bring more resources and opportunities to the marginalized sectors of our society. Conclusion I have given you this morning an overview of the recent changes and future direction of BSP monetary and banking sector policies. The BSP has sought to maintain stable monetary conditions in the country. It has also undertaken wide-ranging reform measures in recent years and we expect this process to continue as our economy develops and as the economic and financial environment evolves. We expect that the initiatives that we have set to pursue will enhance our ability to help create an environment conducive to the expansion of productive activities of the private sector. We hope that the business community will respond positively to our efforts and do its share in achieving a higher, more balanced and sustained growth path for our economy. Thank you and good day. (Note: Business Conference, The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), March 16, 2001, Mandarin Oriental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Moving Forward with Monetary Policy in 2001
Occasion: Business Economics Club, University of Asia and the Pacific
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon: It is my great pleasure to join this distinguished gathering of business and economics professionals to talk about the prospects for monetary policy in 2001. This is indeed a timely opportunity to discuss the Bangko Sentral's conduct of monetary policy. One of the fulcrums of sound and sustainable economic growth is price stability, and preserving price stability is the major challenge that confronts central bankers around the world. The remark made by US Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers that "Monetary policy is destiny" may be an exaggeration, but it carries a fair amount of truth in it. This afternoon I would like to begin with a brief description of present monetary conditions, along with the Bangko Sentral's recent policy actions. I would then like to move on to the broader plan for monetary policy, which is to shift to an inflation targeting framework by the middle part of the year. Recent economic and monetary developments Last year, as you know, was an eventful one for the Philippines, with pressures coming from both the domestic and international fronts. The BSP's monetary policy stance took a generally accommodative path for most of 2000. However, there were some tightening episodes in May, September, and October in response to emerging inflationary pressures and the narrowing interest rate differentials that have contributed to some volatility in the foreign exchange market. The increases in policy rates and the liquidity reserve requirement in 2000 were calibrated carefully to address the underlying price pressures without unduly restricting the pace of economic recovery. Thus, despite domestic and external shocks, the economy managed to register a respectable performance. Real GNP growth strengthened to 4.2 percent in 2000 from 3.7 percent in 1999. At the same time, inflation remained largely subdued despite pressures from supply-side shocks such as record-high world oil prices. Average inflation for the year was recorded at 4.4 percent, well below the government's target of 5-6 percent. Overall economic activity continues to show signs of improvement, as indicated by leading indicators of supply and demand conditions. For example, manufacturing production posted higher growth rates in both value and volume terms for the whole of 2000. Average capacity utilization likewise picked up slightly from 79.3 percent in December 1999 to 80.0 percent in December 2000. Palay production also reached a record high of 12.4 million metric tons in 2000, which could translate into favorable food prices this year. Growth in commercial bank lending has continued to expand, rising by 7.2 percent year-on-year at end-December 2000. Similarly, Meralco power sales grew by 7.1 percent in 2000, compared to 0.6 percent in the previous year. Appliance sales made a turnaround, rising by 7.2 percent last year following an 8.4 percent decline in 1999. These favorable trends augur well for overall economic performance for the year. At the same time, the recent stabilization of the domestic political situation and the peaceful change in political leadership have brought about renewed business confidence and restored stability in our financial markets. This broad stability has provided room for the gradual easing of the BSP's monetary policy stance. The series of reductions in key policy interest rates in December, January and February amounting to a cumulative total of 400 basis points effectively reversed the increases in October 2000 and brought down policy rates back to their pre-crisis levels. The resulting monetary easing should provide a supportive environment for business activity. Outlook for monetary policy What do we expect for monetary policy for the rest of the year? Since February 12, the monetary board has kept the BSP's policy rates steady at 11.0 percent and 13.25 percent for the overnight RRP and RP rates, respectively. The Monetary Board will, however, continue to review the BSP's monetary policy settings, taking its cue from financial markets and other economic indicators before effecting further policy rate reductions. The important precondition for rate cuts in the near term is that price pressures remain subdued so that monetary policy action does not jeopardize the low-inflation environment needed to foster investment and growth. The overall direction for monetary policy in 2001 will thus depend on the assessment of the inflation path for the year. Prevailing inflationary pressures remain relatively benign, and there are indications that cost-push influences may turn out to be weaker than previously expected. For example, the Department of Agriculture has reported that the dry spell associated with the el niño weather phenomenon this year may be milder than previously expected. This implies favorable food supply conditions which, in turn, would translate into stable food prices. Nevertheless, some risks remain. On the external front, the slowdown in the U.S. economy will have a significant impact on emerging economies like the Philippines which have close trade and financial linkages with the U.S. Concerns over the U.S. slowdown could be amplified by continued weakness in the Japanese economy and slow recovery in the Euro area. The prospect of lower foreign interest rates--as these countries try to rev up their economies --creates the risk of exchange rate volatility in emerging economies as interest rate differentials narrow. There are also talks of a new round of oil production cuts, which could lead to higher crude oil prices and create cost-push inflationary pressures. All these could pose a threat to the expected deceleration of domestic inflation in the second half of the year. On the domestic front, the main risks to inflation could come from the large fiscal deficit, although the government has committed to make fiscal discipline a key plank in its economic program. These risks highlight the need for greater vigilance on the part of monetary authorities to ensure that the price stability objective is achieved. For the year, the government is targeting an average inflation rate of 6-7 percent. Moving towards inflation targeting Looking ahead, the BSP's efforts are focused on preparing for the shift to inflation targeting. As some of you may know, on January 24, 2000, the Monetary Board approved in principle the shift to inflation targeting as the framework for monetary policy. Let me explain briefly the thinking that went behind the decision to adopt this framework. Inflation targeting focuses mainly on price stability as the primary objective of monetary policy. This approach has several basic features. First, the central bank announces an explicit inflation target, which it commits to achieve over a suitable time horizon. Second, monetary policy is forward-looking, since it is important for policy to react at an early stage to emerging inflationary risks. Third, the commitment to an explicit inflation target improves the accountability of the central bank and raises transparency in the conduct of monetary policy, two common threads of good governance. Increased accountability enhances the credibility of monetary policy, while greater transparency promotes the efficient functioning of financial markets which, in turn, leads to a stable and predictable macroeconomic environment. Inflation targeting has attracted considerable attention over the past few years from central bankers, academics and other government policymakers. Its growing appeal is based on two factors. First, for many countries, financial liberalization in the past decades has led to the weakening of the relationship between money and prices, and also between broad money and operating targets such as base money and reserve money. This has reduced the effectiveness of standard monetary aggregate targeting and prompted a search for an alternative policy framework. Second, monetary authorities were encouraged by the success of the pioneer countries that have adopted inflation targeting. Countries like Australia, Canada, Finland, Sweden, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Israel and Chile moved from a high-inflation to a low-inflation environment and experienced higher output growth as well as reduced volatility in prices and output growth. This strategy has also been adopted in developing economies, notably Brazil and, more recently, Thailand. Inflation targeting in the Philippines is expected to help advance the cause of economic reform. Specifically, by helping ensure price stability, inflation targeting creates a stable macro environment for continuing reforms. Moreover, the basic preconditions of inflation targeting--the primacy of price stability objective as the objective of monetary policy and central bank independence--are already in place. Republic Act (R.A.) 7653 or the New Central Bank Act (dated 3 July 1993) explicitly identifies price stability consistent with a balanced and sustainable economic growth as the primary objective of the Bangko Sentral. The law specifically provides for the operational (or instrument) independence of the BSP. This means that the BSP is free to choose its own instruments, such as open-market operations, in the conduct of monetary policy. Central bank independence also implies fiscal independence, or the absence of fiscal dominance. the BSP Charter provides for clear limits to any possible financial assistance of the BSP to the National Government. Fiscal independence thus allows the BSP to pursue its main objective of price stability without being constrained by fiscal considerations. Successful inflation targeting also requires a well-developed financial system, to ensure the effectiveness of the monetary transmission mechanism. The Philippine financial system has a long history of reforms, which should further strengthen the foundations and enable it to be an efficient channel for monetary policy. With the basic preconditions in place, the challenges of the shift to inflation targeting involve mainly the operational aspects of the new framework. We began last year with a series of public hearings on inflation targeting to promote better public understanding of the directions of monetary policy. Other important operational issues include the use of the headline inflation rate as the measure of inflation and core inflation as the operating target. Headline inflation is widely known and easily understood by the public, but is also subject to supply-side shocks that are beyond the central bank's control. Thus, the BSP's announced targets would have to take into account the impact of supply-side shocks on inflation. This can be addressed through the adoption of a target band for greater flexibility. Meanwhile, core or underlying inflation makes a good operating target since it excludes volatile CPI components, such as food and energy, that are subject to short-run disturbances. Thus, it is affected mainly by demand factors that can be influenced by monetary policy actions. The National Statistics Office (NSO) currently does not publish a core inflation series, but work is now underway to construct an NSO definition of core inflation. Effective inflation targeting also requires an accurate forward-looking assessment of inflation and output growth over the target horizon. This is to allow policy to react at a relatively early stage to emerging inflationary pressures. To this end, the BSP is at work on further strengthening its econometric modeling and forecasting capabilities with the development of a long-term macroeconomic model to complement its current short-term inflation forecasting models. Lastly, measures to enhance BSP transparency include the adoption of annual inflation targets for the medium-term, publication of monetary board discussions pertaining to monetary policy, publication of a quarterly inflation report, and press releases on both policy actions and assessments of the monetary stance. Concluding remarks In conclusion, improving economic conditions have allowed monetary easing to reverse the temporary tightening in 2000. This should help provide a supportive environment for economic growth objectives. Nevertheless, the presence of upside risks to the inflation outlook requires policymakers to stand alert against threats to price stability. In this regard, the shift to inflation targeting this year will help provide a credible and forward-looking framework that further strengthens the central bank's focus on price stability. In closing, I would like to offer some words from U.S. Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, who said in a recent congressional testimony: "A central bank can best contribute to economic growth and rising standards of living by fostering a financial environment that promotes overall balance in the economy and price stability." In short, the chief importance of monetary policy is in creating the supportive economic conditions necessary for long-term sustainable development. Through strategies such as inflation targeting, the central bank aims to contribute to broad macroeconomic stability through stable prices. This is the abiding commitment of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. Thank you and good afternoon. (Note: Business Economics Club, University of Asia and the Pacific, March 07, 2001, UA&P, Pasig City)

Title: Opening Statement
Occasion: Breakfast Meeting, Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: The year 2000 saw the economy challenged from several sides. On the external front, world oil prices shot up to record levels, leading to higher transport costs and higher wages. A buoyant U.S. economy necessitated the tightening of U.S. monetary policy, which narrowed interest rate differentials and contributed to the generalized weakening of regional currencies. These adverse global developments were compounded by uncertainties on the domestic front, particularly in the political arena. Recent economic developments However, even in the face of domestic and international shocks, the economy managed to pull off a respectable performance. The recovery that started in 1999 was sustained in 2000 as real GDP grew by 3.9 percent and real GNP rose by 4.2 percent. Growth was broad-based, and, in terms of expenditures, exports and personal consumption were the main drivers. This moderate expansion in economic activity was realized amidst a benign inflation environment. Favorable weather conditions--which kept food prices generally stable in 2000--and the BSP's resolve to keep monetary aggregates within programmed levels helped keep inflation at bay. Inflationary pressures were evident toward year-end due to the series of oil price and transport fare increases as well as the depreciation of the peso, which fed into wage adjustments. However, due to good inflation numbers early on, the average inflation for 2000 remained low at 4.4 percent. In January 2001, year-on-year inflation rose slightly to 6.9 percent but it decelerated to 6.7 percent in February, bringing the average inflation to 6.8 percent, within the government's target of 6-7 percent for 2001. Moderate inflation provided the flexibility to keep interest rates low and stable in 2000. the 91-day t-bill rate averaged 9.9 percent in 2000, down from the 10.2 percent average in 1999. At the latest auction, the benchmark T-bill rate averaged 10.3 percent. Mirroring the trend in the T-bill rates, bank lending rates have also begun to ease. Starting December, the BSP has also reduced its own policy rates, as the financial markets showed signs of stability and in response to the future outlook on inflation. Lower lending rates are expected to steer the economic recovery towards a sustained path. In the external sector, the current account posted a hefty surplus of US$7.6 billion for the first eleven months of 2000 due mainly to the strong performance of exports which outpaced the growth in imports. The overall BOP position, however, recorded a deficit of US$918 million due to a weak capital and financial account. Meanwhile, as of end-January 2001, the country's gross international reserves (GIR) stood at $14.4 billion, equivalent to 4.2 months of imports of goods and services. With the speedy and peaceful resolution of the political crisis, and with the Supreme Court ruling on the legitimacy of the Arroyo administration, the peso appreciated to P47.812 on 05 March 2001, the strongest daily average reached this year. On the banking system, Philippine banks have been able to hold their ground amidst a challenging environment despite some stress here and there. Capitalization is more than adequate relative to international standards and the statutory floor. The banking system's capital-to-risk assets ratio as of November 2000 was recorded at 16.4 percent. The NPL ratio of commercial bank remains within the 15-16 percent range. As of end-December 2000, it dropped to 15.10 percent from a peak of 16.26 percent in November 2000. The real estate exposure of commercial banks also remains moderate at 12.3 percent of total loans (as of end-September 2000), well below the Bangko Sentral's ceiling of 20 percent. Recent policy initiatives On money laundering. A number of BSP issuances during the year reflected the efforts and commitment of the BSP in the international fight against money laundering. These efforts, however, have been circumscribed by the legal environment that the BSP has to work with. nonetheless, several administrative measures have been undertaken by the BSP to bring the country's regulatory regime on anti-money laundering closer to international standards. Among others, these measures included: 1) instructing FOREX corporations, which are affiliates or are subsidiaries of banks, to report details of all FOREX transactions; 2) requiring banks and non-banks to establish the true identity of their clients; 3) requiring banks and non-banks to report suspicious transactions; 4) prohibiting banks from issuing cashier's, manager's or certified checks payable to cash or numbered accounts; and 5) requiring FOREX corporations that are subsidiaries or affiliates of banks, quasi-banks and non-bank financial intermediaries to demand supporting documents from residents buyers if FOREX in amounts of $10,000 or more. In order to raise the awareness of the general public and the authorities concerned, the BSP and the BAP institute have and will continue to sponsor seminars on money laundering. In addition, the BSP and the BAP are currently working on guidelines for the proposal that will give banks and regulators the right to examine FCDU accounts under certain conditions. Under the plan, non-Philippine resident depositors will be asked to sign a voluntary waiver on secrecy upon opening an FCDU account in any Philippine-based bank. A number of initiatives are in place but these details may be discussed in the q&a portion. On economic development. The BSP has been supportive of the government's social development objectives within the parameters set by its charter. In particular, the BSP, in January 2001, released a circular to implement the provisions of the General Banking Law of 2000 with respect to microfinancing loans. These are small loans granted to the basic sectors, as defined in the social reform and poverty alleviation act of 1997 and other loans granted to the poor and low-income households for their microenterprises and small businesses. The BSP is also finalizing plans to open a rediscount window for rural and cooperative banks which lend to microfinance activities. This initiative is aimed at supporting rural and cooperative banks which have achieved efficiency in their microfinance activities, without sacrificing prudential standards. In September 1999, the BSP approved the opening of a rediscount window for banking institutions providing financing for socialized and low-cost housing. The measure supports the government's efforts to pump prime the economy through the housing sector, thus, helping bridge the gap in the supply of affordable housing especially to the underprivileged. Policy thrusts Going forward, the thrust of monetary policy will continue to be guided by the pursuit of the BSP's primary mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to a balanced and sustained economic growth. Towards this end, the shift to inflation targeting as the framework of monetary policy will be implemented. This is expected to improve further the transparency and consistency of monetary policy as well as the accountability of monetary authorities to the price stability objective. In the banking sector, the BSP will continue to improve its supervisory framework. This upgrading includes the adoption of a more forward-looking and risk-based bank supervision framework and the implementation of a consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates for a more comprehensive assessment of bank risks. The BSP will also continue to support the ongoing restructuring of the banking system, with a view to developing regionally if not globally competitive banks. Furthermore, the BSP will continue to work for the improvement in the legislative framework particularly the amendments to the BSP charter which, among others, will relax existing legal barriers to the fight against money laundering. In particular, a proposed amendment will allow the Monetary Board to look into deposits of more than P50 million in an individual account, provided that there is reasonable ground to believe that such an account is being used in relation to any fraud or irregularity. This effectively restores the authority of the Monetary Board under the Old Central Bank Act, which was deleted under the New CB Act, to inquire into a deposit account of a suspicious nature. In closing, I wish to thank the organizers of this meeting for the opportunity given to me to share with you my views on the Philippine economy and the future policy thrusts of the BSP in the areas of money and banking. Thank you. (Note: Breakfast Meeting, Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines, March 7, 2001, Manila Hotel, Metro Manila)

Title: Opening Remarks
Occasion: 2001 BSP Monetary Conference
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. George Pickering, Chief Representative for Asia and the Pacific, Bank for International Settlements; Mr. Chee Sung Lee, Division Chief, Monetary and Exchange Affairs Department, International Monetary Fund; Mr. Enoch Ch'ng, Senior Director, Monetary Authority of Singapore; Honorable Dante Canlas, Secretary of Socio-economic Planning; panel discussants, members of the Monetary Board; co-workers at the BSP; distinguished guests; ladies and gentlemen, good morning: Let me begin by saying that I am deeply honored by the presence of many distinguished guests, and delighted by the attendance of friends and colleagues in the banking system, the business community, the academe and the government. This monetary conference is the second in a series that the Bangko Sentral has organized. In 1999, when the BSP held its first monetary conference, I was wearing a different hat. I was invited to serve as one of the panel discussants on the topic, Inflation Targeting: An Alternative Way of Achieving Price Stability. I was then the president of a commercial bank. The theme of today's conference--E-Banking: Challenges and Opportunities for Central Banks--is indeed timely. A barometer of the market's perception of its importance is the number of participants here and the broad spectrum of society that they represent. The exponential growth of the internet, which only a decade ago was limited largely to academic users, clearly shows that electronic technology has become very important to all of us. Dramatic changes are occurring in central banking. They are, in fact, happening even as we speak because the environment has become so dynamic. In part, this is because we continue to grapple with globalization, which has brought about increased interdependence of markets and mobility of capital flows. Admittedly, these changes are oftentimes hard to read but read them we must, so that we do not simply react to events that occur around us. Instead, we must anticipate change. It is in recognition of this that I have always subscribed to the notion that it is better to anticipate change rather than to have it forced upon you. However, to be able to do so, one must first understand the nature of things. Central banks must, therefore, be at the forefront of efforts to discern--even anticipate--the implications of this technological revolution on their own operations. There may be some nay-sayers, who have visions of a meltdown in information technology and its catastrophic effects on society. They will be, therefore, quite reluctant in recognizing the merits of e-banking. However, based on our experience with the Y2K millennium crossover, the largest danger that the year 2000 data change engendered came from the uncertain response of consumers and other market players rather than from any computer failures. Moreover, it seems that this is no longer a question of whether we want to play the game--because this seems to be inevitable. Rather, the question is how prepared are we as we are drawn into the game. The digital divide in technology puts a premium on knowledge. It is imperative, therefore, that we learn as much as we can regarding information technology and e-banking. This conference will hopefully go some distance towards satisfying these imperatives. The progress of e-banking will impact on monetary policy in various ways. For instance, e-banking will bring about changes in the structure of the real economy and this will influence the conduct of monetary policy. I.T.-induced changes to payment and settlement systems will also influence the effectiveness of monetary policy, and affect the central bank's day-to-day operations. E-banking will surely have an impact on financial stability. As more and more people embrace e-banking, payment and settlement systems become more and more dependent on physical information systems such as computers and communication networks. Thus, bottlenecks in such systems, caused by purely technical reasons--not economic or financial ones--could ignite unwanted chain reactions in the payment system that could cause serious financial disruption. This would have important implications on the role of the central bank as the lender of last resort and as a repository of public confidence. The coming of age of e-banking will necessitate regulatory changes congenial to technological change. Invariably, we may have to rewrite the rules of the game to be in tune with the challenges of e-banking. In fact, some steps have already been done in this direction. On May 5, 2000, the BSP has issued a Circular requiring banks to seek prior approval before they can be allowed to provide e-banking services. This will help ensure that these banks have the appropriate risk management systems accompanying their provision of e-banking services. Meanwhile, increased private sector awareness of e-banking would prompt institutions to build up their capability to manage attendant risks, allowing them at the same time to maximize the resulting economic gains. Greater interaction between the private sector and regulators in this kind of forum could also assist the central bank in formulating measures that are more responsive to the needs of market players. On a more general plane, we hope that this conference will go some distance in advancing the cause of economic reform, as the country prepares to join in the growth trajectory of the third millennium. We have an interesting day ahead of us as we discuss the issue of e-banking and how this will impact on its brick-and-mortar counterparts. I look forward to a fruitful and rewarding conference. Thank you and good morning to all of you. (Note: 2001 BSP Monetary Conference, February 26, 2001, Westin Philippine Plaza)

Title: Closing Remarks
Occasion: Bank Analysis and Examination Training Program ADB-APEC Financial Regulators Training Initiative
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Norberto Nazareno, President of PDIC; Mr. Robert Porter, Consultant to ADB on Bank Supervision; Ms. Shamsad Akhtar, Manager, Financial Sector and Industry Division of ADB; distinguished guests, fellow workers of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. First of all, I would like to personally commend the group which initiated the holding of this first "national" session of the APEC Bank Supervision Training Initiative. This is the first group of participants to take part in active classroom training of this large-scale initiative, which is being supported by a wide group of international organizations as well as supervisory authorities of this region. The course is intended to provide our examiners from BSP and PDIC with a fresh understanding of the issues considered in assessing a bank's financial condition including assigning a camels rating. Also included are information on the regulatory approach to assessing risk, definitions of financial terms, descriptions of common financial products and concepts, and the cause and effect relationships of financial strategies. For the past five (5) days, the participants were subjected to an intense training on bank financial analysis, combined with some concepts for on-site examinations, particularly, on risk-focused examination process, and the camels rating system. Let me tell you that the BSP, for its part, has been consistently aligning its policies and procedures, not only on supervision of banks, but also on its examination process, to international standards. I'm sure the PDIC is also undertaking similar initiatives. As early as November 1997, in order to avoid creating dangerous gaps in regulatory oversight, the BSP has adopted a consolidated approach to bank supervision as well as a risk-based examination approach. The consolidated supervisory approach is deemed essential because of the growing complexity of banking organizations and their related interests. On the other hand, the risk-based examination approach is most appropriate given the complexity of risks inherent in banking in a more liberalized and globalized economy. In implementing a risk-based approach to examination, the BSP is shifting the examination focus to: · A review of the bank's corporate governance and internal risk management system; and · An appropriate level of transaction testing. More than determining a bank's financial condition and performance, examiners are required to assess the manner in which a bank identifies, measures, and manages risks. Examination reports now include an evaluation of "bank-wide" risk management. This is a significant departure from the segmented, unit-based examination approach. Existing supervisory processes and systems are also being modified to be more supportive of a pro-active stance in the supervision of banks. The modifications are aimed at enhancing our ability to identify, at an early stage, potential problems in individual banks and in the banking system as a whole through a more effective offsite surveillance system. In fact, we have expanded our analytical range to have in place an early warning system that is more forward looking. Aside from monitoring key historical trends and performance variables on an individual bank level and at an industry level, we have developed or are developing: · A set of statistical bank failure prediction models that can effectively guide and prioritize on-site bank examination; · A comprehensive bank performance reporting system that will facilitate ready analysis of individual bank performance trends, peer group analysis and overall industry trends; and · A corporate borrowing monitoring system that will facilitate a more complete evaluation of the quality of loan portfolio of banks. These changes in BSP supervisory approaches and techniques would certainly require an enhanced set of skills that is supportive of a proactive stance in the supervision and examination of banks. I truly hope that this training program has been beneficial to you as supervisors, as it has equipped you with the appropriate skills and expertise needed to successfully meet the demands of your challenging jobs. Thank you and congratulations! (Note: Bank Analysis and Examination Training Program, ADB-APEC Financial Regulators Training Initiative, BSP Institute, February 23, 2001)

Title: Key Emerging Economies Drive to Participate in the Global Markets - What Role for the Financial Services Industry in the Philippines
Occasion: Annual Governors' Meeting for Finance, World Economic Forum
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction Officers and members of the World Economic Forum, fellow central bankers and distinguished colleagues from the various finance ministries represented in this meeting, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. It is encouraging to see emerging economies and other countries dust themselves from the effects of the recent economic downturn. But as they come out of the slump, these countries will again have to grapple with the forces of globalization brought about by the increased interdependence of markets. While they continue to make headway toward full recovery, there is wide recognition in these countries of the need to go the full distance by ensuring that the recovery does not undercut the will to proceed with essential reforms. Even those economies which are in the path of strong growth acknowledge the wisdom behind the phrase "Peacetime is the right time to get the army in shape". Winds of Globalization It cannot be denied that globalization has brought substantial benefits to countries that have opened up their financial systems. These gains include the introduction of new sources of funds and instruments, which have enabled participants to earn the highest possible returns on their investments and to diversify risk. However, the increased mobility of funds has also heightened the risks associated with the failure to address inappropriate policies, weaknesses in the financial system, problems in corporate and public governance and policy uncertainties that arise from inconsistencies among policy objectives. Key emerging countries in particular are likely to face headwinds in maintaining growth. Hence, as we prepare ourselves to face the new risks emanating from continued participation in global capital markets, the subject of this special session becomes more urgent. The Financial Services Industry A prominent feature of the reform packages adopted in key emerging economies involves the liberalization of their financial systems. This has been achieved through the removal of financially repressive policies (such as directed credit schemes and interest rate controls) as well as the removal of barriers to the cross-border provision of financial services and to the establishment of foreign financial institutions. While financial services are intangible, invisible, and non-storable, economists use some measures of financial intermediation to gauge the extent of financial deepening. In the Philippines, the financial intermediation ratio (defined as the ratio of M3 to GNP) rose from 0.28 in 1992 to 0.42 in 1997. While it dipped slightly to 0.41 in 1998, [1] preliminary estimates for 1999 place the ratio at 0.54.[2] Overall, the trend, which shows more efficient utilization of financial resources, is a testimony of the success of the reform efforts that have been painstakingly adopted in the past 10 years. These measures have led to an increase in the magnitude of financial services transactions. Enhanced competition in the financial system has also led to a broadening of the range of financial products and services available to savers and investors, and to gains in allocative and internal efficiency. The latter, in turn, has contributed to lower financial intermediation cost that has had positive repercussions on the real sector of the economy. Some emerging economies, in fact, have gained enough sophistication to make considerable inroads in supplying financial services internationally through cross-border trade, through the establishment of commercial presence abroad, and through the provision of financial services in the home country to international travelers and foreign residents.[3] Other economies, the Philippines included, see the internationalization of their financial institutions as a long-term, but nevertheless, achievable goal in the march toward global economic integration. The Role of the Financial Services Industry in the Global Integration Process In such a setting, it is important to examine the role of the Philippine financial services industry in the process of global integration. In sum, the industry should strive for flexibility in its capability to respond to changes in the economic environment, both domestic and external, and to the changing funding requirements of the country. This requires that borrowers as well as lenders are able to take into account uncertainty. A pragmatic view of the functioning of financial markets accepts the reality of uncertainty while improving upon the markets' capability to manage risks. Upgrading risk management capabilities requires financial intermediaries to recognize and understand the increased risks associated with financial liberalization, such as credit risk, liquidity risk, exchange risk and interest rate risk. It requires them to design instruments that will allow borrowers and investors to spread and diversify their risks. Increasingly, this involves the use of hedging and other risk management instruments such as commodity and financial futures, options and swaps, and other financing techniques. Financial innovation is not an arbitrary process, however. It is most evident in financial systems where competitive pressures have been allowed. To promote globally competitive and more efficient banks, monetary and financial authorities in the Philippines have encouraged mergers and consolidations in the banking system. Such consolidation will help banks take advantage of their collective experience, services and technological know-how. Complementary Institutional Reforms However, in many countries, domestic financial institutions are unable to effectively manage capital flows because of the inappropriateness of institutional arrangements in integrating cross-border capital flows with financial policy decision-making. Allow me then to discuss what I think the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas' role should be since it is a major participant in the development of the financial services industry in the Philippines. Financial authorities generally have three interrelated objectives in promoting a sound financial system. First, they wish to ensure that financial markets are efficient channels between savers and investors, and that these markets provide the financial services needed by the economy. Second, they wish to ensure that financial markets are stable. And, third, they wish to ensure that adequate protection exists for investors and depositors. In pursuing these objectives, Philippine authorities have put in place a policy environment where finance is used in the context of a voluntary market process for mobilizing and allocating resources rather than as a tool for implementing interventionist development strategies. Toward this end, the Philippines has adopted a largely open financial market policy. This is consistent with the view that an open financial market is necessary for effective market discipline. Several initiatives have also been taken in the microeconomic front to ensure that the supporting financial infrastructure promotes robust financial structures and contributes to lower barriers to cross-border capital flows. These measures include: ensuring an adequate capital base for financial institutions; providing for adequate information flow, credit appraisal and risk rating systems; ensuring efficient, safe and adequate clearing and settlement systems; developing appropriate and effective legal and accounting standards and framework; and strengthening prudential supervision and regulation. Conclusion Whenever I am invited to a forum such as this, the talk invariably drifts into a discussion of the good template for the financial architecture for the future. However, I do not feel comfortable with "one size fits all" prescriptions. I think that there is no single set of policies that is right for every country. Hence, while the measures that I discussed may work for the Philippines, these may not necessarily apply to other emerging economies. I also think that reforms in the financial system will continue to be work-in-progress. Several things are clear though. Emerging economies are in the midst of profound changes in their development process. Hence, without policy changes, financial systems will serve as a drag to the growth process. On the other hand, authorities' high degree of policy commitment in effectively addressing macroeconomic imbalances and in implementing structural reforms in the financial sector will have a markedly uplifting effect on recovery and longer-term growth. Thank you and good day. ------------------------------- [1] M4 consists of M3 (as conventionally defined) and non-bank residents' foreign currency deposits. [2] For the period January-September [3] Tamirasa, Natalia, 1999. Trade in Financial Services and Capital Movements. IMF Working Paper 99/89.

Title: Philippines: Recent Economic Developments and Outlook
Occasion: MOPC Press Forum, Manila Overseas Press Club
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Juan P. Dayang, Chairman of the MOPC press forum, officers and members of MOPC, friends, ladies and gentlemen: good afternoon. It is always a pleasure to break bread with the press, particularly members of the Manila Overseas Press Club. However, this day takes on a different dimension given the momentous events that have transpired in the past few days. Amidst the challenging developments that took place last year, it has been easy to lose sight of the more basic bread-and-butter issues confronting our country. Today, I will put a different focus on these issues by talking about the state of the Philippine economy, particularly the monetary and banking sectors. Recent Economic Developments The year 2000 saw the economy challenged from all sides. On the external front, world oil prices shot up at decade-high levels, and drove up transport costs and wages. The U.S. economy continued to heat up, calling for a tighter monetary stance, which narrowed interest rate differentials across regions and contributed to the weakening of their currencies. On the domestic front, conflicts in Mindanao and issues about public governance contributed to business uncertainty that hindered the economy's growth momentum. Nevertheless, the economy continued to expand. During the first three quarters of 2000, real GNP grew by 4.5 percent, an improvement from the 3.1 percent recorded a year ago. Moreover, the expansion became broad-based, with manufacturing posting a recovery and agriculture and services maintaining their strength and resiliency. The moderate expansion in economic activity was realized amidst a relatively benign inflation environment. Inflation for the whole year averaged 4.4 percent, well below the target of 5-6 percent. This was also despite inflationary pressures coming from increases in oil prices and transport fares during the last half of the year. Moderate inflation helped keep interest rates lower than 1999 levels. For instance, the 91-day T-bill rate averaged 9.861 percent, down from the 10.197 percent recorded in 1999. This was despite the calibrated and temporary upward adjustments in the BSP policy rates starting in the middle of this year. Recently, owing to the broad stability in the financial markets, we have started to gradually bring our policy rates down. Consequently, lending rates have begun to ease toward the end of 2000. Lower interest rates are needed to nurse the economy towards a sustainable growth path. In the banking system, indicators remained positive and stable. Banks' capital-to-risk assets ratio remained high at 16.6 percent as of September last year. The non-performing loans ratio on the other hand, has stayed within the 15-16 percent range during the latter part of last year.
