In the external sector, our current account continued to be in surplus at US$6.75 billion for the first ten months of 2000. However, a weaker financial account resulted in an overall balance of payments deficit of US$950 million during the same period. Investments, however, continued to come in although at a slower pace. The continued surplus in the current account contributed to the build up in our gross international reserves during the last quarter of the year. As of end December 2000, the GIR level reached US$15 billion, enough to cover 4.45 months' worth of imports of goods and payments of services. Meanwhile, we have managed to trim our external debt from us$52.2 billion at end-June 2000 to us$51.8 billion as of September 2000. As a result, and also due to good export numbers, our debt service burden has remained manageable. For the first ten months of 2000, our debt service ratio was lower at 12.3 percent compared to the 17 percent observed in the early 1990s. In the foreign exchange market, the peso was actually making some headway before the political crisis in October came to a head. In fact, it started appreciating slightly toward the end of December 2000, largely on account of foreign exchange inflows and the progress in the impeachment process. However, last week saw mounting public protests over the recent impasse in the impeachment trial, which triggered overreactions from the market. As a result, the peso-dollar rate exhibited substantial fluctuations from the normal trend. While we regretted these adverse developments in the market, we have always held that these movements are temporary and would not permanently reverse the gains that we have made in stabilizing the peso. This has been proven true--with the peso registering the largest ever one-day rally last Friday, as it closed at P47.50: US$1.00. Today, the peso opened even stronger at P47.00 and has been trading at around the same level. Finally, in the fiscal sector, the national government deficit reached P136.1 billion, exceeding the target for the year by P73.6 billion. Nonetheless, this has not resulted in substantial hikes in market lending rates. Moreover, the authorities remain fully aware of the need for fiscal consolidation and are taking steps to ensure maximum prudence in fiscal management. Policy Directions For the year 2001, the Bangko Sentral will continue to pursue its primary mandate of maintaining price stability, both in the domestic and foreign exchange markets, in support of balanced and sustainable economic growth. In order for the Bangko Sentral to best serve this purpose, a shift from monetary targeting to inflation targeting as the framework for conducting monetary policy will be implemented by the middle of this year. Under this new framework, government authorities will announce in advance the inflation target over a given time horizon. If the target is not met, the Bangko Sentral is required to explain the reasons and to spell out the measures that it will take to get back to target. The framework, therefore, allows the Bangko Sentral to build its credibility by demonstrating consistent adherence to the inflation goal. This would help cement inflationary expectations. In the process, the framework also promotes greater transparency in the conduct of monetary policy, thus facilitating more efficient markets. In the banking system, reforms to further strengthen the system will continue to be pursued, even as major policies have already been implemented over the past decade. In particular, major reforms are being implemented to prepare banks for greater international competition as a result of increasing market globalization and liberalization. Hence, the reform agenda in the banking sector is a robust one going forward. On the legislative front, rules and regulations to implement the new general banking law of 2000 are being formulated. Guidelines already issued in the form of circulars include provisions on foreign stockholdings and electronic banking. The reforms contained in the General Banking Law of 2000 will be complemented by proposed amendments to the BSP Charter. These amendments aim to enhance the BSP's supervisory and operational independence, improve prudential standards and promote greater competition in the banking system. To improve its monitoring capability, the BSP is developing a more integrated system of bank reporting. This includes measures to reform the country's settlements and payments system by developing a real-time gross settlements system, and the issuance of new reporting guidelines to simplify and rationalize bank reports. During the year, the BSP has also continued to encourage bank mergers and consolidations to further strengthen the banking system. As of November 2000, a total of 21 banks have entered into such arrangements with both banks and non-bank financial institutions. Despite these consolidations, studies have shown that the level of competition in the banking system remains healthy. Outlook Given the economy's performance last year and the policy thrusts that have been envisioned for this year, government expects that in 2001, the economy will grow by 3.2-3.7 percent in terms of GNP. This expected expansion is based on the strength of all sectors. Meanwhile; inflation is expected to be in the range of 6-7 percent as a result of the pass-through effect of the exchange rate depreciation, higher oil prices and the adjustment in transport fares and wages. In the external sector, the key factors that are expected to have a major impact on the economy include: interest rate movements and the extent of the slowdown of the U.S. economy, the extent of recovery of the Japanese economy, the growth momentum in Europe and the volatility of global financial markets. On the domestic front, the primary task of government is to achieve fiscal consolidation and improve public governance. Conclusion I have provided you an overview of the state of the economy. With the presidential transition completed, we expect the economic recovery to gain further momentum. As business confidence revives, we hope that the Philippines will be back in the radar screens of foreign investors. This could re-launch us on a growth trajectory that would be more sustainable. Let me state right away that these words are not due to the exuberance of the moment. My views are based on the fact that our commitment to much-needed policy reforms has never faltered, and that there has never been any policy inertia, let alone any policy drift. While conditions can turn tough in 2001 due to external factors such as the slowing U.S. economy, surprises can be on the upside, particularly as investors reassess and take a closer look at our economic fundamentals. On the part of the Bangko Sentral, the commitment to maintain stability in the domestic and foreign markets will remain our primary concern. At the same time, reforms in the banking system will continue to be pursued. In the process, we hope to provide the right macroeconomic environment that will be conducive to a sustainable recovery of the economy, and reduce its vulnerability to external shocks. Thank you and good day. (Note: Manila Overseas Press Club, MOPC Press Forum, January 22, 2001, Century park Hotel, Manila)

Title: Year 2000: A Tale of Two Stories
Occasion: Annual Reception of the Banking Community
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Year 2000 was both a challenging year and a fulfilling one. A challenging year It was a challenging year because the economy was confronted by decade-high world oil prices compounded by tight U.S. monetary policy. On one hand, the supply situation was squeezed by higher domestic oil prices leading to higher wages and transport costs. On the other hand, the demand situation had to accommodate the need to keep the interest rate differential between foreign and domestic interest rates from further narrowing. As the U.S. continued to grow in 2000, most of the Asian regional currencies weakened against the U.S. dollar. The peso also declined in exchange value but held its ground towards the end of the year, averaging about P44.13, even as imports showed some increase while the public sector foreign interest expense rose. It was a challenging year because of some political tension adding more pressure to the economic scenario. What was needed at the time was some room for the economy to stabilize and for the market to realize that the problem was neither fundamental nor permanent. It was for these reasons that year 2000 was indeed a challenging year: the monetary authorities went into a cautious, but necessary, mode, adjusting the BSP's policy interest rates a number of times to ensure that the price stability objective was upheld. The BSP also provided some dollar liquidity in the system when required to ensure that legitimate dollar demand was served, and at the same time sought to plug any remaining loopholes in foreign exchange trading. A fulfilling year Notwithstanding these twists and turns, year 2000 also proved to be a fulfilling one. The calibrated adjustment in interest rates did not stand in the way of economic growth. Real GNP expanded by 4.5 percent in the first three quarters exceeding the year-ago performance of only 3.1 percent. Real GDP improved by 4.2 percent against year-ago achievement of only 2.7 percent as growth came from all the sectors of agriculture, services and industry. The cause of price stability was served by the cautious monetary stance. Eleven-month inflation rate averaged only 4.0 percent, well below the government's inflation target range of 5-6 percent for 2000. Although the public sector finances turned out to be more than challenging, the increasing use of domestic financing did not lead to precipitate increase in market lending rates. In fact, domestic credit growth for both public and private sectors showed significant improvement in October, growing by close to 11 percent year on year with the bulk of bank loans going into manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade and business services. The weak market confidence did not also dampen the external sector account. The current account, owing chiefly to brisk exports, sustained its large surplus of more than US$6 billion for the first nine months of 2000 leading to a gross international reserves build-up to US$14.5 billion at end-November 2000. External debt even dropped to US$51.85 billion at end-September 2000 from US$52.16 billion at end-June 2000. The banking system also held its ground against all the domestic and external shocks to its resiliency. Its assets continued to climb, the capital to risk asset ratio remained high at more than 16.5 percent while asset quality was kept manageable with non-performing loans ratio declining from 15.7 percent in September to 15.6 percent in October. Prospects Looking ahead, the main challenge to policymakers is to continue building upon the gains achieved thus far. A sound macroeconomic environment requires the relentless pursuit of key structural reforms. While we expect a moderate growth of output of about 3.2-3.7 percent in terms of GNP and a slightly higher inflation rate of about 6-7 percent, we are optimistic that these initial projections can be bettered by continued hard work by all. For our part, the monetary authorities will continue to focus on the medium-term outlook for inflation and financial markets rather than on the daily gyrations of key parameters. This is the thrust of transparent inflation targeting framework. We will continue to keep our ears tuned to international developments while sustaining our efforts to modernize the banking system. (Note: Regular Membership Meeting, Rotary Club of Manila, January 4, 2001, Manila Hotel)

Title: he Philippine Economy: Recent Developments, Policy Directions and Outlook for 2001
Occasion: Regular Membership Meeting, Rotary Club of Manila
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I. Introduction Mr. Sebastian B. Arrastia, President of the Rotary Club of Manila (RCM), officers and members of RCM, friends, ladies and gentlemen: good afternoon. It is a pleasure for me to be with you on the occasion of your first membership meeting for 2001. During the past few months, political concerns have dominated the news, diverting public attention from other issues that matter in the long haul. Today, the fourth into the new year, I invite you to shift focus--to take stock of our country's economic gains and appreciate the progress we have made in advancing the structural reform agenda as well as in laying the foundations for sustainable growth. I hope that after this talk, you will leave this hall convinced that, through our current challenges, we can face the new year ready to make the most of the opportunities that they present. II. Recent economic developments The year 2000 was indeed a challenging one. Decade-high world oil prices squeezed supply, leading to higher transport costs and higher wages. A buoyant U.S. economy necessitated the tightening of monetary policy, which narrowed interest rate differentials and contributed to the weakening of regional currencies. Adverse global developments were compounded by uncertainty on the domestic front arising from, among other factors, the hostilities in the south and troubling questions about public governance. Nonetheless, the past year was also a fulfilling one. In the face of domestic and international shocks, the Philippine economy managed to pull off a respectable performance. During the first three quarters of 2000, real GNP grew by an average of 4.5 percent, well above the 3.1 percent for the comparable period in 1999. Meanwhile, real GDP improved by 4.2 percent as against the year-ago achievement of only 2.7 percent. The economic expansion was underpinned by the resilience of services and agriculture and the recovery of industry, signaling the economy's shift to a more balanced and broad-based growth path. For the whole of 2000, real GNP is expected to grow by 4.2 percent, while GDP growth is estimated at 4.0 percent. Growth is expected to ride on the continuing strength of agriculture, services and industry. On the demand side, stronger personal consumption and exports are expected to be the drivers for the economic expansion. Notwithstanding the pick-up in economic activity last year, prices have remained generally stable. The average inflation rate for the first 11 months of 2000 of 4.0 percent was well below the full-year target of 5.0-6.0 percent. Moreover, it was achieved despite inflationary pressures from oil price and transport fare increases and the depreciation of the peso, which fed into wage adjustments. Despite posting an uptrend starting October 2000, interest rates settled lower during the year, with the 91-day T-bill rate averaging 9.861 percent, compared to 10.197 percent in 1999. If you will recall, last year, we raised our policy rates three times--in May, September and October. Let me note in this regard, however, that the calibrated adjustments in interest rates appear to not have stood in the way of economic growth, particularly since we have started to gradually bring our policy rates down, owing to broad stability in the financial markets. As a result, lending rates started to ease toward the end of the year. Domestic credits have started to go beyond single digit, with the bulk of bank loans going into manufacturing and other key economic sectors. In the external sector, the current account continued to be in surplus at over US$6 billion for the first nine months of 2000, owing to brisk exports. However, a weaker financial account offset the gains in the current account, resulting in an overall balance-of-payments deficit of US$532 million during the period. The robust current account position helped to build up gross international reserves (GIR) to $14.5 billion as of end-November 2000. This GIR level is enough to cover 4.4 months' worth of imports of goods and payments of services, and is more than enough to cover short-term obligations, twice-over. The country's external debt dropped to US$51.85 billion at end-September 2000 from US$52.16 billion at end-June 2000. Owing to this and good export numbers, the country's debt service burden has remained manageable. For the period January-September 2000, the debt service ratio reached only 13.38 percent compared to 17.0 percent, which was observed in the early 1990s. Meanwhile, the peso-dollar rate has, of late, been subject to substantial gyrations owing to the spate of bombings in the metropolis. We note with regret that these adverse developments have reversed--temporarily, we hope--the gains we have made in stabilizing the peso. It may be worth noting that, prior to these unfortunate events, the peso was making some headway, appreciating slightly toward the end of December, on account of foreign exchange inflows and the progress in the constitutional process. The strengthening of the peso at the close of 2000 may also be attributed in no small part to the measures taken by the BSP toward this end. The financial system remains stable and sound. Total assets continued to climb; the capital-to-risk assets ratio remained high at 16.5 percent; while asset quality was kept manageable, with the non-performing loan ratio declining slightly from 15.73 percent in September 2000 to 15.56 percent in October. In the fiscal sector, the task of consolidation remains a tall order. For the period January-November 2000, the National Government incurred a deficit of P114.4 billion, exceeding the target for the period by P53.03 billion. Nonetheless, it is helpful to note that the increasing use of domestic sources to finance the shortfall did not lead to a precipitate increase in market lending rates. The authorities are fully aware of the need for prudence in fiscal management and are taking steps to ensure that the national coffers will provide ample support for this year's budgetary needs. Overall, if the economy's performance last year is any indication, we are moving toward more broad-based--and thus sturdier and more sustainable--growth, even as we strive to rise to the challenge of fiscal consolidation. III. Policy directions, structural reforms and outlook for 2001 Policy directions This year, the conduct of monetary policy will continue to focus on containing inflationary pressures while maintaining stability in the foreign exchange market. This objective, we believe, will be best served by our shift from monetary targeting to inflation targeting as the framework for conducting monetary policy, by the middle of this year. Under the inflation targeting framework, the Government will announce the inflation target that it is committed to achieve over a given target horizon. In cases when the inflation targets are not achieved, the BSP will have to explain the reasons for the slip and the policy measures that it will need to adopt to bring inflation to target. An indispensable ingredient, therefore, is the BSP's accountability to the price stability objective. Credibility is thus built on a record of adherence to the inflation target. Such a framework enhances the transparency of monetary policy and, therefore, promotes the efficient functioning of markets. Structural reforms Alongside efforts to provide a monetary policy environment conducive to the stability of the general price level, the BSP will continue to pursue reforms to strengthen the financial system. While policies implemented over the past decade have had major positive results--made evident by the resiliency of the domestic financial system in the midst of the 1997 crisis--events over the past three years have highlighted that more needs to be done. To prepare the financial system for the challenges posed by globalization, the BSP is implementing major reforms in financial regulation and legislation. In particular, the BSP has sought to prepare the domestic banking system for the increased international competition brought on by globalization through the adoption of measures in the following areas: Improving the legislative and regulatory framework On the legislative front, the BSP has formed a committee to formulate the implementing rules of the new General Banking Law of 2000 or R.A. no. 8791. The initial output of the committee involves the formulation of the guidelines for implementing provisions on foreign stockholdings, and the deferment by the Monetary Board of the implementation of the provision allowing banks to sell the financial products of their allied undertakings or of their investment house units. These guidelines were issued under Circular No. 256 dated 15 August 2000. The reforms introduced in the GBL 2000 will be complemented by the proposed amendments to the Charter of the BSP. These measures aim to enhance the supervisory and enforcement powers of the BSP, further improve prudential standards for the banking system, intensify competition in the banking sector, and enhance the BSP's independence. Strengthening prudential measures To improve regulatory oversight and monitor bank compliance with the new guidelines, the BSP is developing a more integrated system for bank reporting and a more effective supervisory framework. The significant developments in this area include: - Reform of the settlements and payments system. Settlement risk will be reduced by developing a Real-time Gross Settlements system (RTGS), which will cover equities, fixed income, money, and foreign exchange markets and will effect final settlement on a continuous basis; - Development by the BSP of a risk assessment system in lieu of a checklist-driven approach to on-site bank examination; and - Implementation of a risk management program, which involves the adoption of the BAP's foreign exchange manual and financial markets risk reference manual, and the holding of risk management courses for bank examiners. Encouraging bank mergers and Consolidations The BSP also continues to encourage bank mergers and consolidations as a means of enhancing the strength of the financial system. As of end-November 2000, a total of 21 banks, 15 of which were commercial banks, have entered into such arrangements with both banks and non-bank financial institutions. Two more applications involving five banks are now pending. Let me note at this point that, these consolidations notwithstanding, a BSP study finds that there is a healthy level of competition in the banking system, which is necessary for safeguarding the interests of depositors and borrowers as well as banks' other stakeholders. Outlook These policy thrusts and structural reform measures should help us consolidate and build upon our recent gains. For 2001, the Government expects the economy to grow by 3.2-3.7 percent in terms of GNP and by 3.0-3.5 percent in terms of GDP. Growth is expected to be underpinned by the continued strength of the services sector. Meanwhile, agriculture and industry are also expected to post positive growth. In the external sector, macroeconomic developments in the major industrial countries are expected to continue to exert a major influence on domestic economic developments. Key factors that are being monitored include: the prospects for lower interest rates and soft landing in the U.S., the strength of recovery of the Japanese economy, the momentum of growth in Europe, the volatility in global financial markets, and the divergence of major currency exchange rates from medium-term fundamentals. On the domestic front, downside risks to the country's growth momentum include the state of fiscal finances and the quality of public governance, particularly in the area of transparency and accountability. Meanwhile, inflation is expected to be in the range of 6.0-7.0 percent. IV. Conclusion I have given you some broad-brush strokes on the state of the Philippine economy. Recovery is clearly under way. However, conditions can turn tougher this year. We all know that the ongoing political exercise is an important factor. We should allow it to take its course. At the same time, it is important to recognize that part and parcel of the process of recovery is a strategy of economic reform that will give credibility to the country's economic program, as well as greater clarity and coherence in overall economic management capabilities. For its part, the BSP remains committed to the pursuit of structural reforms in the financial system. We will also continue to provide a macroeconomic policy environment that is both conducive to growth and to the maintenance of price and exchange rate stability. Through these measures, we hope to improve the quality of the country's economic recovery, thereby reducing its vulnerability to external shocks. In the end, these efforts should put the Philippines on the path of sustainable growth. Thank you and I wish you all a prosperous new year. (Note: Regular Membership Meeting, Rotary Club of Manila, January 4, 2001, Manila Hotel)

Title: Moving The Financial Markets Forward
Occasion: Joint General Membership Meeting ACI Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I. Introduction Officers and members of ACI Philippines, Money Market Association of the Philippines, Trust Officers Association of the Philippines; distinguished guests; ladies and gentlemen: I am very pleased to be with you this evening on the occasion of your joint general membership meeting. This is perhaps the biggest single group of financial market practitioners gathered in one place. Together, your views and actions yield considerable influence on the economy. I don't think I am exaggerating if I say that foreign exchange and money markets move in large part on actions taken by people gathered in this hall. This has been demonstrated in the past few weeks when the attention of most people has been focused on the peso exchange rate and interest rates. Recent political concerns have dominated perceptions with respect to the Philippines. As a result, both FX and money markets have been largely sentiment-driven, and long-term economic prospects have been relegated to the background. Our job as economic managers is to see to it that through our current difficulties, the Philippines' long-term economic promise remains intact. In this respect, the BSP performs a dual role. First, as the country's monetary authority, the BSP sees to it that monetary policy is supportive of its mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to sustainable economic growth. With price stability, long-term savings and investments are encouraged, which in turn leads to the growth and development of the financial market. I realized that in a time of uncertainty such as this, a review of the so-called fundamentals of the economy becomes suspect; however, I submit that now is precisely the time when we should be vigilant and take great care that the fundamentals do not deteriorate in such a way that the long-term growth prospects are affected. Second, as the regulator of the financial system, the BSP promotes the stability and soundness of the financial system, which is key to overall economic stability and growth. I will therefore focus on the current thrusts of the BSP along these two main areas of responsibilities. II. Helping the financial market move forward under a globalized environment: Reforms and policy directions Setting the right environment international experience in central banking has shown that the greatest contribution of a central bank to sustainable growth lies in providing a stable price environment. In many ways, the charter and monetary framework of the BSP incorporates the state-of-the-art in thinking about the proper role of a central bank. The process began with the 1986 Philippine Constitution, which guaranteed the independence of the BSP. In 1993, the New Central Bank Act (R. A. No. 7653) then reorganized the Central Bank into the BSP, focused the bank's mandate on the maintenance of price stability, changed the composition of the Monetary Board towards a private sector majority, and granted fiscal and administrative autonomy to the bank. These developments will culminate in our shift to inflation targeting as the monetary policy framework beginning in 2001. Under the inflation targeting framework, the BSP will announce explicit inflation targets to the public. Inflation targeting thus provides a clearer assignment of the BSP's accountability to the objective of promoting price stability and increases the transparency of monetary policy. The shift to inflation targeting is important in view of the growing body of evidence that low inflation helps to promote growth and efficient resource allocation in the long run. Controlling inflation will help us to avoid asset price bubbles, achieve lower interest rates in the long term, stabilize the exchange rate, and therefore help maintain the soundness of the financial system and overall macroeconomic stability. Improving the framework for the development of the financial sector While the preceding macroeconomic-oriented reforms are being implemented, the BSP is also adopting major reforms in financial regulation and legislation to address the concerns raised by globalization on the stability of the financial system. The growth in the size and complexity of financial markets has brought about considerable benefits in terms of a broader menu of alternative sources of funds for investment and a shorter process of technological acquisition. Theoretically, the diversification of funds sources that accompanies globalization should offer expanded opportunities for better risk management. In practice, however, globalization has been characterized by volatility in capital flows to emerging markets, to the detriment of the performance of the real economy. The government has adopted a multi-pronged approach to meeting these challenges. In the case of the banking system, the BSP has sought to make banks more ready to face international competition, by improving the legislative and regulatory framework, by strengthening prudential measures, and by encouraging mergers and consolidations. The main legislative framework is provided by the General Banking Law of 2000 (R.A. No. 8791, or GBL 2000), which supersedes the half-century old General Banking Act of 1949. The reforms introduced in the GBL 2000 will be supported by the proposed amendments to the Charter of the BSP. General Banking Law of 2000. Some of the more important features of the GBL 2000 include (1) granting authority to the Monetary Board to require banks to adopt internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy; (2) providing for stricter rules governing bank exposure to directors, officers, stockholders and related interests (DOSRI); (3) further liberalizing the ownership participation of foreign banks in the local banking system to 100 percent within seven years after the effectivity of the GBL 2000, and (4) granting authority to the BSP to regulate electronic banking. To implement the provisions of the GBL 2000, the BSP has formed a committee to formulate the implementing rules of the new law. The initial output of the committee involves the formulation of the guidelines for implementing section 11 of the GBL, which allows foreign individuals and non-bank corporations to own or control up to forty percent (40%) of the voting stock of a domestic bank, subject to certain conditions, and which also allows a Filipino individual and a domestic non-bank corporation to each own up to forty percent (40%) of the voting stock of a domestic bank, without any limits on the aggregate ownership by such individuals and corporations in a domestic bank. These guidelines were issued under Circular No. 256 dated 15 August 2000. Amendments to the New Central Bank Act. The BSP is also working for amendments to the New Central Bank Act (R. A. No. 7653). Broadly speaking, these legislative measures aim to enhance the supervisory and enforcement powers of the BSP, further improve prudential standards for the banking system, intensify competition in the banking sector, and enhance the BSP's independence. The Senate version of the bill has been finalized, while the House version is set for second reading. The new Speaker of the house has indicated that passage of the bill is included in the priority agenda of the house. Improving risk management. To complement BSP circulars aimed at strengthening prudential regulations, the BSP and the BAP are taking the lead role in developing an informative framework for risk management standards which could be useful for banks in understanding risks and shaping their own risk management infrastructures. Recently, a manual of current best practices in risk management has been released. This documentation of international best practices is expected to help banks understand risks associated with banking activities. Risks need to be better understood especially because they have begun to take different forms and are often off the balance sheets. The manual can also serve as guide to banks in the process of developing their own risk management procedures which could be unique to their respective organizations. Development of risk management manuals for specific products are currently in progress. In addition, a foreign exchange manual has also been developed and released to the banks for their guidance. This manual institutionalizes a system of financial records, operational procedures and control mechanisms applicable to all operating units in a bank to account for foreign exchange transactions. It also allows the banks to monitor its total currency exposure at any given time. Another risk management initiative in progress is the current effort to upgrade the existing payment system and develop it into a Real Rime Gross Settlement system. This will enhance operational efficiency, reliability, speed, and timeliness of payment transactions in the face of the rapidly increasing volume and value of transactions. The RTGS system once in place, will offer a powerful mechanism for limiting settlement and systemic risks in the interbank settlement process thus ensuring stability of the whole financial system. This will also pave the way for the achievement of a delivery versus payment system which should develop further the capital market. Upgrading BSP's supervisory capability. The BSP is continuously upgrading its supervisory capabilities in line with the changing structure of the financial system to ensure that supervision remains effective in fostering the safety and soundness of the country's financial system. This upgrading includes the adoption of a forward-looking and risk-based framework. To operationalize this framework, we have developed our own risk assessment system. A first-generation early warning system has also been developed to facilitate the evaluation of bank solvency. This will assist our supervisors in identifying possible weaknesses in individual banks even before they reach critical proportions. We also continue to send our supervisors to various trainings abroad to sharpen their supervisory capabilities and to expose them to international best practices in supervision and risk-management techniques in other countries. Mergers and consolidations. The BSP continues to support bank mergers and consolidations as a means of enhancing the strength of the financial system, and has extended a package of short-term incentives to support these consolidations. In the future, we feel that the banking system would ideally consist of several major local and foreign banks accounting for the bulk of the total spectrum of the banking system. The rest will be niche players, which will have a competitive advantage in dealing with specific groups of customers. Mergers and consolidations actually complement the opening up of the banking sector to new foreign participants, inasmuch as both measures will increase the ability of the banking system to compete in the globalized environment. Our assessment of the financial system indicates that the industry has enough room for mergers and consolidations while at the same time maintaining the effective competition that is beneficial to depositors and borrowers. III. Conclusion I have given you today the broad contours of the financial reform efforts that are now underway. We are committed to these reforms which we expect will ensure the resiliency of the financial system even through our current difficulties. Finding the right regulatory balance is always difficult. While we need to encourage greater prudence in lending, regulation must not stifle competition and innovation in the financial markets. In the end, however, we hope to be rewarded when we achieve greater competitiveness and efficiency in the Philippine financial system, an enhanced role of intermediation in ensuring broad-based, sustainable development, and a regulatory environment that is up to the challenges of the times. We are quite sanguine about the future because of what we are undertaking today. After all, "the best way to predict the future is to make it happen". Thank you and good night. (Note: Joint General Membership Meeting, ACI Philippines, Money Market Association of the Philippines and Trust Officers Association of the Philippines, November 20, 2000, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati City)

Title: Providing Support to the Corporate Sector
Occasion: Luncheon Meeting, Federation of Philippine Industries, Inc. (FPI)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Raul T. Concepcion, Mr. Antonio M. Garcia, distinguished leaders of the business community, friends and colleagues, good afternoon: I am grateful for this chance to meet with you and discuss some of your concerns on the current economic situation. As leaders of the business community, I very much appreciate your ideas on how we can work together to boost the engines of economic activity. I also share your concerns on the potential impact on business activity of recent BSP policy measures. This afternoon I would like to provide you with some perspective on these policy moves and also address some of the issues raised in your position paper. The issues that you raised fall under three main headings: (1) the use of alternative measures to stabilize the exchange rate; (2) encouraging banks to restructure the loans of financially distressed businesses; and (3) the creation of a rescue fund for these companies. I shall structure my comments accordingly. On using other monetary measures to stabilize the exchange rate Let me clarify first the rationale for the BSP's recent policy rate increases. The Bangko Sentral's decision to raise its policy interest rates was in response mainly to a volatile situation that is becoming a threat to the economy. The BSP took action in order to help stabilize the economic situation while the political concerns are being addressed. Raising interest rates was not an easy choice to make, since the BSP has always been supportive of the economic recovery. However, we believe that there is also a significant potential economic damage from a free fall in the peso, since it weakens consumer and business confidence, discourages investments and inhibits growth. Let me also make clear that the relatively high interest rates will not be there forever. Our policy moves are intended to give time for the political situation to sort itself out. Thus, once the situation stabilizes, we will adjust our monetary policy stance to allow the recovery to proceed. I must also emphasize that in the last few months, the BSP has used policy tools other than interest rates to stabilize the exchange rate. For example, to alleviate demand pressure in the spot FOREX market, we expanded the coverage of the Currency Risk Protection Program (CRPP) to service the foreign exchange requirements of oil companies. We have also tightened the rules covering the foreign exchange units of banks by requiring them to submit documents for dollar sales of over US$10,000. This was intended to curb the speculative activities involving these FOREX corporations and also prevent possible money laundering. In addition, we do not expect the hike in interest rates to translate into an excessive increase in bank lending rates for the following reasons: » There is still ample liquidity in the financial system; » Banks' deposit rates have not gone up in the same proportion. Therefore, banks should not increase their lending rates excessively; » Commercial banks have entered into a gentleman's agreement that puts a cap of 0-5 percentage points on the spread of bank lending rates over the yield on the 42-day cash management bills; and » Most important, the increase in BSP policy rates actually benefits the banks which place their funds with the BSP in the course of this open market operation. The BSP has also exempted thrift banks from the recent increase in liquidity reserves. This is to encourage them to continue to provide credit to their target markets, which are the small and medium-sized enterprises and the housing sector. At the same time, bank lending activity continues to improve. Total outstanding loans of commercial banks grew by 4.4 percent year-on-year in august 2000. Loans to the manufacturing sector have been rising for ten straight months since November 1999, with an annual growth of 11.3 percent in August. On restructuring the loans of financially distressed companies The second set of proposals has to do with encouraging banks to restructure loans and be more liberal and flexible in extending credit. Specific proposals call for relaxing the rules on the classification of restructured loans and on loan loss provisioning. Our sound banking system remains one of the bright areas of our economy, and maintaining the health of the system remains a priority of the BSP. The rules on loan restructuring and loan provisioning were put in place precisely to ensure the soundness of the financial system. The stringent bank requirements and thorough scrutiny are part of the lessons of the Asian crisis, which underscored the importance of maintaining prudential standards. Relaxing these rules would go against established principles of sound banking regulation and financial supervision. Such an approach would strengthen the corporate sector at the expense of weakening the banking system. We must not forget that a strong economy requires a healthy banking system. Moreover, as policymakers, one of our main tasks is to ensure the even-handed application of policy rules. To extend preferential treatment to selected sectors implies an uneven application of policies and distorts the policy environment. Your position paper also calls for the BSP to take a lead role in evaluating rehabilitation proposals, since the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the courts may not be effective in this role. We have taken some crucial steps to address this issue. Secretary Jose Pardo and I have asked President Estrada to certify as urgent proposed House Bill No. 11867, also known as the Corporate Recovery Act (CRA). The Corporate Recovery Act is a comprehensive approach to addressing corporate financial distress. It allows the long-overdue reform of our insolvency laws and provides for the remedy of rehabilitation for distressed companies. The CRA will benefit greatly our efforts in corporate restructuring by providing immediate remedies to troubled corporations, speeding up their recovery and putting them on a more solid financial footing. On the creation of a rescue fund The third set of proposals is on the creation of a rescue fund for distressed but viable businesses. This set of proposals would have a potential impact on the fiscal budget, and would be best addressed by our fiscal authorities. Let me say, however, that such a rescue fund should not become an added fiscal burden. Of course, it is possible to arrange for external financing. However, if external funds will be used, stringent requirements should still apply in choosing the fund's potential beneficiaries, which should be limited to well-managed companies with genuine liquidity problems. Maintaining prudential standards and ensuring good corporate governance should remain a top priority at all times. The idea of providing a rescue fund may result in what economists call a moral hazard problem and, over time, result in a weaker corporate sector. The assurance of a government- funded bailout may be construed by some as carte blanche to spend unwisely and undertake potentially risky investments in the future, and eventually create bigger financial problems. We have already seen how such an approach can have disastrous results, as in the case of Japan and Korea, whose banks remain mired in a sea of bad loans. On the proper role of government I believe that government intervention should not be treated as a blanket solution to all our economic troubles. The government's role is not to ensure the uniform survival of all enterprises, but rather to ensure a properly functioning, conducive business environment that will allow the fittest, most competitive companies to flourish. This is the essence of free market competition. The ideal economic environment likewise includes a solid institutional framework for good corporate governance, to insure against corporate misdeeds. Policymakers should also focus on providing an enabling economic environment conducive to vigorous economic activity. This implies prudent monetary and financial policies as well as a continuing commitment to vital economic reforms. Concluding remarks In closing, I would like to emphasize that the BSP's responses to the FPI's proposals are guided primarily by sound economic principles. We continue to be supportive of the corporate sector, but within the larger context of our main policy objectives of ensuring price stability and maintaining a sound banking system. The key to restoring the confidence of banks to extend credit and maneuvering ourselves out of economic hardship lies in providing an enabling economic environment for sustained economic growth. Asking banks to relax credit standards only invites future trouble in the form of more bad loans and corporate bankruptcies. Corporate restructuring should not be done at the expense of prudential standards. At the same time, the Bangko Sentral is very much aware of the importance of bank financing for the working capital needs of Filipino companies. For this reason, we will continue to review our regulatory framework to make them more responsive to prevailing business conditions. The BSP will also continue its efforts to encourage bank lending activity as soon as market conditions permit. In line with this, let me again emphasize that the relatively high interest rate policy is not going to be a permanent economic fixture. We will continue to monitor the situation with a view to adjusting the monetary stance when the political situation improves. The business community can be assured that the BSP's policy actions will remain broadly supportive of our common objective of sustainable economic growth. Thank you and good day. (Note: Luncheon meeting, Federation of Philippine Industries, Inc. (FPI), November 6, 2000, Dusit Nikko Hotel, Makati City )

Title: The Near-Term prospects for the Philippine Economy
Occasion: European Union Embassies' Economic Counsellors Meeting
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Counsellor Jean-Philippe Quercy, counselors and officials of the European Union Embassies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, good morning: It is a pleasure to have this opportunity to discuss with you the present economic situation of the Philippines and the outlook for the coming months. The European Union has significant economic ties with the Philippines, accounting for about 20 percent of Philippine exports as well as a substantial amount of foreign investment inflows into the country. The EU has been a constant development partner whose confidence has been a continuing source of strength in times of difficulty. You are all aware of the pressures currently facing the Philippines, and of the recent policy moves of the BSP in response to these pressures. I am here today to provide you with some perspective about our recent policy actions. My essential point is that the economy is facing pressures from various fronts, and the BSP's recent policy moves were taken in order to help stabilize the economic situation while the political concerns are being addressed. Recent economic developments The recent pressures on the Philippine economy have come from various sources. On the external front, adverse shocks such as the oil price hikes and shortages, the middle east tension, and the political problems in Thailand and Indonesia, have weakened the peso along with the other currencies both in Asia and elsewhere. On the domestic front, negative political developments such as allegations of high-level corruption have further clouded market sentiment toward the peso. The resulting exchange rate depreciation and the lower level of confidence have created a situation that threatens our nascent economic recovery. Policy responses BSP measures include increases in the BSP's policy interest rates by a cumulative 500 basis points for the September-October period. The increases were intended to address the narrowing differential between foreign and domestic interest rates, which has partly caused the peso to weaken. We also raised the liquidity reserve requirement for commercial banks by a total of 400 basis points in order to siphon off excess liquidity in the system, which we believe is being used for speculative activity against the peso. To alleviate demand pressures in the FOREX market, we expanded the coverage of the Currency Risk Protection Program (CRPP) to service the FOREX requirements of oil companies. More recently, we have tightened the rules covering the foreign exchange units of banks by requiring them to submit the necessary documents for dollar sales of over us$10,000. This was intended to curb the speculative activities involving these FOREX corporations and also prevent money laundering. This is not a form of exchange control. What we want is to provide foreign exchange for legitimate and productive uses. The main result of all these policies is a significant tightening of monetary conditions, leading to higher interest rates. This was a difficult choice to make, given the importance of supporting economic recovery. However, we believe that the potential damage from a currency free-fall is also very significant since it weakens confidence, discourages investments and inhibits growth. Difficult situations require difficult measures, and inaction is no longer a practical alternative. Let me emphasize, however, that the current high interest rate regime is intended to be only temporary. Monetary authorities are very much aware of the serious adverse effects of high interest rates on the economy. The series of actions are intended to give time for the political situation to be sorted out in an orderly manner. I personally am hopeful that due process will prevail and allow an orderly resolution of the issues. At the same time, there is enough reason to expect that in two or three months' time, we will have a clearer outlook for the world oil market as well as the political tensions in the middle east and Asia. As safeguard, monetary authorities have taken steps to help minimize the impact of the recent monetary tightening on lending rates. For example, we have exempted the thrift banks from the higher liquidity reserve requirement, so as not to unduly constrain priority lending to small and medium-sized enterprises and the housing sector. Commercial banks have also entered into a "gentleman's agreement" that puts a 0-5 percentage point spread over the yield on the 42-day cash management bills for their lending rate. Let me again make clear that the relatively high interest rates are expected to be only temporary. For the moment, we have put off further monetary policy actions but we will continue to closely monitor the situation and take any policy action that may be deemed necessary. Once the situation stabilizes, we will adjust the stance of monetary policy to allow the recovery to flourish. Outlook for 2000 and 2001 In looking now at the months ahead, I think our expectations for sustained economic performance should be guided by an appreciation of the Philippines' sound macro fundamentals. So far this year, we have seen broader-based output growth, moderate inflation, a healthy external position with robust export growth, a fundamentally sound banking system. These economic gains have been due to an enabling policy environment borne of a steady commitment to vital economic reforms. In the last few months, we have also continued to see positive trends in various leading indicators of economic activity. For this reason, we expect sustained output growth in the second half of 2000. For the whole of 2000, GDP growth is expected to meet at least the lower end of the target of 4.0-5.0 percent. Inflation is expected to build up in the remaining months of 2000 due to emerging inflationary pressures from exchange rate movements, oil price increases and wage adjustments. However, these factors are expected to be offset in part by low food prices due to strong agriculture output growth and the timely importation of basic food products such as rice and sugar. Thus, the 2000 average inflation target of 5.0-6.0 percent is well within reach. Concluding remarks In closing, Philippine authorities have had to make some tough decisions in this very challenging economic and political environment. It must be underscored that our actions to stem a free fall of the peso have been balanced with the crucial goal of long-term sustainable growth. The relatively high interest rates are intended only as a temporary measure. These policy moves are really meant to allow some time for the political situation to be clarified. Let me make just one final point. The Philippines has faced tight situations before, in both the economic and political fronts. The difference now is that we have better established democratic institutions and a vastly improved policy environment. I strongly believe that our established constitutional processes will allow the orderly resolution of current political concerns, and that we shall overcome such adversity in the end. Thank you and good day. (Note: Economic Counsellors Meeting, European Union Embassies, October 31, 2000, Embassy of France, Makati City )

Title: An Update on the Monetary Situation
Location: Canadian Chamber of Commerce, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It is always a pleasure to break bread with the officers and members of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. With the swiftly unfolding political and economic developments in our country, I welcome this opportunity to update you on the monetary situation, particularly the exchange rate and interest rates. Recent actions of the BSP During the past few weeks, the Bangko Sentral has been implementing a package of measures aimed at stabilizing the foreign exchange market. This package included the following: » The increase in the BSP's policy rates by 100 basis points on September 11 and by another 400 basis points on October 13, partly to widen the interest differential between peso and dollar assets; » The increase in the liquidity reserves of commercial banks by a total of 400 basis points; » The expansion of the coverage of the currency risk protection program to include the requirements of oil companies; and » Just recently, the rationalization of the operations of FOREX corporations which are subsidiaries or affiliates of banks. This latest measure is intended to: »» Further strengthen existing money laundering measures; »» Align our foreign exchange system which is very liberal, with those of other countries like Thailand and Indonesia; and »» Reduce the scope for speculative play by some market players who are sourcing their dollars from FOREX corporations. Moreover, the minimum capital requirement of FOREX corporations has been increased to fifty million pesos. Given the increasing volume of transactions of these corporations, this prudential measure has been deemed necessary. Following this initial package of measures, the peso started to improve somewhat in the first week of October. Nevertheless, it is important to point out that the peso is moving broadly in sync with other currencies. Pressure points on the economy Of late, however, the economy continues to face increasing pressure from several points, as indicated by the peso's substantial weakening and its premium against the Thai baht, which had gone up considerably to about eight pesos from what it was in the early part of the year. On the domestic front, negative political developments--such as the "jueteng" scandal, allegations of cronyism and unexplained wealth--have clouded the outlook on the peso. On the external front, adverse shocks, including the oil price hikes and shortages, the middle east tension, and the political problems in Thailand and Indonesia, have further weakened the peso. The confluence of these aggravating circumstances has created a volatile situation. This could have adverse effects on the economy. Differentiating the economic sphere from the political arena It is therefore important that to the extent possible, we differentiate the economic sphere from the political arena. We should realize that amidst the current political noise, the substantial gains on the economic front have been unfortunately ignored. These include good output numbers, subdued inflation, a favorable external position, and considerable progress in structural reforms. These economic gains can be preserved, given that most leading indicators show the economy's continuing recovery momentum. It is also important to point out that, on the political side, democratic institutions are in place and that we have a constitutional process which should be followed in addressing outstanding political issues. The political turmoil is something expected of, and must be addressed within, a dynamic and democratic political system. A delicate balancing act One cannot overemphasize that a difficult situation requires tough and radical solutions, which may not necessarily sit well with the general public. During the past few weeks, we at the Bangko Sentral have had to make precisely such tough decisions. The underlying premise of our strategy is that there is a need to stabilize the economy while a political solution is being worked out. Stabilization involves, among others, siphoning liquidity that is being used by speculators to buy dollars, thus putting further pressure on the peso. At the same time, measures to make peso assets more attractive are being implemented, including adjustments in the Bangko Sentral's policy rates. Basically, there are two hard choices available to us: (1) letting the peso go, or (2) raising interest rates. Obviously these choices are akin to a razor-sharp, double-edged blade. Hence, it is important that these should be handled carefully lest the economy suffer unnecessarily. We believe, however, that there is a scope for taking the middle ground. The middle way Let us first consider our options if we let the peso go. Filipinos seem to be very sensitive to the peso-dollar rate. This could be partly because there are about five million overseas Filipino workers with five million families to support. These overseas workers maintain dollar accounts with banks and remit dollars to their families. We have also a very strong export sector. On the other side of the ledger, we also have to consider our imports as well as our external debt payments. As a result, the exchange rate, rightly or wrongly, is seen by most people as a barometer of the economy's condition. Thus, if the peso goes on a free fall, then we will be entering unchartered waters. While it may be easy to say that the peso should bear all the brunt of adjustment, in a small, open economy like the Philippines this could have dire consequences. The impact on markets will be almost immediate: oil price increases, transport fare adjustments, and wage hike petitions that go over and beyond productivity increases. All of these could develop eventually into an inflationary spiral, which could undo most--if not all--of the gains that we have achieved thus far. On the alternative choice of raising interest rates, it is important that we remain sensitive to its adverse effects on the real and financial sectors. High interest rates discourage investment and production. High interest rates contribute to further corporate distress and in turn, affect asset quality. This is the reason why we are monitoring the situation very closely with a view to reversing direction as soon as circumstances warrant. Thus, we expect the current relatively high interest rate regime to be temporary. This contingency measure is expected to buy us time. Perhaps, within the next three months, the middle east situation as well as the political situation in Thailand and Indonesia would have stabilized. And in our case, a clearer picture of our own political situation shall have emerged. In fact, except for some extremists, most of us agree that our domestic political concerns can be addressed in an orderly manner, following established constitutional processes. It is important that this is conveyed not only to ourselves but also to foreign investors. I remain fully convinced that the constitutional process will prevail in the quick resolution of our current political problems. Moreover, let me stress that we do not expect the hike in interest rates to translate into a one-to-one increase in bank lending rates for the following reasons: » There is still ample liquidity in the system; » Banks' deposit rates have not gone up in the same proportion. Banks, therefore, should not increase their lending rates excessively; » We recently arrived at a gentlemen's agreement with banks to cap lending rates. The spread will be 0-5 percent over the cash management bills rate; and » We exempted the thrift banks from the recent increase in liquidity reserves. This is to encourage them to continue to provide credit to their target markets, which are the small and medium-sized enterprises and the housing sector. In summary, let me be the first one to assure you that we at the Bangko Sentral are aware that monetary tools should not be used to address a non-monetary problem. Nevertheless, the recent political developments have fed into the economic stream and this has driven the dynamics of our recent actions. Let me also emphasize my view that the basis of the current high interest rate regime is not expected to continue. Hence, this regime is not meant to be prolonged. The interest rate situation will be reviewed continuously and interest rates will be adjusted accordingly as financial markets stabilize. Conclusion Let me close by saying that our guiding strategy is to strike a balance and not take extreme measures that may cause permanent damage to the economy. Not to do something at this point is tragic. Remember that old adage: "If you don't make up your mind, then your unmade mind will unmake you." You are all seasoned businessmen and interested followers of Philippine conditions, and I would be happy to hear your views. Thank you. (Note: Canadian Chamber of Commerce, October 30, 2000, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City )

Title: An Update on the Foreign Exchange Situation
Location: Makati Business Club, Dusit Nikko Hotel, Makati City
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I take great pleasure in joining the officers and members of the Makati Business Club. I assume that the MBC, like other business groups in the country, are watching closely the political and economic developments as they unfold. Actions of the BSP during the past two weeks During the past two weeks, the Bangko Sentral implemented a package of measures to try to stabilize the foreign exchange market. This package included the following: Ø The increase in the BSP's policy rates by 100 basis points on September 11 and by another 400 basis points on October 13, partly to widen the interest differential between peso and dollar assets; Ø The increase in the liquidity reserves of commercial banks by a total of 400 basis points; and Ø The expansion of the coverage of the currency risk protection program to include the requirements of oil companies. At the same time, we continue to strengthen the monitoring of foreign exchange transactions. Following this initial package of measures, the peso started to improve somewhat in the first week of October. However, recently, the premium against the Thai baht has gone up considerably to more than five pesos compared to what it was in the early part of the year. Nevertheless, it is important to point out that the peso is moving broadly in sync with other currencies. Pressure points on the economy Of late, however, the economy continues to face a number of pressure points; new shocks have likewise buffeted the economy. On the domestic front, negative political developments--such as the "jueteng" scandal, allegations of cronyism and unexplained wealth--have clouded the peso outlook. On the external front, adverse shocks, including the oil price hikes and shortages, the middle east tension, and the political problems in Thailand and Indonesia, have further weakened the peso. The confluence of these aggravating circumstances have created a volatile situation that could spell disaster for our fragile and nascent economic recovery. Insulating the economic sector from political noise In this situation, it is important to remember that the BSP will try insulate the economic sphere from the political arena. We would like to point out that gains on the economic front have been made, including good output numbers, subdued inflation, a favorable external position, and considerable progress in structural reforms. These economic gains can be preserved, given that most leading indicators show the economy's continuing growth momentum. It is also important to point out that, on the political side, democratic institutions are in place and that we have a constitutional process which should be followed in addressing outstanding political issues. However, given the current state of Philippine politico-economic dynamics, where political and economic issues are often intertwined, the public may find this way of looking at the issues difficult to appreciate. Having said that, I must admit that, not being a political person, I do not have the competence to talk about politics. And so, my discussion today will focus on economic issues. A delicate balancing act Let me start by saying that a difficult situation requires tough and radical solutions, which may not be popular to the public. During the past two weeks, we at the Bangko Sentral have had to make precisely such tough decisions. This is because inaction on our part is usually perceived by market players as license to engage in all sorts of speculative play. You may recall that the neutral policy stance adopted by the bank of Thailand amidst the gyrating value of the Thai baht in recent weeks was viewed negatively by market players. But the underlying premise of our strategy is that there is a need to stabilize the economy while a political solution is being worked out. Stabilization involves, among others, siphoning liquidity that is being used by speculators to buy dollars, thus putting further pressure on the peso and making peso assets more attractive. In making our decision, there are two choices available: (1) letting the peso go, or (2) raising interest rates. Obviously these choices are akin to a razor-sharp, double-edged blade. Hence, it is important that these should be handled gingerly lest the economy bleed excessively. We believe, however, that by carefully calibrating our responses, we can still walk the middle path. Thus we would avoid having to choose between the devil and the deep blue sea. Which is more dangerous? Which is a less painful solution? Let us first consider our options if we let the peso go. Filipinos seem to be very sensitive to the peso-dollar rate. This is a price that the man on the street seems to watch with much interest, bordering to the point of obsession. This could be partly because there are about five million overseas Filipino workers with five million families. These overseas workers maintain dollar accounts with banks and remit dollars to their families. As a result, the exchange rate, rightly or wrongly, is seen by most people as an anchor of the economy's strength. Thus, if the peso goes on a free fall, we will be entering unchartered waters. While it may be easy to say that the peso should bear all the brunt of adjustment, in a small, open economy like the Philippines this could have dire consequences. The impact on markets will be almost immediate: oil price increases, transport fare adjustments, and wage hike petitions that go over and beyond productivity increases. In addition, inflationary expectations will also be affected. On the alternative choice of raising interest rates, it is important to point out that we are not insensitive to its adverse effects on the real and financial sectors. Thus, we expect the current relatively high interest rate regime to be temporary. Again, let me emphasize that we expect this to be short-lived. This contingency measure is to buy us time. Perhaps, within three months time, the middle east situation as well as the political situation in Thailand and Indonesia would have stabilized. And in our case, a clearer picture of our own political situation shall have emerged. In fact, except for some extremists, our domestic political concerns can be clarified in an orderly manner, following established constitutional processes. It is important that this is conveyed not only to ourselves but also to foreign investors. I remain fully convinced that the constitutional process will prevail in the resolution of our current political problems. Moreover, we do not expect the hike in interest rates to translate into a pari passu increase in bank lending rates for the following reasons: Ø There is still ample liquidity in the system; Ø Banks' deposit rates have not gone up in the same proportion. Banks, therefore, should not increase their lending rates excessively; Ø We recently arrived at a gentlemen's agreement with banks to cap lending rates. The spread will be 0-5 percent over the cash management bills rate; and Ø We exempted the thrift banks from the recent increase in liquidity reserves. This is to encourage them to continue to provide credit to their target markets, which are the small and medium-sized enterprises and the housing sector. In summary, let me emphasize that we at the Bangko Sentral are aware that monetary tools should not be used to address a non-monetary problem. Nevertheless, the recent political developments have fed into the economic stream and this explains our recent actions. Let me also emphasize that the current high interest rate regime is not meant to be prolonged. The interest rate situation will be reviewed continuously and interest rates will be adjusted accordingly as financial markets stabilize. Conclusion In conclusion and as mentioned earlier, we must be careful that we strike a balance and not take extreme measures that may cause permanent damage to the economy. You are all captains of industry and seasoned businessmen and i would be happy to hear your views. I am here to ask your help and cooperation to stabilize the economic situation. Thank you. Title: Recent Developments and Directions for the Philippine Economy and Banking System
Occasion: Le Club Meeting
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I. Introduction It is a pleasure for me to speak before the regular forum of Le Club. In its capacity as the French Chamber of Commerce in the Philippines, Le Club has certainly done much to foster not only French-Philippine economic relations but also understanding and mutual appreciation of our two cultures. In an even broader sense, Le Club offers an important gateway for enhanced economic ties between the Philippines and the European Union, which now accounts for about 20 percent of Philippine exports. This morning, I will argue that the recent economic and political developments have obscured the concrete structural reform measures that have been instituted, and the foundations that have been laid in order to support sustainable development. The Philippines remains an excellent opportunity for investment. In this connection, I will brief you on the latest developments in the Philippine economy in general and the banking system in particular. It is my hope that at the end of our meeting, I would have presented the case for the Philippines. II. Assessments What are some salient features of our recent economic performance? Economic recovery more broad-based in 2000. Industry expanded by 4.1 percent for the first semester of 2000, compared to only 0.3 percent for the whole of 1999. Thus industry figures more importantly in this year's growth, in contrast to last year, where growth was to a large extent due to an agricultural rebound. The structure of economic growth is, therefore, shifting in such a way that growth is becoming more sustainable. The Mindanao conflict has certainly made international headlines, but this is confined only to the central region of Mindanao, which contributes less than 3 percent to total domestic output. Moreover, despite the recent pressures on the exchange rate and political concerns, advance indicators of economic activity have been registering generally positive trends: Indices of the value and volume of manufacturing production increased year-on-year by 35.8 percent and 23.9 percent, respectively, in July 2000. Meralco power sales and car industry sales are recovering and have risen by 8.2 percent and 13.7 percent for January-August, as opposed to contractions experienced during the same period in 1999. Key monetary and financial variables also point to the sustainable growth of the economy. The 5.0-6.0 percent annual target, and was achieved despite inflationary pressures from oil price and transport increases and wage adjustments. The treasury bill rate has experienced some upward pressure recently, but still stands at a manageable 9.892 percent as of the latest auction,[1] while bank lending rates range from 12.27-15.22 percent. [2] As of end-June 2000, the total resources of the Philippine financial system had risen by 43.7 percent compared to the end-1996 or pre-crisis level. Banks' asset quality remains manageable· as of July 2000, the non-performing loan ratio of commercial banks stood at 15.26 percent. A Goldman Sachs survey places the comparable June figures at 21.5 percent for Malaysia, 16.7 percent for Korea, and 39.7 percent for Thailand. Bank lending has shown consistent signs of recovery for several months now, with loans outstanding of commercial banks growing by 5.5 percent year-on-year as of July 2000. In particular, bank lending to the manufacturing sector advanced by 15.3 percent year-on-year in July. In the face of the foregoing positive developments, however, we realize that the current volatility in the foreign exchange represents one of the most serious challenges to the momentum of growth. Current foreign exchange market pressure does not reflect long-term trend. The pressure on the peso emanates from several factors: (1) narrowing of the differential between domestic and foreign interest rates due in large part to the rise in us interest rates since mid-1999; (2) the overall weakening sentiment on regional currencies; (3) an increase in corporate demand for dollars, arising from the pick-up in economic activity; and (4) negative market perception due to non-fundamental factors such as developments in Mindanao and in the political arena. By contrast, measures of the impact of exchange rate movements on the international competitiveness of Philippine industry indicate that the current level of the peso has been out of line with long-term fundamentals. Thus, the BSP views the current weakness of the peso as temporary, and not reflective of economic fundamentals. We believe that, as the international financial markets calm down, as the prospects for additional interest rate increases by the US Fed are reduced, and as concerns about the domestic political situation are resolved, the market will realize that the foreign exchange rate has overadjusted and will correct itself. Moreover, the BSP is carefully monitoring the pass-through effects of the peso weakness into the general price level. Accordingly, the BSP's approach has been to ensure an orderly adjustment in the foreign exchange market. To this end, the BSP has adopted several policy measures, including: - Increases in the BSP's policy rates in may and September 2000, with the cumulative increase reaching 225 basis points each for the BSP's borrowing (RRP) and lending (RP) rates. On top of this, the Monetary Board announced a 400 basis point increase in policy rates effective Friday, 13 October 2000. These adjustments address the narrowing of the differential between domestic and foreign interest rates, which has helped to drive the peso weakening. The adjustments in policy rates are also expected to stave off emerging inflationary pressures due to the impact of exchange rate movements on import prices and on wage settlements; - Increases in banks' and quasi-banks' liquidity reserve requirement by two percentage points effective 13 October 2000, and by another two percentage points for commercial banks and one percentage point for thrift banks effective 20 October 2000; and - Expansion of the coverage of the Currency Risk Protection Program (CRPP) to include the requirements of oil companies. This will alleviate the strain on the spot market due to demand pressure from unhedged borrowers wanting to cover their future foreign exchange requirements due to fears of further peso depreciation. In addition to the foregoing, the following aspects of the Philippine economy are supportive of an orderly foreign exchange adjustment: A low rate of inflation. A healthy trade position. Robust export growth. Improved maturity profile of our foreign debt. Adequate international reserves. Finally, a strong commitment to a floating exchange rate system. III. Reforms and policy directions Globalization counts a lot of merits. It widens the opportunities for emerging markets such as the Philippines, but at the same time punishes policy mistakes much more quickly and more severely. Today, therefore, requires that growth must be continuously nurtured, and the pace of reforms maintained and even accelerated. To a large extent, these concerns will be addressed by recent reform measures which further opened up the economy to foreign investment. Major foreign entrants are expected to come in the banking and retail sectors, with the recent enactment of the General Banking Law of 2000 and retail trade liberalization law, while the E-commerce Act and Regional Headquarters Law make a pitch to the technology industry and to multinationals seeking to enhance their presence in the region. Mergers and consolidations. We envision a future where there are, eventually, several major local banks and foreign banks accounting for the major portion of the total spectrum of the banking system. The rest will be niche players, which will have a competitive advantage in dealing with specific groups of customers.
