To achieve this end, the BSP continues to support bank consolidation, through the extension of a package of short-term incentives. The policy of encouraging mergers and consolidations is actually complementary to that of opening up the banking sector to new foreign participants, inasmuch as both measures will increase the ability of the banking system to compete in the globalized environment. To date, there have been a total of 9 mergers and consolidations involving 16 commercial banks, 1 thrift bank and 2 rural banks. Five more mergers have been approved in principle by the monetary board. General Banking Law of 2000. The recently passed general banking law of 2000 (R. A. No. 8791, or GBL 2000) supersedes the half-century old General Banking Act of 1949. The GBL 2000 now forms the basic legal fabric governing the banking system, and is expected to further strengthen the banking sector by, among others, improving transparency, putting in place internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy, and enhancing competition, including through allowing foreign banks to acquire up to 100 percent of the voting stock of an existing bank within 7 years from the effectivity of the law. Amendments to the New Central Bank Act. The BSP is pushing for amendments to the New Central Bank Act (R. A. No. 7653). Broadly speaking, these legislative measures aim to enhance the supervisory and enforcement powers of the BSP, further improve prudential standards for the banking system, intensify competition in the banking sector, and enhance the BSP's independence. Improving risk management. To improve regulatory oversight and monitor bank compliance with new guidelines, the BSP is developing a more integrated system for bank reporting. Risk management will be enhanced further through the implementation of a risk-based approach to supervision. Also, in line with the growing international awareness of the need for sound risk management in large-value fund transfer systems, the BSP and the BAP are also collaborating in upgrading the Settlements and Payments System into a Real Time Gross Settlements system (RTGS), which will cover equities, fixed income, money, and foreign exchange markets and will effect final settlement on a continuous basis. IV. Conclusion I have today sketched to you the financial reform efforts that are now underway, but I hope that this has gone some distance in convincing you of the Philippine government's commitment to its reform agenda and of our continuing search for a regulatory environment that is up to the demands of the times. Such reform agenda constitutes a key ingredient in the foundation for what we envision to be the banking landscape of the future--one that is characterized by bigger and more stable banks, with a regional orientation. We recognize that the reform process necessary to achieve this vision will be long and arduous, but eventually, we hope to be rewarded in terms of the emergence of Filipino financial institutions with transnational reach. Thank you and good day. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [1] 16 October 2000 [2] for the week 9-13 October 2000

Title: ome Thoughts on the Prospects for Asian Economic Cooperation
Occasion: First International Conference on Asian Political Parties
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Leaders and representatives of the various Asian political parties, distinguished colleagues, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good morning: First of all, I would like to thank the organizers of this conference for inviting me to speak at this forum. It shows vision on their part to establish a dialogue and a broad consensus on the long-term economic and political issues that will be of increasing significance for the Asian region in the coming decades. But you can be assured that my thoughts on Asian cooperation will not border on the political; central bankers are an apolitical tribe but hopefully non-trivial. The outlook for Asia Asia is becoming an increasingly dominant player in the global economy. Already it accounts for about a third of the world GDP, about a quarter of world trade and more than half the world's international reserves. The long-term economic outlook for the region has also remained largely undimmed by the crisis. The factors that made east Asia a high-growth area in the past decade are basically intact, such as the presence of an increasingly educated workforce and high savings rates. At the same time, the increased trade flows among Asian economies have fostered economic cohesiveness and political cooperation among these countries. Asia is, therefore, a force to reckon with, after North America and the Euro currency area. The result of this increased cohesion and growing economic strength is inexorably a serious determination to establish regional institutions geared to look after Asia's needs. Today I would like to offer some personal observations on the initiatives to promote economic cooperation, such as regional financing arrangements and a common Asian currency. These two areas are part of the more dominant trend towards increased regional integration, and, therefore, deserve some amount of consideration. The case for regional cooperation and integration Our collective experience with macroeconomic crises in the 1990s suggests the following: first, macroeconomic crises produce negative spillover effects that tend to affect entire regions; and second, most foreign institutional investors tend to indiscriminately lump emerging markets together instead of making country-specific analyses and investments. Often, a weakness or attack in one currency will provoke a reassessment of the fundamentals of the other comparable countries in the same region. Moreover, losses in one market may lead investors to pull out their funds in other regional markets. These considerations, together with the presence of extensive intra-regional trade and investment linkages, provide the case for a "peer pressure" or "club spirit" that will promote the pursuit of sustainable and prudent macroeconomic policies in individual countries in the region. In this area, soft forms of regional cooperation such as the exchange of economic information and best practices have proven invaluable and should continue to be encouraged. Other, more substantive modes of cooperation may include regional training in finance and macroeconomics to upgrade the quality of both economic research and macro and financial management. Over the years, there has been a growing determination to set up formal regional institutional arrangements in Asia. This is due partly to the desire for a uniquely Asian institution that will have a focused mandate and will be responsive to the region's needs. For example, the regional crisis has spurred interest in policies to promote greater regional economic stability. Particular attention has been paid to, among other things, arrangements to ensure exchange rate stability and improved regional surveillance. The Regional Financing Arrangement Asian central banks have shown the way in establishing the foundations for cooperation. In 1977, the ASEAN Swap Arrangement (ASA) was established with five participating ASEAN countries to provide a short-term liquidity facility to help each participant meet temporary balance of payments difficulties. The main idea was to provide a short-term financial safety net for countries in distress. In May 2000, ASEAN finance ministers agreed, under the "Chiang Mai Initiative" to expand the ASA to include all ten ASEAN members and, in addition, provide a network of bilateral swap and repurchase arrangement facilities among ASEAN, China, Japan, and Korea (or what is known as ASEAN +3). The Chiang Mai Initiative, therefore, expands the short- term financial safety to include all of ASEAN plus Japan, China and Korea. This proposal was further threshed out in Brunei and discussions will likely culminate in Prague this month towards an expanded ASEAN Swap Arrangement. It also provides for the possible creation of a regional surveillance system for East Asia. Thus, by providing the basis for a regional support mechanism, the Chiang Mai Initiative may be considered a major step forward in the efforts to strengthen official financial cooperation in the Asian region. Efforts to further develop the Chiang Mai arrangements into a longer-term scheme are embodied in the current plan for a Regional Financing Agreement (RFA). The RFA is intended to complement existing international financing facilities by bridging the gap between short-term financial arrangements and medium-term schemes such as those of the IMF. Proposals for the mechanisms and features of the RFA--such as funding source, conditionalities, and surveillance--are presently under evaluation by ASEAN. The prospects for an Asian common currency Another factor spurring Asian economic cooperation is the continued expansion of regional arrangements in other parts of the world. The recent successful launching of the Euro has prompted many Asian leaders to ask why Asia cannot work toward creating a common currency of its own. In fact, Europe is increasingly seen as a model for the Asian region's economic future, with a single currency and its own mechanism for responding to macroeconomic crises. The idea for an Asian common currency was first proposed by the Philippines and Hong Kong. The suggestion was for the creation of an Asian Currency Unit (ACU), analogous to the European Currency Unit (ECU) which was the precursor of the Euro. Creating a synthetic currency like the ACU may be a viable route to monetary union in Asia in light of the absence of a single dominant currency or country. The benefits of a single Asian currency are in the form of increased economic integration, higher levels of investment and trade, and lower transaction costs as a result of the elimination of multiple exchange rates and the convergence towards a single price for each good. Lower transaction costs for businesses translate into increased efficiency in regional trade activity. However, a single Asian currency essentially means a single monetary policy implemented by an independent Asian central bank. This means that member countries will have to contend with the prospect of a loss of monetary autonomy under such an institution. On the positive side, such an institution will also have a large amount of international reserves at its disposal, which will help deter speculative attacks against the common currency. All these benefits are still well into the future tense. This is because one of the main requirements for successful monetary union is that member economies should be on broadly similar cycles and have similar structures. As you well know, the various economies of the Asian region are at very different stages of development, and operate under differing cultures and government regimes. These economic disparities, therefore, may necessitate a lengthy period of time for allowing members to comply with the economic preconditions for currency union. These preconditions include, among other things, economic convergence criteria, an interim exchange rate arrangement, rules for fiscal policy, a regional competition policy and labor market integration. Needless to say, these things will take a long time to put together. If the Euro is of any guide, we are looking at some fifty years of preparatory work towards a single currency area. Thus, in view of the extensive preconditions for monetary integration, a currency union for Asia may be more of long-term priority for Asian leaders. Other barriers to regional cooperation Other barriers to regional integration exist. For example, most of the East Asian countries continue to view each other as economic or political rivals more than as potential partners. Hong Kong and Singapore, for example, are competing to become the financial hub of east Asia. Differences in political systems also underlie some rivalries. These contemporary differences have historical and cultural roots, and will tend to complicate any efforts toward integration, at least in the medium term. He agenda should be topped by initiatives to establish common understanding of the key issues in this part of the world and our stakes in making this work for our respective countries and people. Concluding remarks Asia is a force to reckon with in the world economy, one with impressive assets, increasing cohesiveness and bright economic prospects in the long term. This cohesiveness and increasing strength have led to a growing determination to create uniquely Asian regional institutions. Initiatives for increased regional cooperation are expected to produce benefits in the form of increased financial and economic stability. Prospects for regional financial cooperation appear to be good in view of the initial achievements in the form of currency swap and repurchase arrangements. Efforts to create a single Asian currency are expected to be a long-term matter given the complex set of preconditions for monetary union. Nevertheless, the successful example of Europe in this area provides some ground for optimism. Another reason for optimism in the prospects of regional economic integration is the determination of Asian leaders to make it work. Building long-term institutions in Asia requires firm political commitment. For this reason, I am heartened that Asian leaders have venues like this one which would enable us to collectively chart our strategies for the future. The challenge for us all here will be to build on the commonalities and emerging ties of our countries and to overcome the diversities, many as they are, through diplomacy and understanding. At the same time, there remains no substitute for putting one's house in order. No amount of regional cooperation will produce benefits as long as the fundamentals of individual countries remain unsound. Addressing domestic weaknesses in the financial and corporate sectors should remain the foremost priority for Asian governments. Our initiatives as Asian leaders may turn out to be one of the shaping forces of the world economy in the next few years. My hope is that they will continue to be positive and visionary. I am reminded of the words of dr. Robert Scalapino at the recent "Future of Asia" conference in Tokyo: "Never forget that leadership is a critical element in this whole question of economic development and growth." Thank you very much. (Note: First International Conference on Asian Political Parties, September 19, 2000, Manila Hotel)

Title: The Philippines: Recent Economic Development and Policy Thrusts
Location: Rotary Club of Makati, Makati City
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction Ladies and gentlemen, good morning. It is indeed a great pleasure to be here and be able to join the officers and members of the rotary club of Makati in this forum. I always look forward to this kind of interaction with the corporate leaders in business and industry in the country. Macroeconomic performance I am sure that I have already met most of you in various fora this year and have heard me articulate on the positive outlook of the macroeconomy and the soundness of the banking system. As we approach the last quarter of this year, we remain convinced that with the solid economic foundations, our economy will be able to hurdle domestic and external shocks and perform credibly not only this year but more importantly even in the medium-term. In the past few days several important economic indicators were released that tend to affirm our optimism at the start of this year. For the first semester of this year, real GNP showed an expansion of 4.0 percent. This was above market expectations and higher than the 2.8 percent growth registered during the same period last year. Overall growth was driven mainly by the stronger performance in industry and sustained expansion in services as well as in agriculture. Things are also going well on the inflation front. Inflationary pressures have been quite subdued. Inflation last month increased slightly at 4.6 percent. This brings the average inflation for the first eight months of the year to 3.7 percent, well within our target for the year of 5.0 - 6.0 percent. Inflation may continue to rise modestly towards year-end but we are confident that the whole year target will be achieved. The benign inflation numbers have contributed to the maintenance of a low interest rate regime which is needed to spur more productive activities in the economy. For August the benchmark 91-day treasury bill rate averaged 8.926 percent only slightly higher than the 8.898 percent average in December 1999. The exchange rate has been stable for the first four months of the year but has experienced some episodes of volatility and increased depreciation pressures since late may. A large part of the depreciation pressures stemmed from the weakening of regional currencies, the increase in U.S. interest rates and the tensions in Mindanao. With the resolution of the Mindanao crisis and the expectations of stable interest rates in the U.S., as well as the continued inflow of foreign exchange from our export receipts and OFW remittances we expect the peso to recover some of its value towards year-end. Our external position also continues to be solid. Thanks to our exports, which saw robust growth of 11.5 percent for the first half of the year. The remarkable export performance helped the current account register a surplus of US$2.45 billion for the first five months of 2000. The overall balance of payments likewise registered a surplus US$397 million during the same period. Banking sector performance Looking at the banking system, key indicators point to the system's continuing soundness. As of June 2000, the non-performing loan ratio of commercial banks stood at 14.65 percent. A Goldman Sachs survey places the comparable June figures at 21.5 percent for Malaysia, 16.7 percent for Korea, and 39.7 percent for Thailand. In the case of the Philippines, no public funds have been used to restructure the banks. Philippine banks continue to be well-capitalized with the banking sector's Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) recorded at 17.2 percent as of end-March 2000, higher than the end-1999 CAR for Malaysia (12.3 percent) and Thailand (15.2 percent). Policy thrusts Going forward, BSP's efforts will continue to focus on the maintenance of stable overall prices and of sound banking system. To enhance our capability to achieve our primary mandate of price stability, we are shifting to an inflation targeting framework next year. We believe that this framework is useful in conducting monetary policy in an increasingly liberalized and globalized financial environment. Inflation targeting is expected to, among other things: Manage inflation expectations, because of its forward-looking features; Strengthen the BSP's accountability and commitment to the price stability objective; and Enhance transparency in the conduct of monetary policy. We are also considering entering into a post program monitoring arrangement with the IMF without a financial component after the existing standby arrangement expires at the end of this year. The precautionary program will act as a seal of good housekeeping and further boost the credibility of our macroeconomic policies. In the banking sector, the BSP will continue to push for measures supportive of a sound and healthy banking system. An important recent legislative reform is the enactment of the General Banking Law of 2000. This new law addresses the need to make our previous 50 year-old General Banking Act of 1949 more responsive to the needs of the new financial environment. It provides the BSP more flexibility in supervising the banking industry and upgrades the country's banking laws to meet global standards. The law also liberalizes foreign participation in domestic banks, provides stricter rules on DOSRI loans, adopts the fit and proper test in the appointment of senior bank officers and promotes greater transparency in bank practices. The passage of the general banking law will add more clout to the supervision and regulatory functions of the Bangko Sentral, allow the adoption of internationally accepted risk-based capital adequacy formula and enhance competition. With the passage of the GBL 2000, an ongoing concern of the BSP right now is the operationalization of the provisions of the new law. A task force to operationalize the GBL has been formed within the BSP. The implementing rules and regulations for the provisions of the GBL are expected to be completed by the end of the year. New circulars are already being drafted while existing rules and regulations are being reviewed to align current policies with the new GBL. A necessary legislative initiative to complement the general banking law of 2000 is the amendment to the New Central Bank Act. The broad objectives of the amendments to the new central bank include: Strengthening further the BSP's regulatory oversight; Aligning prudential standards with international norms; Fostering greater competition; and Enhancing the supervisory capability and independence of the Bangko Sentral. One important proposed amendment to the New Central Bank Act is the restoration of the tax exempt status of the BSP. We have been actively participating in congressional hearings to enlighten our legislators that exempting the BSP from taxes is not synonymous to the government losing money. We have made the point that, exempting the BSP from taxes will not make the national government financial position worse-off. This is because the loses in the form of taxes would be offset by the higher dividends and interest rebates that the BSP would be remitting to the national government. We have also emphasized that BSP transactions are policy-driven and not aimed at earning any income for itself. This fiscal autonomy of a central bank is not unique to the Philippines, it is practiced elsewhere. Other central banks that enjoy tax exempt status include: the Bank of Thailand, the Bank Negara Malaysia, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Reserve Bank of Australia. To reiterate, tax exemption of the BSP does not necessarily imply a worsening of the government's financial position but contributes to the effectiveness in the conduct of monetary policy. We are also closely watching the growth of the so-called electronic banking activities of domestic banks. We foresee an expansion in the volume of such transactions in the future. We encourage the adoption of these new delivery mechanisms in our domestic system to ensure that we keep in pace with the latest financial innovations. However, such systems entail new risks which have to be clearly understood and accurately priced by our banks. From a regulatory point of view, there is a need to identify, assess and manage these attendant risks. The BSP has undertaken initial steps towards this direction. We have issued some requirements to ensure that banks have in place a risk management process that is adequate to monitor, assess and control the associated risks. Another current undertaking of the BSP is the development of a Real Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS). This is expected to enhance operational efficiency, reliability, and timeliness of payment transactions in the face of the rapidly increasing volume and value of transactions. This new system will limit settlement and systemic risks in the interbank settlement process thus ensuring the stability of the whole financial system. This should be an initial step towards the eventual integration of our payment system with those of the rest of the region. Concluding remarks In closing, I would like to thank the officers and members of the Rotary Club of Makati for inviting me to this gathering and be able to share with you our views on recent economic developments and our future policy thrusts. Once again, I solicit the support of our friends from the Rotary Club in pushing for these plans of the Bangko Sentral. It takes time for these reform measures to be implemented and for these initiatives to take effect. However, with close partnership between policymakers and the private sector, this process can be accelerated. We are confident that as the reforms are implemented, these policy measures will eventually lead to sustained and faster growth for the economy. (Note: Rotary Club of Makati, September 6, 2000, Makati City )

Title: Confidence in the Financial System: How Do We Protect Our Investments?
Occasion: Joint MAP-PCCI-MBC Membership Meeting
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction I am delighted to be able to speak before the General Membership Meeting of the Management Association of the Philippines (MAP), held jointly with the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the Makati Business Club. I am sure that our discussion will be very fruitful for two very important reasons. First, this joint gathering of three of the country's most important business groups is rather rare. Second, the organizers chose an excellent topic for discussion-- for the issue of confidence in the financial system is crucial to the question of confidence in the rest of the economy, and, indeed, to the sustainability of our development agenda. If the Philippines is to catch up with the rest of Asia, then there is no choice but to integrate with the global economy. However, as the Asian financial crisis has demonstrated, globalization heightens demands on both the economy and on economic management. The past decade has witnessed large fluctuations in external financing flows to emerging markets, and recent developments indicate that this volatility is likely to continue. Continued strengthening of the financial sector is, therefore, an imperative. A stable, competitive, and innovative financial sector will help greatly in sustaining and stabilizing the economy's growth path by ensuring that financing flows efficiently towards its most productive uses. The two important areas that impinge upon the financial system's performance are: (1) the state of the overall macroeconomy, and (2) the authorities' commitment to the structural reform program. Accordingly, I shall look into these two areas in detail. The state of the economy Economic recovery without sacrificing price stability. A strong industrial sector recovery contributed greatly to our 3.45 percent real GNP growth for the first quarter of this year. This contrasts with 1999, where the 3.6 percent whole year growth was to a large extent due to an agricultural rebound, and where industry expanded by only 0.3 percent. The sectoral composition of GNP, therefore, argues in favor of a healthier and more sustainable growth compared to last year. It is important to note that this recovery has been achieved without sacrificing broad stability in prices. Inflation averaged 3.6 percent for the first seven months of this year, as against a full-year target of 5-6 percent. Low inflation has also contributed to a trend decline in interest rates. The 91-day treasury bill rate stood at 8.93 percent as of the latest auction on 21 August, while lending rates have been within the range 11.41-14.33 percent for August 2000. External payments risk managed through prudent external debt and international reserve management. Apart from a sound policy framework, the other aspect of macroeconomic management that has an important bearing on confidence in the financial system involves our ability to pay our foreign obligations on time. Two ingredients are important in this respect--the BSP's management of, first, the level and composition of our external debt, and second, our international reserve position. We have improved significantly in both respects. Thus, although the end-march 2000 level of foreign debt increased by 7.8 percent over its year-ago level, the maturity profile of the debt has improved, with medium- and long-term loans accounting for 88.5 percent of the total at end-March 2000, compared to 85.0 percent for the year-ago level. Furthermore, as of 10 August 2000, the GIR level has gone up to $15.455 billion, which is equivalent to 4.6 months of imports of goods and services. This provides us an additional cushion of comfort against external shocks. Finally, our commitment to a floating exchange rate system remains the best means of addressing foreign exchange risk, as this removes a one-way bet on the direction of exchange rate movements and ensures that the risk of exchange rate movements are borne by market players. The state of the banking system At the threshold of the 21st century, the Philippine banking system stands resilient and dynamic. Successive increases in the minimum capitalization requirement of banks and the consequent mergers and consolidations have resulted in bigger and better-capitalized banks. The banking system is also moving toward greater transparency and improved corporate governance. Overall, key indicators point to the system's continuing stability and growth. As of June 2000, the non-performing loan ratio of commercial banks stood at 14.65 percent. A Goldman Sachs survey places the comparable June figures at 21.5 percent for Malaysia, 16.7 percent for Korea, and 39.7 percent for Thailand. The higher level of capitalization has also allowed Philippine banks to post a Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) of 17.2 percent as of end-March 2000, higher than the end-1999 CAR for Malaysia (12.3 percent) and Thailand (15.2 percent). One important benefit of banking system soundness is that, to date, the liquidity assistance of the Bangko Sentral to distressed banks has been significantly lower compared to the levels extended by other Asian monetary authorities. Also very importantly, no public funds have been used to bail out failed banks and financial institutions. Restructuring of banks in the Philippines have involved mainly the consolidation of the banking industry. Reforms and policy directions All the foregoing statements should not be taken as implying in any way that we have become complacent about our growth prospects--far from it. In fact, we recognize the recent existence of some negative market sentiment towards the Philippines. We take this sentiment as a challenge for us to remain ever more committed to the pursuit of structural and social reform. The reform agenda is a robust one going forward. Key reforms have been and are currently being put in place to build the architecture necessary to equip the banking system for globalization. General Banking Law. The passage of the General Banking Law of 2000 (R.A. No. 8791) is expected to further strengthen the banking sector by, among others, improving transparency, putting in place internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy, and enhancing competition, including through allowing foreign banks to acquire up to 100 percent of the voting stock of an existing bank within 7 years from the effectivity of the law. Amendment of the New Central Bank Act. The BSP is pushing for amendments to the New Central Bank Act (R. A. No. 7653). Broadly speaking, these legislative measures aim to enhance the supervisory and enforcement powers of the BSP, further improve prudential standards for the banking system and enhance the BSP's independence. Mergers and consolidations. The BSP continues to support a liberal banking policy that promotes an environment conducive to the development of big, regionally--if not globally-- competitive banking institutions. This policy is actually complementary to that of opening up the banking sector to new foreign participants, inasmuch as both measures will increase the ability of the banking system to compete in the globalized environment. In view of the large number of competitors in the commercial banking sector, we are confident that such mergers will not result in an oligopolistic banking industry. The industry has enough room for mergers and consolidations without staving off the effective competition that is beneficial to depositors and borrowers. Smaller banks will play a significant role as niche players, specializing in products that will give them competitive advantage in catering to specific customers. Enhancement of banks' risk management capability. We have repeatedly emphasized that the dramatic changes in the structure of banking and the increased risks associated with financial liberalization and globalization entail upgrading banks' risk management capabilities. The significant developments in this area include: · Improvements in the financial infrastructure to ensure compliance with international best practices in supervision and risk management, including development by the BSP of a more integrated bank reporting system for monitoring bank compliance with new guidelines. · Reform of settlements and payments system. The BSP and the BAP are collaborating in developing a Real Time Gross Settlements System (RTGS), which will cover equities, fixed income, money, and foreign exchange markets and will effect final settlement on a continuous basis; · Completion by the BSP of a first-generation early warning system for commercial banks, which will provide the BSP with advance indicators of bank solvency; · Development by the BSP of a risk assessment system in lieu of a checklist-driven approach to on-site bank examination. The BSP is also closely monitoring the proposed amendments by the BASLE Committee on Banking Supervision to the capital adequacy framework. The proposed framework aims to eliminate the distortions caused by the existing capital framework and further promote systemic stability. The features of this new framework will be incorporated into the implementing rules and regulations of the General Banking Law of 2000 that the BSP is formulating. Increasing the transparency of the financial market. Transparency is essential for market discipline, for proper market evaluation of risks, and for ensuring that these risks are correctly and promptly reflected in market prices. Recent BSP measures meant to improve market transparency include requiring banks to post information on interest rates and to disclose the levels of non-performing loans, classified loans and other risk assets, and insider loans in their quarterly statements of condition. Challenges ahead With the implementation of our economic reform agenda, we are confident of achieving our program targets. For the year 2000, these targets include a GNP growth rate of 4.5-5.5 percent, an inflation rate of 5.0-6.0 percent, a current account balance of US$6.3 billion, and a foreign reserve position of US$16.1 billion by year-end. However, we must always bear in mind that global and regional stability is very much a work-in-progress. Uneven growth and possible slowdown in certain major economies could still cause destabilizing aftershocks in Asia. In connection with this, recent indications of a soft landing for the us economy are a welcome development. The key feature of globalization is that it confronts us with new combinations of both opportunities and risks. Thus, a financial system that is attuned to the demands of the new environment must be responsive to both the opportunities and risks present in the market. The key challenge is to find the appropriate level of prudential supervision that ensures the safety and soundness of the financial system, while at the same time balancing this consideration with the need to maximize the level of competition and efficiency in the provision of financial services. As policies take hold and the confidence of the business sector builds up, we can expect greater business receptivity to economic opportunities. Such confidence is self-reinforcing, and the task for government is therefore to continue to build the foundations that will allow for a sustained economic take-off. Thank you and good day. (Note: Joint MAP-PCCI-MBC Membership Meeting, August 28, 2000, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati City )

Title: Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City
Location: The BSP and the ECCP: Partners in Promoting Philippine Development
Occasion: European Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines (ECCP)
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It is a pleasure to be invited to this luncheon meeting of the European Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines. Indeed, it is an excellent opportunity to break bread with members of the umbrella organization for European businesses in the country and exchange views on the state of Philippine business and the economy. Europe has been one of the Philippines' strategic partners in the areas of trade and investment. The annual flow of foreign equity investments in the country by European countries has grown steadily during the last ten years from US$30 million in 1990 to US$1.2 billion in 1999. The yearly flow of European portfolio investments in the country also followed the same trend, rising from US$17 million in 1990 to US$4.7 billion in 1999. For the first five months of this year, our balance of trade with the European bloc was positive at US$1.3 billion. In 1999, we also enjoyed a balance of trade surplus with Europe amounting US$3.6 billion. Europe is also an important destination region for our overseas workers, whose remittances from this area have been growing steadily. As long-time trade and investment partners, most of you, I am sure, are no longer strangers to the intricacies of Philippine business. What you need at this time, I think, is an update on the Philippine economy to keep you informed of key developments that may affect the cost and pace of doing business in the country. They say that perception is key and this afternoon, I would like to share with you some developments that would hopefully help you arrive at a more informed assessment of the Philippine economy. One encouraging piece of news is that the economy has continued to expand. In the first quarter of this year, real gross domestic product grew by 3.4 percent, way above the 0.7 percent growth posted during the comparable quarter in 1999. This growth was underpinned by the expansion in industry and services, indicating broad-based recovery. In particular, the manufacturing sector appears to be taking over the reins of growth, as it rose by 5.8 percent during the quarter relative to its level during the same period a year earlier. It is also noteworthy that in contrast to the first quarter of 1999, when the public sector propelled overall growth, private sector activities were behind this year's first quarter expansion, indicating more durable growth prospects. There are other indicators that support this expansionary trend. On the supply side, the value and volume of production indices for the first five months of this year posted positive growth rates, a reversal of the negative growth in 1999. On the demand side, exports growth remained strong at 11.5 percent in the first six months of this year. Meanwhile, import growth continues to be positive, indicating the underlying growth momentum of the economy. Car sales and power sales are also on the rise and these indicators attest to the strengthening of consumer confidence. As the economy positions itself for further expansion, the macroeconomic environment remains fundamentally sound and conducive to doing business. Inflation has remained low and stable at 3.6 percent during the first seven months of this year. This has helped keep interest rates at steady and reasonable levels. Of late, the peso has followed a more stable path after its sentiment-driven weakening in the past few weeks. We expect that this trend will continue as regional currency movements stabilize and the political turmoil in Mindanao subsides. Our external payments position remains solid, reflecting a respectable current account surplus, high level of foreign reserves and an improving maturity structure of external debt. Our banking system remains safe and sound and serves as an efficient channel for business and investment transactions. This overall positive view of the economy's fundamentals has been confirmed by various international research agencies. For instance, Morgan Stanley found that the Philippine stands at a favorable position relative to some international investment benchmarks, including external debt as a percentage of exports, debt service ratio and reserve coverage. Paine Webber, which came up with its ability to pay index, grouped the Philippines with south Korea, Thailand and Malaysia as the countries with the "lowest risk" in East Asia, indicating that it has a low prospect of default due to its sound financing position. But the key event that confirmed the soundness and direction of the Philippine economic program was the endorsement by the international monetary fund last week of the findings of the fifth review of the country's stand-by arrangement. Not only did it pave the way for the release of US$314 million worth of financing for the country, but it also helped in bolstering the country's international credit standing. Meanwhile, the government remains firm in strengthening its efforts at improving tax administration and holding back on non-essential expenditures with a view to keeping the fiscal program on track. In addition to our fundamentally sound economy, our strategic location as a gateway to Asia and the superior quality of our manpower resources are some key positives that prospective investors would do well to consider in their fund allocation decisions. The 1999 survey by the Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk Consulting Limited showed that Philippine labor was second only to India in Asia and ahead of ASEAN countries in terms of quality, cost competitiveness and availability. In another report based on a new global cyber index called "Cyber Atlas" of the US-based Meta group, which measures the "technological vitality" of 47 countries, the Philippines ranked first in terms of available workers who are skilled in information technology. Perhaps this competitive edge of our human resources could find some match with the European investors' expertise and industrial strength not only in information technology but also in other related areas such as power, telecommunications, energy and even banking. Any European-RP venture in this direction will continue to be supported by our firm commitment to structural reforms that have seen the passage in congress of such legislations as the electronic commerce law, the revised General Banking Act and the Regional Headquarters Law. All of which aim to facilitate greater efficiency in business transactions in a globally integrated context. On the part of the Bangko Sentral, continued prudence in monetary policy and in bank supervision will remain our primary thrusts to ensure a stable monetary and financial environment conducive for business and investment transactions in the country. In closing, I wish to thank the officers and organizers of this meeting for the opportunity to address the ECCP members and share my views on the Philippine economy. We have brought this Philippine story to the United States and it was received well. Hopefully, members of this Chamber would be equally receptive to our story and signify their willingness to join the Philippines in a partnership to develop further the economy. After all, prosperity shared is never diminished but grows into an even grander vision for all its beneficiaries. Thank you and good day. (Note: Luncheon Meeting, European Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines (ECCP), August 7, 2000, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City )

Title: Closing Address: SEACEN Workshop on Concepts and Measurements of Core Inflation and Inflation Forecasting
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Monetary Board member Vicente B. Valdepeñas, Jr., Dr. Subarjo Joyosumarto, officials and staff of the SEACEN Centre, distinguished guests, participants, my colleagues at the BSP, ladies and gentlemen, good evening: Tonight we are concluding a very successful and productive SEACEN workshop. Let me take this opportunity to thank all those who have made this event truly successful. Our profound gratitude to the SEACEN Centre for co-sponsoring this workshop--SEACEN has been a historical partner in this type of regional cooperation; the resource persons for generously sharing their expertise--and without whom international flavour would have been wanting; the SEACEN member central banks for sparing their staff for a few days--there is no truth to the saying that those who attend seminars and workshops are those who are dispensable, our representation to this activity are some of our best staff; and members of the Bangko Sentral preparatory committee who helped organize this event. Your contributions to this event cannot be missed. The subject of this workshop, measurements of core inflation and inflation forecasting, is very timely and useful to central bankers, particularly at this time when forward-looking and information-intensive methods of policy-making take a front seat over traditional methods that respond to what has already taken place. I am positive that the workshop was able to shed light on a very critical goal of monetary policymaking--price stability. In a dynamic environment where traditional relationships among macro variables are beginning to, or have in fact weakened, particularly in periods of crises, it is pertinent for policy-makers to be equipped with the proper tools and techniques for monitoring and forecasting that one variable which is at the center of monetary management--the inflation rate. A reasonable tracking of its future movements effectively enables monetary authorities to win half the battle of fighting inflation. After all, nobody says this is easy. This workshop was meant to help our respective research or economic forecasting departments. The other half of the battle, of course, relies on the ability of those who actually shape policy to give the appropriate response in a timely manner. A good prediction of inflation is particularly relevant to the BSP's planned shift to inflation targeting as a monetary policy framework in 2001. I am positive that the participants from Indonesia have benefited in the same way since this country is also on the road to adopting inflation targeting as an alternative policy framework. Equally important to a good prediction of inflation is a better understanding of that part of inflation which monetary authorities have some degree of control--underlying or core inflation. It is true that the literature is far from achieving convergence to a single, acceptable measure of core inflation, but venues such as this provide us with a better understanding of this concept as well as options that are currently available for its measurement. I have been informed that this workshop has been a fruitful learning experience for many of you. It is my hope that whatever insight or even wisdom that you picked up in the past four days will be applied in your respective workplaces. Also, I hope everybody took the opportunity to get to know one another on a more personal level. I hope the acquaintances gained through the interaction among the participants in this workshop will go a long way. The workshop proper ends here but I would like to encourage everyone to join the post-workshop activities which the Bangko Sentral has organized. I have been advised that the members of the BSP preparatory committee will be taking you to Tagaytay highlands where one could have a picturesque view of the famous Taal volcano and lake. We also invite you to enjoy the amenities there. Try your hand in the golf course, swimming pool, or perhaps just take a look at the gardens. There are other sports facilities available. Do enjoy the rest of your stay. Thank you and good evening. (Note: SEACEN Workshop on Concepts and Measurements of Core Inflation and Inflation Forecasting, July 7, 2000, Ilustrado, Intramuros, Manila)

Title: Keynote Speech
Occasion: Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Ives Nisce, newly elected officers of the RBAP, distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good evening: I would like to start by congratulating the new officers of the RBAP for 2000-2001. Rural banks are a key instrument in providing credit to the countryside as well as mobilizing domestic savings. Because you are at the frontlines in providing financial services to the rural areas, you are a vital component of the domestic financial system. In recent years, our experience with crisis conditions has shown the central value of maintaining a sound banking system. This has been one of the major tasks of the BSP since its inception, and progress in the same area has helped us weather the financial storm in 1997-1998. The banking system at present Today, the fundamental strength and soundness of the banking system is shown by the continued growth of its assets to P2.96 trillion as of end-March 2000, and by its capital adequacy ratios which remain well above international standards. The rural banking system also continues to grow apace. Its branch network has more than doubled from 490 branches in 1993 to 1,068 as of end-March 2000. However, we need to address some weak areas. Asset quality, for example, is less favorable compared to the overall banking system. As of end-January 2000, the NPL ratio for rural banks was recorded at 19.6 percent compared to 13.65 percent for the entire banking system. There have also been in recent months more than a few cases of liquidity problems among rural banks as well as reports of DOSRI-related abuses. The BSP, of course, is quite willing to provide help to troubled rural banks. However, bank owners and managers should also do their part in ensuring the basic soundness of their respective institutions, so that these types of problems can be avoided altogether. In short, there is a fair amount of room for improvement in our rural banking sector. Strengthening the sector thus remains a top priority for regulators. Maintaining a sound banking system Our continuing efforts to develop the banking system essentially focus on pushing forward key reform initiatives. Let me spend a few minutes on some of these efforts. The General Banking Law One crucial initiative is the recently signed General Banking Law (GBL) of 2000. The GBL is envisioned to enhance the BSP's supervisory capability and enforcement powers, raise transparency and prudential standards as well as promote greater competition in the industry. Most important, the General Banking Law also tightens the rules on exposure of all banks to DOSRI or insider lending. These tighter rules apply to all banks, rural banks included. The GBL helps establish effective deterrents to unsound banking practices. Addressing this issue is vitally important to preserving public confidence in the banking system. I must firmly emphasize here that, in cases where enough evidence of unsound banking practices is found, authorities are fully committed to imposing appropriate penalties on the concerned parties. This ensures that managers and owners will suffer the consequences of their misdeeds, so that they will not be repeated in the future. We have already taken a major step in this direction recently by filing charges for DOSRI lending violations against officials of two failed commercial banks, a failed thrift bank and a failed rural bank. These actions should make clear to everyone that violations of the law will not be tolerated. Other banking reform priorities focus on improving the system for oversight and supervision of banks. Expected to be passed later in 2000 are the proposed amendments to the New Central Bank Act (R.A. 7653). Among other things, we are pushing for the inclusion of investment houses that offer investment banking services under BSP supervision. This is so that the Bangko Sentral can monitor the activities of investment houses, specially those affiliated with banks. We think this is a timely move in view of the recent liquidity problems of some investment houses involved in direct lending. At the same time, the BSP remains flexible in implementing prudential measures to give banks breathing space, particularly in their capital build-up program. We have already postponed the increase in the minimum capital requirements for all banks for 2000, and extended the compliance period for the 1999 capital requirements to end-2000. This relieves the pressure on our banks so they can concentrate more on business strategy. Concluding remarks All these efforts are aimed at further strengthening the banking system, by increasing transparency and improving governance. They are also aimed at ensuring that the banking system will have a talented and highly qualified pool of managers who are firmly committed to their fiduciary responsibilities to stakeholders. I would therefore like to end by saying our goal of balanced, sustainable growth for the economy also requires a strong and stable partnership with the private sector, and I am glad that the future of rural banking rests on capable hands. I wish you success in all your activities in the coming year and beyond. Thank you very much. (Note: Induction of New Officers, Rural Bankers of the Philippines, July 4, 2000, Century Park Sheraton, Manila)

Title: The BSP in the New Millennium
Occasion: 7th Anniversary of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: This is a special day for me. This is the first time I will be presiding over the celebration of the BSP's founding anniversary since I assumed the governorship last year. And completing one year in room 501 seems eternal to me. Some had their baptism in water, others had their baptism in the spirit. I had my baptism of fire--the issue of interest rates raged last year, the Y2K changeover required tons of liquidity, one failed bank sent tremors through the banking system, the equities market was rocked with scandal, the exchange rate is playing up again. Now my friends beat me occasionally in the fairways. This is one of the hazards of being a signatory to the country's currency. But our collective efforts and teamwork at the BSP enabled us to overcome all of these obstacles. During my first year in office, I have kept my faith in that wonderful adage, that the privilege to work is a gift, that power to work is a blessing, and that love of work is success. As we mark the seventh anniversary of the BSP, let us consider this a rare opportunity to look back and assess our performance with respect to our mandate, the strategies we have adopted, and our broad record of contribution to the sustainability of economic growth. The BSP charter gifted us central bankers with the privilege to look after the macro objective of price stability and the health of the financial system. This is a mandate we need to pursue without wavering, and we need to continue reinventing ourselves, so that we will not fall short of the sine qua non of our mandate. In this connection, let me congratulate you, my colleagues in the Bangko Sentral, for your excellent performance. Path breaking reforms in the financial system have been put in place in order to address the issue of the system's stability and capacity to compete in the globalized setting. This includes the passage of the general banking law 2000, which gives the BSP more flexibility in supervising the banking industry, improving business practices, and upgrading the country's banking laws to meet global standards. The Makati Business Club Executive Survey has again voted the Bangko Sentral, for the 8th time, as the number one performing government agency. That is the blessing of work, and of working hard. Looking forward, what is the major work agenda of the BSP? First, pursuant to the Monetary Board approval, we will be shifting from monetary targeting to inflation targeting as the framework for monetary policy starting 2001. Under an inflation targeting framework, the BSP will give primary importance to the goal of price stability. We will announce inflation targets to the public and will explain how we intend to achieve them. We will then be accountable for the achievement of the inflation target. Such a framework highlights the importance of communication by the BSP of the rationale for its policy decisions to the public. Thus, inflation targeting offers greater transparency and accountability in the conduct of monetary policy. This, in turn, will help increase the credibility of the central bank over time. The second thrust is the implementation of the General Banking Law of 2000. We have created a task force in order to ensure that policies and procedures are in line with the new general banking law. Critical areas of implementation include the issuance of regulations implementing a risk-based capital adequacy standard, guidelines for bank closure and receivership, and the identification of unsafe and unsound practices. Related to this successful advocacy program, the BSP is now pushing for the amendment of the New Central Bank Act (R.A. No. 7653). Broadly speaking, these legislative measures aim to: (a) enhance the supervisory and enforcement powers of the BSP; (b) further improve prudential standards for the banking system; (c) intensify competition in the banking sector; and (d) promote further the independence of the BSP, particularly its ability to deal with threats to the overall stability of the financial system. As is widely anticipated, the amendments to the BSP charter will also enhance its capacity to attract the best talent available. With the removal of legal constraints, we can look forward to a better and more competitive working environment. Finally, let me sound the call to all BSP'ers that at the same time that we attract the best technical and executive talent, we must also attract, encourage, and maintain the best moral talent in this institution. An institution is shaky without its foundation, and I submit that a lasting foundation of the BSP consists of its people with high values and integrity, those people who love their work. Our very choice of working for the BSP, and staying loyal to it all these years, is already an indication of our selflessness. Today, therefore, we are launching our work attitude and values enhancement program. This program will focus on the positive values that all officers and employees of the bank should imbibe, as public servants. Thus the program will support and complement the civil service commission's "mamamayan muna, hindi mamaya na" project. Particular attention will be given to the role of officials and supervisors as role models and implementers. This values enhancement program will ensure that we will always have a deep pool of committed talents, and this is one critical element of success. Let me therefore end these remarks with one final word: "If you can fill the unforgiving minute with sixty seconds worth Of distance run, yours is the earth and everything that's In it...." In our February 2000 Corporate Planning Conference, we noted that there are still certain areas of our work where we can establish shorter timelines for completion. We will be taking stock of these areas early next year. As your chief executive, I therefore encourage you to continue filling up your unforgiving minute with sixty seconds worth of solid work. Then yours will be the earth and everything that is in it. Maraming salamat at mabuhay ang Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. (Note: 7th Anniversary of the BSP, 03 July 2000)

Title: BSP Dividend Remittance fir 1999: P2.97 Billion
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. President, it is my immense privilege to present to you today the symbolic checks for the sum of P2.97 billion, representing the profit remittances of the Bangko Sentral to the National Government. This is the product of the bank's favorable financial operations in fiscal year 1999. Let me clarify, Mr. President, that these remittances are exclusive of the approximately P6 billion in tax payments we remitted to the government for 1999. In fact, over the past seven years, the Bangko Sentral has managed to remit more than P60 billion in dividends and taxes with an initial handicap of only P10 billion capital. The National Government still owes the BSP P40 billion but has received more than P60 billion. I think you will agree that that is a lot of bang for the proverbial buck. Today marks the 7th anniversary of the BSP's establishment in 1993. One of the ways we are celebrating this occasion is by taking the novel step of providing, as part of the 1999 dividends, real estate properties worth P1.5 billion. These properties are targeted for use in the government's low-cost housing projects. It is our 'own' way of helping in the efforts to provide for the needs of the poor. We have also been looking into plans for a similar scheme for our local banks, using their foreclosed real estate properties for housing projects. We want to help speed up the turnaround of the property sector and thereby help pump-prime the economy to boost economic activity. These efforts are part of the Bangko Sentral's long-standing commitment to help build a path towards balanced and sustainable growth for the Philippine economy. The inflation picture continues to be benign and therefore we have a very good flexibility in helping pursue growth. Mr. President, we have also managed to fulfill our 'other mandate' to promote a sound financial system. Many financial indicators are more eloquent proof of our achievements. The macro indicators are as good in terms of the declining interest rates, the external payments surpluses and the ample gross international reserves. Our guiding role in the economy continues with the number of crucial measures that we have managed to put in place just recently. I would like to mention just two of the most important. The first is the planned shift, beginning 2001, to inflation targeting as a framework for conducting monetary policy. Among other things, this change in framework will help the public better understand the workings of monetary policy and also increase the accountability of monetary authorities in achieving this overriding goal. The second is the recently signed General Banking Law of 2000, which is envisioned to enhance the BSP's supervisory capability and enforcement powers, raise transparency and prudential standards as well as promote greater competition in the banking industry. Let me therefore assure his excellency that the Bangko Sentral will continue to build upon the work that it has already managed to achieve so far in these last seven years. We will continue to strive to live up to the trust and confidence that has been placed in us in providing the bedrock of stability that is needed to consolidate the recovery · Thank you very much. (Note: Dividend Turnover Ceremony, 7th Anniversary of the BSP, 03 July 2000, Malacañang Palace, Manila)

Title: The Philippines: Recent Economic Developments
Location: Hong Kong and Shanghai Corporation, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. It is indeed a great pleasure to be here and be able to join all of you in this investor forum. I always look forward to this kind of interaction on economic and financial developments in the Philippines. To the sponsor of this event--Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, thank you--for this opportunity to tell you that the Philippines' macroeconomy remains fundamentally sound. Let me argue this point. Macroeconomy remains fundamentally sound The recovery of the Philippine economy is now well underway. Last year we experienced broad-based output growth with real GDP expanding by 3.3 percent. The recovery process continues to gather momentum as real GDP showed a 3.4 percent growth during the first quarter of this year. Growth was led by industry and services, which grew by 4.8 percent and 3.8 percent, respectively. For the entire year 2000, we expect GNP growth to reach 4.5-5.5 percent while GDP growth is estimated to hit 4.0-5.0 percent. Things are also going well on the inflation front. Inflationary pressures have been quite subdued. Last year, inflation averaged 6.6 percent, well below the target 7-8 percent. This year, the average inflation rate in the first five months was only 3.3 percent, also well below the whole year target average of 5-6 percent. The stability in the general price level is partly on account of good agricultural performance--due to benign weather conditions--and also on the prudent monetary management by the BSP. The benign inflation numbers, together with prudent monetary management, have contributed to the trend decline in interest rates. The benchmark 91-day treasury bill rate has dropped from an average of 13.2 percent in January 1999 to 8.9 percent as of the latest auction on 19 June 2000. Similarly, the range in lending rates of banks dropped from 16-19.5 percent in January 1999 to 11.5-14.3 percent as of 12-16 June 2000. Recently, however, the BSP raised its policy interest rates on three occasions (on May 2, May 17 and May 19). The two most recent policy moves were meant to (1) address the narrowing differential between domestic and foreign interest rates, which have encouraged the movement of capital out of the country, and (2) contain the expected rise in inflationary pressures, consistent with a forward-looking monetary policy stance. At the foreign exchange market, except for the last two weeks of May this year, peso-dollar rate movements have been generally relatively mild, reflective of the country's sound macroeconomic fundamentals. This stability was evident in the significant drop in market price volatility in 1999 and in the first five months of 2000 relative to what it was in 1997 and 1998. Volatility, as measured by monthly standard deviation of daily exchange rates, declined from P3.93 in 1997 to P0.74 in 1998, P0.25 in 1999 and further to P0.22 during the first five months of this year. The significant depreciation of the peso-dollar rate in the last two weeks of May was attributed to both bearish regional sentiments due to the U.S. Fed tightening bias and, to some extent, the conflict in Mindanao and recent aberrations in peace and order in Metro Manila. The peso was under severe speculative pressure on May 24-25 with the peso reaching a high of P43.40/US$1 (May 25) during trading. But since the peso's weakness was not supported by a change in macroeconomic fundamentals, the peso quickly recovered. At the close of trading last 21 June, the peso-dollar rate was at the P42.693/US$1 level. Our external position continues to be solid. Thanks to our exports, which saw robust growth of 19 percent last year. The remarkable export performance helped the current account register a surplus of US$7.2 billion in 1999. Latest figures show an estimated account surplus of US$1.6 billion for the first quarter of this year. For the entire year, we are expecting current account surplus to reach US$6.3 billion. Gross international reserves are also expected to rise to a more comfortable level by the end of 2000 from the US$15 billion level in end-1999. Banking system sustains strength Strengthened by almost two decades of policy and structural reforms, our banking system has withstood well the Asian financial crisis that battered most of our regional counterparts. Growth in banks' resources has been supported by a build-up of capital, thereby keeping the average capital adequacy ratio of our banks well above the international norm. Banks remained adequately capitalized as indicated by their double-digit Capital-to-risk Asset Ratios (CAR). At 18.1 percent as of end-February 2000, the ratio was well above the statutory floor of 10 percent and the international norm of 8 percent. As of end-March, commercial banks' CAR reached 17.2 percent. In addition, the deterioration in banks' asset quality remains manageable. The non-performing loans ratio of commercial banks has remained below the 15 percent mark with the April 2000 ratio at 14.5 percent. This ratio is expected to remain below 15 percent as the positive growth prospects of the economy is expected to impact favorably on the repayment capability of corporates. The real estate exposure of commercial banks continued to be moderate at 11.6 percent as of end-December 1999. This is well below the Bangko Sentral's ceiling of 20 percent. Moreover, banks increased their provisions against loan losses in compliance with the loan loss provisioning requirements of the BSP. As of April 2000, loan loss provisions of commercial banks increased to 6.3 percent of total loans compared to 5.75 percent in end-1999. As a proportion of NPLs, loan loss provisions declined slightly to 43.7 percent in April 2000 from 46.6 percent in 1999 but still higher than the 38.3 percent cover ratio in 1998. Despite the overall stability of the system, isolated cases of banking difficulties have been observed, with the difficulties experienced by a medium-sized commercial bank being the most recent. This was followed by some nervousness in the banking system but the situation quickly normalized following coordinated efforts of both the BSP and the BAP. Cash withdrawals abated quickly and deposits returned, an indication of the restoration of the public's full trust and confidence in the system. Overall, the banking system remains safe and sound. Banks continue to serve as an efficient instrument of financial intermediation and effective transmission channel for monetary policy. Last 23 May 2000, the General Banking Law (GBL) of 2000 was signed by the President. This law is expected to foster greater investor and public confidence in the banking system. Broadly, the law enhances the supervisory capability and enforcement powers of the BSP, improves prudential standards and fosters greater competition in the industry. Moreover, the adoption of the GBL is expected to enable the industry to better withstand shocks and better attune it to the exacting demands of increasingly globalized and, therefore, more competitive financial markets. The law liberalizes foreign participation in domestic banks, provides stricter rules on DOSRI loans, adopts fit and proper principle in the appointment of senior bank officers and promotes greater transparency in bank practices. Charting future policy In the months ahead, the BSP will continue to do its share towards the achievement of balanced and sustainable economic development. In the area of monetary policy, the BSP will continue to focus primarily on price stability. The BSP will continue to adopt a prudent and flexible monetary stance in support of a stable price environment conducive to sustained economic growth. To enhance the BSP's pursuit of its mandate to promote price stability, the BSP will shift from monetary aggregate targeting to an inflation targeting framework for monetary policy in 2001. Inflation targeting is expected to, among other things: Þ Manage inflation expectations, because of its forward-looking features; Þ Strengthen the BSP's accountability and commitment to the price stability objective; and Þ Enhance transparency in the conduct of monetary policy. We believe that inflation targeting is a useful framework for conducting policy in an increasingly liberalized and globalized financial environment. We expect that this methodology can provide a clear link between monetary policy actions and the price stability objective. The BSP interest rate policy will ensure that the price of money will continue to be supportive of the economic recovery process. Thus, the move towards low but sustainable rates will continue to be pursued in line with the objectives of promoting a low-inflation environment and stable conditions in financial markets, including the foreign exchange market. The BSP will also maintain a flexible exchange rate system under which market forces are allowed to determine the exchange rate for the Philippine peso. The BSP may, however, intervene in the market only to temper temporary and abnormal aberrations in the exchange rate with a view to maintaining orderly market conditions. At the same time, the BSP will continue to monitor foreign exchange market developments, with a view to rationalizing foreign exchange trading and minimizing extreme volatility in the foreign exchange market. Recently, we released a circular encouraging banks to improve the reporting and record-keeping in their affiliate foreign exchange corporations. This will also help banks monitor and manage the foreign exchange exposures of their subsidiaries and affiliates. In the banking sector, the BSP will continue to pursue measures to strengthen the regulatory and supervisory framework over banks. With the signing of the GBL 2000, the BSP is now pushing for amendments of the New Central Bank Act or RA 7653. The proposed amendments seeks to enhance the supervisory and enforcement powers of the BSP; continue to improve prudential standards for the banking system; and promote further the independence of the BSP, particularly its ability to deal with threats to the overall stability of the financial system. Concluding remarks The robust performance of the economy in the recent past, amidst external and domestic shocks, confirms that indeed the macroeconomic fundamentals for the Philippines remain solid. Output continues to grow at a respectable pace. Inflation remains subdued while market interest rates remain at reasonable levels. The exchange rate has settled down. The banking system remains healthy and sound. These strong fundamentals will help ensure a strong economic performance this year and pave the way for rapid, as well as sustainable growth in the medium-term. Indeed, the Philippine economy continues to face other challenges. There is the threat of another round of interest rate hikes in the U.S. while recovery in Japan remains fragile. The process of restructuring in the banking system has yet to be completed. But our structural reform efforts are expected to address them. Reforms take time to take effect but we are going there. We are confident that all these policy measures will eventually lead to a sustained and faster growth for the economy. (Note: Investor Forum, HongKong and Shanghai Corporation, June 23, 2000, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Speaking Notes
Location: Greenhills Walking Corporation, Restaurante La Dolce Fontana, Greenhills, San Juan, MM
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Today I would like to offer my views on some of the recent developments in the foreign exchange market, in monetary policy and in the banking system as well. Recent developments on the exchange rate Let me start with a review of what has been happening in the currency market. The depreciation of the peso in the last two weeks of May was due to bearish investor sentiment toward the Asian region in general and, to some extent, local political factors such as the conflict in Mindanao. The negative sentiment on Asia was caused by the U.S. Federal Reserve's perceived bias towards raising interest rates in order to curb nascent inflationary pressures. As you know, an interest rate hike in a major industrial economy like the U.S. tends to draw away capital from emerging markets by narrowing the interest rate differential and encouraging a shift by investors to dollar-denominated assets. This, in turn, puts pressure on the exchange rate. Anticipating a narrowing differential between domestic and foreign interest rates, the BSP raised its key policy rates twice in May this year to keep up with rising U.S. interest rates. To date, the U.S. Fed has raised interest rates by 175 basis points since it adopted a tightening bias in June 1999. With its recent interest rate actions, the BSP effectively raised its rates by a net amount of 100 basis points during the same period. These measures notwithstanding, the peso briefly came under attack in late May, reaching an intraday low of P43.40 against the U.S. dollar at one point (25 May). The adjustment shook the local financial markets a bit, but I think it is important to note that the peso reached a low of around P46 to the dollar in January 1998. Thus, the recent weakening has been comparatively mild and should not be a source of undue concern. Our position at the BSP was that the peso's recent movements have been mainly sentiment-driven and not based on fundamentals. This means that the changes are likely to be reversed in due time, given the Philippines' sound macroeconomic fundamentals. True enough, the peso has since recovered from its recent lows. Yesterday (13 June), it closed at P42.425 against the U.S. dollar at the PDS. For the rest of the year, the trend of the peso will depend on several factors. One is the corporate demand for dollars, which is expected to rise as economic activity continues to strengthen and imports pick up their pace. Another, of course, is the prospect of further increases in U.S. interest rates, which will depend on whether the U.S. economy slows down enough to convince the fed that further rate hikes are no longer necessary. In fact, sentiment appears to be building at the U.S. Fed that they May need to hold off on raising interest rates for the time being due partly to the cooling down of consumer spending. Moreover, downward pressure on the peso is expected to be offset by increased dollar inflows from overseas workers and the continued robust growth of exports. Recent developments in the banking system Meanwhile, developments in the banking system have centered on efforts by authorities to speed up key reform efforts. These efforts include the full privatization of PNB with the sale of the Government's 80 percent stake in the bank. As you know, the recent bidding encountered certain problems. The Department of Finance was forced to declare a failed bidding since only one of two prospective bidders was able to qualify. The other bidder failed to find a bank partner for its consortium and therefore became ineligible. The bidding has also attracted some criticism from certain sectors, in part because of a perceived lack of transparency. I would like to emphasize that the bidding procedure was fully transparent, and was monitored not only by private groups but also by outside institutions such as the IMF and world bank. At the moment, authorities will have to evaluate the various alternatives before taking any further steps. The other major case of topical interest in the banking system is that of Urban Bank. As you know, Urban Bank's financial difficulties stemmed mainly from an NPL ratio and a real estate exposure that was higher than the industry norm, and the inability by the bank to meet large withdrawals due to its investments in non-liquid instruments. The bank is currently under the receivership of PDIC. A private auditing firm will evaluate the various proposals from private groups on how best to rehabilitate the bank. The deadline for proposals or bids was set for yesterday, June 13, and we will know more about the eventual fate of the bank in a few weeks' time. It is important to note that Urban Bank is small compared to the entire banking system and its problems should pose no systemic consequences on the banking industry. Its assets, for example, comprise less that 0.5 percent of that of the commercial banking system, while its deposits comprise less than 0.5 percent of the combined total deposit liabilities of all commercial banks.
