The other important thing to emphasize in the Urban Bank case is the commitment by authorities that, in the event that sufficient evidence of unsound business practices is found, penalties will be imposed on concerned parties. This will help ensure that such occurrences are not repeated in the future. Other developments An important development in the banking system involves the enactment of crucial measures into law. I am referring to the General Banking Law of 2000 (R. A. No. 8791), which was signed by the president on 23 May 2000. The GBL 2000 tightens and updates some of the rules under the 52-year old General Banking Act, which has been long overdue for an overhaul. The new law will help further promote financial stability by enhancing the competitiveness of the banking sector and strengthening the regulatory and supervisory framework. Among other things, it provides for greater competition through increased foreign participation in the banking system. Foreign banks are allowed to acquire up to 100 percent of the voting stock of an existing bank within 7 years of the law's effectivity. The new law also imposes stricter rules on bank exposure to directors, officers, stockholders and related interests (DOSRI). Meanwhile, expected to be passed later this year are the amendments to the Central Banking Act which will further strengthen our capacity for prompt corrective action and our ability to use our supervisory tools. At the same time, the Bangko Sentral remains flexible enough in implementing prudential measures to give banks some breather, particularly in their capital build-up program. There will be no increase in the minimum capital requirement for banks for the year 2000. We have also extended the compliance period for the 1999 capitalization requirements to end-2000. In place of absolute capital requirements, banks will be required to put up differing levels of capital as buffer, depending on the risk level of their respective portfolios. The use of risk-based capital standards allows us to conform with the standards set internationally by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). Such a realignment has been made possible by the passage of the new GBL. Concluding remarks So there you have it, a brief situationer on the state of the currency and the financial system. We have managed to get through some challenging situations by responding to them vigorously, and we are continuing the work we have already started on crucial reforms. Thank you. (Note: Breakfast Forum, Greenhills Walking Corporation, June 14, 2000, Restaurante La Dolce Fontana, Greenhills, San Juan, Metro Manila)

Title: EIU Presentation
Occasion: Economic Intelligence Unit, Philippine Corporate Update Program
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It is always a pleasure to speak at this briefing. I am honored by the presence of many distinguished guests and delighted to see many friends in the audience. I will try to focus my presentation this morning on the developments and policies in the areas of banking and monetary policy, particularly inflation, interest rates and exchange rates. A. Banking sector Recent developments Our banking system has withstood well the crisis that battered most of our regional counterparts. Our banks remain resilient and stable. Growth in banks' resources has been supported by a build-up of capital, thereby keeping the average capital adequacy ratio of our banks well above the international norm. In addition, banks' asset quality has remained manageable. · Total resources of the banking system continued to grow to P2.9 trillion as of end-February 2000 from about P2.1 trillion as of end-1996. · Banks' asset quality remains manageable. The non-performing loans ratio of commercial banks has remained below the 15 percent mark with the March 2000 ratio at 14.1 percent. This ratio is expected to remain below 15 percent as the positive growth prospects of the economy is expected to impact favorably on the repayment capability of corporates. · Moreover, banks increased their provisions against loan losses in compliance with the loan loss provisioning requirements of the BSP. As of March 2000, loan loss provisions of commercial banks increased to 6.2 percent of total loans compared to only 1.4 percent in 1998. As a proportion of NPLs, loan loss provisions likewise rose to 44.0 percent in March 2000 from 38.3 percent in 1998. · Banks remained adequately capitalized as indicated by their double-digit Capital-to- risk Asset Ratios (CAR). At 18.1 percent as of end-February 2000, the ratio was well above the statutory floor of 10 percent and the international norm of 8 percent. As of end-March, commercial banks' CAR reached 17.2 percent. · The real estate exposure of commercial banks continued to be moderate at 11.6 percent as of end-December 1999. This is well below the Bangko Sentral's ceiling of 20 percent. · Despite the overall stability of the system, isolated cases of banking difficulties have been observed, with the difficulties experienced by a medium-sized commercial bank being the most recent. This was followed by some nervousness in the banking system but the situation quickly normalized following coordinated efforts of both the monetary authorities and the BAP. Cash withdrawals abated quickly, an indication of the restoration of the public's full trust and confidence in the system. · Overall, the banking system remains safe and sound. Banks continue to serve as efficient instruments of financial intermediation and effective transmission channels for monetary policy. · Comparative financial indicators show that the Philippine banking system remains sound compared with those of its counterparts. Ø The non-performing loans (NPL) ratio of domestic banks is the lowest among crisis-affected countries. The NPL ratio of Philippine commercial banks stood at 14.1 percent as of March 2000 compared with those of Malaysia (10.9 percent), Korea (20.7 percent), Indonesia (39.8 percent), and Thailand (38.1 percent). Ø The successive increases in the minimum capitalization requirement of Philippine banks in the 1990s strengthened their relative capital position in the region. Based on an independent survey by the BSP, the country's minimum capital requirement--as of 1998--was the fourth largest in Asia, surpassing those of Malaysia, Korea, Hong Kong and Indonesia. Ø Since Philippine banks are well-capitalized, the restructuring process of the banking industry did not involve government capital infusion nor the establishment of asset management corporations for the acquisition of non-performing loans similar to those that took place in Malaysia, Korea, Thailand and Indonesia. Restructuring of banks in the Philippines has involved mainly a consolidation of the banking industry through mergers and acquisition. Policy directions While the banking sector remains stable, the passage of the General Banking Law (GBL) of 2000 is expected to strengthen it further. The GBL, which was signed on 23 May, is expected to foster greater investor and public confidence in the banking system as it enhances the supervisory capability and enforcement powers of the BSP, improves prudential standards, and fosters greater competition in the industry. Moreover, the adoption of the GBL is expected to enable the industry to better withstand shocks and better attune it to the exacting demands of increasingly globalized and, therefore, more competitive financial markets. Some of the more important features of the new law include the following: · It allows for more foreign participation in the system, thus inducing competition. Foreign banks are allowed to acquire up to 100 percent of the voting stock of an existing bank within seven years after the effectivity of the Act. At the same time, however, the Monetary Board has been tasked with ensuring that 70 percent of the resources of the banking system is held by banks that are majority-owned by Filipinos. · Meanwhile, the General Banking Law 2000 provision on the three-year moratorium on the establishment of commercial banks will help hasten the ongoing consolidation process in the banking system. · It provides for stricter rules governing bank exposure to directors, officers, stockholders and related interests (DOSRI). The definition of DOSRI is expanded to include investments of the bank in enterprises owned or controlled by said DOSRI. The monetary board is also given the power to define the term "related interests". · It grants authority to the monetary board to adopt internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital adequacy. · It requires that the integrity, experience, education, training and competence of an individual be part of the assessment of the Monetary Board in determining whether a director or officer is fit and proper to hold the position in a bank (i.e., the fit-and-proper rule test). In this regard, the Monetary Board is empowered to disqualify, remove or suspend a director or officer for acts or omissions which render him unfit for the position. · It strengthens current regulations with respect to transparency practices by explicitly providing these in the law. · It gives the BSP authority to regulate electronic banking to ensure adequate protection of banks' depositors and other clients. B. Monetary developments and policies Inflation Things are going well on the inflation front. Inflationary pressures have been quite subdued on account of good agricultural performance--due to benign weather conditions--and prudent monetary management by the BSP. Last year, inflation averaged 6.6 percent, well below the target 7-8 percent. This year, the average inflation rate during the first four months was only 3.2 percent. This is also well below the target range of 5-6 percent, and was the lowest recorded rate in 13 years. To enhance the BSP's pursuit of its mandate to promote price stability, the BSP will shift from monetary aggregate targeting to an inflation targeting framework for monetary policy in 2001. Inflation targeting is expected to, among other things: Þ Anchor inflation expectations, because of its forward-looking nature; Þ Enhance the BSP's accountability and commitment to the price stability objective; and Þ Enhance transparency in the conduct of monetary policy. We believe that inflation targeting is a useful framework for conducting policy in an increasingly liberalized and globalized financial environment as it provides a clear link between monetary policy actions and the price stability objective. The BSP has been conducting public consultations on this planned policy shift, including in the regions outside metro manila. Another one is scheduled on June 14 in manila for the general public, including banks, other financial institutions, industrial associations and the labor sector. Let us know if you are interested in attending this briefing so that we can extend to you an invitation. Interest Rates Benign inflation numbers, together with prudent monetary management, has contributed to the trend decline in interest rates. The benchmark 91-day treasury bill rate has dropped from an average of 13.2 percent in January 1999 to 8.968 percent as of the latest auction on 29 May 2000. Similarly, the range in lending rates dropped from 16-19.5 percent in January 1999 to 11.5-14.3 percent as of 29 May 2000. The combined effects of declining inflation, broadly stable exchange rate and monetary aggregates that were well generally below programmed targets have given the Bangko Sentral greater flexibility in the conduct of monetary policy. · Greater flexibility enabled the Bangko Sentral to reduce gradually its borrowing rates (RRPs) by 462.5 basis points and its reserve requirements by a total of five percentage points in 1999, in line with the economic objective of promoting investments through market-driven reduction in interest rates. · Recently, however, the BSP raised its policy interest rates on two occasions (on May 17 and May 19). The recent policy moves were meant to (1) address the narrowing differential between domestic and foreign interest rates, which have encouraged the movement of capital out of the country, and (2) contain the rise in inflationary pressures and a build-up in inflationary expectations, consistent with a forward-looking monetary policy stance. · Of late, the BSP has adopted a neutral monetary policy stance. The BSP is convinced that the recent policy rate hikes has sufficiently addressed the narrowing differential between domestic and foreign interest rates and concerns of a potential increase in inflation. Moreover, the BSP believes recent movements in the exchange rate are largely sentiment-driven and are not validated by real factors as the country's macro fundamentals have remained strong. The BSP's interest rate policy adheres to its commitment to ensure that the cost of credit or the price of money will remain low in support of economic recovery. Thus, the move towards low but sustainable rates will continue to be pursued in line with the objectives of promoting a low-inflation environment and stable conditions in financial markets, including the foreign exchange market. Exchange Rates Except for the last two weeks of May this year, foreign exchange rate movements have been relatively mild, reflective of the country's sound macroeconomic fundamentals. · This stability was evident in the significant drop in market price volatility in 1999 and in the first four months of 2000 relative to what it was in 1997 and 1998. · The significant depreciation of the peso-dollar rate in the last two weeks of May was attributed to both bearish regional sentiments due to the U.S. Fed tightening bias and, to some extent, the conflict in Mindanao and recent bomb explosions and threats in metro manila. · The peso was under severe speculative pressure on May 24-25 with the peso reaching a high of P43.40/US$1 (May 25) during trading. But since the peso's weakness is not supported by a change in macroeconomic fundamentals, the peso has recovered. Yesterday (31 May), the peso-dollar rate closed at P42.62:us$1 compared to P42.75:US$1 on Tuesday. · The expected trend of the peso in 2000 will be influenced by various factors, including corporate demand for dollars as the economy continues its recovery and concerns over further adjustments in us interest rates. However, higher dollar inflows from OFWs and direct foreign investments--due in part to the enactment into law of key legislative measures such as the Retail Trade Liberalization Law and the General Banking Act 2000--is expected to offset these factors. The BSP will maintain a floating exchange rate system under which market forces dictate the exchange rate for the Philippine peso. The BSP may, however, intervene in the market only to temper temporary and abnormal aberrations in the exchange rate with a view to maintaining orderly market conditions. At the same time, the BSP will continue to monitor closely foreign exchange market developments. In this regard, it will also review existing measures--including those relating to the reporting and record-keeping of foreign exchange transactions--to rationalize foreign exchange trading and minimize extreme volatility in the foreign exchange market. Thank you and good day. (Note: Economic Intelligence Unit, Philippine Corporate Update Program, June 1, 2000, Intercontinental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Open Conference on Corporate Governance
Location: Institute of Corporate Directors, Peninsula Hotel, Makati
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Distinguished officers, fellow professionals, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning. It is a great pleasure for me to welcome you to this Open Conference on Corporate Governance Reforms in the Philippines. We are fortunate indeed to have a brilliant line-up of resource speakers and discussants today. With your presence lending it added prestige, I am confident that this whole day brainstorming will be a success. Addressing the need for good corporate governance in a climate full of sophisticated and rapidly changing technologies has never been greater. But its critical elements have remained unchanged. Governance is concerned with the systems of law, regulation and practices, which promote enterprise and ensure accountability. Simply stated, it refers to "the way people in power use that power" efficiently and effectively. It is not limited to a specific sector or industry, it exists wherever power is exercised. There is no shortage of theoretical constructs. A great deal has already been said and written about proper governance. In fact various practical standards and guidelines have been put forward. The question now is how can we bring about a higher level of actual adherence to proper corporate governance? For me, looking from a banking industry perspective, the basic principles of good governance are accountability, fairness and transparency. However, I believe these are applicable more universally. Accountability is the ability to require company officials to answer for their actions and decisions. Within the context of good governance, accountability means the presence of a clear-cut segregation of responsibilities and decision-making authorities. It presupposes the existence of a hierarchy of approvals from the rank and file to the key personnel up to the board of directors. It is the responsibility of the Board to ensure that there are written limits on the discretionary powers of each officer, committee, sub-committee and such other groups for the purpose of lending, investing or committing the bank to any financial undertaking and or assumption of risk. Additionally, it is mandatory for the board of directors to establish a system of checks and balances, which applies in the first instance to the board itself. The second element of good governance is fairness. A fair business transaction is one which is conducted in the regular course of business and upon terms not less favorable to the bank than those offered to others. The member of the board of directors should act honestly and in good faith, with loyalty and in the best interest of the bank, its stockholders and other stakeholders. While a director should always strive to promote the interest of the stockholders, he should also give due regard to the rights and interests of other stakeholders such as its depositors, investors, borrowers and other clients. The principle of fairness builds up trust, confidence and rapport. The third element concerns transparency. This entails the accessibility of relevant information and data for its internal and external use. Reliable and timely information and reports are a must for proper governance. The proliferation of modern technology makes information gathering and information dissemination an easier task. This is aside from the fact that it enables management to have an immediate access to a variety of information and feedbacks. However, dissemination of numerous but meaningless information does not improve transparency. What matter is that reports must be relevant and can easily be understood. I would say that banks nowadays have deepened their commitment to matters of governance. This is being given further impetus by market and regulatory incentives to merge and consolidate. More directly, the Bangko Sentral, in line with the newly enacted General Banking Law of 2000, is strengthening the fit and proper criteria for the qualification and disqualification of proposed and incumbent officers and members of the Board of Directors of banks. I am firmly convinced that faithful adherence to principles of good governance will give our banks the necessary resiliency and flexibility to respond quickly to any given crisis as well as opportunity. In retrospect, one of the key lessons we have learned in the recent Asian crisis is the need to improve corporate governance if we are to avoid future crises in an increasingly globalized economy. Unless our institutions are governed better, we shall just be marking time to the next disaster. Bearing this in mind, I now wish all of you a fruitful and mutually rewarding conference. Thank you very much and a pleasant day to all! (Note: Opening Remarks, Open Conference on Corporate Governance and Related Reforms, 29 May 2000, Institute of Corporate Directors, Peninsula Hotel, Makati)

Title: A REGULATOR'S PERSPECTIVE ON BANK CONSOLIDATION
Location: JP Morgan, Grand Hyatt, Hong Kong
Occasion: Mergers and Acquisitions Conference Among Asian Financial Institutions
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It is a great pleasure to be invited to this conference which brings together the pillars of banking in Asia. You have a very interesting conference theme, and as my contribution, I have been requested to provide the view from the regulator's side. While I have worn the hat of Central Bank governor for only ten months now, this subject has been on my mind even when I was in the private sector. Back then, I had already considered mergers and consolidations as the wave of the future. This trend was clearly illustrated by the Citigroup model, which saw the merger of an investment house, a securities company and an insurance company. In this presentation, I hope to revisit this movement in the light of developments in the Philippine banking system. Recent Developments Let me start by sharing with you some pertinent developments. It is common knowledge that the resilience of the Philippine banking system is one of the key factors that explain the relative success of the Philippine economy in weathering the crisis. Reforms implemented before, during and after the crisis helped fortify the system. As a result, since 1990 the average capital adequacy ratio of our commercial banks has always been above, and their NPL ratio has always been below, 15 percent. In these respects, our banking system has performed well vis-a-vis international standards. In 1999, total resources of the banking system rose by 7.9 percent to P3.0 trillion, and the number of head offices and branches continued to increase to 7,689 units. The capital adequacy ratio of commercial banks improved slightly from 17.5 percent in 1998 to 17.8 percent in 1999, and their NPL ratio stayed within the 13-14 percent range. Real estate exposure declined from 13.1 percent of outstanding portfolio in 1998 to 11.6 percent at end 1999. These ratios indicated a wider resource base, stronger capitalization and better asset quality. Of greater interest, we have seen the mergers of several of the major players in the banking system. We expect to see more this year, based on the applications now pending with us. Specifically, six cases have been finalized since an incentive package was offered in 1998. These cases involved nine commercial banks, a thrift bank and two rural banks. We are still reviewing 15 applications, involving six commercial banks, five thrift banks and 20 rural banks. So far, these include only cases in which the Bangko Sentral had been formally notified. I understand that there are other ongoing negotiations that have yet to reach us. Review of the BSP Policies on Mergers and Acquisitions In explaining these developments, let me trace the evolution of the Bangko Sentral's policies on mergers and acquisitions. Our consolidation rules are rooted in our liberal banking policy that promotes an environment conducive to the development of big, globally competitive banks. This is consistent with the transition to convergence model which assumes that domestic financial entities will be able to compete in the increasingly liberalized and globalized financial environment given an appropriate enabling regulatory framework. Our drive towards open financial markets actually accelerated with the passage by congress in 1994 of the law liberalizing the entry and scope of operations of foreign banks in the Philippines. While the intention of this law is to fast track the introduction of better financial products and services, it also requires that local banks strengthen their capital base and increase their resources to better meet the headwinds of foreign competition. This explains the subsequent rounds of increases in capital requirements in our banking industry during the last five years. In fact, further increases are expected by the end of this year. In the process, banks experiencing difficulties in meeting capital build-up requirements have the option to merge or consolidate with other institutions. In several cases, however, mergers occurred between strong banks that merely wanted to further prepare themselves for global competition. To promote further the consolidation process, we issued circular no. 172 in 1998, which provided major incentives to banks that have decided to merge. These incentives include the extension of the booking of the required 2 percent general provision for probable loan losses; temporary relief from full compliance with the prescribed net worth to risk assets ratio; and provision of one-year grace period within which to comply with the ceiling on real estate exposure. Early this year, we also allowed the amortization of goodwill up to a maximum of 40 years, if warranted. But despite the incentives available, not all banks were ready to merge or consolidate. Some banks saw another option: downgrading or conversion to a lower category. For these banks, this option required minimal or no additional capital, at the same time that they maintained their ownership and market identity. While this option is legal, our view is that it poses certain risks in the operations of the downgraded banks that may continue to engage in activities they are no longer authorized to perform. To plug the loopholes arising from this option, we issued circular no. 229 last March, which required the applicant bank to: · Comply with the end-2000 minimum capital requirement and other regulations applicable to the lower bank category in which it is converting; and · Phase out within six months all inherent powers and activities not normally associated with the lower bank category into which it is converting, with major monetary and non- monetary penalties for non-compliance. Concentration Issue In the process of consolidation, bank concentration is expected to increase. But we do not expect this to pose a threat to overall competition levels. Based on our initial studies, the expected mergers would not prevent effective competition. Moreover, we see the alternative option of banks to downgrade as a balancing factor in the opposite direction. Increasing competition from non-bank financial intermediaries, the capital market and even alternative payment systems such as electronic shopping malls via the internet also help ensure that market competition will remain sufficient. Finally, to the extent that the market remains open and contestable, especially by foreign players, then consumer interest should continue to be well-protected. Incidentally, foreign ownership of local banks up to 100 percent for a limited period is now virtually assured with the passage in the Bicameral Committee in Congress of amendments to the General Banking Act. We expect the president of the republic to sign this bill into law very soon. Consolidation Prospects We have seen, so far, that the thrust of the mergers has been on strengthening the banking system's resource and capital base and expanding operational networks. This is the initial phase of the merger process. With the increasing competition banks are now getting from alternative payment systems, we anticipate the consolidation process to go beyond the traditional, basic banking areas. Already we are hearing about mobile banking. The fact that our unibanks are authorized to go into allied and non-allied undertakings ensures that the Citigroup model is possible here. As a regulator of banks, we anticipate attendant risks in the process. But we are confident that our consolidated method of bank supervision will be able to adequately cover any additional risks arising from this transition to convergence. Moreover, for commercial banks, we have started to use our first-generation early warning system that will provide advance indicators on banks' solvency outlook. Other complementary measures include the shift of our payment and settlement system to real-time gross basis within this year, and the introduction of risk rating to allow for early identification of problems and improvements in credit risk management. In the medium term, as our banks gain the necessary expertise and resources to intermediate larger volumes of funds for clients whose needs have grown in size and complexity, we hope to see the emergence of Filipino banks with a regional orientation. Beyond that, perhaps we can eventually be witnesses to the evolution of some Filipino financial institutions with transnational reach. Conclusion In summary, we see in mergers and acquisitions a potent tool for realizing the expanding possibilities for new and better financial products and services. On the other hand, we also see a corresponding increase in our responsibilities in ensuring the stability and robustness of the financial system. Our role as bank regulator is to see to it that the financial system is able to manage the risks attendant to the growth requirements of a rapidly changing economy. Based on this standard, we believe that the Philippine model, particularly in so far as bank consolidation is concerned, has gone some distance in achieving the right balance in the right direction. Finally, we all agree with the old adage that "united we stand; divided we fall". In the increasingly global banking environment, perhaps we can paraphrase it as "consolidated we move forward; downgraded we fall behind". Thank you and good day. (Note: Mergers and Acquisitions Conference Among Asian Financial Institutions, JP Morgan, April 28, 2000, Grand Hyatt, Hong Kong)

Title: The Bangko Sentral and the Economy's Move Toward Broad-Based Growth
Occasion: Signing Ceremony for the US$500 Million BSP Syndicated Term Loan Facility
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I am very pleased to see the successful completion of this undertaking today. For the record, the Bangko Sentral has tapped the international debt market only six times since its establishment in July 1993. Under my term, this is the third facility to be arranged. The continued support of our lending investors to our latest fund raising exercise is much appreciated. This is indicated by the more than ten percent over-subscription in commitments that have been received from 24 banks, 15 of which are based abroad. This underscores investor confidence in the continued soundness and resiliency of the Philippine economy. That this is the case has been validated by the consistent and steady credit ratings that we received from major rating agencies during and after the Asian financial crisis. Indeed, I consider this positive investor response as an encouragement to the Bangko Sentral to sustain its efforts towards establishing the most appropriate monetary environment for a broad-based growth of the economy. And I am pleased to say that our efforts are now reaping very good results. In 1999, the economy forged ahead to sustained growth. Output expanded steadily. Inflation trended down continuously. Interest rates were generally low and reasonable. There was broad stability in the foreign exchange market and our external payment position remained strong. The financial system continued to grow and domestic credit had started to pick up. Looking forward, we are optimistic that over the next two quarters, we should see the economy sustaining more vigorous growth. In particular, industry has started to recover. Manufacturing is expected to propel the economy forward this year, to complement the steady growth in agriculture and services. I must therefore say that this is the most opportune time for market players to ride out the rising growth curve. Ladies and gentlemen, I assure you that the proceeds of this facility will be put to good use to enable the Bangko Sentral to keep the monetary and banking environment conducive to doing business in the country and ensure sustained growth. In particular, our efforts this year will be centered on moving towards a major policy shift to inflation targeting as the framework for conducting a more focused and transparent monetary policy. In closing, I would like to extend my thanks to ABN-AMRO, Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, WestDeusche Landesbank, KBC Bank, and to all those who collaborated with us in completing this undertaking. Thank you and good day. (Note: Signing Ceremony For US$500 Million BSP Syndicated Term Loan Facility, April 6, 2000, Peninsula Hotel, Makati)

Title: THE PHILIPPINE ECONOMY: GEARING UP FOR SUSTAINED AND BROAD-BASED GROWTH
Occasion: Luncheon Meeting, Rotary Club of Manila
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: INTRODUCTION Mr. Fortunato Gupit, Jr., President of the Rotary Club of Manila, other officers and members of the Rotary Club of Manila, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. We are in interesting times. The nation faces the challenges of fiscal consolidation and structural reform that, while subjecting it to powerful headwinds, are expected to buttress its economic foundations in the years ahead. Indeed I welcome opportunities like this to interact with those sectors of the economy with a significant stake in what is happening around us. THE ECONOMY IN BRIEF From all indications, our economy is steadily gearing up toward broad-based growth. Last year, real GNP grew by 3.6 percent, much higher than the 0.1 percent growth registered in 1998. Industry has started to recover. Manufacturing, in particular, has shown three consecutive quarters of accelerating growth and is expected to propel the economy forward as demand picks up. This should complement the expected steady expansion in services and agriculture, which were the main drivers of growth last year. Domestic liquidity grew by 19.3 percent at end-1999 as the economy started to gain momentum, and monetary growth was sustained at 13.6 percent in January this year. Monetary developments continue to reflect a balance between accommodating economic recovery and ensuring that inflation is kept under control. Economic growth has been fostered in a low-inflation environment. Inflationary pressures continue to be tame, with the increase in the general price level averaging only 2.8 percent for the first two months of this year. We think that we would be able to comfortably meet this year's inflation target of 6-7 percent against last year's average of 6.6 percent. Price stability, in turn, paved the way for lower interest rates. The benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate fell from an average of 10.2 percent in 1999 to 8.9 percent at the last auction (27 March) amid the healthy cash position of the national government. Meanwhile, the Bangko Sentral has kept its policy interest rates steady given subdued inflationary pressures and broad stability in the foreign exchange market. The local currency was generally stable in 1999, with the peso-dollar rate averaging P39.09. Of late, the peso has weakened to around P40.90 to a dollar, reflecting in part the trends in other regional currencies. At the same time, problems in the local equities market have had an unfavorable impact on the value of the peso. With the eventual resolution of these issues, we expect the exchange rate to stabilize in the near future. Last year, the fiscal position was viewed by the markets with some concern, as the national government registered a budget deficit of about P112 billion, higher than the target of P85.3 billion, and equivalent to 3.6 percent of GNP. Of course, this was modest compared with other countries in the Asian region where budgetary shortfalls ranged from 5 percent to 8 percent of their national output. This year, the government has committed to a much lower deficit of P62.5 billion, or about half of last year's shortfall, with both hard cuts and soft cuts in the 2000 budget to ensure compliance with such a commitment. The external payments position continues to be strong. In 1999, the balance of payments yielded a surplus of US$3.8 billion, almost twice the year-ago level. This was due mainly to the robust performance of the current account and the considerable inflow of medium- and long-term loans. Exports grew by a hefty 18.8 percent, putting the Philippines as top exporter in the whole of the Asian region. At the same time, imports have started to pick up, growing by 4.1 percent in 1999. The surge in raw materials and intermediate goods imports indicates the resurgence of economic activity and establishes the momentum for future growth. The robust external payments position enabled the BSP to beef up its foreign exchange reserves, which stood at US$14.5 billion as of end-February this year. This level of reserves can support around 4.2 months' worth of imports of goods and services and can cover our short-term external liabilities, twice over. Our external debt continues to be manageable at US$51.2 billion as of end-September 1999. Its maturity profile has improved, with medium- and long-term debt accounting for the bulk of total debt. Due to higher exports, debt servicing has become less onerous compared to what it was at the start of the decade. The debt service ratio was 27.2 percent in 1990; in 1999, it was 13.1 percent. THE IMPORTANCE OF A SOUND FINANCIAL SYSTEM These signs of consolidation provide a litmus test of the soundness and robustness of the macroeconomic policies that are in place. Echoing this view, the Asian Development Bank, in its latest Asia recovery report, has noted that the country's fundamentals remain intact. Overall, this mix of prudent macroeconomic policies should stand the economy in good stead and enable economic authorities to manage well the transition to stronger and broader-based growth. At the end of the day, however, the strength of the financial system is one of the pillars upon which the effectiveness of macroeconomic policy rests. This is because weak financial institutions will not be able to channel efficiently the country's scarce resources to productive activities. A weak banking system will also hinder the transmission of monetary policies. Hence, long-term growth and stability will be conditioned partly by the reforms undertaken in the financial system. For this reason, the Philippine financial sector has gone through several episodes of policy reform from the 1980s that included allowing greater role for market forces, higher bank capitalization and better bank supervision. When the recent crisis struck, a further program of reform was adopted aimed at improving disclosure, strengthening compliance and upgrading the quality of bank management. As a result, the Philippine financial system has fared relatively well both during and after the crisis. The system's strength is evident in the sustained rise in its total resources, compliance with prudential norms, more than adequate capital position, and relatively good asset quality. The non-performing loan (NPL) ratio of Philippine commercial banks reached 13.4 percent as of January 2000, one of the lowest in the region. As the operating environment reacts more warmly to domestic economic growth prospects, we should see perkier lending ahead and an improvement in asset quality. THE REFORM AGENDA CONTINUES They say that peacetime is the right time to get the army in shape. Thus, while the banking system remains sound and healthy, we continue to pursue an activist stance in monetary and banking policy. One major policy shift is our adoption of inflation targeting as the framework for conducting monetary policy. Among other things, this involves setting an explicit inflation target, announcing it and publishing and submitting regular reports on the performance of monetary policy. We believe that such a framework will enable monetary authorities to focus more singularly on the price stability objective. It will also increase transparency in the conduct of monetary policy as well as the Bangko Sentral's accountability to the inflation objective. At the same time, it could enhance the credibility of policymakers in containing inflationary pressures. While we are still working on some operational details, we see no hindrance to the adoption of inflation targeting as the monetary policy framework, since we already have the basic preconditions in place, such as central bank independence and a strong commitment to price stability. In fact, we have started to conduct public consultations on this issue. Moreover, as you probably know already, there are two major reform measures in the pipeline, which aim to strengthen the financial sector. These involve the amendments of the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act. Among other things, the proposed amendments seek to enhance competition in the banking sector, further strengthen banking supervision, and promote further the independence of the Bangko Sentral. CONCLUSION In the same breath, however, I have to admit that there are some overhangs that threaten to take the wind from the economy's sails. In pointing this out, my intention is to highlight those areas where we need to strengthen policies and take pre-emptive measures to minimize vulnerabilities. Without policy changes, we will essentially be attacking just the symptoms. However, with carefully formulated strategies to address the economy's weaknesses, we would go down to the very root of the problem and address it accordingly. A major overhang involves the delayed passage of key structural reforms such as the Omnibus Power Sector Reform Bill, Securities Act, banking reforms, and E-commerce bill. These particular reforms are meant to improve governance, a key issue, since investors need to know that there is predictability in policies and their implementation. The passage of these measures into law will go a long way in bolstering investor confidence. Thus, it is reassuring that these are all in the advanced stage of legislation. Our congress leaders have committed to pass these important pieces of legislation before the end of June this year. We look forward to this as it would fortify our commitment to put in place an enabling environment that nurtures productive activity. Countries that face the headwinds of the forces of economic growth need to undertake broad policy responses and to institute economic reforms at the structural level. In globally integrated economies, like the Philippines, economic management is increasingly getting more complex. Margins of error have been significantly reduced, and the importance of maintaining sound, and consistent economic policies cannot be sufficiently emphasized. Thus, let me conclude with the writer Charles F. Kettering's wonderful remarks: "Think a dynamic future--work in a dynamic present. We should all be concerned about the future because we will have to spend the rest of our lives there." We are all stakeholders of the future. Thank you and good afternoon. (Note: Luncheon Meeting, Rotary Club of Manila, March 30, 2000,Manila Hotel)

Title: Financial Sector Reform: Building a Banking System for a Global Economy
Occasion: 33rd International General meeting, Pacific Basin Economic Council
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It is a great honor to be invited to speak before this 33rd Annual General Meeting of the Pacific Basin Economic Council. It also gives me great pleasure to be here in beautiful Hawaii, the center of the Asia pacific, and the heart of the PBEC family. For this second plenary session, our topic is, "Financial Sector Reform: Building a Banking System for a Global Economy". Indeed, given the focus of this meeting, which is to find ways to adjust to the changing global landscape, it is natural that the banking system should emerge as a key sector for consideration. For the banking system is the backbone of any economy. It is the nerve center where financial transactions flow. But like any other system, it is a two-edged sword. At the same time that it facilitates greater efficiency, it also has the potential for excesses. What we need to look at in this session are the strategies and reforms needed to build a banking system that can respond more effectively to the fast-changing global environment. Major Areas for Reform Based on our experience during the Asian financial crisis, I have identified two major areas for reforms, which I think are very familiar now to the participants in this conference. These are the system's regulatory framework and its corporate culture. Let me start with an overview of these two areas. A key element in the reform process is to ensure that the regulatory environment is at par with the increased risks that go with the globalized landscape. Thus, prudential regulations have to be strengthened in terms of stringency, coverage and enforcement. A more harmonized and comprehensive system of supervision across financial institutions is a necessity for greater scope and effectiveness. To ensure enforcement, the capability and independence of supervisory authorities must also be strengthened. But improving the regulatory framework cannot be undertaken in isolation from the rest of the elements of the reform process. Weaknesses in banks' balance sheets and operating procedures must be identified and remedied to enable them to respond better to and comply adequately with the requirements of a stricter regulatory regime. Since banks are corporate entities, corporate restructuring must also take place. This means improving the underlying legal and institutional frameworks for financial and operational restructuring. The bottomline for all these reforms is to prevent future crises by upgrading the risk management capability of banks and the supervisory authorities. The Philippine Experience Using these imperatives for financial sector reforms, let me now outline the Philippine experience towards building a globally competitive banking system. The Philippine banking system had gone through several episodes of policy reforms since the 1980s. These reforms included allowing a greater role for market forces such as the deregulation of interest rates, increases in bank capitalization and improvements in bank supervision. Hence, even before the crisis, there was already a high degree of market orientation in the system and the regulatory framework was continuously being improved. Consequently, the Philippine banking system was not severely affected by the crisis. Total resources continued to rise and asset quality remained relatively sound. The NPL ratio of commercial banks remained below 20 percent, well below those observed in other Asian neighbors, which ranged from 20 to 75 percent. Banks' exposure to the property sector was also limited at a little over 10 percent, compared to 15-35 percent in other neighboring countries. As a result, we saw only a moderate correction in asset prices and a limited supply glut in selected segments of the property market. Our commercial banks remained highly capitalized as indicated by their capital adequacy ratio of 17.8 percent as of November 1999. This developed from the Bangko Sentral's policy of encouraging big, globally competitive banks. To date, four major and four minor bank mergers have taken place, involving ten commercial banks, four thrift banks and two rural banks. We expect a few more mergers this year. It is important to note that while the recent mergers increased bank concentration, initial studies conducted by the Bangko Sentral indicated that these mergers were not enough to pose a threat to overall competition levels. In terms of corporate reforms, the Philippines has undertaken significant steps in aligning its regulatory, risk management and disclosure practices to international norms. Disclosure statements for audited financial statements of banks are generally consistent with international accounting standards. Incidentally, the Philippines is one of the first signatories to the Special Data Dissemination Standards of the International Monetary Fund. With respect to banking governance, the Bangko Sentral has established guidelines to govern the responsibilities and duties of the Boards of Directors of banks to ensure prudent and efficient bank administration. Overseeing all these reforms is the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, which in 1993, was granted increased fiscal and administrative autonomy under the new central bank charter. Increased autonomy enabled it to formulate more flexible policies that resulted in greater stability in the macro-economic environment, which in turn promoted greater market confidence in the banking system. Future Policy Thrusts Looking forward, further reforms in the Philippine banking system, and in any banking system for that matter, will have to deal with the challenges of increasing sophistication and globalization in the financial environment. Toward this end, major banking reforms have been submitted to the Philippine congress. These proposed legislations seek to further align our prudential standards with international norms, enhance competition in the banking sector and strengthen further the supervisory and regulatory capability of the Bangko Sentral. The amendments are also expected to enable the system to adapt to the latest innovations in banking technology, including electronic banking. With the spread of electronic commerce, banks will have to contend with the growing competition posed by alternative payment systems such as electronic shopping malls and digicash. In the process, the supervisory scope of the Bangko Sentral will have to be widened. Reforms related to corporate restructuring are also in the pipeline. Pending in Congress are proposed amendments to the Philippine Securities Act which seek to update the operating rules for corporate debt resolution. In the meantime that these proposed reforms are still pending in congress, other complementary measures are also being pursued. The settlement and payment system is being upgraded to move into a real-time basis. Risk rating is being introduced to allow for early identification of problems and improve credit risk management. We have started to use the first-generation early warning system of commercial banks that will provide advance indicators on banks' solvency outlook. To complement the system on a macro basis, we are also in the process of finalizing a set of leading indicators that will enable us to detect potential, system-wide currency and financial crises. Concluding Notes In closing, I leave you some notes on reforming the financial system, based on the Philippine experience. Structural reforms, and for that matter banking reforms, take time to design and implement. While the initial impact is mostly painful, the benefits are less apparent since they are spread over a longer period of time. Hence, significant political courage is often needed to see the reform process through its conclusion. For one, the cooperation of the legislature is crucial in putting in place reforms that are expected to have a major impact on the banking system and the economy. In terms of enforcement, a key factor is the degree of independence of the supervisory authorities from other government agencies and from other vested interests. This inspires greater confidence from the private sector, which is the most crucial factor that determines the success or failure of the reform process. Thank you and good day. (Note: 33rd International General Meeting, Pacific Basic Economic Council, 20 March 2000, Honolulu, Hawaii)

Title: THE PHILIPPINES: CONSOLIDATING ECONOMIC GROWTH
Occasion: Investors' Briefing, ABN-AMRO
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I. INTRODUCTION Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Let me welcome you to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. I am sure our potential investors will agree that year 1999 saw encouraging signs that the world economy was on the mend. In Asia, most indicators were looking up. Within Asia, the Philippine economy made good progress in most economic fronts. II. RECENT DEVELOPMENTS Our thrust this year, therefore, is to consolidate the economic gains so far achieved. Now let me walk you through recent developments in key areas of the economy. An Early Rebound The economy started its recovery during the first quarter of 1999 and continued into the fourth quarter, with GDP growing by an average of 3.2 percent. This was driven mainly by a strong rebound in agriculture and the sustained growth in services. Low Inflation Rate Inflation rate continued to decline as a result of stable food supply and prudent monetary management. Inflation has posted a record low of 2.6 percent in January and 3.0 percent in February 2000. Favorable External Payments Position For the period January to November 1999, overall balance of payments and current account position posted surpluses of $3.54 billion and $6.45 billion, respectively, boosted by sustained growth in exports and higher capital flows from loans and portfolio investments. A Robust Export Sector One of the key factors behind our continued economic strength is our exports. Even during the crisis, when exports were declining in most of the region, Philippine exports, which consisted largely of electronics, machinery and transport equipment, managed to post double-digit growth. In 1999, our exports grew by 18.8 percent. Growing Foreign Reserves As a result of the country's favorable external position, our gross international reserves has broken record levels, reaching $15 billion at end-December 1999 equivalent to about 4.3 months of imports of goods and services. More recent data indicate that international reserves remain sizeable at $14.8 billion as of end-January 2000. Continued Stability of the Peso In the case of the peso, while the Bangko Sentral sustained the market orientation of the exchange rate, it also implemented policies to rationalize the foreign exchange market and limit opportunities for speculative play. As a result, exchange rate movements in 1999 were less volatile compared to the second half of 1997 and in 1998. A Manageable Level of External Debt Turning now to our foreign obligations, our external debt remains relatively manageable at US$51.2 billion as of September 1999 or 69.1 percent of annual GDP. It is also important to note that the proceeds of our foreign borrowings have been channeled to productive sectors, including infrastructure, capital goods, exports, and education. Our private external debt is among the lowest in the region. Our foreign debt burden is also low relative to most other emerging economies. A Relatively Strong Banking Sector In the banking sector, our well-regulated banking system has helped significantly in insulating the Philippines from problems being experienced in other Asian countries. As a result of banking sector reforms implemented before and during the crisis, our banks have remained relatively strong as evidenced by their low NPL ratio and strong capital adequacy ratio. As of December 1999, the banking system's NPL ratio was 12.8 percent. This is one of the lowest in the region. Moreover, for commercial banks, the NPL ratio was lower at 12.3 percent as of December 1999. Meanwhile, capital adequacy ratio of banks at 18.0 percent as of end-September 1999 is above the 10 percent minimum requirement and the 8 percent BIS standard. Limited Exposure of Banks to Property Sector In addition, our banks' real estate exposure at 12.2 percent of total loan portfolio as of September 1999 is way below the 20 percent ceiling imposed by the BSP. It also compares favorably with most other Asian banking systems. As a result, we saw only a moderate correction in asset prices and a limited supply glut in selected segments of the property market. Overall, save for a few thrift banks and a number of small rural banks that had to be closed, the banking system remains sound and continues to be an efficient channel of monetary policy. This was validated further by the system's smooth crossover into the new millennium last January. Effective Counter-Cyclical Policies The continued stability of the peso and the fall in inflation starting in February 1999, have afforded the BSP enough flexibility in monetary management. This flexibility enabled the BSP to reduce its policy interest rates several times by more than 400 basis points and its reserve requirements by five percentage points in 1999. These, in turn, provided strong support for the reduction in market interest rates, which have fallen to pre-crisis levels since May 1999. Flexible Fiscal Response On the fiscal side, the government continued to pump-prime the economy to boost domestic demand and enhance an early recovery. Endorsement From the IMF We also need to tell you that in march 1998, a two-year stand-by arrangement was agreed with the IMF, with $1.4 billion in available funds. This modest amount was in contrast to the huge rescue packages for the other crisis-hit economies in the region. So far, the country has drawn $755 million from the facility. While the facility ends this march, we have formally requested from the IMF an initial three-month extension of the standby arrangement to complete the reforms we have begun. The Country's Performance Exceeded Program Targets Most of the macroeconomic objectives of the program for 1999 were met. I refer to our over performance in output, inflation and the current account. The economy's performance was within the criteria set in the program. These criteria cover base money, net international reserves, short-term debt availments and BSP approvals of medium and long-term loans. These favorable developments were confirmed in our recent discussions with the IMF. We wish to assure you that the Philippines remains committed to continue the reforms begun under this facility. III. BSP Financial Highlights Let me now brief you on the Bangko Sentral operations. In sum, we were able to sustain a fairly sound financial condition during the last three years. Assets increased to P967 billion in December 1999 from P730 billion in 1998, or an expansion of 32 percent, while net worth increased by 7 percent to P75 billion. Net income for 1999 was P2.0 billion or a return on equity of 20 percent, given its paid-up capital of only P10 billion. For 1999, the Bangko Sentral had paid p6.0 billion in taxes to the national government. As a result, total taxes paid to the national government since its tax-exemption status expired last July 1998 amounted to P14.7 billion. From July 1993 to June 1999, the Bangko Sentral has remitted to the national government P43.8 billion in dividends and interest rebates. Including taxes paid as of December 1999 of P14.7 billion, total funds transferred to the national government since July 1993 amounted to P58.5 billion, an amount higher than the total statutory capital of the BSP itself. IV. OUTLOOK Looking forward, we do anticipate an acceleration of economic growth at a rate of 4.5-5.5 percent this year. Inflation is expected to average 6.0-7.0 percent for the whole year. For the first two months of this year, inflation averaged 2.8 percent. With falling inflation and a stable peso, interest rates are seen to remain relatively low this year, ranging from 9.5 to 10.5 percent. For the year, the current account is estimated to post a US$5.1 billion surplus, resulting in a US $2.8 billion surplus in our balance of payments. By end-2000, our foreign reserves are estimated to rise to US $17.4 billion. Economic Reforms to Continue In terms of our policies, most of the reforms initiated in 1999 will be continued. These include: the implementation of prudent fiscal and monetary policies; adoption of a liberal foreign exchange regime; liberalization and privatization of the banking and power sectors; proactive management of the external debt; and progressive development of the capital market. On the part of the Bangko Sentral, focus will be on the continuation of structural reforms to make the economy, in particular the banking system, more market-oriented. Towards this end, the Bangko Sentral will continue to encourage mergers in the banking system to promote big, globally competitive banks. We intend to further liberalize the banking environment by working for the entry of more foreign banks, possibly for a limited period. V. CONCLUSION In closing, let me assure you that the Bangko Sentral will remain committed to its strategic role in promoting early and sustainable recovery of the economy. This role covers the objectives of: keeping prices low, the peso relatively stable, interest rates reasonable and the banking system safe and sound. As the new century dawns, we look forward to a gradual but sustained growth in the economy as government renews its commitment to continue the process of economic reforms. Thank you very much. (Note: "The Philippines: Consolidating Economic Growth", ABN-AMRO Investors' Briefing, March 13, 2000, Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas)

Title: Fostering the Proper Environment in Developing the Philippine Capital Market
Occasion: 1st Annual Finance Asia-TRP Philippine Local Debt Conference, Thomson Ratings Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It gives me great pleasure to be invited to this First Annual Philippine Local Debt Conference under the auspices of Finance Asia and Thomson Ratings Philippines. Indeed, it is a privilege to address this first major gathering in the new millennium of the issuers, investors, regulators, underwriters and other key players in the Philippine capital market. The BSP and the Philippine Capital Market Let me assure you that the development of the local capital market has been the driving force of the government and the private sector since the opening of the manila stock exchange in 1927. Since then, numerous developments in the market had transpired. And since 1949, the Bangko Sentral has consistently implemented and supported measures to strengthen the market. In 1980 for instance, the then Central Bank of the Philippines instituted financial reforms that removed various distinctions among financial institutions. This introduced the modified universal banking concept that required higher levels of capitalization, thus increasing the capacity of banks to engage in long-term funding and to venture into such activities as underwriting, securities dealership and equity investments in allied and non-allied undertakings. During the same period, the Central Bank implemented a number of measures to increase the yield of debt instruments by eliminating administrative ceilings on interest rates. In 1986, the government securities network was mobilized and the auction system for treasury issues was installed. These were essential not only in ensuring marketability in the primary market but also in developing a strong secondary market. During the same period, the Central Bank adopted a phase-out policy with regard to central bank bills. To avoid competition in the market, regular CB bills were withdrawn to give way to treasury issues as open market instruments. At the same time, the debt-to-equity conversion program was introduced, enabling the country to generate foreign equity investments that could help advance the cause of capital market development. The Central Bank was also instrumental in the establishment of the Credit Information Bureau in 1982, which has provided vital credit information and helped reduce risks involved in investments in capital market instruments. But it was the establishment of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas in 1993 that gave the major boost to the development of the capital market in the country. The establishment of a financially stronger and more policy independent Bangko Sentral spelled greater stability in the financial system. It ensured a firmer handle on price and exchange rate movements. These, in turn, provided the primary incentives for investors to go into long-term investments in the country and eventually benefit the capital market. The financial restructuring of the Bangko Sentral also promoted the government securities market with the issuance by the National Government of P170 billion in special treasury bills to the New Central Monetary Authority. This not only widened the Bangko Sentral's open market flexibility but also increased the supply of treasury securities in the market. The complete transfer of the Bangko Sentral's fiscal functions to the Bureau of the Treasury in 1998 signaled the shift of the public debt management function to the Finance Department and the strengthening of the Bangko Sentral's monetary policy independence. These developments further ensured a more efficiently functioning capital market. Current Issues Ladies and gentlemen, today, the Philippine capital market has gone a long way. With the increasing globalization and deregulation of the financial system, the market is facing a different set of challenges in the new millennium. A long-term yield curve has to be established; market infrastructure and mechanisms have to be put in place; and finally, various taxation issues have to be resolved. The country's credit rating capability also needs to be improved. BSP's Main Policy Thrusts Against all these new challenges, the Bangko Sentral remains committed to fostering the proper environment in further developing the Philippine capital market. In pursuing this goal, we have two major roles to play: one is to foster macroeconomic conditions conducive to the further development of the market and two, is to ensure the strength and stability of the financial system that will serve as an efficient channel for capital market transactions. I am pleased to report to you that the Bangko Sentral has been doing its homework in fostering the appropriate macroeconomic conditions for capital market growth. In carrying out its primary mandate of maintaining stable prices, the Bangko Sentral generates the most basic incentive that inspires investor confidence in the market. In 1999, the inflation rate exhibited a steady downtrend. From a high of 11.5 percent in January, it steadily declined to 4.3 percent in December, bringing the full year average for the year to 6.6 percent. The decline in inflation and maintenance of monetary aggregates at levels below program, as well as the relative stability in the foreign exchange market, provided the Bangko Sentral with some flexibility in substantially bringing down its key policy rates and in lowering reserve requirements against bank deposits. These facilitated appropriate adjustments in the price of credit that eventually benefited the capital market. Inflationary expectations, the bane of capital market development, have thus been favorable. To the extent that the Bangko Sentral gives more emphasis on indirect and market-based policy instruments such as open market operations, it influences the availability and rate of return on assets in the securities market. In addition to its own measures, the Bangko Sentral also supports the undertakings of other government and private entities that seek to enhance the efficiency of the market. Ensure a Strong Financial System The second major role of the Bangko Sentral is to ensure the existence of a strong and stable financial system. In this area, the bank has also been doing a good job. This is one of the reasons why the Philippine economy was not severely affected by the Asian financial crisis. In 1999, the banking system continued to make significant inroads in containing the lingering effects of the regional crisis. Non-performing loans of commercial banks at 14.6 percent in November remained one of the lowest among crisis-affected nations even without the benefit of a systemic financial restructuring. Commercial banks' capital adequacy ratio during the same period was recorded at 17.8 percent, well above the Bangko Sentral and international standards. During the year, we continued to promote an environment conducive to the development of big, globally competitive banks. To date, nine mergers involving twelve commercial banks, four thrift banks and two rural banks, have taken place. All these measures promoted the mobilization of more resources that will be made available to the market. To promote quality and transparency in investor information, we have required banks to include additional key information in their regular reports, properly certified by accredited external auditors. We have also required banks to list in the Philippine Stock Exchange for greater transparency and regulatory oversight. Speaking of regulations, in 1998 we transferred to the Securities and Exchange Commission the regulatory power over most non-bank financial institutions without quasi-banking functions. This is expected to facilitate greater consistency in the regulation of these institutions and allow the Bangko Sentral to concentrate on its core function of supervising banks. In the area of clearing and settlements, the Bangko Sentral is poised to move into the real-time-gross-settlement arrangement within the year or early next year. Complementary to these measures that we have implemented, we have also supported pending legislations in congress that are expected to foster greater competition, raise prudential standards to international norms and strengthen further the Bangko Sentral's regulatory and supervisory capability. These include amendments to the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act. We also support the proposed revisions to the Revised Securities Act that will further strengthen the regulatory powers of the sec. Future Policy Thrusts In closing, let me underscore that the development of the capital market is not an end in itself. It is only a means for mobilizing savings and channeling them into productive enterprises that would facilitate rather than disrupt economic growth and improve the standard of living of our people. To achieve this objective, the Bangko Sentral is prepared to play its role and continue the following policy thrusts: » Maintenance of price and exchange rate stability as the basic foundation for economic growth. We are gradually moving into inflation targeting as a framework for conducting monetary policy and further ensuring price stability. » Strengthening further the financial system and other key institutions participating in the capital market. We shall intensify prudential regulation and advance the concept of competition through mergers and consolidation. We shall continue to monitor the health of the banking system through our macro and micro early warning systems. » Promotion of greater transparency and timeliness in financial and corporate reporting. We shall put premium on greater disclosures to the market to avoid surprises and help solidify market confidence. The BSP will also continue to support measures to reduce taxation obstacles to capital market development and the improvement of the country's credit rating capability. Toward this end, we support the activities of Thomson Rating Philippines and other existing and potential domestic rating agencies in the country. We welcome benchmarking exercises to ensure the appropriate direction of the market. Conclusion Finally, let us allow ourselves to be reminded by that Jewish girl, Anne Frank, who said: "How wonderful it is that nobody need to wait a single minute before starting to improve the world." We shall not wait a single minute before we undertake our future moves to help improve the capital market. I hope that market participants shall not also wait a single minute to advance their own share that, together, we shall not have to wonder at the dynamics of change in the capital market, but we shall always be driven by the goal to do something positive for the market and necessarily, for all. Thank you and good day. (Note: Philippine Local Debt Conference, Thomson Ratings Philippines, February 17, 2000, Peninsula Hotel, Makati City)

Title: PHILIPPINE BANKS: THE LANDSCAPE BEYOND 2000
Occasion: Asian Banking Conference, Salomon Smith Barney
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: INTRODUCTION Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. Allow me to say, first of all, that it is indeed a pleasure to speak at this forum. I understand this conference seeks to take stock and look ahead in the banking sector after the Asian crisis and into the new millennium. Let me say at the outset that I am putting myself above the fray on whether the new millennium has started this year or still has to start in 2001. Levity aside, the region became the focus of grave investor concern during the recent financial turmoil. The crisis exposed fundamental weaknesses in Asian financial systems that were masked by one of the longest periods of sustained economic growth in recent history. This growth was accompanied by large capital inflows that were encouraged by prevailing economic policies, including financial system and capital account liberalization. Greater openness, however, implied that external shocks were more easily transmitted through the financial system, and from there, to the rest of the economy. The increased mobility of funds also heightened the risks associated with inappropriate domestic policies and weaknesses in the financial system. Surges in capital inflows brought about excessive demand expansion, and their abrupt reversal following changes in investor sentiment caused destabilizing asset price volatility and demand contraction. Maturity and currency mismatches exacerbated the weaknesses in domestic financial systems. POLICY RESPONSES TO THE ASIAN FINANCIAL CRISIS All of us are probably somewhat wiser now. Dealing with the problems brought up by the crisis necessitated both broad, macroeconomic policy responses and the adoption of structural reforms, including in the banking system. In the Philippines, the financial sector had gone through several episodes of policy reform from the 1980s that included allowing greater role for market forces, higher bank capitalization and better bank supervision. Thus, before the crisis, there was already a relatively high degree of market orientation in the financial system and the regulatory framework was being continuously improved. When the crisis struck, a further program of reform was adopted aimed at improving disclosure, strengthening compliance and upgrading the quality of bank management. Consequently, the Philippine financial system fared relatively well during the crisis. The system's strength was evident in the sustained rise in its total resources, compliance with prudential norms, and relatively good asset quality. The NPL ratio of Philippine commercial banks reached 14.6 percent as of November 1999, one of the lowest in the region. In the months ahead, the NPL ratio is expected to decline as the downtrend in interest rates and broad stability in the exchange rate are expected to increase the repayment capability of corporates. Overall, banks have remained an efficient channel of monetary policy, an important element in our efforts to stabilize the macroeconomy. ECONOMIC PERFORMANCE Post-crisis, macroeconomic conditions have improved considerably. The Philippine economy grew by 3.6 percent in terms of GNP in 1999 and average inflation was kept at 6.6 percent. Lending rates are now even lower than pre-crisis levels. The country's external payments position is comfortable--helped in large part by robust exports--and gross international reserves are at record-highs. CHALLENGES OF GLOBALIZATION In the period ahead, further reforms in the banking system will have to clearly deal with the challenges of increasing sophistication and globalization. I have always subscribed to the notion that it is better to anticipate change rather than to have it forced upon you. The liberalization of the Philippine financial system has brought about significant benefits in terms of encouraging efficiency and competition, and allowing our banks to take advantage of international opportunities. However, the events of the past years have demonstrated that such an environment has attendant risks. We are ever mindful of this. Maintaining stability in a globalized environment requires enhanced prudence in financial intermediation by banks. At the same time, we need to have stronger supervisory institutions. In terms of future changes, we have submitted major banking reforms to the Philippine legislature. The proposed revisions seek to align our prudential standards with international norms, enhance competition in the banking sector, and strengthen the powers of the Monetary Board. The amendments will also enable the regulatory structure to adapt to the latest innovations in response to powerful changes occurring in banking technology. Electronic banking, including banking through the internet, will be placed under the authority of the BSP. Upgrading risk management capabilities requires that financial intermediaries recognize and adequately deal with the increased risks associated with financial liberalization and globalization. In this connection, improvements are being made in the financial infrastructure to comply with the best practices in risk management. The settlement and payments system is being reformed with a view to effecting final settlement on a continuous basis, via RTGs. The system is now in the development stage and will cover equities, fixed income, money and FX markets. Risk rating is also being introduced. Among other things, this will allow early identification of problems, improve credit risk management, provide basis for a portfolio management process and improve loan loss reserve methodology and support. We have also started to use the first-generation early warning system for commercial banks that will give us an indication of banks' solvency outlook well in advance. To reinforce the system on a macro basis, we are also in the process of finalizing a set of leading indicators that will enable us to detect potential, system-wide currency and financial crises. Financial innovation is an integral component in meeting the challenges posed by globalization. It is not surprising that financial innovation is most evident in systems where the competitive spirit has been fostered. In the Philippines, monetary authorities have encouraged mergers and consolidations in the banking system to promote competitive and efficient banks. Such consolidation will help local banks take advantage of their collective experience, services, and technological know-how to extend the perimeters of their businesses, with a view to realizing gains in terms of expanded markets and enhanced expertise. To-date, two mergers of commercial banks have been approved, and two more are in the final stages of the merger process. On the number of surviving banks, I see four or five big domestic banks plus the foreign banks accounting for about 70-80 percent of the resources of the commercial banking system. At present, roughly 57 percent of commercial banks' assets are attributable to the top five domestic banks and Philippine branches of foreign banks. In the end, the market, on its own, will determine the exact number of all banks. While size will increase, appropriate prudential measures are expected to check any tendency of big banks toward excessive risk-taking. Institutional changes also involve ongoing programs to upgrade our supervisory skills through intensified training of our personnel. This is consistent with the shift in supervisory focus from a compliance-based and checklist-driven assessment of banks' conditions to a forward-looking and risk-based approach.
