We are also promoting a culture of learning in our bank, through the exchange of best practices with local and foreign institutions, and through the conduct of dialogues. These would help us obtain insights that would strengthen our appreciation of key issues and take the reform process forward. Before I end, let me clarify that the new 90-day guideline on foreign capital lodged as peso time deposits is meant to limit the movement of speculative money in and out of the country. By doing this, we hope to minimize foreign exchange volatility, which should be good for the economy over the longer term. The other objective of the new rules is to strengthen the monitoring of foreign investment flows in the Philippines. They in no way presage the introduction of controls. We in the Philippines remain committed to market-oriented policies. CONCLUSION Recently, Alan Greenspan remarked that the challenge faced by U.S. Monetary Authorities involves fostering, as best as they can, the financial conditions that will allow the economic expansion to continue as long and as vigorously as possible. We hope that someday we will be met with the same challenge in our home shores, and we hope that we will be up to the task. Our commitment to a transparent and carefully formulated strategy to strengthen our banking system should serve us in good stead. Thank you and good day. (Note: Asia Banking Conference, Salomon Smith Barney, 14-15 February 2000, Hong Kong)

Title: THE PHILIPPINES: GEARING UP FOR HIGHER GROWTH
Occasion: Presentation at the CSFB Meeting, Credit Issue First Boston
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I take great pleasure to be invited to this very prestigious organization to present the Philippine story. I always welcome the opportunity to touch base with the key players in the international capital markets like you who closely monitor our performance, policy actions and pronouncements because of the large stake that you have on these matters. This morning allow me to walk you through the key developments in the Philippine economy and the direction where the economy is heading. Recent Economic Developments We take pride in the fact that the Philippine economy made substantial progress in most economic fronts. Let me cite some of the macroeconomic indicators. » Output performance better than expected The Philippine economy staged a strong rebound during the first three quarters of 1999 as real GNP grew at a higher-than-expected rate of 3.0 percent from a 0.5-percent growth for the same period in 1998. The leading indicators of demand particularly from the external sector and the expansion in domestic credit are telling us that growth will continue through the last quarter of 1999. » Prices have remained broadly stable It must be emphasized that the economic expansion was achieved amidst a broadly stable price situation and a sustained fall in domestic interest rates. Notwithstanding inflationary pressures emanating from the series of oil price increases and the wage and transport fare hikes, the country's inflation rate exhibited a steady downtrend during the year. From a high of 11.5 percent in January 1999, the inflation rate fell to 4.3 percent in December, bringing the 1999 inflation average to 6.6 percent. » Domestic interest rates on the downtrend Domestic interest rates continued their general downtrend for most of 1999. The benchmark 91-day t-bill rate declined from an average of 13.2 percent in January to almost 8.9 percent by December. » Foreign exchange market broadly stable There continues to be broad stability in the FOREX market, consistent with the country's stable macro fundamentals and robust external payments position. Market price volatility has dropped significantly in 1999 relative to what it was in 1997 and 1998. This was due largely to the package of reforms implemented by the BSP to stabilize the FOREX market as well as its strong commitment to a floating rate system. » External position remains strong The rebound in the Philippine economy was supported by strong performance in the external sector: a strong export growth, and substantial capital inflows funded from foreign investments and proceeds from government international bond offerings. For the first 10 months of 1999, the BOP recorded a surplus of $3.4 billion, a dramatic improvement from the $1.4 billion recorded for the same period in 1998. In particular, the current account - buttressed by strong exports, which grew by 19 percent - has strengthened considerably, increasing nearly ninefold to $5.5 billion from January-October 1999 from $575 million for the same period in 1998. Non-resident gross portfolio investments grew by over 170 percent for the first 10 months but due to some withdrawals, net portfolio investments grew by only 143 percent. » Gross international reserves (GIR) up to historic highs As a result of our improved external payments position, we were able to build up our GIR to a record level of $15.02 billion by end-1999, equivalent to 4.3 months' worth of imports of goods and services. At this level, GIR is roughly two and a half times more than sufficient to cover the country's total short-term external debt. » External debt manageable The Philippines' outstanding external debt remains manageable at $48.1 billion as of end-June 1999, with the creditor and maturity profile improving. The share of short-term debt to total has declined from 15.0 percent in 1998 to 13.6 percent as of end-June 1999. Meanwhile, debt service burden as a ratio to exports of goods and services has dropped through the years: from 17.4 percent in 1994 to 13.7 percent from January-September 1999. » Expansionary fiscal policy pump-primed the economy On the fiscal side, the National Government overshot the fiscal target for 1999 due largely to pump-priming efforts aimed at rejuvenating demand. The government expects that with the revival of economic growth, it can revert to fiscal consolidation by 2003, with the private sector taking over the reins of growth. » Banking sector remains relatively strong The resilience of the banking system has helped save us from the worst effects of the Asian financial crisis. This strength is evident in the sustained rise in the total resources, the strong capital base, healthy asset quality, and the continued broad compliance with prudential norms. Operations in the first nine months of 1999 resulted in a modest expansion in the assets of the banking system. Our banks continue to be adequately capitalized as reflected in their 18 percent networth to risk asset ratio as of end-September 1999. Meanwhile, the non-performing loans ratio of commercial banks remains manageable at 14.6 percent as of end-November 1999. Aided by the stricter provisioning requirements, banks have also built up their reserves against loan losses to adequate levels. Banks' exposure to the real estate sector remains moderate at 12.2 percent of total loan portfolio as of September 1999 from 10.6 percent in March 1997, well within the 20-percent ceiling prescribed by the BSP in mid-1997. Overall, the banking system remains to be financially healthy and operationally sound and continues as an efficient channel of monetary policy. Performance Under the IMF Program The economy's performance remains broadly on track relative to the IMF performance criteria. Monetary aggregates were below programmed ceilings for the first 11 months of the year. However, the monetary targets were exceeded by some margin in December due to the precautionary preparations for the Y2K changeover, but already liquidity in the system is going back to normal levels. Net international reserves was maintained above the floor in 1999, while ceilings on medium- and long-term approvals of external borrowings remained below limits. The National Government overshot its fiscal target for 1999 of P85.3 billion by over P26 billion. Fiscal transactions for 1999 resulted in a deficit of P111.7 billion. Challenges and Prospects While the economy is well geared up for growth, certain challenges have to be addressed squarely to ensure a faster yet sustainable rate of growth. We at the Bangko Sentral are conscious of the fact that global and regional stability is still a work-in-progress. Uneven growth and possible slowdowns in key industrial economies, particularly the U.S. and Japan, could still cause destabilizing aftershocks in Asia. For this reason, efforts should continue to complete the needed structural reforms to address the remaining weaknesses. In terms of monetary policy, the mix will continue to aim for a continued decline in inflation and broad stability in the exchange rate, while seeing to it that interest rates are reasonably low to support economic growth. In the banking system, the thrust will be to deepen further banking reforms that carried the system through the Asian crisis. We will seek to foster greater competition, raise prudential standards to international norms, and strengthen further the Bangko Sentral's regulatory oversight and supervisory capability. Complementary to these, we have completed the first-generation early warning system for commercial banks that will allow us to predict the banks' solvency outlook one year in advance. To reinforce the system on a macro basis, we are also in the process of finalizing a set of leading indicators that will allow us to detect in advance potential, system-wide currency and banking crises. New Reform Initiatives of the BSP We are now exploring new initiatives for possible implementation this year. We are reviewing our policy on bank mergers and acquisitions to determine and assess its total impact on the banking system. Relatedly, the moratorium on the granting of new branch licenses is also being reviewed for possible relaxation in areas, which can still accommodate additional bank branches. We are also looking into the practice of banks of using "off-balance sheet" transactions that add unnecessary risks into their portfolios and preparing guidelines that will discourage such risky practices. Outlook for 1999 and 2000 As policy reforms are implemented in the various sectors and as the global economic and financial conditions continue to improve, we see the improvements in the Philippine economy continuing and further strengthening this year. Inflation, having registered a rate well below the 7.0-8.0 percent target for 1999 at 6.6 percent, is targeted to average around 6.0-7.0 percent in 2000. On the balance of payments, a surplus of around $2.4 billion or 2.8 percent of GNP is projected for the current year compared to the estimated $3.8 billion surplus for 1999. Gross International Reserves are expected to increase further to over $17 billion by end-2000. Concluding Remarks Let me conclude my presentation by saying that while the economy tracks the path for higher economic growth, the Bangko Sentral is ever mindful of the tasks ahead. Indeed, after hurdling the initial challenges of stabilization, the new environment calls us to enlarge the place of our tent, lengthen our cords and strengthen our stakes (Isaiah 54:2). Bangko Sentral is therefore committed to the continuous review of its monetary and banking policies with a view to adapting to contemporary demands and to helping propel the economy toward self-sustaining growth. Thank you and good day. (Note: Presentation during the Credit Suisse First Boston Meeting, 27 January 2000, Zurich, Switzerland)

Title: THE FINANCIAL EXECUTIVE: IN PURSUIT OF EXCELLENCE IN A GLOBAL SETTING FROM THE POINT OF VIEW OF A CENTRAL BANKER
Occasion: First General Membership Meeting, Financial Executives Institute of the Phils.,
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Distinguished officers and members of the Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines (FINEX), colleagues, guests, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. First of all, allow me to congratulate the newly elected officers and members of the FINEX board. I am extremely glad for this opportunity to join you today in marking another year, the very first of the new millennium. Like you, my sincere hope is that it will prove to be a fruitful one for all of us. I think it is very timely that for this year, FINEX will be driven by the theme "The Financial Executive: Pursuing Excellence in a Global Setting". The pursuit of excellence demands that we prepare ourselves to manage the challenge of greater competition and an increased potential for risk even on a global scale. This should imply not only the adoption of international best practices but also, on a personal level, being a responsible and competent corporate citizen. Our common experience with globalization and increased financial integration in the last few years has shown that individual actions can have systemic consequences, that excessive risk-taking by individual players and disobedience to prudential regulations can lead to systemic collapse. This was one of the main lessons of the Asian financial crisis. At the same time, there is also a need to address the weaknesses in the system that contributed to the Asian banking crisis. An ADB study pointed out that one of the root causes of the Asian debacle is inadequate bank governance that allowed excessive risk-taking by financial institutions. It is the realization of the benefits of good governance that prompted countries in the Asian region to work hard at instituting governance reforms. Therefore, this is a very timely occasion to discuss good governance with financial executives on whom the success of the reform effort greatly rests. A Call for Governance Reforms Corporate governance refers to a set of rules that define the behavior of company managers while ensuring their accountability to stakeholders. Good governance, whether applied to banks or non-bank corporates, is essential for a well functioning economy as it provides incentives for management to act in ways that improve the firm's financial position and assure shareholders of an adequate return. At the same time, good corporate governance helps create an environment conducive to the sustained growth of the industry. Good corporate governance always asks us in the face: "Is there a better way?" Elements of Good Governance in the Banking System In my recent lecture at the Asian Institute of Management, I emphasized that good governance at the individual bank level hinges in part on the business practices adopted by the board of directors and management. In the same lecture, I outlined some of the key elements of a good governance system at the individual bank level, which are the following: » Management with high integrity, adequate training and experience, which concerns all of you; » A good internal information and control system to ensure that decisions affecting the rights and obligations of the bank are never made solely by one individual; » Prudent credit approval procedures and risk limitation procedures; and » Effective external and internal audit procedures to ensure that established policies and procedures are followed and special interests are not allowed to influence decisions. At the same time, experiences in the past showed that there are factors by which the quality of corporate governance can be enhanced in the banking system. Most important of these factors include: » The existence of independent and effective bank supervisors, who ensure that prudential standards are adhered to; » The requirement to list in the stock exchange, which promotes transparency and market discipline; » An active merger and acquisitions market, which compels banks' best behavior to avoid a takeover or merger; and » Effective anti-corruption laws, which prevent, among other things, abuses in connected lending. These are the four pillars of corporate governance in the banking system. BSP: GUARDIAN OF BANK GOVERNANCE An important ingredient that helped spare the country from the worst effects of the Asian crisis has been the relative strength of the Philippine banking system. This derives from the combination of a past history of banking reforms and the timely pre-emptive measures taken to address any potential financial sector weakness. The reform efforts of the BSP took different dimensions, from tightening of minimum capital and bringing regulatory standards closer to international best practices to re-orienting bank supervision toward risk-based analysis and strengthening bank exit policies. Together with the other measures on provisioning, portfolio valuation, public disclosure, and consolidated bank supervision, the BSP has covered practically the whole range of critical policies in banking supervision. As a result of these initiatives, Goldman Sachs in its recent cross-country study found that prudential standards in the Philippines remained strong and compared favorably with the standards used in the Asian region. Moreover, the performance of the Philippine banking system in terms of NPL, profitability and capital adequacy during the crisis was generally positive. These reflect in part the good governance structure existing in Philippine banks. Concluding Remarks Let me conclude these remarks by saying that the banking system has undergone a substantial period of reform in the last decade to achieve the goal of strengthening the system itself, including through development of a culture of good corporate governance. However, the caveat has to be mentioned: the reform effort is a continuing process as we try to keep pace with the demands of globalization and liberalization. Therefore, it will require the Bangko Sentral to maintain an activist stance in the reform program. This is evident in the range of proposed reforms submitted to the legislature as amendments to the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act. There is a final caveat. Good governance in the banking system cannot be effected by the BSP alone. It also requires active participation of other sectors in the economy, particularly the corporate sector. You as financial executives have the responsibility to raise the code of conduct in your chosen field and to pursue excellence in such endeavor. Let this goal be pursued by working towards and adhering to good corporate governance. Through our combined efforts, the challenges of the new global setting will indeed be much less daunting. Thank you and good afternoon. (Note: First General Membership Meeting, Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines (FINEX), January 19, 2000, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati City)

Title: BSP Policy Thrusts for the New Millenium
Occasion: Luncheon Meeting, Rotary Club of Makati
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I take great pleasure in joining the officers and members of the premier Rotary Club in Makati today. While this club is the oldest and largest of the 29 Rotary Clubs in Makati, counting among your membership major professionals and corporate leaders in business and industry in the country, I am very confident your organization has maintained fresh and dynamic perspectives especially at this time of the new millennium. Coming at the heels of a major revamp in the cabinet and the virtual end of the watch for the millennium bug, this meeting is a perfect opportunity to brief you about recent economic and financial developments and the new policy initiatives of the Bangko Sentral. Recent Developments I start with key economic and financial developments in the past year. The year 1999 saw the economies of the crisis-affected countries recover from the Asian financial crisis. Most economic indicators were looking up. Output growth expanded. Inflation continued to decline. Exports sustained their growth. Domestic demand began to pick up. As a result, market confidence started to return, allowing Asia to remain on top of the other emerging economies in other parts of the world. We take pride in the fact that the Philippine economy made good progress in most economic fronts. Let us look at some of these key economic indicators. Output growth has rebounded, with GNP growing at an average of 3.0 percent during the first three quarters of the year. We are also optimistic that growth will be higher in the last quarter given the very good leading indicators of growth. Inflation remained single-digit, averaging 6.6 percent for the whole year of 1999. Interest rates had trended down during the same period, even reaching pre-crisis levels. In the external front, the exchange rate was relatively stable in 1999 compared to 1998. We continued to post positive gains in our external payments position, with our balance of payments recording a surplus of $3.8 billion. As a result, our gross international reserves continued to rise, posting a record level of $15.0 billion as of end-December last year. This is expected to boost further investor confidence and reduce our vulnerability to potential external shocks. Turning to the banking system, Philippine banks remained financially healthy and operationally sound. In 1999, reforms focused on further strengthening the financial system in order to support economic recovery and to enhance its resiliency to domestic and external shocks. As a result, banks continued to be adequately capitalized as reflected in their 18 percent net worth to risk asset ratio as of end-September 1999. This ratio far exceeded the statutory requirement of 10 percent and the international standard of 8 percent. As of end-September 1999, banks' NPL ratio was recorded at 14.5 percent. This ratio compared favorably with those of our Asian neighbors, which ranged from 19 percent in Malaysia to 75 percent in Indonesia, already incorporating the impact of financial restructuring. Moreover, as of end-June 1999, total exposure of commercial banks to the real estate sector was contained at 12.3 percent of their loan portfolio. This was well within the prescribed ceiling of 20 percent. Overall, while there were some banks that failed in the aftermath of the Asian crisis, the banking system continued to be a sound and efficient channel of monetary policy. This was further confirmed during the millennium bug watch, when there were no major glitches that surfaced in the banking sector. Challenges and Prospects Although the economy is now in a much better shape compared to a year ago, certain challenges have to be addressed squarely to ensure a faster yet sustainable rate of growth capable of attracting more foreign investments. We should keep in mind that global and regional stability is still a work-in-progress. Uneven growth and possible slowdowns in key industrial economies, particularly the U.S. and Japan, could still cause destabilizing aftershocks in Asia. For this reason, efforts should continue to complete the needed structural reforms in the financial and corporate sectors, which are the main transmission lines of outside shocks in the economy. In particular, vital economic legislations related to these reforms will have to be passed and implemented as soon as possible. The fact that the Philippines was least affected by the crisis should challenge us to undertake even more significant policy and structural improvements to sustain our good economic fortune. On the part of the Bangko Sentral, future policy actions will support the government's thrust for a broad-based and sustainable economic recovery. This means Bangko Sentral will be working for a more efficient and competitive economy and a safer, stronger and globally-competitive banking system. Our monetary policy mix will continue to aim for a continued decline in inflation and broad stability in the exchange rate, while seeing to it that interest rates are reasonably low to support economic growth. The exchange rate will remain market-determined and the build up in foreign exchange reserves will be pursued to the extent allowed by monetary and foreign exchange market conditions. In the banking system, the thrust will be to deepen further banking reforms that carried the system through the Asian crisis. We will seek to foster greater competition, raise prudential standards to international norms, and strengthen further the Bangko Sentral's regulatory oversight and supervisory capability. While most of the changes are embodied in the proposed amendments to the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act, which we expect to pass Congress early this year, several policy initiatives have been implemented by the Bangko Sentral to support these major improvements in banking laws. To promote bigger and stronger banks capable of competing globally, we have encouraged bank mergers and consolidations by providing incentives and suspending the grant of new bank branch licenses. So far, three bank mergers have been completed, while several others are in various stages of negotiation. At the same time, banks' compliance to the phased increase in minimum capitalization was monitored closely and loan classification and provisioning requirements were tightened further to enhance the capability of banks to withstand shocks. Complementary to these, we have completed the first-generation early warning system for commercial banks that will allow us to predict the banks' solvency outlook one year in advance. To reinforce the system on a macro basis, we are also in the process of finalizing a set of leading indicators that will allow us to detect in advance potential, system-wide currency and banking crises. New Initiatives We are now exploring new initiatives for possible implementation this year. We recognize that the economic and banking system blooms with more vigor after each pruning. For one, we are reviewing our policy on bank mergers and acquisitions to determine and assess its total impact on the banking system. Relatedly, the moratorium on the granting of new branch licenses is also being reviewed for possible relaxation in areas, which can still accommodate additional bank branches. These initiatives are aimed at enhancing competition on a greater scale, even allowing existing banks with comprehensive networks to expand, to ensure that economies of scale and the benefit of efficiency are realized by surviving market players. We are likewise reviewing the guidelines on FCDU licensing, with the end in view of making the banking system more resilient to external shocks. In particular, we will be looking at the capability of certain types of banks in handling FCDUs. In fact, we have instructed our technical staff to suggest ways of addressing the problems associated with indiscriminate traffic between the banks' regular books and FCDU books. In particular, matters of taxation will be addressed to remove the distortionary aspects of maintaining the difference between regular and FCDU books. We are also looking into the practice of banks of using "off balance sheet" transactions that add unnecessary risks into their portfolios. The Bangko Sentral is preparing guidelines that will discourage the use of such risky practices as "off balance sheet" repos and direct lending facilities. We are also looking at engineered swaps to see how arbitrage opportunities between peso and dollar deposits can be reduced. In order to monitor compliance by banks to the new guidelines, a more integrated bank reportorial system is also being developed. At the end of the day, all these new initiatives are meant to usher in an improved regulatory environment that emphasizes a higher level of competition based on stronger, more globalized banks. Indeed, the Philippine banking system is entering a new era of banking which we are glad to be a part of. Conclusion In closing, I would like to thank the officers and members of the Rotary Club of Makati for inviting me to this gathering and to be able to share with you some of our important plans for the new millennium. I solicit the support of our friends from the Rotary Club in pushing for these plans of the Bangko Sentral. Let me encourage our Rotarians that, paraphrasing Jimmy Carter in 1978, "If we fear making anyone mad, then we ultimately probe for the lowest common denominator of human achievement." Thank you and good day. (Note: Luncheon Meeting, Rotary Club of Makati, 18 January 2000, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati City)

Title: Building the Infrastructure for Effective Governance in the Banking System
Occasion: JBF Center Lecture Series, Asian Institute of Management
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction: The Analytics of Banking Governance Ladies and gentlemen, good evening. I am deeply honored to be invited to deliver the first lecture in this year's edition of the Jose B. Fernandez Center Lecture Series. I always welcome opportunities, such as tonight's forum, to interact with practitioners in the financial system regarding relevant issues confronting our economy. The theme of tonight's discussion is The Establishment of an Adequate Infrastructure for the Effective Governance in the Banking System. Banks and other financial institutions by virtue of their deposit and borrowing functions are custodian of the country's liquid reserves. As such, they play an important role in the efficient functioning of a modern economy. They constitute a system that serves as a pooling mechanism for savings and an efficient allocation device that channels these funds to the most productive economic activities. Any disruption in the intermediation process by the financial system will inevitably lead to negative effects on the whole economy. There is, therefore, strong public interest in the safety and liquidity of the banking system's financial condition. As such, much attention has been devoted to the issue of building a strong and stable financial system. In the recent Asian regional financial crisis, among the factors identified to be behind the collapse of some of the banking systems in the region has been the inadequacies in the corporate governance of banks. Its been said that one of the lessons from the 1997 Asian debacle is that good governance of banks is an essential element of a sound banking system. Moreover, the financial sector has grown remarkably in recent years to even exceed the size of the real sector. As a result, a financial crisis can readily spill over to the real sector. Elements of Good Corporate Governance of Banks [1] Corporate governance refers to the set of rules that define the relationships between shareholders, managers, creditors, government and other stakeholders and a set of mechanisms that help directly or indirectly to enforce these rules.[2] Good governance, whether applied to banks or non-bank corporates, is essential for a well functioning economy as it provides incentives for management to act in ways that raise the firm's net present value and assure shareholders an adequate return. At the same time, good corporate governance can help create an environment conducive to the sustained growth of the industry - in this case the banking system. To be sure, a good governance structure in the banking system by itself cannot build a strong and stable financial system on its own. It needs to be complemented by, among other things, similarly appropriate governance structures in the regulatory agencies and the general corporate sector. Good governance at the individual bank level hinges in part on the business practices adopted by the board of directors and management. A competent management is the first line of defense against excessive risk taking by banks. Most bank failures can be attributed to inadequate management that allows the bank to acquire low quality assets and take inappropriate risk positions, and that fails to detect and resolve deterioration in existing assets and risk positions. Briefly, some of the key elements of a good governance system at the individual bank level are: Management that possesses high integrity and has adequate training and experience; Good internal information and control system to ensure that decisions affecting the rights and obligations of the bank never rest with just one individual; Prudent credit approval procedures and risk limitation procedures; and Effective external and internal audit procedures to ensure that established policies and procedures are followed and special interests are not allowed to influence decisions. Let me focus on the elements of good corporate governance at the industry level. Specifically, what are some of the factors that can contribute in the creation of an environment conducive to the adoption of good governance practice by banks? 1. Independent and capable banking supervisors A key element of good governance of the banking industry is the quality of governance of monetary authorities and bank supervision agencies as the regulators set an example for the industry and as they are able to effectively perform their responsibilities/functions/duties. The importance of independence of bank supervisors has been emphasized in the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) paper entitled "Core Principles For Effective Banking Supervision" which states that "an effective system of banking supervision will have clear responsibilities and objectives for each agency involved in the supervision of banking organizations. Each such agency should possess operational independence and adequate resource." 2. Adequate bank rating system The traditional system of analyzing and rating the soundness of financial institutions used by regulators, supervisors, credit rating agencies or corporate analysts has been the camel methodology. Bank soundness is evaluated based on capital adequacy, asset quality, management capability, earnings potential and liquidity. However, this methodology may not be able to fully cover the entire range of governance risks faced by banks. Thus, there is a need to augment the camel methodology to include explicitly governance as a risk factor. This can be done, for example, by taking a closer look at the board of directors in terms of independence, accountability, interlocking interests, integrity, experience and ability to assume their duties, among other things. 3. Active merger and consolidation market A more dynamic industrial environment characterized by an active merger and acquisition market can also induce good governance in banks. The threat of a corporate takeover or a merger should provide an impetus for the adoption of appropriate governance practices. To facilitate merger and consolidation activities, issues such as the limits on foreign ownership of banks, existence of dual classes of shares and tax and accounting regulations hampering mergers should be addressed. 4. Effective anti-corruption framework The campaign to improve governance practices in banks should be accompanied by an anti-corruption framework that is strictly enforced by the relevant agencies. Banks are often a target of corruption activities such that bank collapse often blamed on some form corrupt practice. One of the core principles for effective supervision of banks identified by the BIS relates to connected lending, a form of corruption in banks. The BIS core principles for effective banking supervision states that "in order to prevent abuses from connected lending, banking supervisors must have in place requirements that banks lend to related companies and individuals on an arm's length basis such that extensions of credit are officially monitored, and that other appropriate steps are taken to control or mitigate the risks." 5. Others Other factors essential to the creation of an environment for the good governance of banks are: the codification of the fiduciary duties of care and loyalty and the liabilities of bank directors; the requirement for banks listed in the stock exchange to disclose their governance practices as part of their annual reports; and the promotion of education, training and information on governance and professional directorship. BSP Towards an Environment of Good Governance How does the Philippines rate against these elements of good governance? In a number of regional conferences I have attended, the observation has been made that the Philippines has fared relatively better than some other countries during the financial crisis. It did not undergo a similar degree of capital outflows, banking sector distress and other forms of financial upheavals as was experienced by the other countries in the region. An important ingredient to this performance has been the relative strength of its banking system which derives from the combination of past history of reforms in the banking system and the timely pre-emptive measures taken by the authorities to address any potential financial sector weakness. This effectively spared the Philippines from the wrenching adjustments that have had to be made. Such reforms took different dimensions from tightening of minimum capital and bringing regulatory standards closer to international best practices to re-orienting bank supervision toward the analysis of risk and strengthening bank exit policies. Let me discuss some of the more important measures: Bank capital requirements Minimum capital requirements for banks were raised through end-2000, with intermediate minimum levels for end-1998 and end-1999. The larger banks have not encountered meeting the new requirements. In some cases, mergers have been resorted to. Marking to market The BSP has also required banks to start marking to market their trading securities portfolio so that significant changes in their market values are properly accounted for. Accounting standards have been agreed upon with the BAP, and the relevant price benchmarks have been discussed with market operators. Transparency and disclosure To enhance transparency and market discipline, the BSP has instructed all banks to disclose publicly, whether listed in the stock exchange or not, detailed information on a quarterly basis, their non-performing loans, classified loans and other risk assets, amount of general and specific loan-loss reserves, return on equity, and insider (DOSRI) loans. Consolidated supervision We have also started to supervise financial conglomerates in a consolidated fashion in order to address bank solvency on a consolidated basis. Since legislative changes are needed to fully impose consolidated capital requirements and extend consolidated supervision of financial institutions to include their interests in non-financial ventures, the authorities have proposed an amendment of the GBA in this regard which is currently under consideration by Congress. The BSP has already begun to consolidate limits on foreign currency exposures between banks and their affiliated FCDUs. Supervisory methods The BSP has also changed the focus of its supervision activities from a purely compliance-based and check-list driven assessment of banks' condition to a forward-looking and risk-based framework. Together with the change in emphasis towards a risk-based approach, significant improvements have taken place in the area of rating methodologies. In July 1998, "sensitivity to market risk(s) was added to arrive at a camels rating system". Others Other reforms include the intensified bank monitoring of selected banks especially those in potential distress. The BSP has also adopted explicit procedures to be used when banks fail to reach certain thresholds of capital adequacy. External auditors of banks have been required to report to the BSP all matters that could adversely affect the financial condition of their clients, any serious irregularity that may jeopardize the interest of depositors and creditors, and any losses incurred which substantially reduce bank's capital. Stricter provisioning regulations have also been put in place. How have these actions by the regulators been perceived by the observers? An independent assessment made recently by Goldman Sachs found that prudential standards in the Philippines remained strong and compare favorably with the standards used in the Asian region. Moreover, the performance of the Philippine banking system in terms of NPL, profitability and capital adequacy during the crisis was generally positive. These reflect in part the good governance structure existing in the Philippine banks. Let me quote part of that report, "bank managements are generally seasoned and cautious, having gone through a decade of economic depression and political upheaval. We also regard the BSP as a more transparent and effective regulator among Asian banks, though continued closer, preemptive supervision of bank is vital. The BSP appears to be more vigilant in bank supervision, particularly in terms of related-party lending. It now conducts more off-site examinations and monitors banks' FOREX activities on a daily basis." Concluding Remarks In the last decade, the banking system has undergone a substantial period of reform not only to build a culture of good corporate governance but also to achieve the broader goal of strengthening the banking system. However, the reform process is a continuing process as we try to keep pace with the demands of globalization and liberalization. Thus, the Bangko Sentral continues to take an activist stance in the reform efforts as evident in the range of proposed reforms that have been submitted to the legislature as amendments to the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act. The proposed revisions seek to achieve the following: further strengthen banking supervision; enhance competition in the banking sector; promote further the independence of the BSP, particularly its ability to effectively conduct monetary policy, and strengthen the framework for failure resolution to ensure the speedy settlement of potential problems in the banking system. Finally, let me emphasize that good governance of the banking system may not work in isolation. It has to be accompanied by good governance in the major components of the economy, particularly the corporate sector. Given the concentrated ownership in some parts of the corporate sector as well as the cross shareholdings between banks and corporations, there is a need to address governance issues in both the banking and corporate sectors. Let me close this lecture with the quote on good corporate governance...."Corporate governance is not rocket science. All its principles are derived from common principles of business ethics. Nevertheless, its importance should not be underplayed since the consequences can be costly or catastrophic in the worst case. Being an intangible asset, good governance requires attention and investment of time, money and the need for recourse to sources of professional governance expertise and advice." Thank you and good evening. -------------------------- [1] This section is based largely on 'The Corporate Governance of Banks: CAMEL-in-a-Cage" by Arvind Mathur and Jimmy Burhan of the Asian Development Bank. [2] "A Consolidated Report on Corporate Governance and Financing in East Asia: Executive Summary", Asian Development Bank, November 1999, p.1.

Title: Keynote Address
Occasion: BSP-IMF Conference on Framework for Monetary Policy in Post-Crisis Asia
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: BSP Monetary Board members Vicente Valdepeñas, Jr. and Melito Salazar, Jr., Mr. Kunio Saito, Mr. Stefan Ingves and Mr. Yusuke Horiguchi of the International Monetary Fund, participants to the BSP-IMF conference on "Framework for Monetary Policy in Post-Crisis Asia: Policy Options and Inflation Targeting",friends, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. First of all, let me say that I deeply appreciate the efforts of the International Monetary Fund in mounting this conference in collaboration with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. The BSP is honored to co-host this event which gathers some of the most seasoned practitioners in the field of monetary policy. Belatedly perhaps, let me also welcome you all to Cebu, the Philippines' Queen City of the South, known for its vibrant economy and colorful past. It was on the shores of Limasawa, a small island off Sugbu--now known as Cebu--that the Portuguese explorer, Fernando de Magallanes, landed in March 1521, after an arduous two-year voyage from Seville, Spain. A month later, he would set foot on Sugbu itself, and learn that he had discovered not just two islands, but a group of islands, which would eventually be named Filipinas--or Philippines--in honor of Felipe, then king of Spain. This brief visit into the past helps to emphasize that crossroads are true not only in history but also in contemporary economic and financial interactions. And we are honored that this very important interaction among central bankers around the world is taking place in this historic island of Cebu. POSITIVE PROSPECTS AND CHALLENGES FOR THE REGION As the title of this conference indicates, Asia is now on the mend: the region has emerged from two-and-a-half years of arduous maneuvering through rough waters. The foundations for broad-based economic recovery in the region are beginning to be laid. Recent trends continue to support this view. Starting the second quarter of this year, there has been an upturn in domestic demand along with increased industrial activity, rising exports and an improving investment climate. Relative stability in international financial markets has also been restored. These factors bode well for the region's growth prospects. However, while affirming these positive prospects, let me stress that a lot of hard work lies ahead to ensure lasting economic growth. This conference, which seeks to provide Asia's central bankers the opportunity to discuss options for monetary policy regimes in an environment, which for most countries involves greater exchange rate flexibility is, therefore, timely. Choosing the appropriate monetary policy framework is crucial to preserving monetary stability, establishing stronger macroeconomic fundamentals and sustaining economic growth. THE ROLE OF THE MONETARY POLICY IN ECONOMIC GROWTH As you well know, there has been a shift in the understanding of the role of monetary policy in the past two decades. Prior to the 1980s, monetary policy was seen as a vehicle for promoting economic development by supporting production and employment. Thus, slightly higher inflation, on account of accommodative monetary policy, was considered permissible as it allowed for faster economic growth. This old view of the role of monetary policy assumed the existence of a trade-off between inflation, on the one hand, and employment and growth, on the other. However, developments in the past twenty years or so have required a review of this paradigm. Accommodative monetary policy has almost always led to higher inflation without necessarily promoting economic growth. The link between expansionary monetary policy--hence higher inflation--and economic growth, if it existed at all, proved to be operative only in the short run. Thus, we saw the shift in the focus of monetary policy from the promotion of production and employment to maintaining price stability. It is widely accepted in policy circles that price stability can be best achieved by constraining discretionary policy, which may give rise to an inflationary bias in the conduct of monetary policy. Discretionary policy, in turn, may be curbed through the adoption of a nominal anchor. Depending on the choice of a nominal anchor, monetary policy may follow one of four basic approaches: monetary targeting, interest-rate targeting, exchange rate targeting and inflation targeting. Nobody but nobody can prescribe what is best for a particular economy except those who have a stake in public policy. And the choice will be a function of the behavior of that economy's liquidity as it relates to prices, income and employment; the independence of its monetary authorities; and the extent of development of its financial system as a channel of monetary policy. THE CONDUCT OF MONETARY POLICY IN THE PHILIPPINES As the Philippines' central monetary authority, the BSP's primary mandate is to maintain price stability conducive to a balanced and sustainable growth of the economy. In fulfilling this mission, the BSP is vested with policy independence by the Philippine constitution itself, as well as the BSP charter. Given this responsibility, how does the BSP conduct monetary policy? The BSP currently follows a monetary targeting framework. Under this approach, the demand for money is estimated, given the government's targets for inflation and output growth. The appropriate level of money supply is then chosen to match estimated money demand so as to bring about basic equilibrium in the money market. To attain the targeted level of money supply, the BSP manages the level of base money (BM), taking into account the link between base money and the money supply. This it does by employing a variety of monetary policy instruments. Thus far, monetary targeting has worked for us. Since the establishment of the Bangko Sentral in 1993, various forms of inflationary pressures have challenged its task of maintaining price stability. Nevertheless, the BSP has managed to keep inflation within single-digit levels. I am fully aware, of course, of the other monetary frameworks, including inflation targeting. The BSP's efforts to ensure price stability has given it the flexibility to conduct monetary policy in support of the economic recovery. With inflation within target levels and monetary aggregates below programmed ceilings, adjustments have been made--in the BSP's policy interest rates and the reserve requirements--to lower the cost of lending and to improve the availability of credit. This monetary stance has helped nurture the economic recovery. During the first three quarters of the year, the Philippines performed better than expected, with real GNP expanding by 3.0 percent compared to the programmed 1.9 percent. Growth was promoted in a low-inflation environment amidst generally stable foreign exchange market conditions, a sound external position and a healthy financial system. However, successful monetary targeting has certain requisites. Foremost among these is a stable and predictable relationship between monetary and real sector variables. We are well aware, however, that financial deregulation and liberalization have given rise to a new financial architecture and a continuously evolving array of financial products and services. These developments have caused large and frequent fluctuations in the velocity of money, thus weakening the link between monetary and real sector variables. In the Philippines, we have experienced this "de-linking" in at least two instances: first, when inflation remained low, even as monetary aggregates were breached, and second, when inflation continued to accelerate, while monetary aggregates were kept well within targets. These experiences have led the BSP to explore other options for monetary policy, among them, inflation targeting. During the symposium commemorating the 50th anniversary of central banking in the Philippines, which was held in Manila last January, inflation targeting was one of the topics for discussion. Governor Donald Brash of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand presented the main paper and I was privileged to have been invited as one of the reactors. Let me discuss some of the points I raised in my reaction paper. First, inflation here in the Philippines is affected, to a large extent, by non-monetary factors. In fact, food accounts for more than 50 percent of our CPI basket. Clearly, in our case, inflation cannot be addressed by monetary policy alone. Our experience has proven that inflation can be triggered by weather-related disturbances and structural factors such as weaknesses in the food distribution system. Aside from non-monetary factors, another possible hindrance to the implementation of inflation targeting in the Philippines is the difficulty of formulating a forecasting framework with a very high degree of accuracy, and which is easily understood by the public.On the latter point, it is important to underscore that the effectiveness of monetary policy is strengthened if the goals and instruments of policy are known to the public and if the authorities can make a credible commitment to meeting them. In addition, inflation targeting requires the strict accountability of the head of the central bank. Of course, holding a public official accountable for his performance is a basic tenet of public governance. However, putting the job of the central bank governor on the line even when inflation is not necessarily driven by central bank policy is-in my view-quite harsh and would undermine stability in the monetary system. And let me quickly add that when I advanced these points, I had not assumed the post at room 501 of the Executive Building of the Bangko Sentral. Assuredly, there are varying views on the subject-which is why I look forward to the discussions ahead. I am certain we will leave this island of Cebu very much refreshed and imbued with new ideas. There is much to be learned from the experiences of our colleagues from across continents. REGIONAL COOPERATION As I noted earlier, patterns of recovery are emerging in Asia, with the pace and magnitude of recovery stronger for some countries. Sustaining the recovery requires firm commitment on the part of the governments in the region to pursue structural reforms, as well as implement consistent macroeconomic policies. These twin thrusts will help ensure the soundness of the financial system and create a more robust macroeconomic environment, which will minimize the effects of any external shock on the domestic economy. However, in an increasingly globalized economic environment, efforts on the national level are unlikely to be very effective in reducing the likelihood of the recurrence of a similar crisis. Regional collaboration is crucial. Cooperation is particularly needed in the areas of bank supervision, information exchange, surveillance and possibly, the establishment of a regional financing facility. There is need to improve bank supervision in the region by developing standards that adhere to international best practices and to foster information exchange among countries, by establishing accessible data banks on the financial system and developing high-quality, credible, and transparent reporting and disclosure standards. There is also a need to sustain the surveillance process on the global and regional level. Such a surveillance process enables us to anticipate the emergence of potential instability, and react in a timely fashion to limit the spread of contagion. There is likewise a need to examine the possibility of establishing a regional financing facility, which can help solve liquidity problems during speculative attacks, and help maintain stability in the region. CONCLUDING REMARKS Earlier, I said that information exchange is one area where regional cooperation can be enhanced. This conference provides a very important venue for this exchange, as it provides Asia's central bankers and other policymakers the opportunity to discuss how some of the analytical developments, such as inflation targeting frameworks, might apply in Asia. The discussion will be all the richer as it draws on the experience of central banks from around the world that have adopted these frameworks. With the impressive list of participants, we can look forward to two-and-a-half more days of highly stimulating discussions. In closing, let me invite you to the dinner, which I am hosting tonight at the beachfront of the hotel. For now, let us proceed to our lunch date. Thank you and good day. (Note: "Framework for Monetary Policy in Post-Crisis Asia: Policy Options and Inflation Targeting", 8-10 December 1999, Cebu City)

Title: Keynote Address - Euromoney
Occasion: 7th Annual Asia pacific Issuers and Investors Forum, Euromoney
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction Mr. Adrian H. Thomas, Conference Manager and Head of the Asian Division of Euromoney, distinguished participants to this Seventh Annual Asia Pacific Issuers and Investors Forum organized by Euromoney: Let me begin by expressing my deep appreciation to the conference organizers for inviting me to keynote the Euromoney Investors Forum, which is the leading regional gathering for the capital markets in Asia. For more than two years now, developments in Asia have been the focus of grave investor concern. But I am sure that you will agree with me that the foundations for economic recovery in the region are now beginning to be laid, in almost all cases being accompanied by a painful restructuring and reform program. Relative stability in international markets have been restored starting the second quarter of this year, and the International Monetary Fund has also projected a stronger growth in most Asian economies in the first year of the new millennium. The fundamentals of the Asian economies can be now be said to be better than at any time since the 1997 crisis. The regional financial crisis has highlighted the importance of nurturing investor confidence in national policies. In particular, the key role played by transparency in policy formulation, and the timeliness and accuracy of financial and economic information has been underscored. This forum, therefore, is an important step in maintaining this confidence. Please do not interpret my statements as indicating that we have become sanguine about our growth prospects. In the Philippines, we are only too acutely aware that sustained recovery and sustainable growth requires continued hard work. This is reflected in our commitment to our economic reform agenda. In the spirit of transparency, therefore, let me now provide you with greater detail about how we have coped with the crisis. My focus will necessarily be on the Philippines, but you will find me drawing on issues of current regional concern. The Role of the BSP At this point, let me underscore certain distinguishing features of the Philippine monetary system, which served it in good stead in weathering the Asian financial crisis. As the Philippine central monetary authority, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) is mandated by the Philippine Constitution to provide policy directions in the areas of money, banking and credit; to supervise the banking system, and to regulate other financial institutions such as finance companies. The BSP's primary mission is to deliver price stability conducive to a balanced growth of the economy. The BSP enjoys policy independence in the pursuit of this mission. This is guaranteed not just by ordinary law but by the Philippine constitution itself. The onset of the financial crisis in Asia has provided a major challenge to the bank's adherence to this mission, and at times has subjected the bank to criticism and pressure to sacrifice this objective in the pursuit of short-term, more popular goals. The BSP responded to this challenge by adjusting its monetary and financial policies and striking a delicate balance between restoring order in the foreign exchange market, containing inflationary pressures, and limiting the adverse impact of the crisis on the banking and corporate sectors. At no time was the BSP's pursuit of its mission of delivering price stability compromised. This policy stance was rewarded by the containment of the annual inflation rate to single digit levels even at the height of the crisis. Belying dire predictions arising from the current increases in world oil prices, the general price level has remained broadly stable, with the inflation rate settling at 5.4 percent in October this year, for a year-to-date average of 7.2 percent. Economic Growth Performance and Prospects With the economy recovering from the Asian financial storm and with improvement in weather conditions, the Philippines performed better than expected during the first three quarters of this year, with gross national product (GNP) expanding by 3.0 percent in real terms. The evidence is now clear that industry has begun to recover. Our growth prospects-especially in terms of our exports-have been helped in large part by the recent marked improvement in global economic and financial conditions. Of late, some concerns have been raised over the eventual demand slowdown of the US economy. However, with adept management especially by the U.S. Fed, we believe that if there is any slowdown at some point, it will be a soft landing. This could be offset by the strengthening economies of Japan and Europe, as well as of other Asian countries. Our commitment to price stability has also paid off, in that the resulting low inflation rates have given monetary policy the necessary flexibility in supporting the economic recovery. Thus, sustained policy adjustments have been made to lower the cost of lending and to improve the availability of credit. The benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate was 8.894 percent at the auction held this Monday [29 November 1999], much lower than the 15.3 percent average for 1998. Last November 3, we trimmed our overnight borrowing rate by 25 basis points to 8.75 percent. We assure you that at no point will this compromise our inflation targets. Facing External Challenges Focusing now on the external sector, risk management will be pursued through the maintenance of an adequate level of foreign exchange reserves and through careful management of our external debt position. There continues to be broad stability in the foreign exchange market, with reduced market volatility in 1999 relative to 1997 and 1998. The improvement should continue as regional factors become more positive and as we continue to see a surplus in our external accounts. For the first ten months of 1999, the balance of payments posted a surplus of US$3.4 billion. This was a significant increase over the US$1.4 billion surplus recorded during the comparable period in 1998. In particular, the current account-buttressed by strong exports-has strengthened considerably, registering a surplus of US$3.3 billion in the first eight months from a surplus of only US$14 million during the same period a year ago. As a result, we have been able to build up our foreign exchange reserves to a record high of US$14.6 billion as of the end of October. This is equivalent to 4.2 months of imports of goods and payments of services, and is more than enough to cover our short-term external liabilities, even if these are doubled. Apart from being a precautionary measure-particularly against the volatile, short-term capital-our reserve build-up program is also a confidence-building measure. And let me report to you that our external debt continues to be manageable. Total foreign indebtedness amounted to US$48.1 billion as of end-June 1999. While there has been some increase in the aggregate level, the maturity and creditor profiles have improved. The share of short-term debt to total debt has declined from 16.4 percent as of end-1992 to 13.6 percent as of the end of the first half of 1999. Reflecting the judicious sourcing and utilization of foreign borrowings, the debt service burden has dropped through the years: from 17.1 percent in 1992 to 13.5 percent for the first semester of 1999. This means that-dollar for dollar-we are using less resources to service our foreign obligations. Financial Sector Reforms The strength of the Philippine financial system effectively shielded the country from the worst impacts of the regional financial crisis. This strength is evident in the sustained rise in the total resources of the financial system, underpinned by higher deposits and a stronger capital base, as well as in the improvements in banks' asset quality and compliance with several prudential norms. Banks' capital adequacy ratio was recorded at 17.6 percent as of end-June. This was well above the 8 percent standard of the bank for international settlements and the 10 percent statutory requirement. The real estate exposure of commercial banks dropped to 12.3 percent as of end-June 1999 from 13.1 percent as of end-December 1998. Meanwhile, the non-performing loans ratio of commercial banks remains manageable at 13.4 percent as of end-September 1999. Provisioning against loan losses is also adequate, with loan loss reserves equivalent to 5.1 percent of total loans as of end-August 1999. The non-performing loan (NPL) situation is expected to improve as the economy gains further momentum, resulting in increased lending, and as the effects of lower interest rates and relatively stable exchange rates impact positively on the repayment capability of corporates. We have started to see some signs of recovery in bank lending. As of end-September, outstanding loans of commercial banks were still down from last year, but the contraction was miniscule, at 0.15 percent, compared to 3.4 percent in August and 4.8 percent in July. Moreover, outstanding loans registered a 1.1 percent growth on a month-on-month basis. This follows the 2.0 percent month-on-month increase in August, as well as the increases in June and July. Some of the important factors that were responsible for the respectable performance of the banking system include: the long history of financial sector reforms, complemented by appropriate and timely implementation by the authorities of regulatory changes before and during the crisis and the vigilant and close supervision by the banks' major stakeholders. The relatively high equity ratios in Philippine commercial banks have ensured, through stakeholders' rights, that these institutions are managed as sound and profitable entities. Moreover, the management teams of Philippine banks have had prior experience in dealing with the crisis in the Philippine economy in the early 1980s. We also realize the necessity of continuing the structural reform program. Thus, major reform packages have been submitted to the legislature as amendments to the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act. Broadly speaking, the proposed revisions seek to achieve the following: enhance prudential standards; enhance competition in the banking sector; and promote further the independence of the BSP, particularly its ability to effectively conduct monetary policy. Need for Regional Cooperation In my earlier address before the east Asia economic summit, 1 enumerated certain measures that can be adopted at the regional level in order to reduce the chance of future occurrence of a crisis of this magnitude. Inasmuch as international investor opinion can go a long way towards their adoption, let me take the occasion of this forum to re-enumerate some of the main areas that I feel need to be addressed. First, there is need to develop national standards in bank supervision that adhere to international best practices. Collaborative initiatives along this line would reduce systemic risks in global and regional financial markets. Key components of these efforts include the development of accessible data banks on the financial system and of high-quality, credible, and transparent reporting and disclosure standards. In recognition of the importance of these issues, the BSP has enlisted as one of the first of the IMF member countries to enlist in the IMF Special Data Dissemination System (SDDS). While significant progress in international cooperation has been achieved, this is too important a task to be left to national and international organizations alone. Active private sector participation is a requirement for success. Second, the foundation of these efforts to achieve market transparency is the timeliness and accuracy of the data that countries provide the public. This is an important issue to be addressed, as the move to increase the accessibility and speed of availability of financial sector data must not be at the expense of accuracy of information. The risk is that greater openness in information might be attended to by greater volatility in financial markets. In this respect, international conferences such as this present gathering serve as important avenues for linking economic decision makers in the region, both from the government and private sectors. The challenge is therefore for us to utilize for a such as this to come up with concrete vehicles for government-private sector cooperation. Third, it is also important to sustain the surveillance process both globally and regionally. On a global scale, multilateral institutions need to intensify such a process with the cooperative support of the member nations. In this part of the world, regional surveillance should continue under the umbrella of the Asean and the three partners such as China, Japan, and Korea. Peer review is a very useful mechanism of ensuring regional awareness of key developments and possible roadblocks to economic advance. Such a surveillance process indeed buys us time to anticipate the emergence of potential instability and the possibility of contagion. Thank you and good day. ----------------------------------------------- 1 held in Singapore, 20 October 1999

Title: Monetary and Fiscal Policy: Looking Ahead
Occasion: Philippine Association of Hong Kong (PAHK) and Philippine Bankers Club of Hong Kong
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Chief executives, officers and members of the Philippine Association of Hong Kong (PAHK) and the Philippine Bankers Club of Hong Kong (PBHK), good afternoon: Hong Kong is a very suitable place to discuss our country's monetary and fiscal policies. This economic entrepot is a bastion of free market principles; and it therefore serves as a very good setting to present our essentially market-based monetary and fiscal policies. Our meeting this afternoon is also auspicious because we are at such a decisive juncture of the economic recovery of the Philippines when we begin to look ahead to the challenges of the new millennium. But let me preface my remarks this afternoon cautioning you that I will be a one-handed speaker; I will focus on monetary policy and touch on, as necessary, -- in passing -- the acts of the fiscal authorities. Our responsibilities are sufficiently cut and dried that we can easily discern where one should end and the other should begin. Current Economic Policy Current macroeconomic policy aims to foster the recovery and shield against domestic and external shocks. We have had our learning curve flattened by our interesting experiences in the 1990s including the surge in foreign money in 1993-97, the Tequila effect of 1994-95 and the Tom Yang effect of 1997-99. We have kept the course in the two and a half years of the Asian financial crisis. Monetary policy, in particular, has tried to contain inflation while being flexible enough to enable lower interest rates and a stable exchange rate. Fiscal policy, on the other hand, continues to aim to stimulate demand through pump-priming without necessarily crowding out private investment. Recent Economic Results This overall approach produced very good results in 1999, with signs of returning stability and a reviving economy. Our first three quarter data show that growth has indeed rebounded as agriculture continued to perform strongly and manufacturing made a turnaround. Inflation was mostly tame because of ample food supply, and the ten-month average inflation rate of 7.2 percent is quite close to the full-year target of 7 percent. The foreign exchange market was relatively stable in the first three quarters thanks to strong capital inflows. Bank lending has improved, with a smaller rate of decline in September, and domestic demand strengthened, based on data on imports, car sales and power consumption. The recovery was due partly to the accommodative policy adopted in the first semester, with measures to help bring down interest rates combined with fiscal pump-priming to stimulate demand. Monetary stance was afforded greater flexibility because of the subdued inflation trend and the stable foreign exchange market. Actual monetary growth was also significantly below our target ceilings. In a word, conditions were suitable for an easier stance of monetary policy. In the first seven months of 1999, accommodative monetary policy brought down the Reverse Repurchase (RRP) rate to 9 percent in a series of 20 policy rate cuts. The reserve requirement for banks was also cut by a total of 5 percentage points to 12 percent. These measures enabled a decline in both the 91-day Treasury bill rate and bank lending rates. As a precautionary measure, the Bangko Sentral also kept base money and reserve money comfortably below the IMF program ceilings. Meanwhile, expansionary fiscal policy took the form of a P22-billion fiscal stimulus package featured under the 1999 budget. The package set aside some P14 billion for quick-gestating infrastructure projects and some P8 billion for the acceleration of back payments owed to government contractors. It was not entirely smooth sailing, however. Steering the economic ship through the Charybdis waters of the Asian crisis would be everything but smooth. Our fiscal authorities also have to deal with revenue shortfalls that threatened the fiscal targets. To cope with this, policymakers resorted to virtual belt-tightening by cutting down on non-essential expenditures. Also, in July, in response to short-term foreign exchange volatility, the Bangko Sentral switched to a neutral monetary stance and kept policy rates steady. As external factors such as the weakening Thai baht put pressure on the peso, our neutral stance allowed us to closely study the impact of accommodative policy before deciding to relax the stance further. Since then, the currency market has re-stabilized, allowing us to make another 25-basis point cut in overnight RRP rates to 8.75 percent effective November 3. Earlier, we adopted the two-tier approach in our interest rate policy with the end result of achieving lower interest payments of the Bangko Sentral to the banks. Our aim is to induce banks to lend out their excess liquid funds, instead of parking them in the overnight window of the Bangko Sentral. In this way we hope to sustain the improvement in credit growth. Given these recent economic developments and expected turn of events for the rest of the year and the next, we believe that at this point, our banks, while watching their bottomlines, would need to be more aggressive to protect their present market share of the credit market. We have reached the lowest point of the economic cycle, and the only way for the various indicators of demand is up. The banks, coming from the supply side, should therefore assume the leadership in optimism. It is up to them to break the economic stalemate. We are, therefore, encouraged by the trend in credit growth. More and more banks have started to open their doors to borrowers and investors. In due time, we should see the fruits of this positive trend. PRESENT AND FUTURE POLICY STANCE The question now is, what is our present stance? And looking ahead, do we need to modify our existing one? To begin with, policy actions in the near future -- such as the decision to further ease the monetary stance -- will indeed depend on the final shape of the economic outlook and on prevailing market conditions. For this year, we are targeting an average inflation rate of 7 percent and a GNP growth rate of 3.5 to 4 percent. Both goals are well within reach. In 2000, we expect economic conditions to improve further as the recovery gets underway. GDP growth is expected to be stronger, reaching 4 to 5 percent for the year. Improved agriculture performance and a stable foreign exchange market will help temper inflation in 2000 to an average of 6 to 7 percent. There are a number of challenges, of course, and further stimulation may be required to help achieve our broad economic targets. Over the next few quarters, we will need to continue to nurture the industrial sector and make sure that the turnaround in manufacturing is sustained. We would also like to see bank lending strengthen further and convince our local banks to gradually ease their cautious lending stance. And most important, we should be able to sustain our actions to intensify our reform agenda in banking, in tax administration as well as in corporate and public governance. The crisis has taught us to be humble for change. The November rate cut reflects our belief that there is still some room for monetary easing, particularly since average inflation remains close to the year's overall target. Monetary policy will continue to support growth while keeping inflation at bay, but further relaxation will be done carefully, in order to sustain the stability of the currency. To put it briefly, our monetary stance will remain cautious yet flexible. The art of monetary policy is essentially a juggling act; you try to keep several balls in the air all at once. We try to balance the objective of stimulating the economy with the goals of price stability and exchange rate stability. That means taking it one step at a time. This means we are not targeting all monetary goals at the same time. Our monetary instruments are limited. Similarly, if we may speak about it, fiscal policy is also trying to balance the need to stimulate private demand with the goal of fiscal prudence. Hence the fiscal stimulus package was combined with some belt-tightening. Unfortunately, the target budget deficit of P85.3 billion this year may still be exceeded. Personally, however, I don't think that should be the main concern. To my mind, at this early stage of economic recovery, we can afford to accommodate some deficits, at least temporarily, if it would also mean having increased economic activity. At any rate, fiscal pressures may begin to ease soon. Revenue collection is expected to improve as economic growth resumes normal levels. More importantly, because of the more favorable economic scenario, there will be less need for government pump-priming. Therefore, fiscal policy in 2000 will be slightly less expansionary compared to this year. Instead, the main focus will be on fiscal consolidation. As the economy continues to recover, authorities need to focus on sustainability in the long haul. For the fiscal sector, the main concern will be balancing the budget in the medium term, say within the next two or three years. There are two key strategies to do this. First is strengthening the revenue base by improving tax administration. Higher revenues will reduce the deficit and help pay for priority projects and programs. The fiscal authorities also plan to rationalize the investment incentive structure by narrowing down the list of tax and duty exemptions. The second fiscal strategy is expenditure control, or cutting down on non-essential spending. With these measures, authorities hope to narrow down the deficit to P62.5 billion in 2000 and hopefully reduce it to zero later on. Ladies and gentlemen, I took the liberty of venturing onto fiscal ground. I wanted to put across at this important gathering the crucial role of a healthy fiscal sector to the conduct of an independent monetary policy. To the extent that the fiscal balance is in good shape, the Bangko Sentral can continue focusing on its primary mandate of keeping inflation low and the banking system robust. These are the basic elements of vibrant economic growth. Short of this scenario, however, we might also have to watch for a possible current account deficit and a weak currency. The curse of high interest rates could very well be again on our laundry list of priority concerns. At this point, we have fundamentally put this behind us. And the challenge therefore is to ensure that it stays behind us as we strengthen our path to economic recovery. THE CHALLENGES AHEAD Part of our job as policymakers is anticipating and responding to emerging issues on both the domestic and external front.
