On the home front, the major concern will be the potential inflationary pressure from rising oil prices and adjustments in wages and transport costs. Here there should be less concern since we expect that strong agricultural output will help keep down prices for the basic food items, which comprise about 55 percent of the CPI. This was what happened in the October inflation data. More important, greater competition is expected to water down the inflationary impact of higher petroleum prices, transport and wage adjustments. On the external front, we will need to watch for large fluctuations in the regional currency market. Further adverse shifts in regional sentiment cannot be ruled out completely yet, and we must remain alert to instability in other Asian countries. Over the medium term, market expectations of rising foreign interest rates, particularly in the US, may prompt investors to reallocate their portfolio to foreign assets, thereby affecting short-term movements of the peso and limiting the extent to which interest rates can be brought down. The main lesson from these challenges that I have outlined to you is the importance of prudent but forward-looking policy that keeps a sharp eye on new developments. Monetary policy will continue to be cautious yet flexible, and fiscal policy, as we read it, will focus on consolidation. The basic overall thrust is the same: we will try to nurse the recovery but preserve stability and guard against potential shocks to the economy. In the old days when trains ran on steam, the train engineer kept the train running smoothly by putting coal into the boiler. We have already managed to get the train going, and it is running steadily. We have done our part and will continue to do so. And let me add that I hope that you will come on board and join us as we push full steam ahead into the new millennium. And I assure you, the coalfed locomotive is only metaphorical; when you board the Philippine train, it will run on our people's ingenuity and productivity and global competitiveness. Thank you and good afternoon. (Note: Philippine Association of Hong Kong (PAHK) and Philippine Bankers Club of Hong Kong (PBHK), 6 December 1999, Conrad Hilton Hotel, Hong Kong)

Title: THE PHILIPPINES: ECONOMIC RECOVERY WITH A STRONGER BANKING SYSTEM
Occasion: 3rd General Membership Meeting, MART-FOREX-TOAP
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: INTRODUCTION Officers and members of the Money Market Association of the Philippines, the Foreign Exchange Association of the Philippines, and the Trust Officers Association of the Philippines, distinguished guests, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good evening. It is not often that a speaker is able to address three organizations at the same time. This three-in-one affair is also very convenient since it collapses what would have been three dinners into one, thus helping me keep my waistline in shape while requiring me to speak only once. This arrangement is also efficient since it cuts travel time and lessens the ordeal of going through Manila's traffic jams. This gathering thus bespeaks good planning. Given this propitious start and the impressive roster of participants, this evening's activity should be a stimulating and fruitful undertaking. I am indeed honored to speak before major players in the country's money, foreign exchange and capital markets. Developments since July 1997 have brought to the fore the importance of a stable currency market in the efficient functioning of the economy on the path to sustained growth. We are all painfully aware--on both the professional and personal levels--of the costs inflicted by currency attacks on Asia's economic tigers. The Asian crisis also highlighted the importance of well-functioning money and capital markets in achieving broad-based economic growth. For instance, there is wide agreement with the view that one of the causes of the region-wide crisis is the underdevelopment of the capital market, which encouraged not only over-investment in the money and asset markets but also over-reliance on short-term bank resources. The resulting asset bubbles placed the countries' financial systems at risk, some more so than others. It is true that the Philippine financial system was relatively unscathed by the recent financial storm. Though sustaining some cuts and bruises here and there, the system remained essentially sound and unbowed, as prudential measures adopted much earlier supported the viability of the system. Thus, our financial system did not have to undertake the scale of restructuring that its counterparts in neighboring countries had--and for some time still, will have--to go through. Nor did the Philippine government--and thus the tax-paying public--have to pay the enormous costs associated with such a restructuring. However, I have never been one for self-congratulations. Aside from a typical Filipino's aversion to such a trait, I think it is a dangerous stance to have, since it could mean that you are letting your guard down. Let me assure you, therefore, that we are resolute in our commitment to further strengthen our financial system. This would help ensure that financial resources are efficiently intermediated, thus providing the wherewithal for our shared goal of sustained and strong economic growth. Let me say that we are fortunate to have strong foundations to build on. Allow me then to give you a brief exposition on the Philippine economy. RECENT ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS The country's recent economic performance bodes well for its prospects in the near term. During the first half of this year, output performance was better than expected, with the real gross national product (GNP) expanding by 2.9 percent. Growth was underpinned by the strong expansion of the agricultural sector and the renewed strength of the services sector. Moreover, the contraction in industry appears to have been arrested, with manufacturing in particular showing signs of resurgence. The improving economies of Japan and Europe as well as the recovery of many of the crisis-afflicted emerging countries in Asia should impact favorably on our growth prospects, even if the much-hailed strengthening of the U.S. economy should simmer down. Consumer prices have remained broadly stable, with the inflation rate for October settling at 5.4 percent, for an average of 7.2 percent during the first ten months of the year. We have been able to promote growth in a low-inflation environment by reducing interest rates to low and sustainable levels. Interest rates have been on a steady downtrend since the height of the financial crisis. The benchmark 91-day Treasury bill rate was 8.9 percent at the last auction (15 November), much lower than the 15.3 percent average for 1998. There continues to be broad stability in the foreign exchange market, consistent with the country's stable macroeconomic fundamentals and strong external payments position. Market price volatility has dropped significantly in 1999 relative to what it was in 1997 and 1998. This was due in large part to the measures implemented by the authorities to stabilize the foreign exchange market as well as to the credibility of their commitment to the floating exchange rate system. The external payments position is more than comfortable. Surpluses in both the current account and the overall balance of payments were recorded for the first seven months of the year. A robust export performance was a major factor behind this trend. Altogether, these developments have allowed the Bangko Sentral to further increase its foreign exchange reserves to US$14.6 billion as of end-October this year from only US$8.8 billion at end-1997. We see the build-up in our foreign reserves as both a precautionary and confidence-building measure, and we intend to add to these reserves some more by year-end. Our external debt continues to be manageable. While the level of foreign indebtedness has risen to US$48.1 billion as of end-June 1999, its maturity profile has continued to improve. The share of short-term debt to total debt has declined, and, dollar for dollar, we are using less resources to service our foreign obligations in 1999 relative to earlier years. All these developments lower the vulnerability of our external payments position to possible abrupt changes in the global financial environment. The fiscal position bears close watching, though. It has been reported that the P85 billion programmed deficit for 1999 has already been exceeded in the first ten months. However, let me cite three factors that could mollify your concern about the fiscal picture. First, the government has observed that the financing for this year's deficit had already been secured; thus there should be no undue pressure on domestic interest rates from this end. Second, the government went into deficit spending deliberately to pump-prime the economy and provide the safety nets needed to cushion the social costs of the crisis. Third, it went into deficit spending with the intention that such a policy will have a limited shelf-life. The government expects that, with the revival of economic growth, fiscal consolidation can be realized starting mid-2002. MONETARY AND FINANCIAL SECTOR POLICIES In terms of our monetary policy stance, we will continue to promote growth in a low-inflation environment through the reduction in interest rates to low but sustainable levels. Operationally, this means that we are committed to providing sufficient liquidity for the strengthening economy, which is expected to grow at around 3.5-4 percent this year. Moreover, last November 3, we trimmed our overnight borrowing rate by 25 basis points to 8.75 percent. With inflation within the programmed level and monetary aggregates comfortably below program ceilings, we have adequate flexibility in monetary policy. We expect that the reduction in our overnight policy interest rate would create a more normal yield curve, and encourage more active bank lending activity, which is a necessary condition for the resurgence of economic growth. Having said all of these, it must also be pointed out that we will calibrate policy interest rates in the event of marked changes in the external interest rate environment, and significant shifts in domestic inflation and exchange rate conditions. As a channel of monetary policy, the Philippine financial system remains sound and healthy. Not once during the crisis has there been any concern about a possible disruption of the financial intermediation process. The system's strength is evident in the continued increase in its aggregate resources, the compliance with prudential norms, and the fact that while asset quality--though weakened somewhat--remains manageable and compares well with those of other countries in the region. The quality of the loan portfolio of the country's commercial banks improved significantly as of end-September as non-performing loans dropped to 13.4 percent of total outstanding loans from 14.4 percent in August. The sharp decline in the industry's non-performing loans bolstered overall asset quality. This significant improvement in banks' asset quality is expected to continue in the coming months as banks build up further their loan books and as bad loans are worked out. This owes in large part to the sustained implementation of major financial reforms. The reform efforts included, among others, measures to improve the quality of bank management, increase capital requirements, improve bank asset quality, enhance transparency in the system, and align prudential rules with international norms. Let me add that we continue to take an activist stance in these matters, in order to be attuned to the dynamic mode of financial markets. In particular, measures have been proposed to amend the general banking act and the new central bank act with a view to enabling the Monetary Board to adopt internationally accepted standards relating to risk-based capital requirements and to clearly define unsound banking practices, among other things. We also continue to focus on structural reforms that will make our banking system more market oriented. Towards this end, we have encouraged mergers and consolidations in the banking system to promote globally competitive and more efficient banks. The prudential supervision of financial institutions is crucial in maintaining the safety and soundness of the financial system during normal times. But it is during periods of strong pressure on financial markets that the stability of the system is really put to the test. Just as financial systems under inadequate prudential supervision would tend to be more vulnerable to the adverse effects of a crisis, financial institutions in those jurisdictions where supervisory authorities have succeeded in implementing appropriate safeguards are likely to be affected less and come out of the crisis much better than poorly supervised financial institutions. TOWARDS BETTER RISK MANAGEMENT However, there is still much to be done in bringing about a smoothly functioning and strong financial system that can advance economic growth. In particular, a key lesson from the recent financial crisis is the importance of transparency in reforming financial institutions. Greater transparency is expected to reduce problems arising from asymmetric information by ensuring the free flow of information to all market players so that risk can be borne by appropriate parties. For this reason, I commend recent efforts to develop a system of risk rating of Philippine banks. This risk rating system can embody the application of the best financial theory in managing our banks and, in particular, in managing levels of risk and, therefore, capital requirements. In this task, cooperation and dialogue between the private sector, particularly the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) and the Bangko Sentral is indispensable. Just last week, the BSP and the BAP organized a conference on risk ratings, and hopefully, the discussions there will go some distance in encouraging the BAP to take the lead in developing the risk rating concept for the Philippine banking system. Going further, at the 29th Asean Banking Council meeting held last week, we proposed the establishment of an Asean-based credit-rating firm. As you know, banks in the region currently depend on US- or Europe-based risk evaluators, which may not be quite familiar with the region. By contrast, a region-based credit-rating firm would be more sensitive to the nature, characteristics and practices of regional banks, which have more or less comparable standards. Moreover, for improved risk management, the BSP will start requiring foreign and local banks to renew their expanded derivatives licenses every year, commencing in the first quarter of next year at the earliest. With risks getting exponentially greater owing to the dynamic nature of the derivatives market, it is vital that banks with licenses pose no danger to the soundness of the banking system. The BSP is continuously reviewing current rules and would adopt additional regulations and guidelines concerning accounting, booking and evaluation of risks. Y2K-RELATED LIQUIDITY MEASURES We are hoping that the Y2K crossover is going to be a smooth business-as-usual event, We have nevertheless set in place contingency measures in case these are needed. To provide assistance to banking institutions in relation to any Y2K-related liquidity problem, the Monetary Board of the Bangko Sentral has recently approved a menu of schemes which includes (1) the establishment of an Emergency Year 2000 loan facility, (2) the establishment of a special repurchase facility, (3) the lengthening of the period for compliance with the reserve position, and (4) the lowering of the reserve requirement on inter-bank loans from one percent to zero percent. The Emergency Year 2000 loan facility, meanwhile, is intended to provide temporary back-up assistance to banks in the event that they are unable to obtain funding from the market to meet any unusual increase in liquidity demand during the millennium changeover. It is believed that the very availability of a special Y2K financing facility could be a reassuring factor to help forestall potential liquidity problems. This facility is consistent with the relevant provisions of R.A. No. 7653, which state that the Bangko Sentral can provide liquidity to the banking system in periods of national and/or local emergency which directly threaten monetary and banking stability. Availments under this facility is allowed from 1 December 1999 to 31 January 2000. The pre-qualification period to gain quick-disbursing access to this facility has been set for the period on or before 26 November. The special repurchase facility shall be open during the period 15 December 1999-15 January 2000 for qualified borrowers. Acceptable collateral for availments under this facility includes peso-denominated government securities (under a relaxed valuation schedule) and selected foreign currency-denominated government securities. The relaxed valuation will allow banks to borrow greater amount from this facility. The Monetary Board also approved the lengthening of the compliance period for reserve position to cover the reserve period 17 December 1999 - 6 January 2000. The objective of this policy measure is to spread out the time required for banks to cover their reserves, thus reducing the pressure on interest rates. Meanwhile, the reserve requirement of interbank loans was also reduced from one percent to zero percent, consistent with the broad policy thrust of the Bangko Sentral to reduce banks' intermediation cost and bring down interest rates. Moreover, the policy will not significantly affect liquidity since interbank transactions involve only a transfer of funds among banks. The Monetary Board emphasized that all these privileges, accommodations and facilities will be made available to ease whatever liquidity pressure may be occasioned by the millennium crossover. Proceeds of availments are not, therefore, to be used for speculative investments. CONCLUSION The mood is cautiously upbeat for the Philippines. There is much to look forward to, but also much to be prepared for. Our increasing integration with the world economy has provided numerous and major benefits to the country. Yet, it also entails new set of challenges. The ability of the financial system to efficiently intermediate funds, always a concern, assumes greater importance as flows through the system increase with globalization and growth. Against such a backdrop, I believe that the best posture that can be adopted is to be aware of the opportunities and the challenges, and to be prepared to always grasp the opportunities and turn challenges into yet new opportunities. The past two years and a half of the Asian crisis were both challenges and opportunities for us; we did not let go of the opportunities to strengthen our macroeconomy and the banking sector, yet the difficult times also forced us precisely to undertake measures that would help us avoid another of those crisis episodes. This underscores the synergy between the government and the private sector in developing and strengthening of financial markets. This evening's gathering provides another opportunity for you in the private sector to explore the possibilities by which this collaboration can be further enhanced, in support of our common vision of sustained economic development where free enterprise can thrive. Thank you and good evening. (Note: 3rd General Membership Meeting of the Money Market Association of the Philippines (MART) held jointly with the Foreign Exchange Association of the Philippines (FOREX) and Trust Officers Association of the Philippines (TOAP), 22 November 1999, Hotel Intercontinental, Makati City)

Title: The Bangko Sentral and the International Capital Market
Location: ABN-AMRO Bank, Shagri-La Hotel, Makati City
Occasion: Signing Ceremony for the US$400M BSP Syndicated Credit Facility
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: I am very pleased to see the successful completion of this joint undertaking today. For the record, the Bangko Sentral has tapped the international debt market only five times since its establishment in July 1993. During my term, the first issuance was made in August 1999, involving 8.5% notes worth US$300 million. But I consider this one as a milestone because it is the first facility to be arranged under my watch. The strong response of our lending investors to our latest fund raising exercise is much appreciated. This is more than indicated by the over-subscription in commitments that resulted in the increase in the facility amount from the initial US$250 million to US $400 million. I must also say that I am satisfied with the terms covering the facility. This underscores investor confidence in the continued soundness and resiliency of the Philippine economy. That this is the case has been validated by the consistent and steady credit ratings that we received from major rating agencies even at the height of the Asian financial crisis when most of our Asian neighbors suffered downgrades. Indeed, I consider this positive investor response as an encouragement to the Bangko Sentral to continue in its present policy direction and to keep on working to provide the most appropriate environment for the sustained recovery of the economy. And I am pleased to say that our efforts are now bearing very good fruit. The key economic indicators speak for themselves. Real GNP has rebounded. Inflation has been reduced from double to single digit levels, despite the recent hike in the prices of oil products. Interest rates are down and remain reasonable. Bank lending is picking up and the banking system continues to be healthy and strong. The exchange rate remains broadly stable. Our exports are soaring, our bop is sustaining a huge surplus and as a result, our international reserves are breaking record levels. I must therefore say that the greatest compliment of the market is to lend us the rope when we feel that it is still long enough. This is one of those good ironies surrounding the decisions of countries to borrow. Ladies and gentlemen, I assure you that the proceeds of this facility will be put to good use to enable the Bangko Sentral to keep the monetary and banking environment conducive to doing business in the country. In closing, I would like to extend my thanks to the joint coordinating arrangers and to all those who collaborated with us in completing this undertaking. Thank you and good day. (Note: Signing Ceremony for the US$400M BSP Syndicated Credit Facility, ABN-AMRO Bank, 19 November 1999, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Banking Reform and the Role of the Thrift Banking Industry
Occasion: Signing Ceremony for the US$400M BSP Syndicated Credit Facility
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Mr. Dionisio C. Ong, president of the Chamber of Thrift Banks, officers and members of the chamber, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, a pleasant day! First of all, thank you for this opportunity to be in touch with you again. We at the Bangko Sentral always appreciate having a close and active communication with the banking community. On the occasion, let me try to assess where we are now on the banking reform process and what that may imply for the thrift banking industry. Recent developments As you are well aware, the entire banking community, including the thrift banking industry, underwent significant stress during the 1997-1998 Asian financial crisis. Those effects continue to linger despite recent signs of economic recovery. Fortunately, our banking system has been quite resilient. It is now in the process of consolidation that will provide a strong basis for renewed growth once the economy fully recovers. Looking at the thrift banking industry as a whole, I think we should take heart in some recent improvements. As of end-June 1999, total resources of thrift banks already recorded a 4.4 percent annual growth. Although modest, this still represents a complete turnaround from the 5.8 percent decline previously. It is also a pleasant surprise to note that the total number of thrift bank offices actually showed a net increase of 22 offices between June 1998 and June 1999. Total deposits likewise increased by 3.8 percent and profitability was restored as the combined loss of P 224 million a year ago was turned around into a net income of P 990 million as of end-June 1999. In terms of loan quality, there are clear signs that at least the situation has stabilized. The industry NPL ratio stood at 16.7 percent, almost the same as last year's. Loan loss coverage also improved significantly to about 34 percent from just 23 percent last year and is now roughly at par with commercial banks. Nevertheless, overall asset quality remains a problem as evidenced by the steady increase in acquired assets. Thrift banks also enjoyed high capitalization levels relative to risk assets equivalent to almost 21 percent. This compares with the 10 percent statutory requirement. However, the aggregate story conceals some very real problems especially affecting a handful of problem banks and the relatively smaller thrift banks that have experienced a declining asset and deposit base, operating losses and capital deficiencies in today's tough banking environment. But the flip-side to this is the fact that many thrift banks are actually on very sound and solid financial footing. Yes, the critical core of the thrift banking system is fundamentally healthy. For the record, as of end-June 1999, 74 out of the 120 operating thrift banks have already complied with the latest prescribed minimum capitalization requirements. Right now, these are P 250 million for thrift banks based in metro manila and P40 million for those based outside metro manila. And by December 2000, these go up further to P400 million and P 64 million respectively. Of the 46 banks still unable to meet the new standards so far, 22 intend to convert into rural banks. These thrift banks are mostly based outside metro manila. The remaining banks are either negotiating for merger and/or acquisition or have submitted a capital build-up plan based on commitments from shareholders to infuse new capital. The Changing Banking Environment Let me now stand back to look at the evolving overall financial environment and try to situate the thrift banking industry within that. One of the most important lessons of the Asian financial crisis is the need to promote and maintain a sound financial system if economic growth is to be sustainable. On this basis, we have intensified our own financial reforms, even if that may be painful in the short-run, to ensure that our financial system remains competitive and efficient and so that it will continue to retain investors' confidence. We are hoping that the reform process would pave the way for an even more resilient and effective banking system complemented by a vigorous domestic capital market. Together these can more fully meet the complex and enormous financing needs of our developing economy. Within the banking industry, the reforms are taking deep root. Already, it has spurred unprecedented changes that are changing the face of Philippine banking. In the commercial banking industry, which will continue to be the core of the banking industry, we are steadily moving to a scenario of fewer but more financially powerful main banks that are better able to compete in a world of more open borders. That logic is the most compelling driving force behind the current wave of bank mergers and acquisitions. The Bangko Sentral certainly welcomes this development and we have been actively promoting it through our regulatory policies. However, this is not to say that there will be no place in the evolving financial firmament for smaller banks especially thrift banks. Ideally, what will emerge is a backbone of big banks whose services will be well complemented by smaller specialist players that can more effectively cover important niche markets that have their own unique needs. Important niches for example include consumer lending, housing loans, small business loans, agri-business loans, as well as niches based on specific geographic markets. This is a role that the thrift banking industry should be able to play very well especially given certain regulatory advantages that are already existing. In fact, many players have already identified this opportunity. Looking at the thrift banking industry today, many large domestic and even foreign banks as well as other financial service organizations have already established their own thrift banking subsidiaries as part of broader corporate strategy to service a wide range of client markets. At present, there are 18 such thrift bank subsidiaries representing just 15 percent of the number of thrift banks but they already account for more than 40 percent of total banking offices and about half of the total resources of the entire thrift banking industry. For the rest of the thrift banking industry, composed of smaller and independent banks, you will need more than ever to carefully define your place in the market and muster the necessary resources to compete effectively and survive. In a sense, the Bangko Sentral's increased minimum capitalization requirement, apart from the prudential aspects, concretely reinforces the market signal that may have been missed by some players. As a result, marginal banks must now decide in accordance with the set time frame whether to merge or be acquired, to put up more capital, or to compete in another more appropriate division. Admittedly, these may not be very easy choices especially for banks that have long been used to an easy and quiet life. But it is no longer realistic nor constructive to think of banking life that way. Whether we like or not, the business of banking has changed irreversibly and you must step up to meet your clients' higher expectations for greater safety, for better returns, and for more choices. As far as the Bangko Sentral is concerned, it is vitally important that we are able to shape our own banking policies in line with the public's expectations. This has been our primary guide in instituting various reforms that promote financial strength, better management, greater transparency and more accountability. And you can expect that we will continue to move in this direction. A Commitment to Monetary Stability Let me conclude my speech today with another critical lesson learned from the Asian financial crisis. And this is the importance of ensuring basic macroeconomic stability in protecting the health of the financial system. We all know how destabilizing very high interest rates and a large peso depreciation can be to the banking system and to the whole economy. For this reason, we are determined to act pro-actively on monetary policy to ensure continuous monetary and price stability even if sometimes this involves nudging up interest rates a little bit. This is the duty of an independent central bank. We are of course well aware that the economy is currently in a fragile state of recovery. For this reason, it is vitally important that we all cooperate to ensure the sustainability of the fiscal position and support government's efforts to keep the fiscal deficit within reasonable levels. This is the key to lower interest rates that are sustainable. It is also the critical battle that will determine our credibility and our ability to keep the delicate financial balance. Thank you and good day. (Note: General Membership Luncheon Meeting, Chamber of Thrift Banks, 18 November 1999, Shangri-La Hotel, Makati City)

Title: Commitment to Banking Reforms: A Pillar of Asian Recovery
Location: New World Renaissance Hotel, Makati City
Occasion: 29th ASEAN Banking Council Meeting, ASEAN Banking Council
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction Mr. Secretary General Tay Kay Chye, distinguished officers and members of the ASEAN Banking Council, honored guests, ladies and gentlemen: At the onset, I would like to congratulate the council for its many accomplishments. Judging from the steady increase in its membership, it continues to demonstrate its vitality and relevance in a period of sweeping change in ASEAN banking. I am glad to note the presence of the new members representing Laos and Cambodia. I understand that preparations are also underway so that Myanmar will be represented in the next council meeting. When this happens, the council shall have all the banking associations of the Ten (10) ASEAN nations at the turn of the century. This provides the council a golden opportunity to further enhance cooperation among member banking associations to promote faster regional growth in a globalized environment. The Tasks at Hand The Asian financial crisis may be abating but greater challenges still lie ahead as the globalization of banking markets gathers a new momentum in the third millennium. The greatest challenge is in making banks evolve along with the society it serves. Doing so would ensure that they remain efficient and relevant catalysts for growth. A decisive follow-through on banking and corporate reforms is crucial for sustained recovery. Structural weaknesses which were brought to the fore by the Asian crisis should not remain unresolved as these would only impede recovery prospects and could lead to a repeat of the recent regional experience. Asia Poised for a Resumption of Rapid Growth The probability of putting Asia back on a fast-growth track is high considering the following factors: (1) The general socio-political stability prevailing in the region; (2) The limited inflationary pressures which were different from those seen in Latin America in the 1980s; (3 The continued savings mobilization despite the economic slack; (4) The enhanced ability of our banks to capture these savings; (5) The strength of government balance sheets in absorbing their banking system's losses; and (6) The obvious commitment and courage of governments in reforming and restructuring the region's financial architecture. Our prospects are made even brighter with the improving trends of currencies, interest rates, a recovery of confidence in banking systems, and improved liquidity in the financial system of the member countries. Policy Directions for the Philippine Banking System In the Philippines, we are continuing to build upon the many banking reform initiatives that have been started even before the Asian financial crisis struck. Our main goal is to promote a sound, stable and globally competitive financial system anchored on prudent risk management practices. Our major thrust in this regard is two-pronged. First, we are strengthening the legislative framework; and second, we are adopting internationally accepted practices into our supervisory processes. The major legislative reforms are to be effected mainly through the amendment of both the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank act. The major changes involve: » Providing the legal basis for the consolidated supervision of banks; » Lifting the restriction on Bangko Sentral's authority to examine banks on-site which is presently limited to only once every 12 months; » Providing legal protection to supervisors in the conduct of their duties; » Further strengthening the framework for failure resolution and ensuring speedy settlement of potential problems; » Raising fines and penalties for non-compliance with prescribed prudential requirements, as well as adopting a mechanism for prompt corrective action; and » Clarifying conditions for access to the BSP's lender-of-last resort facility. The proposed amendments will further enhance the Bangko Sentral's independence. The monetary board will have the necessary authority to adopt internationally accepted standards of banking operations, including those related to capital adequacy requirements. The creation of stronger and globally competitive institutions anchored on sound risk management practices shall be facilitated through the progressive increase in minimum capitalization and encouragement of bank consolidations. We are also promoting greater efficiency through competition. In this regard, we are considering allowing the entry of more foreign banks, especially through the acquisition of weak and undercapitalized banks, through appropriate changes in legislation. We need banks which have the expertise in intermediating large volume of funds as well as in responding to the growing demands of their clients. Furthermore, we need banks that can offer superior financial advice and services. We need banks that have the capability to operate confidently and efficiently across borders. Complementary Reforms In addition to the restructuring of the banking sector, we have also embarked on the broadening and deepening reforms in the domestic capital market. The reforms involve the strengthening of the regulatory framework for securities and the strengthening of the debt resolution process. The taxation framework on financial transactions and instruments are also currently under review to ease the tax burden of financial intermediation and to promote a more level playing field. Consequently, these should facilitate the introduction of new financial instruments for trading and investments and the development of institutions that will harness savings and channel them into investments. Capital market reforms are essential in reducing our reliance on the banking system for financing development. Our experience during the recent regional crisis showed us clearly the danger of this over reliance. Outlook for the Economy As the Philippine economy continues to make progress under its economic and financial program, the country's banking sector is expected to perform even better in the near future. The first semester economic performance has so far been encouraging. Our real gross national product exceeded expectations as it expanded by 2.9 percent in the first half of 1999 from the 0.1 percent growth in 1998. We continue to keep inflation under control. Inflation rate settled at 5.7 percent in September, for an average of 7.4 percent during the first three quarters of the year. We have also been successful in stabilizing the peso. The volatility of the exchange rate was lessened in 1999 compared to that of 1997 and 1998. We have also continued to sustain prudent monetary management to provide sufficient liquidity to the economy. The benchmark 91-day treasury bill rate is currently at around 8.8 percent. This is much lower than the 15.3 percent average for 1998. We have a relatively strong balance of payments. As a result of the robust growth in export averaging 14.7, the surplus in current account rose to US$2.5 billion from a deficit of US$111 million for the same period last year. The balance of payments surplus was US$ 2.8 billion during the first seven months of 1999. Consequently, our gross international reserves are again back at all-time high levels. Finally, we managed to maintain the stability and promote growth of the Philippine financial system during and after the crisis. The steady improvement in bank asset quality, capital adequacy ratio, liquidity and profitability manifest its strength. Concluding Remarks As a final note, let me call on the support of your council in vigorously promoting the restructuring of the Asian banking and financial system. Your steadfast commitment for continuous reforms of banking sectors will be the single most important contribution to regional prosperity. Thank you and more power to your future undertakings! (Note: 29th ASEAN Banking Council Meeting,13 November 1999, New World Renaissance Hotel, Makati City)

Title: The Bangko Sentral and the Banking System
Occasion: Induction of Officers and Board of Trustees, Clearing Officers Club
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: It gives me great pleasure to be invited to the Induction of the Officers and Board of Trustees of the Clearing Officers Club, Inc. Indeed, occasions like this always evoke new beginnings and great expectations. At the same time, they remind us of new challenges and of course, whether one welcomes them or not, additional responsibilities. I can say these with conviction because four months ago, I was precisely in the same situation. When I took my oath in Malacañang as the new Bangko Sentral Governor last July, it was a new beginning for me. From international banking with Citibank and domestic banking with PCIBank, I have made that important changeover from the supervised to the supervisor. And I can assure you at this point that I find the change in my career very exciting. I am quite familiar with the script and the subtext of our market players on the other side of the fence. I've been there. Yet having said that, in the four months that I have chaired the Monetary Board, what I realized most of all is the awesome responsibility of having to pull the levers of monetary policy with the full recognition of their implications on both markets and people. When I accepted the mantle of leadership from Governor Singson, he has intimated to me this truth, but it is only now that I am beginning to appreciate every grain of monetary policy. And so, during the last couple of months, I learned the hard truth behind the goal of preserving the policy independence of the Bangko Sentral. The episode was the period when interest rates were plummeting beyond those levels consistent with market fundamentals, while the peso was weakening because of adverse shifts in regional conditions. On the issue of interest rate, the BSP maintained the importance of keeping such price variable market-determined. We dread the day when market players would refuse to touch financial instruments of savings and investments whether public or private, knowing that they scarcely reflect market sentiments. On the issue of the exchange rate, your monetary authorities kept their hands off the market even as the peso hovered around P41 to a dollar. We believed, and we were proved correct by events, that the pressures on the currency were regional and temporary. Thus, not long after, the weakness of the peso diminished, consistent with our strong balance of payments. Thus today, I encourage the Clearing Officers Club of the Philippines to maintain the pure ideals of your organization. The clearing officers club was organized to promote professionalism among its members. This is done thru intensive study of established bank clearing procedures and functions. In the process, you are fulfilling a key role in the overall intermediation function of the banking system. When the clearing of checks is not efficiently done, the banking system suffers. We all know that the backbone of the banking system is the integrity and efficiency of the payment and settlement system. It is the link that connects the banks with one another and the banks with the public. Everyday, thousands of checks worth billions of pesos are drawn and cleared through the banking system. It is your main responsibility to ensure that the transactions underlying these checks are correctly accounted for on a timely basis. This is your call, this is your mandate. On this you will be challenged and will be expected to perform. On the part of the Bangko Sentral, we fully support the activities of your organization. In fact, in case of checks drawn within Metro Manila, the clearing office is right in the BSP complex. The Bangko Sentral, in cooperation with the bankers association of the Philippines and the Philippine Clearing House Corporation, has also been working to build up the electronic capability of our payment system. Of course, this is not only in preparation for the Y2K compliance of the banking system, but also for the long-term goal of enhancing the payment system in the Philippines. Financial intermediation can only be as effective as the completion of the whole financial settlement loop. Focusing on the Y2K issue, let me advise you that the Bangko Sentral is addressing this not only in terms of its externally-supported systems but also of its in-house maintained systems. As regulator of the banking industry, the BSP is also devoting significant efforts and resources to ensure the Y2K preparedness of the Philippine banking system. It monitors the banks' Y2K readiness by conducting on site verification of their Y2K efforts. To enhance monitoring, a banking industry year 2000 task force was created, headed by the BSP, and composed of representatives from the bankers association of the Philippines, the Chamber of Thrift Banks and the Rural Bankers Association of the Philippines. Close coordination is also being maintained with the Presidential Commission on Year 2000 Compliance and other regulatory bodies, including other banking supervisory authorities around the globe to address cross-border Y2K issues. And so, in closing, I would say that the Bangko Sentral and the COCI are not really completely distinct and separate entities. We have common goals that keep us connected. The most important and basic of which is to keep the banking system efficient and effective channel of monetary policy. I challenge you today, as I was challenged before, to muster your collective spirit to uphold the pure ideals of your organization. You can never be wrong when you pursue your mandated goals. Congratulations to the new officers and the members of the Board of Trustees of the Clearing Officers Club, Inc. Thank you. (Note: Induction of Officers and Board of Trustees, Clearing Officers Club, Inc., 2 November 1999, Mandarin Oriental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: The BSP's Short-and Medium-Term Plans
Occasion: Silver Anniversary, Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Distinguished officers and members of the Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines, honored guests, ladies and gentlemen: Let me first congratulate the members of the association on your silver anniversary. It gives me great pleasure to celebrate this special occasion with you and share some of my thoughts on the Philippine banking industry. It is a recognized fact that a sound financial system is one of the main pillars of a strong and healthy economy. In the Philippines, the banking industry is presently the single most influential player in the financial system and its importance has been clearly manifested in recent times. The Asian financial crisis that started in 1997 is a strong testimony to this. Many of our neighbors were severely affected by the crisis, owing in large part, to weaknesses in their respective financial systems. THE STATE OF THE BANKING SYSTEM Our banking system has played a key role in insulating the country from the more serious problems that confronted other countries in the region. This is not to say that the industry has not been adversely affected by the crisis, as I'm sure all of you are aware. However, many indicators are encouraging and signal a gradual return to normalcy. For instance, the expansion of the total resources of the banking system slowed down from an average of 28 percent during the preceding five years to only 1 percent in 1998. By mid-1999, however, bank assets stood at P2.86 trillion, slightly up by 1.3 percent over figures for end-1998. Bank earnings declined starting 1997. From 16.3% in 1996, return on equity dropped to 5.8% in 1998 and further to 1.8% in March 1999. The dramatic rise in non-performing loans (NPLs) is probably the most telling indicator of the impact of the crisis on the financial sector. From 2.8 percent in December 1996, NPLs of commercial banks in relation to total loan portfolio surged to 14.3 percent in July 1999. Still, the situation remains manageable as the level is moderate compared to others in the region. With the recent uptick in business activity such as the 6.1 percent year-on-year growth in imports in august 1999, the NPL ratio is expected to gradually decline as companies recover and improve their capability to meet their obligations to banks and other financial institutions. Banks are also expected to expand their lending operations as positive developments continue. Bank capitalization has remained adequate. At end-June 1999, the capital-to-risk assets ratio of commercial banks stood at 17.6 percent, way above the prescribed minimum of 10 percent and the international benchmark of 8 percent. Commercial bank exposures to the real estate sector of 12.3 percent as of June 1999 is way below the 20 percent limit which the Bangko Sentral imposed even before the crisis started. The ratio likewise compares favorably with most Asian countries. Finally, while there were bank failures, these were isolated cases. The combined assets of these banks represented less than half a percent of total resources of the system while their loans were no more than 0.6 percent of the system's total exposure. The relative resiliency of our banking system vis-à-vis its counterparts in the region could be traced to the numerous prudential measures implemented by the Bangko Sentral before and during the height of the Asian crisis. These included: imposition of a lower ceiling on real estate lending; introduction of the general loan loss provisioning; stricter definition of past due loans; higher minimum capital requirements; shift to risk-based approach in bank examination and greater transparency in reporting banks' lending and borrowing operations. The Philippine banking system thus remains safe and sound. But there is no room for complacency or reform fatigue. The globalization of the financial and capital markets presents important challenges that need to be addressed. At the same time, it offers new windows of opportunity just waiting to be recognized and tapped. POLICY DIRECTIONS FOR THE BANKING SYSTEM Our top priority then is to ensure continued stability in the financial system by promoting stronger and globally competitive institutions anchored on sound risk management practices. We intend to do this by continuing to pursue a program of structural reforms in the banking system. Our major thrusts in this regard are two-pronged: first, we are strengthening the legislative framework; and second, we are adopting internationally accepted practices into our supervisory processes. The approach aims at enhancing Bangko Sentral's supervisory and enforcement powers; improving prudential standards for the banking system; fostering greater competition and competitiveness of banks; and promoting further the independence of the Bangko Sentral, particularly its ability to deal with threats to the overall stability of the financial system. We have proposed to congress amendments to both the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act. These include making explicit the power of the BSP to issue and revoke banking licenses, promulgate more objective guidelines and additional penalties for unsafe and unsound practices, and require periodic submission and publication of financial reports. The proposed legislative amendments also seek to: »Provide the legal basis for the consolidated supervision of banks; »Lift the restriction on BSP's authority to examine banks on-site which is presently limited to only once every 12 months; »Provide legal protection to supervisors in the conduct of their duties; »Further strengthen the framework for failure resolution to ensure speedy settlement of potential problems; »Raise fines and penalties for non-compliance with prescribed prudential requirements, as well as adopt a mechanism for prompt corrective action for such non-compliance; and »Clarify conditions for access to the BSP's lender-of-last resort facility. The foregoing changes will give the monetary board the authority to adopt internationally-accepted standards on banking operations, including those related to capital adequacy requirements. Other proposals involve the strengthening of provisions on insider loans, limits for borrowings and allied and non-allied investments of banks. Moreover, BSP guidelines will focus on ensuring more competent bank management, greater transparency, reduced moral hazard and more effective bank regulation and supervision. To promote greater competition within the industry, we are seeking to allow the entry of more foreign banks within a limited time period. At the same time, we are proposing that foreign investors be allowed to own 100 percent of local banks. Mechanisms will be put in place to ensure that local banks maintain dominance of our banking sector. A major feature of the reform initiatives undertaken even prior to the Asian crisis was the progressive increase in minimum capitalization and encouragement of mergers and consolidations. The increase in bank capitalization is being implemented on a phased approach over a three-year time frame from 1998 to the year 2000. We believe that a strong capital position provides cushion against adverse shocks. It also results in lower cost of funds due to the improvement in the bank's credit standing. Here, I would like to point that while our banks are among the highly capitalized in the region, most of them remain relatively small by regional standards. Given the rapid pace of globalization, we need to have forward-looking banks with the expertise to intermediate large volume of funds and to respond to the growing demands of their clients. We need banks that can offer superior financial advice and services with the capability to operate confidently and efficiently across borders. Consolidation will enable banks to harness with greater efficiency their collective experiences, expertise and technological know-how. These are the overriding considerations for encouraging bank mergers and consolidations for which we have offered short-term incentives. I'm confident that this will lead to the emergence of Philippine banks with regional and eventually, transnational reach. COMPLEMENTARY REFORMS The restructuring of the banking industry, however, needs to be complemented by a broadening and deepening of reforms in the domestic capital market. While the banking sector is the dominant player in the Philippine financial system, there is danger in relying excessively on this sector for financing as the recent regional crisis so vividly showed us. Thus, the BSP, in coordination with the SEC, the Department of Finance, private institutions such as the Philippine Stock Exchange and business organizations will continue to vigorously push measures to develop the local capital market. These include the introduction of new financial instruments for trading and investments and the development of institutions that will harness savings and channel them into investments. In addition, the Bangko Sentral supports the further lowering of over-all credit costs to stimulate investment, e.g., through the progressive lowering and eventual abolition of the gross receipts tax on banks and financial institutions. SUMMARY To summarize, the Bangko Sentral will continue to pursue a two-fold mission for the banking system. The first is to safeguard stability; the second is to drive the development of the system towards greater strength, global competitiveness and responsiveness to the requirements of economic development. We count on your support in the achievement of this mission. Thank you and good evening. (Note: Silver Anniversary, Bank Marketing Association of the Philippines, October 28, 1999, Mandarin Oriental Hotel, Makati City)

Title: REFLECTIONS ON MONETARY AND BANKING POLICIES IN THE PHILIPPINES
Location: Rigodon Ballroom, Peninsula Manila Hotel, Makati City
Occasion: Joint General Membership Meeting of the MART, FOREX and TOAP
Speaker: Gabriel Singson
Text: Monetary and Exchange Rate Management Our primary mission is to deliver price stability conducive to a balanced and sustainable growth of the economy. This is the clear instruction of our charter and the financial crisis in Asia has not changed this at all. To ensure price stability, we have been carefully managing the growth of monetary aggregates particularly the base money within levels consistent with our best reading of the economy's underlying requirements. As the market knows well, we have formalized this approach in the form of a well-defined monetary program that we have also committed to meet under our economic program endorsed by the IMF. The monetary program should not, however, be seen as cast in stone. An essential part of the process are the periodic reviews to constantly test the validity of our assessments that may lead to the modification of targets. A flexible, market-determined exchange rate policy supports this monetary management approach to allow the economy to cope with the unavoidable external shocks. The sharp adjustments in the exchange rate that have taken place in recent months in the face of large capital outflows from the region clearly illustrates this. Nevertheless, the BSP cannot also be totally indifferent to the sharp fluctuations of the exchange rate because that also affects market psychology and confidence in a way that can destabilize the economy. The BSP has therefore also responded with various measures, especially when speculators are at work, to reduce excessive exchange rate volatility without necessarily altering fundamental market direction. Our primary concern is to see to it that the exchange rate is being set by a market that is reasonably free from panic and speculation. The BSP is also prepared to take a leadership role in moderating bank lending rates whenever these are perceived to have become excessively high. However, we have avoided openly regulating bank lending rates because that too will be counter-productive because credits will only dry up. The fundamental solution to this problem is to restore basic market confidence as soon as possible so that the credit process will normalize. However, that is of course easier said than done in today's rather hostile market environment although we are confident that the government's comprehensive policy response to the Asian crisis will eventually lead to this. In general, despite the daunting challenges of a very difficult market, we have been aiming for a reasonable balance in the behavior of critical financial market variables. We believe this is important to regain a sense of stability that will bring back the confidence. Our recent policy moves are fully consistent with our careful balancing act. The recent hike in required reserves, from 8 percent back to 10 percent that was prevailing in May 1998, was prompted by the need to siphon off excess liquidity given the observed contraction in aggregate demand. At the same time, we have cushioned the potential impact on bank lending rates by increasing the rate of return on the interest-bearing component of bank reserves. We also reduced our overnight borrowing rate to 13.75 percent from 16 percent. Finally, we increased the rediscount budget from P10 billion to P15 billion to further protect the credit access of the agricultural sector, of exporters, and of small borrowers. Major Results We all know that the Philippines has not escaped the effects of the Asian crisis. But we should not also lose sight of the fact that we have managed to avoid a deep recession. Moreover, inflation, although significantly higher than last year, has not accelerated out of control. In fact, in August and September, it has gradually decelerated. With inflation averaging 8.5 percent for the first nine months of 1998, we are in a good position to be within our revised target of 9.5 percent for the whole year. Likewise, our external accounts have been adjusting in an orderly way. The current account deficit was reduced to only $109 million as of January to July 1998 versus $3.1 billion over the same period last year. The underlying decline in imports did not have to be too deep as merchandise exports remained strong and remittances remained steady. This is in marked contrast with the quality of adjustment in other affected countries. The corresponding overall balance of payments for the period yielded a $1.4 billion surplus as against a $2.3 billion deficit over the same period last year. This has facilitated an improvement in gross international reserves to $10.342 billion, up from $8.8 billion at end-1997. The external debt situation also remains firmly under control. As of end-June 1998, total external debt was stable at $45.8 billion. The share of short-term external debt, at 17.8 percent, is also significantly lower than at end-March which was at 19.4 percent. Meanwhile, the current debt service requirement is equivalent to only 12.1 percent of total exports of goods and services. Banking Sector Developments Let me now turn to the banking system. In my view, the real damage from the Asian crisis will likely come from the underlying banking crisis rather than the large currency adjustments. After all, other countries have also experienced large currency depreciations before but they were able to eventually recover and even benefit from the increased export competitiveness. But the failure of a banking system is always costly and recovery will take a long time based on the historical experience in many countries. Fortunately, the Philippines has successfully avoided a banking crisis. In contrast, other countries are now forced to spend massive amounts of public funds to clean up and recapitalize their banking systems or face worse consequences. Japan alone has announced a bailout package amounting to $520 billion. In the Philippines, we do not need to do this at all since there is no systemic failure. At most, we have provided limited amounts of collateralized emergency advances (about $300 million for 1997 up to October 1998) to some banks strictly in accordance with law. Moreover, the collection record is generally very good especially if the bank is saved. This form of liquidity assistance is a very typical lending operation of a central bank as a lender-of-last-resort. I think we should be careful to distinguish between failure of individual banks and systemic failure. Individual bank failures do not always lead to a systemic crisis and are in fact part of life in any free market banking system whether it is in the United States, United Kingdom, Japan, the Philippines or anywhere else. In the US, for example, a total of 202 savings and loan banks were closed in 1981-1985. In the Philippines, we have been almost routinely closing troubled banks over these years without much fuss. In the last 10 years, we have closed down a total of 122 banks (mostly rural banks) due to insolvency. According to the BIS Core Principles on Effective Banking Supervision: "x x x Supervision cannot and should not, provide an assurance that banks will not fail. In a market-economy, failures are a part of risk-taking x x x ". Finally, the combined deposits of all 22 banks we were forced to close since July 1997 (the start of the crisis) account for less than one third of one percent of total deposits of the banking system. This is far too insignificant to put the entire system at risk unless people panic. This is one area where we are hoping that all concerned will be responsible enough to help calm down the situation rather than fan the hysteria. The World Bank and other independent observers have on numerous occasions publicly stated their confidence in the Philippine banking system. In its August 1998 issue, Institutional Investor magazine cited the Philippine banking system along with those of Hong Kong, Singapore, and Taiwan as "... those that are sound, despite troubles of individual banks...". In sharp contrast, it said that the banking systems in the rest of Southeast Asia and South Korea, where the damage is so severe, required "... nothing less than reconstructive surgery -- even amputation...".

Title: Promoting Monetary and Financial Stability in Asia
Occasion: 1999 East Asia Economic Summit
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction Officers and members of the world economic forum and the Singapore Economic Development Board, distinguished guests, friends, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. May I thank the conference organizers for inviting me to speak at this plenary session. I find the air in this conference quite invigorating. It is not that Singapore's humidity is easing up. But the agenda of this conference and the list of highly esteemed speakers, in whose company I am honored to be included, raise the promise, if not the threat, of a highly stimulating discussion. The theme for this session is "promoting monetary and financial stability in Asia". Two years ago, in all of Asia, "stability" sounded like a word that belonged to a foreign language. It is an encouraging sign that we can now understand again what the word means. What is monetary and financial stability? In defining this, I call your attention to the use of the conjunction "and". Monetary and financial stability indicates a state of affairs where there is a close tracking between the amount of money available and the amount of credit being sought. Stability requires, as key conditions, the strength and viability of the financial intermediation process as well as the soundness of a country's macroeconomic fundamentals. A breakdown in either the monetary or the financial process would lead to an impasse where growth could be stuck. It is also important to recognize that monetary and financial stability has both domestic and global dimensions. This is a point that I would like to revisit in some detail later. Signs of Stability There are encouraging signs that things are looking up once again for Asia, suggesting that we have pulled back from the financial doldrums and are facing favorable prospects in the near term. According to the World Bank's 1999 annual report, the hard work of recovery has started this year for many Asian economies, with the foundations of growth being rebuilt and reformed. The BIS share this view. It observed that stability in international financial markets has been restored to a certain extent starting the second quarter of 1999. The IMF also projects stronger growth in most Asian countries for the year 2000, with improvements in economic confidence and activity being reflected in a modest but nevertheless broadly-based upturn in domestic demand, the recovery of industrial production and exports, and the flow-back of international capital. Yet we should be aware that self-congratulations might be premature. The Asian recovery remains fragile and tentative. Some say that while the region is recovering better than expected from the recent economic crisis, the risk of aftershocks is still high. For one, while growth has re-started in most of the affected countries, investment remains below pre-crisis levels. Some financial markets -- such as equities and foreign exchange -- remain quite volatile. In many instances, reforms in the corporate sector have encountered difficulties in taking off. And in a number of countries, most of the improvement owes to fiscal pump priming rather than to much-needed structural reforms. We expect, therefore, that stabilization on all fronts will be a work-in-progress for some time still. Hence, we must make sure that the early signs of recovery do not undercut our will to proceed with the necessary structural reforms and to establish stronger macroeconomic fundamentals. As recovery strengthens, our sense of the urgency of reforms tends to weaken. This is the false sense of complacency that we must guard against. Interdependence in the Region If there is anything that differentiates today's age from the past, it is the intimate interdependencies that exist among countries, particularly those in the same region. We live in an increasingly internationalized economy where national borders once considered sacrosanct are now being rendered irrelevant. Just as no man is an island, no country is a fortress. Domestic policies can no longer be isolated - or unplugged -- from regional and global developments. To deny this is to tune out of reality. The recent crisis brought this fact to the forefront. The conference on capital flows and financial crises sponsored by the IMF, the World Bank, and the World Trade Organization in April this year brought out clearly that the correlation of market movements within regions greatly increases at times of crisis, thus confirming the existence of contagion. The conference report cited a study conducted by Carmen Reinhart, which found, among other things, that contagion is mostly regional (but may change with globalization), that it is highly non-linear (that is, a crisis tends to intensify as more countries are hit by crisis), and that financial links are highly correlated with commercial links. A Regional Approach to Promoting Monetary and Financial Stability in Asia It is no surprise then that there has been a multitude of calls for a new global financial architecture to shelter countries from similar crises and to make the world a financially safer place. However, a truly coordinated action plan has been made difficult by the lack of international -- or even regional -- agreement on how this should come about. Since each economy faces a different set of circumstances, there can be no uniform solutions, no common prescriptions, no generic responses Nevertheless, let me discuss those areas where consensus is emerging as to how best to get closer to the goal of monetary and financial stability. Within each country, there is a need to maintain strong fundamentals and a healthy financial sector. Within the region, it is necessary to promote policy coordination in the following areas: preventing future liquidity crises, improving bank supervision, promoting orderly currency arrangements, minimizing moral hazard, enhancing the effectiveness of crisis management, and promoting regional information exchange, policy dialogues, training and research· let me discuss each of these briefly in sequence. 1. Maintaining strong fundamentals and a healthy financial sector On each domestic front, there is no gainsaying the need for strong macroeconomic fundamentals and a robust financial sector. Consistent macroeconomic and complementary structural policies will not only reduce economic imbalances but also give confidence to the markets. Monetary policy and the financial sector are intimately interactive. The effectiveness of monetary policy depends on the health of the financial system. The effective transmission of monetary policy depends on an efficient financial intermediation process. Thus, a breakdown in the financial systems impedes and cripples monetary policy. A weak financial system also hinders the expansion of output and employment. Correspondingly, weaknesses in the conduct of monetary policy undermine the stability of the financial system. One issue that deserves close examination is the possible role of monetary policy in allowing asset price bubbles to develop at the onset of the Asian financial crisis. It is widely agreed that the uncontrolled expansion of domestic credit led to the rapid growth of, and inflation in, asset markets. On the other hand, over-investment in these markets may be traced to the lack of alternative long-term investment instruments in the domestic markets. Thus, the development of the capital market is another concern that should be addressed by appropriate monetary policies. Sound macroeconomic fundamentals and well-developed financial and capital systems serve as a strong defense against external shocks. They not only help the economy to better absorb them, but they also help minimize their severity. In the process, they ensure that economic growth advances and remains robust. 2. Promoting regional policy coordination We need a more coherent regional perspective and plan of action for the promotion of monetary and financial stability. As the world evolves into a more integrated and cohesive economic unit, the need has increased for Asia to consider the policy settings of other countries, especially in the neighboring regions. In other words, it is imperative for Asia to develop a regional mind-set in its policy decisions. a. Preventing future liquidity crises First, Asia must appreciate the role of regional cooperation in preventing future liquidity crises. In some of our countries, the currency and financial crisis began its life primarily as a liquidity problem, as foreign exchange reserves were depleted while staving off speculative attacks against the domestic currency. This highlighted the importance of establishing a regional financing facility. Thus, the inaugural meeting of the Asian Central Bank Forum almost two years ago established an Asean/ Asian financing facility. The facility was envisioned as a mechanism to help maintain stability in the region. Shortly after this, the meeting of the Asian finance and central bank deputies took further measures to preserve stability in the regional financial system. It formulated the manila framework, which proposed, among other initiatives, the establishment of a mechanism for regional surveillance to complement global surveillance by the IMF, and the enhancement of economic and technical cooperation particularly in strengthening domestic financial systems and regulatory capacities. More recently, the experts' group at the last APEC symposium suggested the formation of the regional stability forum, which could serve as a regional surveillance body complementary to the existing surveillance activities of international financial institutions, particularly the IMF. b. Improving bank supervision Second, the effectiveness of bank supervision must be enhanced by closer cooperation between national supervisors in the region with the view to developing standards that adhere to international best practices. The benefits of cooperation are obvious. Domestic regulatory and supervisory bodies stand to benefit from the experience and expertise of other economies as well as of regional and international financial institutions. Collaborative initiatives along this line would reduce systemic risks in global and regional financial markets and decrease the possibility that a crisis in one country would have a domino effect on neighboring economies. It would also strengthen the supervision and regulation of internationally active financial institutions, which Asia would be seeing more of, given the region's immense financial intermediation needs. A great deal of effort has been directed at promoting acceptable practices that would enable financial market participants to better assess and manage risks. These include the development of high-quality, credible, transparent and comparable reporting and disclosure standards and the establishment of easily accessible data banks on the financial system. These would allow market participants to make more informed assessments of both the returns and risks involved in participating in the markets, thus creating a more favorable investment climate. These would also go a long way in helping financial authorities balance better the tasks of enhancing competition in the sector and sustaining the private sector's confidence in the sector's health and stability. It is in recognition of these principles that the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas signed up as one of the first IMF member-countries to subscribe (in August 1996) to the fund's Special Data Dissemination System (SDDS). A caveat is in order. Injecting greater transparency into the workings of the market means that the economy, and particularly the domestic financial sector, is exposed to new and more risks. Hence, an imperative of the new paradigm involves the development of an appropriate system of risk management so that risks are identified, measured, priced appropriately, and controlled. c. Promoting orderly currency arrangements Third, considering that there are already in place cooperative ventures among Asian economies to bring about orderly currency arrangements, Asia must explore how such initiatives can be further developed. Under these agreements, the countries are able to raise the dollars needed to stabilize their foreign exchange markets by drawing on the reserves of their counterparts against their US securities holdings. These repurchase agreements are thus designed to increase the countries' capability to defend their respective currencies in the face of speculative attacks, enhancing their ability to withstand potential financial crises. Moreover, in 1997, ASEAN central banks signed an agreement renewing a currency swap accord. Under this accord, a member country in need of liquidity can exchange its local currency for US dollars provided by other members under the agreement. Another such initiative involves bilateral payments arrangements, which conserves the use of foreign exchange, enhances intra-Asian trade and strengthens Asian economic and financial cooperation. The Philippines has existing bilateral payment arrangements with some countries and is exploring similar arrangements with others. d. Minimizing moral hazard Fourth, Asia should launch a concerted effort to minimize moral hazard. It is widely recognized that the prospect of a public sector bailout in the event of serious difficulties in the financial system within the crisis countries led to the weakening of market discipline in the past. This, in turn, gave rise to lax credit and provisioning policies which undermined the financial infrastructure. On an international dimension, therefore, measures should be put in place to ensure that credit extended to emerging market countries do not reach excessive levels. e. Enhancing crisis management Fifth, Asia must institute measures to enhance the effectiveness of crisis management. Some of the crisis-hit countries saw the need to put up restructuring institutions to help restore order in the financial system. Their basic mandate was the purchase of the bad loans of ailing institutions and the recapitalization of failing institutions. The Philippines saw no need for such restructuring institutions. The non-performing assets of our financial institutions were at relatively more manageable levels than elsewhere in the region. In fact, as of July this year, the Philippines had the lowest level of non-performing loans among the crisis-hit countries. Moreover, while the cost of restructuring in some of the worst hit countries has reached some US$60 billion, the Philippine monetary authorities have had to shoulder only around US$400 million in emergency loans and overdrafts in the aftermath of the crisis. Issues concerning the health of the corporate sector also need to be addressed. These include the impact on the corporate sector of high domestic interest rates and unhedged external borrowings, and measures to facilitate corporate debt restructuring. The effort to restore the health of the corporate sector consists of many components, among them, stimulating demand, accelerating the restructuring of banks and other financial institutions, strengthening the institutional framework for corporate finance to promote the efficiency of credit allocation, and formulating laws to regulate the processes of bankruptcies, foreclosures, mergers and acquisitions. As part of the effort to strengthen corporate governance in the Philippines, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has adopted a new set of rules for dealing with debts of distressed corporates, including simple suspension of payments, rehabilitation, and, when this is not possible, liquidation.
