Beyond strengthening the SEC-led debt resolution process, the government intends to review the legal and institutional framework for insolvency in the Philippines. F. Regional information exchange, policy dialogues, training and research The most basic form of cooperation--which also involves the least constraint on national policymaking--is the exchange of information among countries. Hence, other avenues for monetary cooperation within the Asian region include policy dialogues, joint efforts at training and research, and information exchange on monetary and financial issues that affect the region. On the latter, there is a need to improve upon the timeliness and accuracy of the data that countries provide the public. Of course this means that we are ready to adhere to greater standards of transparency, and that which goes with it: greater accountability. Our voluntary commitment toward this should be stronger given one of the lessons that the crisis has imparted: that is, the role of data opacity in contributing to the financial distress experienced in some degree or other in most Asian countries. Earlier, I said that greater openness is attended by certain risks including greater volatility. It is in this light that frequent dialogues and frank consultations are quite useful, even indispensable. Periodic summits and dialogues enable economic policy managers of participating countries to gather together to exchange views and information, and to consult with one another. Meetings, conferences, seminars and workshops thus effectively serve as hot lines linking key economic movers and thinkers in the region. They might cramp our schedules, but the returns from these personal encounters - whether on or off the golf course -- are immeasurable. For example, the executives' meeting of East Asian and Pacific Central Banks and Monetary Authorities (EMEAP) -- a grouping of monetary authorities of 11 Asian and oceanic countries -- has become quite active of late. Other fora for financial cooperation in terms of research and training activities are the South East Asian Central Banks (SEACEN) Research and Training Centre and the South East Asia, New Zealand and Australia group of Central Banks and Monetary Authorities (SEANZA). The Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation or the APEC, initially envisioned to focus on trade and investment liberalization, has increased its scope to include financial issues. Multilateral institutions are also aiding these initiatives. This December, the IMF and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas will be jointly hosting a conference on monetary policy framework in post-crisis Asia. We believe that monetary policy should feature prominently in discussions because of its critical role in the reforms currently taking place throughout Asia. These pooling of information on important macroeconomic developments and on the policy stance of various governments permit participating countries to formulate policies that are in their national interest but are also in tune with regional and even global initiatives. Information sharing also helps policymakers to appreciate how the intended effects of domestic monetary and financial policies could be modified by events abroad, including the policies and developments in other countries. Of course, aside from the exchange of information and ideas, countries can also explore the coordination of policy initiatives, when appropriate. Cooperative endeavors along these lines are essential in enabling Asian countries to sustain progress toward strong growth. It is also through these dialogues that Asian policymakers are able to think "outside the box", since the wealth of lessons, experiences and insights that other countries have to share with them challenge and disturb their conventional wisdoms and could provoke creative solutions and approaches. Conclusion There are naysayers who remain unconvinced that real reform has taken place in Asia. In fact, one pundit has said that he sees a repeat of the financial crisis within a year. They could be right or they could be wrong: in support of either case is that the reform process takes time. However, I think that two years of hard-knocks have taught us important lessons although, for some countries, the learning curve may be flat and long. Nevertheless, the lessons have led to the adoption of concrete initiatives that have yielded appreciable results. Specifically, Asian monetary authorities are now monitoring cross-border flows more closely and more comprehensively. They are now more responsive to the need for effective -- yet balanced -- prudential regulation of their banking sectors. They are now more open to the idea of transparency. Every age must contend with its own definitive challenge. The challenge for us may well be how to sustain our recovery and reform efforts individually and collectively. Individual countries face mutual pressures from one another to clean up their acts and implement necessary reforms. Because of interdependencies, one country's failure causes another country's failure. And each country's success depends on the success of others. Thank you and good day.

Title: The Philippine Economy: Turning the Corner
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Introduction Officers and members of the Manila Overseas Press Club, ladies and gentlemen: This is my first address before the MOPC and it gives me great pleasure to be able to discuss with you some of the issues that have preoccupied me since I assumed the driver's seat at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas· What you see now in the Bangko Sentral as an institution is largely a result of the fine leadership and steadfast commitment to the bank's objectives by past governors, the last one being my distinguished predecessor, Governor Gabriel Singson· The fruits of their labor are readily apparent in the high public regard of the Bangko Sentral. I would also like to say that I am delighted and inspired by the strong working relationships that I have formed with the staff at the Bangko Sentral · I see 1999 and the coming years as a period of important changes and great opportunities· It is timely for us at the Bangko Sentral to take stock of our bearing in order to prepare to meet the demands and expectations of the new millennium· As James Wolfensohn asked when he took over the leadership of the World Bank group in 1995: "What then will you expect of me after my first few months with the bank? Weighty pronouncements? Headline news? I hope not...what I am about to give is a progress report, an indication of my approach to my new responsibilities, and some insight into the direction in which I would like to lead the bank". These words have stayed with me, and I find them especially relevant at this point in my career· Alchemy of economic growth: developments and policy intentions Recent Gains In spite of a difficult external environment, our country has successfully contained the Asian contagion· We hope that the recovery that we are now seeing will be more durable· this year, we are projecting a real GNP growth of between 1.5 and 3.5 percent· The first quarter growth performance of 2 percent shows that the economy is on track toward achieving our growth aspirations· We have also achieved price stability, the bedrock of our Central Bank's effectiveness, and the primary objective of the BSP· inflation is not an abstract concept; our commitment to low inflation is premised on our belief that it makes a real and substantial difference in the lives of our people· The latest inflation rate was 5.7 percent for July. We have also been able to promote growth in a low-inflation environment by lowering interest rates· The reduction in banks' reserve requirements is a key factor behind lower intermediation costs and lower interest rates· Broad stability in the foreign exchange rate has also been established, with the peso's volatility lower than what it was in 1998· Recent movements in the exchange rate reflect external factors such as concerns arising from a possible Yuan devaluation and another hike in us interest rates· However, with the continuing favorable macroeconomic outlook, we expect the exchange rate to settle and trade within a tighter range· Robust export performance has contributed to a strong external position· Foreign investments are flowing back· Our gross international reserves--at about US$14 billion as of end-July--are at record level. We continue to ensure that our external indebtedness remains manageable. Total external debt totaled us$48.6 billion as of end-March 1999, more than 86 percent of which were medium- and long-term, while more than half were owed to multilateral and bilateral creditors· Policy Intentions This "alchemy of growth"--if I may refer to it as such--was not achieved by chance· It was crafted by policy. We have been careful to complement the standard levers of macroeconomic policies with appropriate structural reforms so that the fruits of growth could be spread more widely and more equitably· The government will further push structural reforms including measures to strengthen further the banking system, improve tax administration, institute public sector expenditure reforms, and strengthen corporate governance· While the signs showing that the economy has turned the corner toward sustained growth are encouraging, let me hasten to add that there is no room for complacency or reform fatigue as important challenges continue to be present· These take the form of a constantly evolving global and regional environment, the pressing need to put our fiscal house in order, and the need to further spur growth in bank lending· Regarding bank lending, empirical evidence on other countries suggests that good banks get on board once an expansion gets well underway· The buzzword here is market perception· Thus, we will continue to promote the proper, even if challenging, environment under which banks will be encouraged to lend· Recognizing these challenges, it is imperative that we study carefully the parameters of our integrated economy so that we can put in place additional measures to prevent another crisis from occurring, or at least mitigate its harmful effects on the economy· We need to think of what we should be doing when t+1 comes along, even if data are only available for the period t-1· to succeed in this, our policies must be forward-looking and well-thought out· The Financial System: The Role of an Activist Policy Far-reaching restructuring has taken place in the financial market· I should know· Before I joined the Bangko Sentral, I was in the private banking industry for more than 30 years· But let me emphasize that careful consideration is being taken so that existing as well as prospective prudential regulations do not impact unduly on the financial viability of banks· We have done so by observing a balance between fostering greater financial discipline on banks and creating an environment conducive to the growth of private enterprise· State of the Financial System At this point, let me assure you that the Philippine financial system, as shown by relevant financial indicators, on the whole, is robust and sturdy· Non-performing loans of commercial banks remain manageable as preliminary estimates put their NPL ratio at 13.6 percent for June. Provisioning against loan losses is also adequate, with loan loss reserves equivalent to 4.8 percent of total loans as of may 1999· The BSP's prudent attitude toward real estate lending has kept commercial banks' exposure to the property sector at a manageable level at 13.2 percent as of march 1999, well within the prescribed ceiling of 20 percent· Commercial banks are well-capitalized· their capital adequacy ratio of 17.7 percent as of end-march 1999 is higher than the minimum statutory requirement of 10 percent and the 8 percent BIS standard· In spite of the challenging environment, total resources of the financial system managed to grow by 2.0 percent to P3.5 trillion in 1998, underpinned by higher deposits and a stronger capital base· While there have been some bank failures, these were isolated cases and they constituted only about a third of one percent of the total resources of the banking system· There is, therefore, no worry of any disruption in the financial intermediation process· Need for an Activist Financial Sector Policies There is a need for us to intensify our activist stance in banking reforms· The Bangko Sentral shall continue to put in place prudential measures to promote stronger and more stable banks and help them withstand potential shocks· These will include reforms to strengthen further the framework for failure resolution to ensure the speedy settlement of potential problems in the banking system· Furthermore, legislative measures are in the pipeline to amend the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank Act in order to, among others, improve prudential standards for the banking system and further enhance the competitiveness of the banking sector· Another key challenge is the internationalization of financial markets· How should our game plan evolve in this respect? With competitive forces staring us squarely in the face, we need banks that are forward-looking, banks that can muster the expertise to intermediate large volumes of funds, banks that have the resources to complete deals for clients whose needs have grown in size and complexity· We need banks that can offer superior financial advice, banks that can operate across borders· As we enter the new millennium, we must adapt our thoughts and actions to these realities· It is for these reasons that consolidations and mergers in the banking system are being encouraged· Such consolidation will help merged banks take advantage of their collective experience, services and technological know-how· To achieve this, we have extended short-term incentives to banks that plan to merge. We also intend to further liberalize the banking environment by working for the entry of more foreign banks, possibly for a limited period· We are also planning to allow foreign players to acquire 100 percent of local banks· in addition to promoting greater competition, the freer entry of foreign banks would send an important signal of confidence to foreign investors· However, some macroeconomic mechanisms would have to be put in place to ensure that majority of the assets of the banking industry will remain with Filipinos· This policy stance should not, however, be taken to mean that smaller banks do not have a place in the financial system· They do· They cater to a different segment of the population, and they reach markets that larger banks may be unable to service· The Bangko Sentral as an Institution Let me just say a few words on how I see the Bangko Sentral's evolving role as an institution· The BSP, like any dynamic institution, has to contend with many forces, particularly with the force of change· While the overriding task of the Bangko Sentral is to remain true to its primary mandate of maintaining price stability conducive to balanced and sustainable growth, the Bangko Sentral must constantly adjust to new developments that affect its pursuit of this mandate· Recognizing this, we must promote a culture of learning in the bank, particularly through the exchange of best practices within the bank, as well as with outside institutions· Toward this end, we plan to host--together with the IMF--a conference on monetary policy frameworks in the post-crisis period at the end of this year. In fact, we plan to conduct an annual Monetary Conference that will bring together prime movers and key thinkers on central banking concerns· we intend to maximize the effectiveness of these dialogues, since they would help us obtain insights that would strengthen our appreciation of key issues and developments· This would also take the process of transparency forward, with these dialogues serving as FORA through which the analytical base of our policy actions could be discussed and examined· Concluding Remarks Our prospects have changed considerably, and for the better. We hope that this is a trend that we can sustain. We stand to gain over the longer term if we heed the lessons that the Asian crisis presents to us· One paramount lesson is that there is no substitute for sound macroeconomic policies and appropriate prudential banking and financial regulations that encourage strong financial institutions· I know that the statements I make and the decisions I take, together with those in the newly constituted Monetary Board, will be scrutinized· While the scrutiny is so much palpable in these early days, I know that this scrutiny will not flag because the Bangko Sentral and the objectives for which it stands have very significant effects on the lives of our people· I am at once challenged and humbled by this· Let me therefore tell you this· We at the Bangko Sentral will remain true to our mandate to pursue price stability and to uphold the integrity of our financial system· We intend--we fully intend--to convert these words into actions that will yield measurable results· Thank you and good day

Title: Continuity and Focus: Pathways to Sustained Growth
Occasion: Joint General Membership Meeting MAP-BAP-ECOP-FINEX-MBC-PCCI
Speaker: Rafael Buenaventura
Text: Let me confess at the outset to a great sense of relief -- that my very first audience as Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is a gathering of friends. At least, that's what I like to believe. This assures me that my inaugural speech will not be a baptism of fire. At least, that's what I like to hope. Let me make another confession. I have three different feelings about succeeding Governor Gabby Singson. The first is a feeling of intimidation. The second is a feeling of comfort. And the third is a feeling of luck. Intimidation, because Gabby leaves behind a performance that is easily the most outstanding among all the past Central Bank Governors of this country. Comfort, because Gabby has done most of the heavy work of building or remodeling the structures that strengthen the monetary, financial, and banking systems in this country. He saved me all that work. Luck, because while Gabby had to contend with the severe financial storm that hit the Asian region from mid-1997 onward, I take his place when the winds have settled down and the sun is shining again. There is actually a fourth feeling, but I saved it for the last. And that is a feeling of honor. It is a real privilege to be given the opportunity of - I will not say, following in his footsteps -- but of taking the torch from him and carrying it forward into the future. Everyone knows that he carried that torch quite a distance during his term. As you know, the Management Association of the Philippines named him the Management Man of the year for 1998. Obviously, the map knows a class act when it sees one. Now that I've made my confession, I wonder whether Gabby is prepared to confess as to who is the better golfer between us. And now, for the good news and the bad news. The bad news is, I have nothing spectacular to say. That is unforgivable for a luncheon speaker. The good news is, I have nothing spectacular to say. That is what the business and banking communities want to hear from their central bank Governor. No one wants to hear spectacular news from his central bank, just as no one wants to hear it from his doctor. The Bangko Sentral's overriding concern is stability, just as your doctor's primary concern is your health. And health and stability have one thing in common: they are no big deal, and you take them for granted, until you stand to lose them. Then it becomes not only distressing news, but interesting news. And no one wants to be on the receiving end of that old Chinese curse: "May you live in interesting times." Stability has returned, at least to the Philippines. Interest rates are at pre-crisis low levels; inflation is down; the peso has strengthened from last year's weakness; and the exchange rate has stabilized. How could interest rates drop, inflation go down, and the peso strengthen all at the same time? Conventional wisdom says that what you achieve with one you lose with the other. This phenomenon was not achieved by luck or chance or "tsamba", as critics say, but by adroit management by president Estrada and his economic team. The stability we enjoy now is due in large part to the success of the BSP in counter- acting speculative attacks on the peso, while by and large allowing the market to set the exchange rate at which the peso will rest without intervention. These were, of course, short-term operations. The more permanent contribution of the BSP to stability against storms were its push for higher bank capitalization requirements, tighter disclosure rules and reporting requirements for bank auditors, new provisioning for loan loss reserves, and the improved quality of bank management and supervision. These and other bank reform measures gave our banking system a sturdiness that the institutions in the neighboring countries did not have. Thus, when the financial storm huffed and puffed, the financial houses in other countries were blown away, while ours remained standing. Some are saying that the Philippines was not as badly affected by the Asian crisis as our neighbors because we hadn't grown as fast as they did to begin with. I believe otherwise. The others had grown more rapidly than we did, but on a weaker financial, structural, and regulatory base. Our foundations and our structures were stronger. The return of relative tranquility and the settling of financial markets do not give the BSP any time or space to rest. It must remain alert and flexible. It must continually scan the local, global and regional environments for signs of disturbances, and respond in advance or at least on time. However, the BSP now also has more productive time for participating in the strengthening of the Philippine economy. The economic vision of the Estrada administration aims for three broad objectives: stability, growth and equity. Stability is both political and economic: it ranges from peace and order, internal and external security, and a functioning justice system to minimal movements in prices, interest rates, and exchange rates. Growth is the continuing and sustainable rise in output, income and employment. And equity is the widening of the sharing of the fruits of growth, with preferential attention to the poor. Growth is the business of the private sector working in a free market, with the government supporting it with basic services, infrastructure, and a sound policy and regulatory environment. Equity results from a whole host of factors, including the efficiency of the investment and labor markets, the profile of investments made, the structure of investment incentives, the pattern of government expenditures, tax laws, labor laws, and the like. The overriding day-to-day responsibility of the Bangko Sentral is stability. It must keep the inflation rate as low as feasible, and it must balance and fine-tune the relationship between interest rates and the exchange rate. Any instability in their behavior, or uncertainties with respect to their future - such as rapid inflation, or disorderly movements in interest rates and in exchange rates - either discourage investments or distort their patterns, away from the long-term and into the short-term, away from fixed assets and into more liquid assets, away from production and into speculation. In other words, by acting as the guardian of stability, the BSP provides the right environment for investments to build productive capacity - and thus expand output, income and employment -- and for businesses to operate efficiently. To repeat, a stable environment is something nobody notices but which everybody thrives in. Disturb the stability, and everybody scrambles either for cover or for quick deals, to avoid getting killed or to make a killing. But one thing many people do not realize. The preservation of stability is different from the promotion of growth. The BSP has the tools of monetary policy for preserving stability. But, contrary to what many may think, monetary policy does not have the tools for promoting growth. It can generate the proper environment conducive to growth, but it cannot itself promote growth. These tools for growth are in the hands of the private sector and of the fiscal sector. Monetary policy is like a string: it can be used for pulling back, but not for pushing forward. And a central bank governor is like a car driver with one foot: he can step on the brake, but not on the accelerator. It is the consumers, investors and the government who have their feet on the accelerator. If they overspeed (and risk inflation), the Bangko Sentral can step on the brake. But if they do not step deeply enough on the accelerator (and risk a slowdown), the BSP cannot force them. To change metaphors, the central bank can lead businessmen and bankers to water, but it can't force them to drink. I think we have all seen this phenomenon in recent periods. Interest rates kept falling, but banks were not keen on lending, and businesses were unable to borrow or hesitate to borrow. With its tools of monetary policy, the BSP can provide stability, but it cannot push growth. It cannot push a string. It has no foot to step on the accelerator. That is the very nature of central banking. But the maintenance of stability in itself is a tall order. We could maintain our internal house in order, but if a storm comes from overseas, we have to waive our right to sleep. Just watch Gabby Singson's face in the next few weeks. Watch him look younger and younger. And watch me as well grow, well, younger and younger also. That is because I thrive on challenges, and challenges keep me young. Many of you may be asking what to expect of my stewardship of the BSP. My answer is simple: continuing monetary stability and continuing banking reform. The BSP will strive to maintain domestic price stability. If liquidity from other sources threatens to heat up domestic price levels, in other words, inflation, the BSP will counteract it. We will see to it that enough liquidity is provided to satisfy the operations and growth requirements of business, but with a wary eye on the inflation rate and on the exchange rate. We will work towards the lowest interest rates possible, consistent with keeping the real interest rate positive and without jeopardizing the stability of domestic price levels and of the peso's exchange rate. We will fine-tune and balance the movements of domestic interest rates and the exchange rate and keep them within a general band, to maintain a stable environment. We will balance the levels of domestic with foreign interest rates, to prevent speculative capital movements whether inward or outward. We will maintain the present free market in foreign exchange. The foreign exchange rate will be essentially market-determined, under a floating rate system. Any intervention by the BSP in the FOREX market will be temporary and will be aimed at minimizing the volatility of the exchange rate, not at setting its level or its trend. We will strive to build up further our international reserves, beyond the present record levels. The higher our reserves, the greater our ability to withstand shocks, and the stronger the confidence of the public in the health of the economy. One thing the BSP will not do: it will not resort to capital controls, or to regulating the inward and outward movement of financial flows. There are other defenses possible against the in-and-out movements of so-called hot money, which generally comes in to buy shares and other assets, and then disposes of them and leaves. Capital controls are not the answer. Total foreign exchange controls are worse, and will not be adopted. They distort investments and, as our history shows, they simply breed corruption. A Russian American songstress once said: "I've been rich and I've been poor. Rich is better." with respect to our foreign exchange market, and indeed of our economy in general, we can also say, "we've been controlled and we've been free. Free is better." In addition to adopting these monetary guidelines, the BSP will continue to pursue its program of institutional and structural reform in the banking system. This is to enhance the strength of the banking system and its capability to serve the financial requirements of our development, and to withstand the kind of shocks that it experienced with the Asian crisis. The BSP will continue to upgrade its monitoring and supervision systems, tightening prudential practices, building strong risk management mechanisms, improving problem recognition processes and capabilities of banks, and providing training to bank examiners and reviewers of the Bangko Sentral. The BSP will continue to support certain bills in the legislative pipeline. These include bills to amend the General Banking Act and the New Central Bank act. These amendments aim at strengthening further our regulatory oversight, raise prudential standards to international norms, foster greater competition, and enhance the supervisory capability and independence of the Bangko Sentral. The BSP will foster a more efficient, strong, and stable financial system in a deregulated environment. These efforts include: initiatives to further increase the minimum capitalization of banks; to provide incentives for mergers; and to liberalize the equity and citizenship structure of banks. The fact that our banking system is already well capitalized has made them structurally better prepared to cope with crises. Our banks are among the region's highest capitalized banks. Its capital adequacy ratio, or CAR, was 17.65% in 1998, well above global standards. On the other hand, most of our banks remain small by regional standards. Bank mergers will further strengthen the banking system. The BSP will continue to extend short-term incentives to banks that plan to merge. As the promoters of "Godzilla, the movie," contend, size does matter. Big banks possess financial strength and are able to meet the needs of large technology investments, a more demanding customer base, and more open markets. They are able to compete more aggressively without compromising their financial soundness. Opening up our banking sector to the entry of more foreign banks will enhance competitive conditions locally, induce mergers and consolidations, and serve the legitimate credit needs of business and personal borrowers better. In fact, I believe that the competition to be encouraged by these trends will so strengthen even local banks that we will someday see a Filipino regional bank emerge, and beyond that a Filipino bank with trans-national reach. The BSP - in coordination with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the department of finance, private institutions such as the Philippine stock exchange, and business organizations such as those present here today - will push vigorously for the rapid development of the local capital market. These include the design and introduction of new financial instruments for use in trading and investments, and the formation of various types of investor institutions and funds to harness savings and channel them into investments. We aim to attain and eventually surpass the levels of sophistication of the capital markets of our most advanced neighbors. The BSP will also support the lowering of over-all credit costs to local borrowers, in order to stimulate new investments and expansions of operations. It will support the progressive lowering and ultimate disappearance of the gross receipts tax imposed on banks and financial institutions. In sum, the BSP will pursue a two-fold mission. The first is to guard and maintain stability. The second is to lead and drive the development of the banking and financial system towards greater strength, sophistication, competitiveness, and responsiveness to the requirements of the country's growth. Globalization, liberalization, and technological developments are going on at a rapid pace, and confront us with threats as well as opportunities. We must be fast enough to keep up with that pace, strong enough to meet the threats, and smart enough to avail of the opportunities. At the beginning, I spoke of escaping a baptism of fire here. We are told by scripture of a baptism of water and a baptism of the spirit. I would appreciate it if the water remained in your glasses. But if you could assure me your spirit of support, then I am assured of success. Thank you. (Note: Joint General Membership Meeting MAP-BAP-ECOP-FINEX-MBC-PCCI, July 20, 1999, Grand Ballroom, Hotel Intercontinental)

Title: IS THE WORST REALLY OVER?
Occasion: 16th Mid-Year Economic Briefing of Urban Bank
Speaker: Gabriel Singson
Text: Introduction I am very pleased and honored to again have this opportunity to provide you a briefing on the current economic situation and prospects. Since my last briefing here at this same venue approximately a year ago, so many important developments have occurred. The picture has increasingly clarified and I am happy to report to you that our fundamental conviction, that our economy will survive the Asian crisis in relatively good shape, is being validated by events. Main Developments After a setback in 1998, the Philippine economy is now beginning to show signs of recovery. GDP grew by 1.2 percent and GNP by 2.0 percent in the first quarter of 1999 after 3 successive quarters of retreat. Palay and corn production is staging a strong double-digit growth. Imports finally started to rebound in March 1999 registering a positive 1.5 percent growth. The month-to-month decline in bank credits to the private sector slowed down to -0.59 percent in March 1999 from a peak of -3.17 percent in January 1999. Unemployment declined to 9.0 percent in the first quarter of 1999 compared with 9.6 percent in the previous quarter. The stock market has staged a major recovery from a composite index low of 1,192 in August 1998 to the current 2,400 level. In a recent speech at a regional conference of central bank governors in Seoul, Korea which I attended, no less than the Managing Director of the IMF, Mr. Michel Camdessus, cited the Philippines' improving prospects. He said, "...The countries at the heart of the crisis are close to or even past the turning point. Most clearly in Korea, the Philippines, and increasingly in Thailand and Malaysia, we see signs of an upturn in activity..." On the basis of our latest projections as of April 1999 which were validated by an IMF mission, we are projecting a GDP growth of 1-3 percent and GNP growth of 1.5-3.5 percent in 1999. Moreover, I am more and more convinced we'll actually be closer to the top end of the forecast range. We have also made steady and significant gains towards stabilizing prices and removing the pressure on our external financial position. Price stability has been primarily sustained through careful liquidity management. The average inflation in 1998 of 9.0 percent was even lower than the target range of 9.25 to 9.75 percent. Moreover, from 11.5 percent in January 1999, inflation has slowed down to 8.0 percent as of April 1999. We are expecting inflation to come down to 7.5 percent by December this year. For the year as a whole, we are projecting an average inflation of 8-9 percent. Meanwhile, the current account of the balance of payments improved dramatically from a deficit of $4.4 billion in 1997 to a surplus of $1.3 billion in 1998. As of January 1999, even the merchandise trade deficit has turned into a $183 million surplus. The current account surplus reached $570 million and the overall balance of payments recorded an $881 million surplus. Gross international reserves have now reached an all-time high of $13.9 billion as of mid-May. This represents a big recovery from less than $8.8 billion as of the start of 1998. Due to the strong early results, we have increased our target current account surplus for 1999 from $444 million to $1.7 billion. The target balance of payments surplus was also increased from $1.6 billion to $3.2 billion. Moreover, the improvement in the balance of payments has been consistent with a manageable external debt situation. Only 15.0 percent of our total foreign debt of $47.8 billion as of end-December 1998 is short-term. Our debt service ratio, or the ratio of foreign debt service payments to total exports of goods and services, has actually declined from 17.1 percent in 1993 to 11.7 percent in 1998. This used to be more than 36 percent in the mid-1980s. The improvements in the external transactions have led to the recovery of the peso to the current level of around P38 to the dollar. Moreover, there is now also more normal movement of the peso in the context of a floating exchange rate policy. The Monetary Policy Stance The recent positive developments especially on inflation and in the foreign exchange market have made possible the significant lowering of interest rates that will support economic recovery. Since the start of the year, the BSP has already cut its market-setting overnight borrowing and lending rates no less than 15 times resulting in a cumulative reduction totaling 350 basis points as of May 24, 1999. We have also cut the liquidity reserve requirement by a total three percentage points this year. With the statutory reserve requirement at 10 percent and the liquidity reserve at 4 percent, the overall reserve requirement is now down to only 14 percent which is even lower than the pre-crisis level of 15 percent (13 percent statutory, 2 percent liquidity). Reflecting the easing of liquidity, the market benchmark 91-day bill rate has dropped to single-digit at 9.741 percent as of the May 31 auction. Meanwhile, bank prime lending rates have eased to around 12-13 percent. Bank lending spreads have also come down to 3-4 percent. We are anticipating that the lower and more reasonable interest rate environment will help in sustaining economic recovery. An Update on the Banking System One of the key reasons why the Philippines is able to lead the way to economic recovery in crisis-stricken Asia is the resiliency and relative soundness of the banking system. Bank failures have continued to be very limited. The total assets of failed banks, including Orient Bank, account for less than one-third of one percent of total banking system assets. As a result, it has not been necessary to commit massive amounts of public funds just to bail-out the banking system. In sharp contrast, the fiscal costs of bank rehabilitation in other countries have been staggering. For example, very recently we were informed by Korean authorities that they are now projecting to spend about $54 billion purely for cleaning up the balance sheets of their surviving banking system. In Thailand, the Governor of the Bank of Thailand told me they have already spent about $22 billion and still counting. Looking forward, I am confident that our banking system will continue to remain viable and resilient especially with economic recovery in clear prospect. Asset quality, as revealed in the NPL ratio is respectable. The NPL ratio of the commercial banking system, which accounts for about 91 percent of total banking system assets, was estimated at 13.18 percent as of March 1999. In comparison, private sector estimates of NPL ratios in other severely affected countries are much higher, ranging from 30 percent in Korea to about 75 percent in Indonesia. Capital adequacy also remains at a very comfortable level. At 17.7 percent as of the latest report, the ratio of net worth to risk assets is presently among the highest in the region. Finally, and more importantly, the future stability of the banking system is being secured with the vigorous implementation of banking reforms. The key measures have been increased minimum capitalization requirements, higher loan loss requirements and their stricter enforcement, and strengthened banking supervision. In response to the banking reforms as well as the competitive environment, we are already witnessing a market-driven, voluntary, and orderly consolidation in the banking industry. In the long-run, this is for the better and will result in a stronger banking system. Is the Worst Really Over? Is the worst really over? Summing up the overall picture, I believe the evidence is quite clear that we have already regained a reasonable degree of financial stability. This stability has given us the solid foundation to pursue our economic growth objectives. I believe the worst is behind us. However, realistically speaking, we must also admit that significant challenges remain. The prospects could be particularly affected by external events that have a domestic impact. Some of the key challenges that we have to look out for include: (1) the ability of the high-flying US economy to achieve a soft landing that can ensure the sustainable growth of the U.S. and world economies; (2) the ability of the Japanese economy to finally turn around; (3) fresh crisis in major developing economies; (4) a major adjustment in the Chinese currency; and (5) major disasters and weather-related disturbances. On the U.S. economy, it is already widely expected that the U.S. economy will have to slow down and correct. In fact, our own projections anticipate this eventuality. The real issue is whether this landing can be achieved without having to dramatically raise U.S. interest rates in a destabilizing way. On the Japanese economy, the authorities there have been taking major initiatives both to stimulate the economy and to clean up the banking system. There is therefore reasonable basis to expect progress. On the other hand, the chances of a fresh crisis in key markets have also been significantly reduced in view of strong actions being taken by the most vulnerable countries like Brazil and Argentina. Even in Russia, the policy dialogue appears to be moving forward according to the IMF. We are also not expecting a major adjustment in the Chinese currency in the near future. During a recent conference in Macau held last May 14, Governor Dai Xianglong of the People's Bank of China vigorously defended the case for the continued stability of the renminbi not only in terms of their international responsibility but also in terms of their own economic self-interest. These are the key risks that we have to face in the period ahead but I believe, on balance, the probability of more success rather than reversal is sufficiently encouraging. Concluding Remarks I would like to finish my presentation today with an update on the financial condition of the BSP. In fiscal year 1998, we were able to remit as a result of profitable operations P14.96 billion to the National coffers in the form of taxes, dividends, and interest rebates. This comes on top of the P37.56 billion we had already remitted during 1993-1997. Altogether, during my term, the BSP has remitted P52.52 billion to the government on a seed capital of only P10 billion. I have had the honor of addressing this regular economic briefing for Urban Bank clients for four straight years now since 1996. I must admit that I have always enjoyed speaking at this forum especially because of the good attendance that the sponsor always manages to mobilize. And you have always been a good and patient audience. On July 5, I will finish my six-year term. I have been blessed and privileged enough to be able to do so with both our economy and the BSP in reasonable shape despite an unprecedented Asian crisis. Thank you and farewell. Delivered during the 16th Mid-Year Economic Briefing of Urban Bank held on 31 May 1999 at the Manila Polo Club

Title: Towards a Sound Financial System: The Philippine Experience
Occasion: The International Conference on Central Banking Policies
Speaker: Gabriel Singson
Text: Introduction It is a great pleasure and honor for me to participate in this high-level conference on central banking policies organized by the Monetary and Foreign Exchange Authority of Macau. I find it quite appropriate that this conference takes place in the context of celebrations on the transition this year of sovereignty of Macau to the People's Republic of China. The common underlying theme of these two events is that of promoting orderly transition. For their part, central bankers have always been concerned with the maintenance of financial system stability as one of their core responsibilities. The Asian financial crisis has powerfully underscored the importance of ensuring the underlying soundness of financial systems, particularly banking systems, in a regime of heightened capital mobility and more open economies. Unfortunately, the message was delivered at great social, economic, and political cost to the countries that have been most affected. Nevertheless, significant progress is already being achieved around the region beginning with the costly clean-up of ravaged banking systems in individual economies. Progress is also being achieved in adapting new banking reforms based on current international best practices as a way of preventing future crises. More importantly, financial system reform is being supported by the reform of the broader corporate sector. Pre-Crisia Financial System Reforms We have often been asked why the Philippines has been less severely affected by the Asian crisis. Looking back, among other reasons, I think we were fortunate in having a fundamentally sound banking system when crisis struck. This was critical from the point of view of overall financial system stability because the banking system, with over 92 percent of total assets, dominated the financial system. The banking system benefited from many painful lessons learned from an earlier banking crisis in the 1980s which saw the failure of a number of banks including medium-sized commercial banks. The Central Bank of the Philippines itself became bankrupt mainly due to the assumption of foreign liabilities and other quasi-fiscal activities. From this experience, the private banking sector learned to manage their banks better and more prudently. Government also learned to be less interventionist in credit decisions and to leave the banking system largely in private sector hands. The Central Bank was formally rehabilitated in 1993 at great fiscal cost. In the process, it gained independence in formulating policy in the areas of money, banking and credit as well as in the supervision of the banking system. Its primary objective was price stability conducive to a balanced and sustainable growth of the economy. Its policy independence was deeply enshrined, guaranteed by no less than the Constitution rather than mere ordinary law. The strengthening of the Central Bank significantly altered the policy environment. Under the leadership of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), the name of the new Central Bank, major financial system reforms were undertaken. A key reform was the opening up of the banking system to domestic and foreign competition. The Foreign Bank Entry Liberalization Law of 1994 allowed, for the first time since 1949, the entry of foreign banks subject to certain conditions. The foreign exchange regime was also liberalized culminating in the country's acquiring IMF Article VIII status in 1995, signifying full liberalization of current account transactions. Capital account transactions were also significantly liberalized. Statutory reserve requirements on deposits and deposit substitutes were also cut from a peak of 24 percent in 1993 to the present 10 percent. This reform was essential to lowering the cost of bank intermediation. The banking system responded vigorously to these reforms and the process of financial disintermediation starting in the 1980s was reversed. Total resources of the banking system increased by an average 28 percent per year from 1992 to 1997. Operational efficiency was also strengthened as banks prepared for a more competitive banking environment. However, the BSP also anticipated the potential risks from the rapid expansion of the banking system by increasing minimum bank capitalization requirements. In late 1995, a first round of significant capital increases was approved for implementation in 1996. In late 1996, another round of capital increases was approved for staggered implementation in 1997 and 1998. As a result of these early initiatives, the banking system was relatively well capitalized at the start of the Asian crisis. The ratio of net worth to risk assets was 16.8 percent at end-1996. In early 1997 and even before the Asian currency crisis, the BSP took a number of defensive measures to strengthen the prudential framework. This included imposing a 20 percent portfolio limit on property-related loans and reducing the allowable loan value on real estate collaterals to 60 percent of appraised value. A 30 percent liquidity requirement was also imposed on banks' foreign exchange assets to slow down foreign intermediation. These measures probably helped mitigate the full impact of the crisis. The conduct of monetary and exchange rate policy during the crisis also explicitly took into account the stability of the financial system. We consciously avoided an excessive currency depreciation through the lowering of interest rates on one hand as advocated by some economists from the academe, like Professor Sachs. We also avoided excessively punitive interest rates to defend the currency as preferred by the IMF. We were convinced that either development would lack credibility and seriously destabilize the banking system by fomenting even more panic. Past experience has taught us that the first order of business in a situation like this should be to make every effort to calm down the market. Recent Reforms However, we also backed up a pragmatic crisis response with further initiatives to strengthen and build confidence in the banking system. In October 1997, we announced another round of staggered increases in minimum capitalization to be implemented through year 2000. Tighter standards for classifying loan accounts were adopted. Tougher loan loss provisioning requirements were also adopted which were at least equal to or even tougher than recommended international best practice. Additional measures included stricter qualification and competency criteria for the issuance of new banking licenses. To enhance transparency and market discipline, the BSP obligated listed banks to disclose more information to the public particularly those that are critical to the assessment of asset quality. Banks were also obligated to mark-to-market their trading portfolios. External auditors were also obliged to inform the BSP of factors that materially affect the soundness of a bank. Finally, bank examination became more risk-based and the focus broadened to cover the consolidated banking group to avoid circumvention. The Current Banking Situation Let me now give you a quick update on the current banking situation. The Philippines continues to avoid a systemic crisis in the banking system. The limited bank failures that have occurred have mainly affected a few small thrift and rural banks. Only one (1) small commercial bank collapsed. Total resources of these banks that failed constitute less than one-half of one percent of the resources of the banking system. As a result, unlike in other countries, it has not been necessary to commit public funds to bail out the banking system. The underlying asset quality of the commercial banking system, which accounts for more than 90 percent of total resources of the banking system, is reflected in a much lower and more manageable non-performing loan ratio of 12.87 percent as of February 1999. Capital adequacy, which gives our banking system the ability to withstand adversity, is also among the highest in the region at nearly 18 percent of risk assets as of latest report. This is comparable with current levels in Singapore and Hong Kong. It is also much higher than the minimum statutory requirement of 10 percent and the BIS recommendation of 8 percent.** Bank profitability in 1998, however, was severely affected by the need to build up loan loss provisions and by reduced operating income growth. As a result, net income dropped by nearly 47 percent to yield a meager 6.0 percent return on average equity. Summing up the various developments, the Philippine banking system is presently in a stable but weakened position arguably similar to the situation of Singapore and Hong Kong. The key to the Philippine banking system's full recovery is seen to be in the early resumption of economic growth which will ease potential collection problems on existing loans as well as improve operating revenues through increased business. On the other hand, prolonged economic weakness can only further strain the banking system. The reforms initiated during the crisis have to be sustained beyond the crisis period if threats of a future crisis will be minimized. While strengthening the banking system is of the utmost priority, complementary reforms will also be needed to enhance the capacity to resolve corporate financial difficulties and bankruptcies, encourage capital market development, and increase domestic saving and the efficiency of its allocation. * Delivered during the International Conference on Central Banking Policies held on May 14, 1999 in Macau. ** There are some differences between the statutory risk asset ratio measure in the Philippines and the BIS formula. However, since the differences tend to cancel each other out, the net results of either formula are nearly the same when applied to the Philippine banking system.

Title: Out of the Asian Crisis
Occasion: Regular membership meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila
Speaker: Gabriel Singson
Text: INTRODUCTION A year ago, on January 8, 1998, I appeared before you and this is what I said: "When I accepted this invitation in early December, the peso was rather steady at P35 to the dollar. Some economists were actually expecting the peso to recover to around P28-P30 by year-end. Many bankers predicted that the peso will end the year at P32-P33 to a dollar. The BSP itself did not have any official exchange rate forecast but we would have been happy to see them proven correct. Unfortunately, today, a month later, the peso had just sharply fallen further to a shaky P45 signaling a clear turn for the worse in the on-going regional crisis affecting our economy. It is not exactly an auspicious way to welcome the new year and totally unexpected a year ago. How did we get into this situation?" THE YEAR IN REVIEW Indeed I found myself in such a difficult situation when I addressed you last year. Speculation was rife. Many feared the worst. The criticism was intense. However, we deeply felt that our economy was fundamentally sound and that panic and speculation were the culprits in the sudden and sharp depreciation of the peso. We therefore immediately adopted measures to reduce the panic and the speculation. Soon thereafter, the peso strengthened and stabilized. In the course of 1998, most economic forecasts, whether official or private, have had to be progressively revised to better reflect the much more difficult economic conditions. This happened in the Philippines. This happened in Asia. This happened even in the major economies. That's how difficult it was to call the economic environment. It is now likely that our GNP growth in 1998 will just be slightly positive. Although looking at things in perspective, this is not such a bad performance considering the deep recession now paralyzing many of our neighbors. Indonesia is looking at a possible -15.3 percent GDP in 1998, Thailand -8.0 percent, Malaysia -7.5 percent, Korea -7.0 percent, Hong Kong -5.0 percent and even Japan -2.8 percent. Inflation accelerated in 1998 due mainly to supply shortages created by the El Niño as well as the sharp depreciation of the peso. Nevertheless, we were still able to keep inflation under control despite all the pressures. According to just recently released data, inflation began to stabilize in December at 10.5 percent. This was below what most analysts expected who had earlier expressed concern that inflation was getting out of control. As a result, average inflation for the year was limited to 9.0 percent (1988 base), well below the target 9.5 percent agreed with the IMF under our economic program. Looking at the silver lining, the weakening and consolidation of the economy in 1998 nevertheless facilitated a rapid improvement in our external accounts. As of the first nine months of 1998, the trade deficit had significantly narrowed to just $824 million compared with an over $8.7 billion deficit the previous year. This reflected both a 19 percent export growth and a 16 percent slow down in imports. On the other hand, the external current account balance which mainly sums up our net international trade in goods and services including workers' remittances has turned into a $333 million surplus versus a $3.6 billion deficit a year ago. For the whole year of 1998, we estimate the current account surplus at about $0.8 billion. Finally, taking into account net capital inflows, our overall balance of payments position recorded a nearly $1.6 billion surplus over the same period. For the whole year, the BOP surplus would be around $1.2 billion. This trend has helped build up our gross international reserve position from a low of $8.8 billion at end-1997 to an estimated $10.8 billion at end-1998 or an increase of $2 billion. These positive developments in our external accounts have led to a significant recovery of the peso. After peaking at P46 to the dollar around this time last year, the peso is now much firmer at P38. In turn, the more stable peso has allowed interest rates to return to more normal levels. As of last Monday's auction, the benchmark 91-day T-bill rate was quite stable at 13.46 percent. This compares with a peak of 20.13 percent nearly a year ago. Lower T-bill rates have correspondingly eased bank lending rates. From a high of over 30 percent, bank lending rates have fallen to around 17 percent on average. BANKING SYSTEM DEVELOPMENTS One of the consequences of economic slow down has been the stress on the banking system as mainly reflected in rising levels of non-performing loans. As of October 1998, commercial bank's NPL ratio had deteriorated to 11.97 percent. However, our banking system as a whole is still able to cope even with this level of stress in view of a fundamentally strong balance sheet as evidenced by a high capitalization ratio, at par with those found in Singapore and Hong Kong, and adequate loss provisioning levels equivalent to 28.5 percent of non-performing loans. The stress on our banking system was also reflected in the increased volume of emergency loans the BSP extended to a few banks to help them overcome temporary liquidity problems mainly as a result of panic withdrawals. However, these emergency loans were equivalent to less than one percent of total deposits of the banking system and 0.6 percent of GDP. This is considerably lower, for example, than the reported large scale liquidity assistance equivalent to 15 percent of GDP extended in Thailand and in Indonesia where banking problems are far more severe. Moreover, based on past performance, we are confident we will be able to collect on these emergency loans. All of these facts support our assessment that banking problems here are quite manageable and do not pose a systemic problem. Summing up the current situation, I strongly believe that we have been fairly successful in stabilizing our economic situation in 1998 despite a very difficult environment. It was not the best of times but it could have been easily much worse. WHAT LIES AHEAD What can we expect in the coming year? I think I can risk being a little bit more upbeat in my prognosis compared to the last time I stood before you. I am, of course, mainly emboldened by the significant stability that had returned to our market as well as the much improved outlook for agriculture. However, I would not advise any excess exuberance just yet. There are enough potential risks still around especially from international shocks that we should be prepared to respond to. Having said these caveats, we believe a moderate recovery in GNP to around 3-3.5 percent is quite attainable. We are also looking at a lower inflation of around 8.5 percent on the basis of a more stable exchange rate, lower oil prices, and a recovery in agricultural production. Many independent analysts believe, and we tend to agree with them, that the peso will be more stable this year especially as capital starts returning to the region. This is consistent with our 1999 projection of a $444 million surplus in the current account and a $1.6 billion surplus in the overall balance of payments. A more stable peso will have beneficial effects on interest rates that will promote further recovery. A recovery scenario will ease the pressure on our banking system that can provide even more support for a sustainable recovery. I believe that our economy's ability to recover has been significantly enhanced by all the reforms we have painstakingly put in place even during the height of crisis. For example, the reforms we have introduced in our banking sector over the past year alone as well as those that we have committed to doing under agreements reached with the IMF and the World Bank are among the most rigorous that any country has dared to embark upon. I am certain that these will all pay off once the overall environment improves. To me, it is just a question of time. BSP PERFORMANCE Before I conclude, let me also say something about the BSP's financial status. From time to time, criticism surfaces in the media expressing alarm about possible huge losses of the BSP linked to alleged bank bail-outs. And as I keep saying, this has no basis. Indeed, since the establishment of the BSP in 1993 up to 1997, we have already remitted to the National Government over P37 billion in profits against an initial capitalization of only P10 billion. For 1998, we expect net operating profits of about P12.0 billion. As of November 1998, our profits had already reached P11.2 billion. We are again planning to remit most of these profits to the government. Lately, there's also criticism that the BSP has not been paying taxes. In fact, since our tax-exempt status expired last July 1998, we have been religiously paying our taxes, P5.5 billion so far, despite the fact that we are probably the only central bank in the world that is required to pay taxes even on our open market operations essential to the conduct of monetary policy. We plan to work with Congress to have this anomalous situation corrected. Taxing the Central Bank is both counter-productive and unnecessary. It is counter-productive because it will eventually undermine the financial viability and credit standing of the BSP and thus weaken its ability to conduct independent monetary policy. It is unnecessary because under existing arrangements the BSP, as a government-owned corporation, is already remitting most of its profits to the National Government by way of dividends. Moreover, despite the current profitable operations of the BSP, we would still like to follow-up with the government the balance of P40 billion in capitalization that it is supposed to put up in addition to the original P10 billion. First, because that is what the law provides and we should follow the law in the same way that the BSP is following the law in the matter of taxes although we don't necessarily agree with its wisdom. Second, it is good public policy to ensure the financial stability of the BSP especially during this period of heightened volatility in financial markets. CONCLUDING REMARKS This year we are celebrating 50 years of central banking in the Philippines. I consider myself very fortunate indeed that I have been part of it for 43 years. Because of the nature of its responsibility, the central bank has invariably found itself at the center of events that have shaped our economic fortunes as a nation. The country's economic record has been far from smooth and impeccable. In fact, we have had to weather so many crises in the past. Along the way, the original Central Bank of the Philippines was itself a casualty and had to be rehabilitated. The new Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas has replaced the old Central Bank with the important difference that it now enjoys independence guaranteed by the Constitution itself. But the core mission remains the same. It is to provide the monetary and financial stability that is the bedrock of the nation's confidence. (Note: Taken from Gov. Singson's speech delivered during the regular membership meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila held on 7 January 1999 at the Fiesta Pavilion, Manila Hotel)

Title: THE PHILIPPINES: CAPITALIZING ON SUSTAINED FINANCIAL STABILITY
Occasion: Euromoney Conference
Speaker: Gabriel Singson
Text: INTRODUCTION It is quite clear that Asia is still some distance away from full recovery. However, financial stability is slowly being regained. The painful process of adjustment is most evident in the sharp improvement in external current account balances that have been principally realized through significant cutbacks in imports and economic recessions. At the same time, Asian governments have actively sought to rapidly rebuild confidence by putting in place major reforms especially in their financial systems which bore the brunt of the bursting of the Asian asset bubble. Smart investors are seeing in all of these an opportunity to position early and take advantage of an expected Asian economic comeback. The Philippines has been more fortunate in avoiding the worst effects of the Asian crisis although it has not been unscathed. Moreover, we have not lost time in doing what we have to do to build better economic foundations. THE ROLE OF THE BSP In line with our mandate, the BSP has been at the forefront of the Philippine team effort to secure overall financial stability during this crisis period. We have also initiated major reforms to protect the health of the banking system amid mounting pressures. One of the strongest institutional features in the Philippines is the independence of the BSP that is directly guaranteed by the Philippine Constitution. This has given us the ability to respond more objectively, more quickly and more decisively to changing economic conditions as circumstances require. This independence has been especially useful in taking decisive actions even during a period of political transition in the Philippines. THE KEY RESULT AREAS Going by the results, the Philippines has not done too badly given the depth of the Asian crisis. In contrast with most of the other affected economies in the region, the Philippines may yet avoid a full-blown economic recession. We will also likely meet our revised inflation target of 9.5 percent despite the adverse impact of the El Niño phenomenon and recent destructive typhoons on food prices. Interest rates have also moderated significantly. Benchmark bank lending rates are currently at around 17-18 percent versus around 30 percent earlier this year. Before the crisis, these were at 13-14 percent. The peso has also recently rallied to around P40-P41 to the U.S. dollar, broadly in line with the cumulative depreciations of the Korean won, the Thai baht, and the Malaysian ringgit. In the external account, the underlying adjustment process is going very well. As of January to August 1998, the current account balance registered a small surplus of $38 million versus a deficit of $3.4 billion over the same period last year. More encouraging, merchandise export growth has remained strong at close to 19 percent and this has been backed up by sustained inflows of workers remittances. The decline of imports has also been much more moderate than in other countries which partly explains why economic output in the Philippines has not collapsed as much. In recognition of the real progress that has been achieved, the IMF Executive Board last October 30 completed its review of the country's economic performance and policies. It also approved the release of a $280 million initial drawing against a total stand-by facility of about $1.4 billion. Significantly, in endorsing the country's economic policies, the IMF recognized the necessity of allowing greater fiscal flexibility to avoid a recession. STATUS OF THE BANKING SYSTEM At this point, I would now like to devote some time to the banking situation in the Philippines. As we all know, this area has been the object of much concern in countries around the region as a consequence of the Asian crisis. I think it is useful to start by understanding the structure of our banking system to appreciate the relative importance of specific banking institutions from the point of view of overall systemic risk. This is critical to putting incidences of bank failure in proper perspective. In our system, the relatively much smaller rural banks and thrift banks are numerically dominant but they account for a mere 9 percent of total system resources. However, the commercial banking system, consisting of 53 operating banks at present, account for 91 percent of total resources. The commercial banking system also accounts for nearly two-thirds of total banking offices nationwide. Relatively speaking, current banking problems here are relatively limited and much smaller compared to other affected countries. They do not constitute a systemic crisis such as are being experienced now in Japan, Indonesia, Thailand, Korea and, perhaps, Malaysia and China. To begin with, the bad loan problem here is still relatively much milder despite a significant deterioration as a result of the Asian crisis. The non-performing loan ratio for all commercial banks was measured at 10.5 percent of total loans as of August 1998. However, this compares with 75 percent in Indonesia, 50 percent in Thailand, 45 percent in Korea, and 35 percent in Malaysia according to one private estimate (Warburg Dillon Read). Moreover, our commercial banks have already faced up to the higher credit risk by setting up loss provisions equivalent to about 29 percent of estimated non-performing loans. There are several reasons for our banks' better asset quality and stronger balance sheet. First, the asset bubble here was smaller since we received a smaller share of the massive capital inflows to the region especially in the 1990s. Second, since our banking industry is private sector-dominated, banks have been able to exercise more objective and critical credit judgment that also reflected their experience, especially bad experience in the 1980s. Third, the BSP has been mindful of its job of preserving the stability of the banking system through effective regulation and supervision. Even before the onset of the Asian crisis, the BSP already adopted some defensive measures to protect the banking system. This included a 20 percent limit on real estate lending relative to loan portfolio, reduction of allowable real estate collateral valuation from 70 percent to 60 percent, and a 30 percent liquidity requirement on foreign assets. In 1996, the BSP also ordered a phased increase to be completed by December 1998 in the minimum capitalization requirement of universal banks by 80 percent, of regular commercial banks by 60 percent and of the bigger Metro-Manila based thrift banks by 67 percent. As a result, our banking system today has one of the highest capital adequacy ratios in the region, at over 17 percent of risk assets as of June 1998. This is comparable to those of Singapore and Hong Kong. Moreover, our capital ratios are well in excess of either our 10 percent minimum requirement as prescribed in the General Banking Act or the minimum of 8 percent as recommended by the BIS. This situation enables our banks to better cope, on their own, with possibly higher loan losses due to a slowing economy. Since the start of the Asian crisis (July 1997), one commercial bank and 7 thrift banks have failed. However, their combined deposits of P4.7 billion account for slightly higher than one-fourth of one percent (0.27 percent) of the total deposits of the banking system of P1.7 trillion. Their combined assets are equivalent to only about 0.41 percent of GDP. These are far too insignificant to threaten the banking system. Because we have successfully avoided a banking crisis, we do not need to spend massive amounts of public funds to clean up bad loans and recapitalize our banking system. Government financial support to the banking system has been primarily in the form of fully collateralized emergency loans provided to stabilize banks when bank runs have occurred due to panic. A basically healthy banking system has also meant that our banks are able to operate normally. Both peso and dollar deposits continue to grow. On the other hand, net domestic credits to the private sector has slowed down to 9.1 percent as of August 1998 but it remains positive. This situation can hardly qualify as a credit crunch where credit supply essentially dries up. Moreover, overall credit growth picked up in August versus July. Further credit expansion can be expected as the agriculture sector and real estate sector recover. MEASURES TO STRENGTHEN FURTHER THE BANKING SYSTEM The BSP has adopted new banking reforms since the crisis. The major new measures included: (1) a further capital increase ranging from 20 to 60 percent over 1998 minimum levels to be completed by year 2000; (2) a 2 percent general loan loss provisioning requirement; (3) stricter specific loan loss provisioning requirement; (4) consolidated supervision of banking units and their affiliates; (5) enhanced disclosure requirements; and (6) more stringent bank licensing requirements. These reforms are strongly endorsed by both the IMF and the World Bank. We have recently agreed with the World Bank on a banking sector reform loan to further support banking reforms. Commenting on the Philippine banking situation, Mr. Wolfensohn, President of the World Bank, when he visited here early this year remarked, "... What is very clear is the Philippine situation is vastly different from Korea, Thailand and Indonesia... I think you all know you are weakened far less than anyone else in the region with the exception of Singapore..." CONCLUDING REMARKS On previous occasions both here and abroad, I have given out essentially the same positive message about the Philippine economy. The passage of time as this crisis unfolded has only given me more confidence in repeating this assessment on the basis of the hard results. I have much faith in the economic future of Asia and the Philippines' ability to play a leading role in it. The underlying values of hard work, sacrifice, respect for learning, and entrepreneurship that we all share are much bigger and more powerful than the Asian crisis. (Note: Taken from Gov. Singson's speech delivered during the Euromoney Conference "The Philippines in Asia: Leading a New Era in Investment" held on 11 November 1998 at the Shangri-La Manila Hotel, Makati City)

Title: BSP ON ITS 5TH YEAR ANNIVERSARY: MANAGING THE CURRENCY CRISIS AS WE PREPARE FOR THE NEXT MILLENNIUM
Occasion: unknown
Speaker: Gabriel Singson
Text: Our 5th anniversary celebrations today follow closely behind two significant milestones in our history -- the Centennial celebration of our independence and the swearing in of a President of and for the masses. And we are especially fortunate that our new President has honored us with his presence. Already this is the second time that he has visited us since winning the presidential elections last May. No other government agency has been that fortunate. Our Fifth Year In Review Our fifth year was characterized by extraordinary challenges due to the onset of the Asian currency crisis shortly after our anniversary last year. Yet the Philippines has shown greater resilience than most other countries in managing the turbulence. Our contributions to the country's economic stabilization efforts in the last twelve months were focused on four major areas: (1) containing inflation; (2) stabilizing the exchange rate; (3) mitigating business distress due to high interest rates; and (4) ensuring a stable and healthy banking system. Containing Inflation We are pleased to report that the inflation rate in 1997 settled at a decade low of 5.1 percent. For the first five months of 1998, average inflation was recorded at 7.6 percent, although for May it went up to 9.3 percent. This performance compares favorably with much more rapid inflation in other affected countries. Mitigating the Impact of Peso Depreciation and High Interest Rates To stabilize the foreign exchange market, the BSP implemented several measures to limit the scope of foreign exchange speculation. After declining sharply in January 1998 to almost P46 to US$1.00, the peso recovered steadily to reach an average of about P41 per US dollar today. As of end-May 1998, the country's gross international reserves (GIR) rose to $10.9 billion from $8.8 billion as of end-December 1997. The decline in the peso exchange rate and the inevitable increase in interest rates adversely affected the business sector. To stem prolonged corporate stress, the BSP implemented various measures including a restructuring of reserve requirements to reduce intermediation cost and induce a decline in domestic interest rates. We are now seeing more normal interest rates. Prime lending rates trended down to a range of 16.5 percent to 21 percent in June 1998. This compares with around 26 percent to 31 percent in February 1998. Maintaining a Healthy Banking System One of the keys to our better performance amid the regional turmoil is the relative soundness of our banking system. Early initiatives to raise the required capital of banks have reinforced the resource base of the banking industry. As of end-March 1998, the total assets of the banking system reached P2.7 trillion. The number of operating network of banks expanded to 7,316 from 6,569 a year ago. The capital adequacy ratio of commercial banks measured as a proportion of net worth to risk assets was recorded at 17 percent in March 1998, an improvement over the 16 percent in December 1997. This ratio is well above the 10 percent ratio prescribed under the law. On the other hand, the non-performing loan ratio of commercial banks was placed at 7.6 percent as of March 1998. This ratio remains quite moderate relative to those of our neighboring countries which hit upwards of 30 percent. International Assessment Our performance has been recognized by knowledgeable observers abroad like the World Bank and Bankers Trust. "What is clear is that the Philippine situation is vastly different from the Koreas, Thailands and Indonesias of the region. While there are difficulties, these difficulties can be overcome... " James Wolfensohn, President - World Bank, February 6, 1998 "In our view, the Philippines has outperformed its neighbors in terms of economic and financial stability, despite not being immune to region-wide volatility" Bankers Trust-Asia, Economic Watch, June 22, 1998 BSP's Corporate Performance Even with the constraining impact of the regional contagion, BSP's financial condition remained strong. In 1997, our resources still grew by 11 percent to reach P683.3 billion. As a result of our strong earnings, we are remitting P5.1 billion today to the National Government. This brings up our total profit remittances to the National Government to P37.6 billion since 1993 on a paid-up equity of only P10.0 billion.
